steps: Education

Many 3D artists earn a bachelor’s degree in animation, game art, computer graphics or fine arts. Others take a shorter certificate program or teach themselves through online courses. Employers care more about skill than the credential, but formal study builds drawing, anatomy and design basics.
Learn the core software

Get comfortable with industry tools such as Maya, Blender, 3ds Max, ZBrush and Substance Painter, plus a game engine like Unreal Engine or Unity for game work. Learn modeling, UV mapping, texturing, lighting and rendering, and practice turning concept art into finished assets.
No license required

No state license, registration or exam is required to work as a 3D artist in the US. Software vendors offer optional certifications, such as Autodesk certifications, but most employers rarely ask for them and judge candidates by their work instead.
Build a portfolio

Your portfolio or demo reel is what gets you hired. Show a small number of polished pieces aimed at the field you want, such as game-ready props, characters or product renders. Include wireframes and texture breakdowns so reviewers can judge your technique.
Time it takes

Most people need about two to four years of study and steady practice to reach a hireable level. Someone with a strong art background who studies full time may get there faster, while self-taught artists working part time often take longer.
First job

Common entry points are junior 3D artist, environment or prop artist, asset artist and internships at game or visual effects studios. Some start in freelance work, product visualization or architectural rendering, then move into games or film once their portfolio grows.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a 3D artist?

No. A degree in animation, game art or a related field helps many people learn the basics and make contacts, but it is not required. Studios hire mainly based on your portfolio or demo reel, so self-taught artists with strong, polished work can get hired without one.
How long does it take to become a 3D artist?

It usually takes about two to four years of training and practice to become job ready. That covers learning the software, building art fundamentals and creating a portfolio. How fast you progress depends on how much time you put in and how focused your portfolio is on one area.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s in business, marketing, communications or a related field, but many hire on sales results alone. Technical sales roles may favor a background in engineering, IT or the industry you sell into.
First sales job

Most account executives start as a sales development representative (SDR) or business development representative (BDR). You make cold calls, send outreach emails, qualify leads and book meetings for senior reps. Inside sales, retail sales and customer success jobs can also lead into the role.
Core sales skills

Learn to run discovery calls, give product demos, handle objections, negotiate terms and track deals in a CRM system. Many companies train new hires in a named sales method. Optional sales certificates exist, but employers weigh your record of hitting quota far more.
License if your industry needs it

Most account executive jobs need no license. Some industries do. Selling insurance requires a state insurance producer license, and selling securities usually requires FINRA exams such as the SIE and Series 7. Requirements vary by state and product.
Time it takes

Most people spend about one to three years as an SDR or BDR before promotion to account executive. New AEs often start with small-business or commercial accounts and move to mid-market or enterprise accounts as they close larger deals.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an account executive?

Not always. Many employers list a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing or a related field as preferred, but sales hiring leans heavily on results. A strong record as an SDR or BDR, such as consistently hitting meeting or pipeline targets, often matters more than a diploma when you are up for promotion.
How long does it take to become an account executive?

It usually takes one to three years. Most people first work as a sales development or business development representative, booking meetings and qualifying leads. After proving they can hit targets, they are promoted to account executive and start running deals from first meeting to signed contract. People with prior sales experience can move faster.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in business, marketing, communications or a field tied to the industry you want to serve. Some hire people with an associate degree or strong customer-facing experience instead, especially for smaller accounts.
First job

Few people start as account managers. Common entry roles are account coordinator, customer service representative, inside sales representative, sales development representative and customer success associate. These jobs teach you how to handle questions, renewals and complaints, and how to use CRM software to track every customer.
Industry licenses

Account management itself needs no license. Some industries add one. Insurance account managers often need a state insurance license, such as property and casualty, and requirements vary by state. Roles that handle securities may require FINRA registrations, usually sponsored by the employer.
Optional certifications

No certification is required. Some people take short courses in negotiation, consultative selling or CRM tools to stand out. Product or industry knowledge, for example in software, advertising or medical supplies, often matters more to employers than any certificate.
Time it takes

With a degree, moving into an account manager role usually takes one to three years in an entry-level sales or customer service job. Managing larger or key accounts usually takes several more years of steady renewals and account growth.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an account manager?

Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing or communications, but it is not a legal requirement. People without a degree often get in by working first in customer service, inside sales or as an account coordinator, then showing they can keep customers happy, handle renewals and grow sales.
How long does it take to become an account manager?

Most people spend one to three years in an entry-level role, such as sales development, customer service or account coordinator, before becoming an account manager. Add four years if you earn a bachelor’s degree first. In regulated fields like insurance, you may also need time to pass a state licensing exam.

steps: Education

Most employers want a bachelor’s degree in accounting, or in business or finance with accounting courses. Classes cover financial accounting, cost accounting, auditing, tax and business law. Some people start with an associate degree and work as a bookkeeper or accounting clerk while they finish a bachelor’s degree.
First job

The usual way in is a staff accountant or junior accountant role, or an audit or tax associate job at a public accounting firm. Others start as accounts payable, accounts receivable or general ledger clerks. They learn journal entries, account reconciliations and the month-end close.
CPA requirements

No license is needed to keep books or work as a staff accountant. A CPA license, issued by each state’s board of accountancy, is required to sign audit reports and is expected for many senior roles. Requirements vary by state, but most call for extra college credit beyond a bachelor’s degree or added work experience.
Exams

CPA candidates must pass the Uniform CPA Exam, which has three core sections and one discipline section of their choice. Most states also require an ethics exam. Accountants in corporate roles may instead earn the CMA from the Institute of Management Accountants, which has its own exam and experience rules.
Supervised experience

Most states require one to two years of accounting work before granting a CPA license, usually verified by a licensed CPA. The work can be in public accounting, industry or government, depending on the state. Hours spent as a staff accountant often count toward this.
Time it takes

A bachelor’s degree usually takes four years, and many people land a staff accountant job right after. Becoming a CPA usually adds one to two more years for extra credits, the exam and required experience, so about five to seven years in total.
qa: Do you need a CPA license to be an accountant?

No. Many accountants work in company accounting departments without a CPA license, doing bookkeeping, month-end close and financial reports. A CPA license is required to sign audit opinions for public companies and others, and employers often expect it for controller, audit and senior tax roles. Licensing is handled by each state’s board of accountancy, and rules vary by state.
How long does it take to become an accountant?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in accounting, which qualifies them for entry-level staff accountant jobs. Becoming a CPA usually takes one to two more years to meet state education and experience rules and pass the Uniform CPA Exam. Someone starting as a clerk with an associate degree may take longer.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma. Many prefer an associate degree or college coursework in accounting or business. A bachelor’s degree is not usually required, but it helps if you plan to move into staff accountant or AP manager roles later.
Core skills

Learn basic bookkeeping, debits and credits, and how invoices, purchase orders and receiving reports fit together in a three-way match. Build solid Excel skills, including lookups and pivot tables. Also practice careful data entry, since the job depends on catching duplicate or wrong payments.
First job

Most people start as an accounts payable clerk, accounting clerk, billing clerk or data entry clerk. There you key invoices, match them to purchase orders, chase missing approvals and answer vendor questions. Training on the company’s accounting or ERP software usually happens on the job.
Optional certification

No license or exam is required to do this work in any state. Some people earn voluntary accounts payable certifications from industry groups such as the Institute of Finance & Management (IOFM). These can strengthen a resume but are rarely a hiring requirement.
Time it takes

You can land an entry clerk role with little or no experience. Moving up to an accounts payable specialist title usually takes one to three years of hands-on work, including vendor setup, payment runs, 1099 reporting and month-end close tasks.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an accounts payable specialist?

Usually not. Many employers hire with a high school diploma plus experience as an AP or accounting clerk. An associate degree or some accounting courses can help you get hired faster. A bachelor’s degree in accounting matters more if you want to grow into accountant, controller or AP manager roles later.
How long does it take to become an accounts payable specialist?

You can start as an accounts payable clerk with little or no experience, and on-the-job training often takes a few weeks to a few months. Reaching a specialist role, where you handle vendor issues, payment runs and month-end work on your own, usually takes one to three years.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Many prefer some college coursework or an associate degree in accounting, business or bookkeeping. Classes in basic accounting, business math and spreadsheets help you understand invoices, ledgers and how payments are recorded.
Spreadsheet and software skills

Learn spreadsheets well, including sorting, filters, lookups and pivot tables. Get comfortable with accounting software and the billing modules of larger business systems. Much of the job is matching incoming payments to open invoices, so careful data entry matters as much as speed.
First job

Many people start as a billing clerk, accounting clerk, data entry clerk or customer service representative. Those roles teach invoicing, account lookups and handling customer calls. From there, moving into an accounts receivable or collections specialist role is a common next step.
On-the-job training

There is no apprenticeship or required supervised hours. New hires usually learn the company’s credit terms, payment posting rules, dispute handling and collection call scripts on the job. Most people work on their own after a few weeks to a few months.
Licensing and rules

In-house accounts receivable staff do not need a license. Collectors who work for third-party collection agencies must follow the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and many states license collection agencies. Requirements vary by state, so check before taking an agency collections job.
Optional certification

Certification is not required, but it can help with promotion to credit or collections lead roles. The National Association of Credit Management offers credentials such as the Credit Business Associate (CBA). Most people earn these after some years of experience in credit or collections.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an accounts receivable specialist?

No. Many employers hire with a high school diploma or GED plus spreadsheet skills and some office experience. An associate degree or coursework in accounting or business can make you more competitive and help you move into senior receivables, credit or general accounting roles later.
Do you need a license to work in collections?

Not if you collect for your own employer’s customers as part of an in-house accounts receivable team. Third-party collection agencies are covered by the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and many states license those agencies. Rules vary by state, so agency collectors should check the requirements where they work.

steps: Education

Most actuaries earn a bachelor’s degree in actuarial science, mathematics, statistics, economics or finance. Coursework in probability, calculus, statistics and programming matters most. SOA candidates also need VEE credit in economics, accounting and corporate finance, and mathematical statistics, which many earn through approved college courses.
First exams

Most students pass one or two preliminary exams before graduating, usually Exam P (Probability) and Exam FM (Financial Mathematics). These are shared by the SOA and the CAS. Employers hiring entry-level analysts often expect at least one passed exam, and many hire through summer internships.
First job

The usual way in is an entry-level actuarial analyst or actuarial assistant role at an insurer, consulting firm or pension plan. Many employers give paid study hours and cover exam costs, and some raise pay as each exam is passed.
Associate credential

Candidates choose a track. The SOA covers life, health, retirement and investment work and leads to the ASA. The CAS covers property and casualty insurance and leads to the ACAS. Both require more exams and modules, and associateship usually takes about four to seven years.
Fellowship and qualification

Many go on to the FSA or FCAS, which usually takes several more years. There is no state license, but actuaries who sign statements of actuarial opinion must meet American Academy of Actuaries qualification standards. Pension actuaries certifying ERISA plans need enrollment by the Joint Board for the Enrollment of Actuaries.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a degree, then roughly four to seven years of work and study to reach associateship. Full fellowship often takes seven to ten years after starting exams, depending on how quickly a person passes.
qa: Do you need a license to be an actuary?

No state license is required to work as an actuary. Instead, the profession relies on exams and credentials from the SOA or CAS. Actuaries who sign certain public opinions must meet American Academy of Actuaries qualification standards, and pension actuaries certifying ERISA plans must be enrolled by the Joint Board for the Enrollment of Actuaries.
How long does it take to become an actuary?

You can start as an entry-level actuarial analyst right after a bachelor’s degree, often with one or two exams passed. Reaching associateship (ASA or ACAS) usually takes about four to seven years of study while working. Becoming a fellow (FSA or FCAS) often takes seven to ten years in total.

steps: Education

Most additive manufacturing engineers have a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, materials, manufacturing or aerospace engineering. Courses in materials science, metallurgy, CAD and design for manufacturing matter most. Some technicians start with a community college certificate in additive or advanced manufacturing.
Hands-on printing

Employers value real experience with printers. Students often join university labs, design teams or makerspaces, and learn to prepare builds, set process parameters, remove supports and post-process parts. Experience with metal powder bed fusion is especially sought after.
First job

Common first jobs are additive manufacturing technician, process engineer, manufacturing engineer or R&D engineer in aerospace, medical devices, defense or at contract printing shops. You run machines, document builds and help qualify materials and processes.
Standards and safety

Aerospace and medical parts must be made under strict quality systems, such as AS9100 for aerospace and FDA rules for medical devices. Metal powders bring fire and health hazards, so employers train engineers in safe powder handling. Defense work often requires US person status under ITAR.
Training and certificates

No license is required. Groups such as SME and ASTM International offer additive manufacturing courses and certificates, and machine makers often train users on their systems. A few engineers later earn a PE license, but most additive jobs do not need it.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, plus internships or lab work. Most engineers become independent on builds within one to two years. Qualifying flight or implant parts, or leading a production line, usually takes five or more years of experience.
qa: How long does it take to become an additive manufacturing engineer?

Usually about four years for a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, materials or manufacturing engineering, plus internships or lab experience with 3D printers. Many start as process or manufacturing engineers and become independent on builds within one to two years. Senior roles qualifying aerospace or medical parts often take five or more years.
What certification helps in additive manufacturing?

No certification is required. SME and ASTM International offer additive manufacturing courses and certificates, and printer makers train users on their machines. For aerospace work, knowing the AS9100 quality standard helps. Employers usually care more about hands-on experience with real builds, especially metal printing, than about any certificate.

steps: Education

Most administrative assistant jobs require a high school diploma or GED. Many people take community college or vocational courses in office administration, which can lead to a certificate or associate degree. Executive assistant roles at large employers often prefer a bachelor’s degree.
First job

Many start as a receptionist, office clerk, data entry clerk or front desk agent. These jobs teach phone etiquette, filing, scheduling and office software. Temporary staffing agencies are another common way in, since short assignments build experience quickly.
Core skills

Employers expect fast, accurate typing, strong spreadsheet, word processing and email skills, and careful calendar management. You also learn to book travel, order supplies, prepare expense reports and take meeting notes. Most of this is learned on the job within a few months.
Certification

No license is required. Some assistants earn the CAP (Certified Administrative Professional) from the International Association of Administrative Professionals, which requires work experience and an exam. Medical and legal assistants may take specialized courses, and certificates in common office software are also popular.
Notary public

Some employers ask assistants to become a notary public so they can notarize documents in the office. Each state issues notary commissions and sets its own rules, which may include a short course, an exam, an application and a bond.
Time it takes

You can often get an entry-level administrative assistant job within weeks to a few months. Moving up to executive assistant, supporting senior leaders, usually takes three to five years of experience and good judgment with confidential information.
qa: How long does it take to become an administrative assistant?

Often just a few weeks to a few months. Many people are hired with a high school diploma and basic computer skills, then learn on the job. A community college certificate in office administration usually takes under a year. Becoming an executive assistant typically takes three to five years of experience.
What certification helps an administrative assistant?

No certification is required, but some help. The CAP (Certified Administrative Professional) from the International Association of Administrative Professionals is the best-known credential and requires work experience. Certificates in common office software show practical skill. Assistants in medical offices sometimes earn the CMAA from the National Healthcareer Association, and some become a notary public.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in advertising, marketing, communications or business. People who want to work on the systems that sell and show ads often study computer science, information systems or data analytics instead. Courses in statistics, consumer behavior and digital marketing help in both paths.
No license required

Advertising has no state license, registration or required exam in the US. Employers judge you on your degree, internships and what you can show, such as campaigns you helped run, budgets you managed and results you can explain with numbers.
Internships and hands-on work

Internships at agencies, media companies or in-house marketing teams are the usual way in. Running small paid campaigns for a club, a local business or yourself also counts. Keep notes on spend, targeting and results so you can talk through them in interviews.
Platform certifications

Certifications are optional but common. The major search and social ad platforms offer free certifications in their own ad tools, and the IAB offers certifications in digital media buying and planning and in ad operations. They show employers you know the tools and terms of the trade.
First job

Most people start as a media coordinator, assistant media planner or buyer, account coordinator or ad operations coordinator. These roles involve setting up campaigns, trafficking ads, checking delivery, pulling reports and supporting senior planners and buyers.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree. After that, moving from a coordinator or assistant role into an advertising specialist, media buyer or ad operations specialist role usually takes one to three years of on-the-job experience.
qa: Do you need a license to work in advertising?

No. There is no state or federal license for advertising specialists, media buyers or ad operations staff in the US. Many people earn optional certifications from the major ad platforms or the IAB to show they know the tools, but hiring is based mostly on education, internships and proven campaign experience.
How long does it take to become an advertising specialist?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree in advertising, marketing, communications or a related field. They then usually work one to three years in an entry-level role, such as media coordinator or ad operations coordinator, before moving into a specialist, planner or buyer position.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most aerospace engineers start with a four-year bachelor’s degree in aerospace engineering from an ABET-accredited program. Courses cover aerodynamics, propulsion, structures, flight dynamics and controls. Degrees in mechanical or electrical engineering, or physics, also lead into the field, especially for systems, avionics and test roles.
Internships and co-ops

Students usually complete one or more internships or co-op terms with aircraft, spacecraft or defense employers. Student design teams that build rockets, drones or small satellites also count. This hands-on work often leads directly to a full-time offer after graduation.
FE exam

Many graduates take the Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam from NCEES near the end of school. Passing it earns Engineer in Training or Engineer Intern status in most states. Most aerospace employers do not require it, but it is the first step toward a PE license.
Citizenship and clearance

Many defense and space jobs fall under export control rules such as ITAR, so employers often require US citizenship or permanent residency. Some roles also need a government security clearance, which the employer sponsors after hiring. The background check can take several months.
First job

The usual first job is an entry-level design, test, systems, structures or manufacturing engineer, working under senior engineers. New hires often spend two to four years learning company processes, analysis tools and certification standards before leading their own parts of a project.
Graduate study and PE

Some engineers earn a master’s degree, often while working, to move into specialized analysis or research. A Professional Engineer (PE) license is optional for most industry roles. It usually requires passing the FE and PE exams plus about four years of supervised experience, and rules vary by state.
qa: Do you need a license to be an aerospace engineer?

Usually not. Most aerospace engineers work for companies or government agencies where a Professional Engineer (PE) license is not required. A PE license matters mainly if you offer engineering services directly to the public or sign off on certain public work. Getting one means passing the FE and PE exams and gaining supervised experience, and requirements vary by state.
How long does it take to become an aerospace engineer?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in aerospace engineering or a related field, then start in an entry-level engineering job. Becoming a fully independent engineer usually takes another few years on the job. A master’s degree adds one to two years, and a PE license typically requires about four years of experience after graduation.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications or a related field. Some hire on proven results alone. Useful coursework covers digital marketing, analytics, basic contracts and spreadsheet work. No license or required exam exists for this role in any state.
Core technical skills

Learn how tracking links, cookies, attribution windows and commission structures work. Get comfortable with spreadsheets, web analytics and affiliate network dashboards. Optional certificates from analytics or ad platforms can show the basics, but employers rarely require them.
Compliance knowledge

Know the FTC Endorsement Guides, which require affiliates to clearly disclose paid relationships. Learn to spot coupon abuse, trademark bidding and fake leads. You should also be able to write program terms that prevent them.
First job

Common entry roles are affiliate coordinator, affiliate or partnerships associate, or account coordinator at a performance marketing agency or affiliate network. Others move over from SEO, paid search or influencer marketing, or from running their own affiliate websites.
Time it takes

Moving from an entry role to affiliate marketing manager usually takes two to five years. Employers expect managers to have grown a program, recruited and negotiated with publishers, and reported on revenue and return on spend.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an affiliate marketing manager?

Most job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business or a related field, but it is not legally required. Many managers get hired on experience instead. That can mean running affiliate sites, working at an affiliate network, or showing they grew a partner program’s revenue.
Is there a required certification for affiliate marketing?

No. There is no license, state registration or standard certification for affiliate marketing in the US. Some people take optional courses or analytics certificates to learn the basics. Employers care more about hands-on results and knowledge of FTC disclosure rules. They also want to see skill with tracking platforms and the ability to recruit and manage publishers.

steps: Education

Most AI engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering, math or a related field. A degree is common but not strictly required. Some people come from self-study or other technical degrees and prove their skills through work. A master’s degree helps for research-heavy roles but is rarely needed to build products.
Software engineering skills

This work is software engineering first. You need solid Python, and often TypeScript, plus APIs, databases, version control, testing and cloud deployment. Many employers want people who can ship a working backend or web app, not only run models in a notebook.
Language model skills

Learn to build on language model APIs and open models. Core topics include prompt design, retrieval-augmented generation over documents, embeddings and vector search, tool calling and agents, fine-tuning basics, and evaluation. Knowing how to measure quality, cost and latency, and how to handle errors and unsafe output, matters a lot.
Portfolio

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work. Employers judge you on what you have built. Publish a few working projects, such as a document search assistant or an agent that completes a real task, with code, a short write-up and how you tested it.
First job

Many people enter as software engineers, backend developers or data engineers, then move onto a team building AI features. Others come from data science or machine learning roles. Junior titles that mention AI exist but are fewer, so an internal move after a first engineering job is a common route.
Time it takes

From scratch, it usually takes about four years of school plus one to three years of engineering work before people land AI engineer roles. Experienced software engineers can often make the switch in several months to a year of focused project work.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an AI engineer?

Not always. Many employers list a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field, but this is a skills-driven field. People without a degree do get hired when they can show strong software engineering experience and working projects built on language models. A degree still makes the first job easier to get.
Is there a certification required to be an AI engineer?

No. There is no license, state registration or required exam for AI engineers in the US. Cloud providers and other groups offer optional AI and machine learning certificates, and some employers like them. Most hiring decisions rest on your engineering experience, your portfolio and how you do in technical interviews.

steps: Education

Most AI product managers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, engineering, data science, statistics or business. A technical degree helps when working closely with machine learning teams. Some add an MBA or a master’s degree, but employers rarely require one.
Technical grounding

Learn how machine learning models are built and judged: training data, evaluation metrics like precision and recall, bias, errors and hallucinations in language models, and the difference between offline tests and live experiments. Many people build this through online courses and small side projects using model APIs.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in the US. Private groups offer product management and AI certificates, but none is an industry standard. Employers care more about products you have shipped and how you reason about model quality.
First job

Few people start as AI product managers. The usual way in is a first role as a product manager on a regular software product, or as a software engineer, data scientist, analyst or UX researcher who then moves into product. Internal transfers onto AI teams are common.
Time it takes

It usually takes several years. Many AI product managers spend a few years in product, engineering or data roles before they own an AI product or feature. Associate product manager programs can give new graduates a faster start.
qa: Do you need a certification to become an AI product manager?

No. No US license or certification is required to work as an AI product manager. Certificates in product management or AI can show interest, but none is an industry standard. Employers mostly look for experience shipping software products and a working understanding of how machine learning models are trained, tested and improved.
How long does it take to become an AI product manager?

It usually takes several years. Most people first earn a bachelor’s degree, then work a few years as a product manager, software engineer, data scientist or analyst. They move into an AI product role once they have shipped products and learned how to judge model quality and set the bar a feature must meet before launch.

steps: Education

Most people enter with a bachelor’s degree in computer science, mathematics, statistics or a related field. Research roles often ask for a master’s or PhD in machine learning. Some come from philosophy, policy or cybersecurity, especially for evaluation and governance work.
Machine learning skills

Learn Python, a deep learning framework such as PyTorch, and how large language models are trained and fine-tuned. Reproducing published safety papers on interpretability, adversarial attacks or model evaluations is a common way to show you can do the work.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam for this work in the US. No single certification is standard. Employers judge candidates on research output, code quality and track record rather than credentials.
Portfolio and research

Build public evidence of your skills. This can include open-source code, write-ups of red-teaming or evaluation experiments, and papers at machine learning conferences or workshops. Many people join short research fellowships or mentorship programs before applying.
Time it takes

Usually four years for a bachelor’s degree plus one to three years of machine learning experience for engineering roles. Research scientist roles often follow a PhD, which commonly takes five to six years. Software engineers switching over may need one to two years.
First job

Common entry points are research engineer, machine learning engineer, or model evaluation and red-teaming roles, including contract work testing models for harmful outputs. Some people start as software engineers at AI companies and move onto safety teams internally.
qa: Do you need a PhD to work in AI safety?

No. Many research engineers and evaluation staff hold a bachelor’s or master’s degree and have strong coding skills. A PhD is common for research scientist roles that set new research directions. Employers weigh published work, open-source code and hands-on experience with large models heavily, so a strong portfolio can stand in for an advanced degree on many teams.
Is there a certification for AI safety?

There is no license or standard certification required to work in AI safety in the US. Employers mostly look at a degree in a technical field, research papers, code and practical experience testing models. Short research fellowships and mentorship programs are a common way for newcomers to build credibility and get noticed.

steps: Education

No degree or license is legally required. Many projects still prefer a bachelor’s degree. Specialist work in coding, math, science, medicine, law or finance usually asks for a degree or professional experience in that field. Some pay more for a master’s or doctorate.
Core skills

You need clean, clear writing, strong grammar, careful fact-checking and the patience to follow long, detailed guidelines. Coding projects expect working skill in a language such as Python. Language projects expect native or near-native fluency in the target language.
Qualification tests

There is no standard exam or certification. Instead, each platform screens applicants with its own unpaid or paid assessments. These often include writing samples, reasoning questions, coding tasks and quizzes on project guidelines. Many also require identity checks and proof of US work authorization.
First job

Most people start as a contract rater, data annotator or general AI trainer on writing and evaluation tasks. Work is usually remote, paid by the hour or task, and done as an independent contractor. Hours can be irregular, and projects can end with little notice.
Time it takes

If you already have the skills, you can often start within a few weeks of applying and passing the tests. Moving into reviewer, quality assurance or specialist projects usually takes several months of consistently high quality scores.
Moving up

Experienced trainers move into reviewer, team lead or project quality roles. Some use the experience to apply for full-time jobs in data operations, content evaluation or model evaluation, where employers often look for a related degree.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an AI trainer?

Not always. General writing and rating projects often accept people without a degree if they pass the platform’s tests. Many projects prefer a bachelor’s degree, though. Specialist work in areas like coding, math, medicine or law usually requires a degree or solid professional experience in that field, and these projects typically pay more.
Is there a certification to become an AI trainer?

No. There is no license or standard industry certification for AI training work in the US. Platforms decide who gets in through their own qualification tests, such as writing samples, reasoning questions and guideline quizzes. Your quality scores on real tasks then decide whether you get more work and access to better projects.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting, economics, criminal justice or business. Some banks hire people with an associate degree or solid banking experience instead. Courses in accounting, law and data analysis help most.
Learn the rules

Study the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act, FinCEN’s customer due diligence rule and OFAC sanctions programs. Employers expect you to understand customer identification, enhanced due diligence, red flags for money laundering and how suspicious activity reports (SARs) work.
First job

Most people start as a KYC or onboarding analyst, or as a level 1 transaction monitoring analyst clearing alerts at a bank, fintech, money services business or broker-dealer. Others move over from teller, fraud, customer service or bank operations roles.
Certification

No state or federal license is required. Many analysts earn the CAMS (Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialist) from ACAMS after a year or two on the job. Its eligibility uses credits for education, experience and training. Some later add the CFE or the ACAMS CGSS sanctions credential.
Time it takes

With a degree, you can usually get an entry-level KYC or alert review job soon after graduating. Moving up to senior analyst or investigator, where you handle complex cases and write SARs, usually takes two to four years.
qa: Do you need a certification to be an AML analyst?

No. There is no license for AML or KYC work in the US, and many entry-level jobs require no certification. Employers do value the CAMS from ACAMS, and it often helps with promotion to senior analyst or investigator roles. Most people earn it after gaining some experience on the job.
How long does it take to become a KYC analyst?

Most people need a bachelor’s degree, which usually takes four years. After that, entry-level KYC and onboarding jobs often train new hires in a few weeks to a few months. People already working in banking operations or fraud can sometimes move into KYC work without a degree.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most people start with a four-year bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, sometimes computer engineering. The key courses are circuit analysis, electronics, semiconductor devices, signals and systems, control and electromagnetics. Taking analog circuits and lab electives early helps you find out whether transistor-level design suits you.
Graduate study

Many employers prefer a master’s degree for analog and mixed-signal design roles, and some research-heavy or RF jobs favor a PhD. Graduate courses cover analog IC design, data converters, RF circuits, power management and device modeling. Some students also design and test a real chip during their research.
Internships and lab skills

Internships at chip, power or communications firms matter a lot for getting hired. Build hands-on skill with SPICE circuit simulation, schematic and layout tools, and lab equipment such as oscilloscopes, spectrum analyzers and signal generators. Being able to measure and debug real silicon makes you stand out.
No license needed

No license, registration or exam is required to do this work in the US. The Professional Engineer (PE) license exists, but chip and electronics companies rarely ask for it. Employers judge you on your degree, projects, internships and how you handle technical interviews about circuits.
First job

The usual entry point is a junior or associate analog design engineer role, designing smaller circuit blocks under a senior designer. Others start in validation, characterization, test or layout engineering, then move into design after learning how circuits behave on real silicon.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, plus usually one and a half to two years for a master’s or five to six years for a PhD. After hiring, it often takes several more years before you own complex blocks or lead a full design.
qa: Do you need a master’s degree to be an analog engineer?

Not always, but it helps a lot. Many analog and mixed-signal design jobs prefer or expect a master’s degree in electrical engineering, and some RF and research roles favor a PhD. People with only a bachelor’s degree often start in test, validation or layout roles and move into design as they gain experience.
Do analog engineers need a license?

No. Analog and mixed-signal engineers in the US do not need a license, certification or exam to work. The Professional Engineer (PE) license is rarely required in the chip and electronics industry. Employers focus on your electrical engineering degree, circuit design coursework, internships and your skill with simulation and lab tools.

steps: Education

Most analytics engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in a field such as computer science, statistics, economics, mathematics or information systems. A degree is common but not strictly required. Employers care most about proven skill in writing SQL and shaping raw data into reliable tables.
Core technical skills

Learn advanced SQL, dimensional data modeling, and how cloud data warehouses work. Add version control with Git, a scripting language such as Python, and the habit of testing and documenting every data transformation. Many people learn these through online courses and self-study alongside work.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in the US. Data tool and cloud vendors offer optional certifications. These can strengthen a resume, but hiring managers usually weigh real project work and experience more heavily.
First job

Most people start as a data analyst or business intelligence analyst, writing SQL queries and building dashboards. Others come from junior data engineering or software roles. In these jobs you see firsthand why clean, well-named, trusted tables matter to the people using the numbers.
Build a portfolio

Show work that proves you can model data well. Examples include a public project that turns messy source data into tested, documented tables, or internal work where you rebuilt reporting tables so dashboards agreed with each other. Share code through a version control repository.
Time it takes

Moving into an analytics engineer title usually takes two to four years after starting in an analyst or data role. People with a strong technical degree and a solid portfolio sometimes move in faster, especially at smaller companies.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an analytics engineer?

A degree is not required, though many analytics engineers have one in computer science, statistics, economics or a related field. Employers mainly look for strong SQL, data modeling, version control and testing skills. Experience as a data analyst plus a portfolio of well-built data models can open the door without a degree.
How long does it take to become an analytics engineer?

Most people take two to four years after starting their first data job. A common route is working as a data analyst or business intelligence analyst, learning data modeling and transformation tools along the way, and then moving into an analytics engineer role. No license or exam is needed, so the timeline depends on skills and experience.

steps: Education

Many Android developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science or software engineering, but employers often accept self-taught candidates. Others take community college courses or online classes. Focus on Kotlin, object-oriented programming, data structures, and how mobile apps handle memory, networking, and battery life.
Core Android skills

Learn Android Studio, the Android SDK, and Jetpack libraries, including Jetpack Compose for building screens. Practice app architecture such as MVVM, working with REST APIs, local storage with Room, coroutines, Gradle, and Git. Reading Java helps too, because many older apps still use it.
Portfolio of apps

Build two or three complete apps that solve real problems, keep the code on GitHub, and publish at least one on Google Play through a developer account. Hiring managers often care more about working, well-structured apps than about certificates. No license or required exam exists for this work.
Time it takes

A degree usually takes four years. People who teach themselves or switch from another programming job often become job-ready in about six months to two years, depending on prior coding experience and how much time they put into practice and building apps.
First job

Common entry points are a software engineering internship, a junior Android or mobile developer role, or work at an agency building apps for clients. Some people start in QA testing or general web development and move to the Android team once they show their apps.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an Android developer?

No. Many employers list a computer science degree, but plenty hire developers without one if they can show strong skills. A portfolio of published apps on Google Play, clean Kotlin code on GitHub, and a solid grasp of Android architecture often matter more in interviews. Larger companies are more likely to prefer a degree.
Is there a certification required to be an Android developer?

No license or certification is required to work as an Android developer in the US. Employers judge candidates mainly on their apps, code samples, and technical interviews. Some people take online courses that award certificates, which can help structure learning, but they rarely replace a strong portfolio and real project experience.

steps: Education

No license or specific degree is required. Some Angular and Vue developers studied computer science, and many came through bootcamps or self-study. Learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript well first, then TypeScript, which Angular uses by default and many Vue teams also use.
Framework skills

For Angular, learn components, services, dependency injection, routing, forms and RxJS. For Vue, learn single-file components, the Composition API, Vue Router and Pinia for state. Both paths need testing, API calls and responsive layouts.
Portfolio

Build and deploy a few complete projects in your chosen framework, such as an admin dashboard with forms and charts or a store front end. Publish the code publicly. Angular is common in large organizations, so business-style apps make strong samples.
Certifications

Neither framework requires a certification, and US employers rarely ask for one. Some third-party Angular and Vue certificates exist, but hiring depends mostly on take-home projects, live coding and questions about TypeScript, components and state management.
First job

Common first jobs are junior front-end developer, junior Angular or Vue developer, or junior web developer. Angular roles often cluster at banks, insurers, government contractors and large enterprises, while Vue is often used by agencies and smaller product teams.
Time it takes

Career changers often need one to two years of focused study and projects before a first front-end job. A computer science degree takes about four years. Developers who already know another framework can usually learn Angular or Vue in a few months.
qa: How long does it take to become an Angular developer?

Starting from zero, expect one to two years of focused study to learn HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript and Angular, and to build projects that get interviews. Angular has a steeper learning curve than some frameworks because of RxJS and dependency injection. Developers who already know React or Vue can usually switch in a few months.
Is there a certification for Vue or Angular developers?

Neither framework requires a certification, and US employers rarely ask for one. Some third-party Angular and Vue certificates exist and can help you structure your learning. Most hiring decisions, though, rest on deployed projects, public code, take-home assignments and technical interviews about components, state and TypeScript.

steps: Education

Most API and SDK developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. Employers also hire self-taught programmers and bootcamp graduates who can show strong skills in languages like Java, Python, Go, JavaScript or C#, plus a solid grasp of HTTP and networking.
Core API skills

Learn to design and build REST APIs, and get familiar with GraphQL and gRPC. Practice versioning, authentication with OAuth 2.0, rate limiting and error handling. Learn to describe APIs with the OpenAPI Specification and to write clear reference docs and code samples.
Portfolio projects

Build a public API and a small client library or SDK for it, ideally in two languages. Publish packages to registries like npm or PyPI and contribute to open-source SDKs. Hiring managers often review GitHub work to judge code quality, testing and documentation.
Optional certifications

There is no license or required exam for this work. Some developers earn cloud certifications, such as AWS Certified Developer – Associate, or a vendor’s API platform certificate. These can help with screening, but employers usually weigh real code and experience more heavily.
First job

Most people start as a junior backend or software engineer, building services and integrations. Some come in through developer support, solutions engineering or technical writing roles that work closely with APIs, then move onto a platform, integrations or SDK team.
Time it takes

Plan on a four-year degree or one to two years of focused self-study, followed by about two to four years of backend experience. Roles that own an SDK or public API design usually go to developers who already have that experience.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an API developer?

No law requires a degree, and there is no license for API work. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s in computer science or a related field. Others hire developers who show strong backend skills through a portfolio of published APIs, SDKs or open-source contributions. Experience building and documenting real integrations often matters as much as formal education.
How long does it take to become an SDK developer?

It usually takes several years. Most people spend about four years earning a degree or one to two years teaching themselves to code. They then work two to four years as backend or software engineers. SDK roles expect solid skills in more than one language, clean API design and good documentation habits, which come mostly from on-the-job experience.

steps: Education

Most application security engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or cybersecurity. No degree is legally required, and some people get in through self-study. Employers care most that you can read and write code well and understand how web apps, APIs and networks work.
Software development experience

Many people start as software developers. Writing, testing and shipping real code teaches how bugs get introduced and how engineering teams work. Comfort with languages such as Java, Python, JavaScript, C# or Go makes it far easier to review code and suggest fixes developers will accept.
Security skills

Learn the OWASP Top 10, secure code review, threat modeling and common attacks such as injection, broken access control and cross-site scripting. Practice with static and dynamic scanning tools, capture-the-flag challenges and public bug bounty programs. A record of findings or write-ups helps show real skill.
Optional certifications

There is no license for this work. Some employers value certifications such as CompTIA Security+ for beginners, or OSCP, OSWE, GIAC GWAPT and ISC2 CSSLP for more experienced people. CSSLP requires several years of related work experience before you can earn the full credential.
First job

Common ways in are software developer, QA or test engineer, security analyst, or junior penetration tester. Many people move into application security by joining a company’s security champions effort or by taking on code review and security fixes within their own development team.
Time it takes

After a degree, it usually takes two to five years of development or security work before landing an application security engineer role. Strong coders who already practice security testing can move faster, while people new to programming often need longer.
qa: Do you need a certification to be an application security engineer?

No. There is no license or required certification for this work in the US. Many employers hire based on coding skill and security experience. Certifications such as OSCP, OSWE, GIAC GWAPT or ISC2 CSSLP can help your resume stand out, and some government or contractor roles ask for specific credentials, but none are mandatory everywhere.
How long does it take to become an application security engineer?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree, then two to five years working as a software developer, tester or security analyst first. That puts the typical path at roughly six to nine years from starting college. People who already code professionally and study security on the side can often switch sooner.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering, data science, statistics or a related field. A master’s degree helps for some roles but is not required. People from business analysis or IT also move in by learning programming and machine learning on their own or through courses.
Core technical skills

Learn Python, working with APIs, SQL and data handling, and the basics of machine learning. Then learn how to build with large language models: prompt design, retrieval over company documents, evaluation of outputs, and deployment on a major cloud platform. Knowing data privacy and security basics matters because clients ask about them.
Portfolio of real projects

Build a few working projects that solve a business problem, such as a document search assistant, a support ticket classifier or an automated report. Show the problem, the result and how you measured it. Employers weigh this more than coursework, since there is no standard credential for this work.
Optional certifications

No license or required exam exists for applied AI work in the US. Some people earn cloud provider certifications in machine learning or AI services to show they can deploy on a given platform. These are optional and help most when a client or employer already uses that platform.
First job

Common entry points are software engineer, data analyst, data scientist, machine learning engineer or solutions engineer roles. Consulting and implementation jobs also work well, because they build the client-facing skills this work needs: finding where AI pays off, setting it up and training staff to use it.
Time it takes

With a related degree, most people reach an applied AI role in about two to five years, counting time in a first technical job. Career changers with strong programming skills sometimes move over faster by shipping AI projects inside their current company.
qa: Do you need a license or certification to be an applied AI engineer?

No. There is no state license or required exam for applied AI engineers in the US. Employers judge candidates by their skills, past projects and work history. Some people add cloud provider certifications in machine learning or AI services, but these are optional and are not a substitute for showing working systems you have built.
Can you become an applied AI engineer without a computer science degree?

Yes. Many people come from data analysis, IT, consulting or other technical fields. You still need solid programming skills, usually in Python, plus experience building and deploying AI tools. A portfolio of real projects that solved business problems, along with a first job in a related technical role, is the most common way in without a computer science degree.

steps: Education

Most art directors hold a bachelor’s degree in graphic design, fine arts, illustration, communication design or a related field. Those aiming at games often study animation, game art or digital media. Useful coursework covers typography, layout, color theory, drawing and industry-standard design software.
Build a portfolio

Hiring depends on a portfolio more than a diploma. Start one in school with class projects, internships and freelance work. Show finished pieces and the thinking behind them, and tailor it to the field you want, such as advertising, publishing or games.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam to work as an art director in the US. Software or design certificates exist, but employers rarely ask for them. Your portfolio, references and track record of shipped work do the job a license would.
First job

Almost nobody starts as an art director. The usual way in is a junior role such as graphic designer, production artist, layout designer, illustrator, concept artist or photographer at an agency, publisher, game studio or in-house marketing team.
Grow into leadership

Over several years, move up to senior or lead designer. Take ownership of whole campaigns or projects, present ideas to clients or producers, give feedback to other artists, and learn to manage budgets, schedules and brand guidelines.
Time it takes

Employers usually want five or more years of hands-on design or art experience before they hire an art director. Counting a four-year degree, reaching the role commonly takes eight to ten years, though a strong portfolio can shorten that.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an art director?

No law requires one, but most employers expect a bachelor’s degree in graphic design, fine arts, illustration or a related field. In practice, a strong portfolio and years of relevant experience matter most. Some art directors without degrees get hired on the strength of their shipped work, especially in game studios and smaller agencies.
How long does it take to become an art director?

It usually takes eight to ten years. That includes about four years for a bachelor’s degree and then five or more years working as a designer, illustrator, production artist or similar role. Many people step up to senior or lead designer before moving into an art director title.

steps: Education

Most ASIC engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering or computer engineering. Key courses include digital logic, computer architecture, VLSI design and semiconductor devices. Many employers prefer a master’s degree for design and physical design roles. Some architecture and research roles ask for a PhD.
Hardware design skills

Learn a hardware description language such as Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL. Verification roles also expect UVM and scripting in Python, Perl or Tcl. Build projects on FPGA boards. Take designs through simulation, synthesis and timing analysis so you understand the full chip flow.
Internships

Internships at semiconductor companies are a main way in. They give hands-on time with commercial EDA tools that students rarely use in class. Many new graduate hires come straight from intern programs, so most students apply during the second or third year of their degree.
License and clearance

No state license or required exam exists for this work, and a PE license is not expected. Some defense and government chip projects require a security clearance. Some roles also limit hiring to people who meet US export control rules.
First job

Most people start as a design verification engineer, junior RTL design engineer or physical design engineer. Verification often has the most entry-level openings. Some move into chip design from FPGA engineering, test engineering or product engineering roles.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, plus one to two years if you earn a master’s. Owning a block design usually takes a few years on the job. Leading a full chip or architecture effort typically takes five to ten years or more.
qa: Do you need a master’s degree to become an ASIC engineer?

Not always, but it helps. Many ASIC engineers are hired with a bachelor’s in electrical or computer engineering, especially into verification roles. A master’s degree is common for RTL design and physical design jobs because it adds VLSI coursework and project depth. Strong internships and FPGA or chip projects can make up for not having one.
Do ASIC engineers need a license or certification?

No. There is no state license or required certification to design chips in the US, and employers do not expect a PE license. They judge candidates on their degree, knowledge of Verilog or SystemVerilog, and experience with design and verification tools. Some defense projects require a security clearance, and some roles must meet export control rules.

steps: Education

Most associate product managers hold a bachelor’s degree. Computer science, engineering, business, economics and design are common choices. Many structured APM programs at tech companies favor technical degrees, but no single major is required. Coursework in statistics, user research or software development helps.
Product internship

Many people enter through a product management internship during college, usually the summer before senior year. Rotational APM programs often hire most of their new graduates from their own intern classes. Internships in software engineering, data analysis or UX design also count as strong preparation.
Build product evidence

Employers want proof you can ship something. Students and career changers build apps, run side projects, write product teardowns or lead a feature in a student or volunteer team. A short portfolio showing the problem, your decisions and the results often helps more than any credential.
Optional certifications

There is no license or required exam for this work. Some people earn an agile credential such as the Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) from Scrum Alliance. These can help career changers show basic knowledge, but most hiring managers weigh internships, projects and interviews more heavily.
Time it takes

Recent graduates usually land an APM role straight out of a four-year degree. Career changers often spend one to three years in an adjacent role first, such as engineer, business analyst, UX designer or customer success, before moving into product.
First job

The associate product manager role is itself the usual first job in product. You own a small feature or area under a senior product manager, often rotating across teams. After about one to three years, most APMs are promoted to product manager.
qa: Do you need a certification to be an associate product manager?

No. There is no license, required exam or mandatory certification for associate product managers in the US. Some people earn an agile credential like the Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO), but employers mostly hire based on a relevant degree, product internships, side projects and how well candidates handle product sense and analytical interviews.
How long does it take to become an associate product manager?

For most people it takes about four years, the length of a bachelor’s degree, ideally with a product internship along the way. Career changers usually spend one to three years in a related role, such as software engineer, analyst or designer, before moving into an associate product manager position.

steps: Education

No degree is legally required. Many people take an associate’s or bachelor’s program in audio engineering, recording arts, music technology or sound design. Others learn through short courses and self-study. Basic knowledge of acoustics, signal flow, microphones and music theory helps in every path.
Learn the core tools

Get fluent in at least one digital audio workstation, such as Pro Tools, which many studios expect. For game work, learn audio middleware like Wwise or FMOD and how sound is implemented in game engines. Some scripting knowledge helps for programming interactive sound.
Optional certifications

There is no license for audio engineers in any state. Some employers value vendor certifications, such as Avid’s Pro Tools certifications or Audiokinetic’s Wwise certification. These show tool skills but do not replace a strong portfolio.
Build a portfolio

Create a demo reel of recordings, mixes and sound design. Game audio candidates often redesign the sound for existing gameplay or video clips. Show before and after work, list your role on each piece, and keep it short and easy to browse online.
First job

Most people start as a studio intern, runner or assistant engineer, a junior sound designer, an audio editor, or a live sound technician. Some enter game companies through QA testing and move into the audio team. Freelance work on small projects also builds credits.
Time it takes

Training usually takes one to four years, depending on whether you choose a short program or a full degree. Moving from assistant or junior roles to working as a lead engineer or senior sound designer often takes several more years of steady project work.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an audio engineer?

No. There is no legal requirement for a degree, and many audio engineers are self-taught or trained through short courses. Some employers, especially game and media companies, prefer a degree in audio engineering, music technology or a related field. In practice, a strong demo reel and solid skill with industry tools often matter more than formal education.
Do audio engineers need a license or certification?

No state requires a license to work as an audio engineer. Certifications are optional. Vendor credentials, such as Avid’s Pro Tools certifications or Audiokinetic’s Wwise certification, can help show tool skills to employers. Most hiring decisions still depend on your portfolio, your credits on past projects and your experience as an assistant or junior engineer.

steps: Education

Most internal auditors hold a bachelor’s degree in accounting, finance, business or information systems. Courses in auditing, financial accounting, internal controls and data analysis matter most. Some later add a master’s degree in accounting or business to move up faster.
First job

Common entry points are staff internal auditor or audit associate roles. Many people start in external audit at a public accounting firm, or in accounting or compliance, then move into internal audit after two or three years.
No license required

No state license is required to work as an internal auditor. Only auditors who sign opinions on financial statements must be licensed CPAs. Some internal auditors still earn a CPA license, which means meeting their state board’s education and experience rules and passing the CPA exam.
CIA certification

The Certified Internal Auditor (CIA) credential from The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA) is the main certification in the field. It requires passing a three-part exam and showing relevant work experience. Many employers prefer it, and it is often expected for senior roles.
Specialty credentials

Auditors who focus on technology often earn the CISA from ISACA. Those who focus on fraud may earn the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential from the ACFE. These are optional but help in IT audit, risk and investigation roles.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then entry-level audit work right away. Moving up to senior internal auditor usually takes another two to four years, and many people earn the CIA during that time.
qa: Do you need to be a CPA to be an internal auditor?

No. Internal auditors do not need a CPA license, and no state licenses this role. Many employers prefer the Certified Internal Auditor (CIA) credential instead. A CPA can still help, especially for roles close to financial reporting, and many internal auditors come from public accounting where the CPA is common.
How long does it take to become an internal auditor?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in accounting, finance or a related field, then can start as a staff internal auditor. Earning the CIA usually takes one to three more years of study and work experience, and reaching a senior role typically takes two to four years on the job.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information systems, software engineering or a related field. Some hire people without a degree if they can show working scripts and integrations they built. Courses in programming, databases and networking help most.
Core technical skills

Learn a scripting language such as Python or JavaScript, plus SQL. Understand REST APIs, JSON, XML, webhooks and authentication methods like OAuth. Practice moving data between two real applications and handling errors, retries and logging.
Platform certifications

No license is required for this work. Many employers value vendor certifications for the tools they use, such as MuleSoft, Boomi, UiPath, Microsoft Power Platform, AWS or Azure. These are optional and earned by passing the vendor’s exam.
First job

Most people start in a related role: junior developer, IT support, systems administrator, business or systems analyst, or CRM or ERP administrator. In these jobs they begin automating tasks and building small integrations, which leads into the integration or automation title.
Time it takes

With a degree, expect four years of school and then usually one to three years in a related role. People already in IT or analyst jobs can sometimes move over sooner by taking on integration projects at work.
qa: Do you need a license or certification to be an integration and automation engineer?

No license is required in any state. Certifications are optional, but many employers like vendor credentials for the platforms they run, such as MuleSoft, Boomi, UiPath, Microsoft Power Platform or a cloud provider. Proven experience connecting systems through APIs and scripts usually matters more than any single certificate.
How long does it take to become an automation engineer?

It usually takes four to seven years. Most people complete a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field, then spend one to three years as a developer, analyst or IT administrator. People who already work in IT can often move into the role faster by automating tasks in their current job.

steps: Education

Most automotive engineers earn a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering. Electrical, computer, and automotive engineering degrees also lead in, especially for electronics, software, and electric vehicle work. Employers often prefer ABET-accredited programs. Key courses include dynamics, thermodynamics, materials, and control systems.
Student vehicle projects

Many students join SAE International collegiate teams such as Formula SAE or Baja SAE. They design, build, and test a real vehicle. Hiring managers value this hands-on work and the CAD, testing, and teamwork skills it builds.
Internships and co-ops

Internships or co-op terms at automakers or parts suppliers are a common route to a full-time offer. Students do design, testing, or manufacturing support work under experienced engineers. Some programs add a semester or more for co-op rotations.
Licensing

No state license is required for most automotive engineering jobs. Engineers who design products for a manufacturer are usually covered by industry exemptions in state law. Some take the NCEES FE exam early in their career, but the PE license is optional and uncommon in this field.
Time it takes

It usually takes four to five years, including any co-op terms, to finish a bachelor’s degree and land a first role. A master’s degree adds one to two years. It is common in specialties like powertrain, vehicle dynamics, controls, and battery systems.
First job

Most people start as an entry-level design, product, test, validation, or release engineer at an automaker or supplier. They often own a single component or system, such as brakes or seats, and take on larger systems with experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be an automotive engineer?

Usually not. Most automotive engineers work for manufacturers or suppliers, and state laws generally exempt engineers who design products for their employer. Some engineers pass the FE exam to keep options open. A PE license is optional and rarely required in this field, though rules vary by state for engineers who offer services to the public.
How long does it take to become an automotive engineer?

It usually takes about four to five years. That covers a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, electrical, or automotive engineering, often with internships or co-op terms. Many graduates start right away as entry-level engineers. Those who pursue a master’s degree for specialties like controls or electric powertrains add one to two more years.

steps: Basic requirements

There is no degree requirement. Dealerships usually ask for a high school diploma or GED, a valid driver’s license, a clean driving record and a background check, since you will drive dealership cars on test drives. Sales, retail or customer service experience helps.
State license

Many states require car salespeople to hold a vehicle salesperson license from the DMV or a motor vehicle dealer board, usually applied for through the hiring dealership. It may involve fingerprints, a background check and, in some states, a short course or exam. Other states have no salesperson license.
First job

Most people start directly as a sales consultant on the showroom floor. Others begin in the dealership’s business development center, answering online leads and phone calls, or as a lot attendant or porter, then move into sales.
Training

Dealerships train new hires in the sales process, the vehicle lineup and trade-in basics. Manufacturers often require online product certification courses for their brand. Expect training on federal rules that cover car sales, such as the FTC Used Car Rule, financing disclosures and customer privacy.
Time it takes

You can start selling within a few days to a few weeks of being hired, once training is done and any state license is issued. Building a steady base of repeat and referral customers usually takes a year or more.
Moving up

Strong sellers often move to finance and insurance (F&I) manager, sales manager or general sales manager. F&I roles add work with lenders, loan contracts and add-on products such as service contracts.
qa: Do you need a license to sell cars?

It depends on the state. Many states require a vehicle salesperson license from the DMV or a motor vehicle dealer board, usually applied for through the hiring dealership and involving a background check and fingerprints. Some states add a short course or exam, while others require no salesperson license at all. Check your state’s rules.
Can you become a car salesperson without experience?

Yes. Many dealerships hire people with no sales experience and train them in the sales process and vehicle lineup. They usually want a valid driver’s license, a clean driving record and good communication skills. Retail, hospitality or customer service experience helps, and new hires often start selling within a few weeks.

steps: Driver’s license and record

You need a valid driver’s license, usually held for several years, and a clean driving record. Many employers ask for a minimum age of 21 or older, and most run a criminal background check and a drug test before hiring.
Education

A high school diploma or GED is the usual minimum. No degree is required, though some test roles prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree or a technical background. Clear writing matters, since operators report what the vehicle did after each drive.
CDL for trucks

Operators of self-driving heavy trucks need a commercial driver’s license, usually Class A. Since 2022, new CDL drivers must finish entry-level driver training with a provider on FMCSA’s Training Provider Registry, pass knowledge and skills tests, and hold a DOT medical card.
Employer training

Employers train operators themselves, often over several weeks. Training covers the self-driving system, closed-course practice, when and how to take over, and how to log issues. States that allow testing, such as California, require companies to train and vet their safety drivers.
First job

Most people start as a vehicle operator or safety driver on a test fleet. Many come from rideshare, delivery or trucking jobs. Remote operators who monitor vehicles from a control center often start as in-vehicle operators first.
Time it takes

With a regular driver’s license and a clean record, you can start within weeks of applying. Truck roles take longer, since earning a CDL usually takes several weeks of training. Moving to lead operator or test specialist often takes one to two years.
qa: Do you need a CDL to be an autonomous vehicle operator?

Only for trucks. Operators of self-driving cars and robotaxis need a regular driver’s license and a clean record.
