Operators of self-driving heavy trucks need a commercial driver’s license, usually Class A, which requires entry-level driver training, knowledge and skills tests, and a DOT medical card. Employers then add their own training on the system.
Can you become an autonomous vehicle operator without experience?

Yes, in most cases. Employers hire drivers with a valid license, several years of driving, a clean record and a passed background check and drug test, then train them over several weeks. Experience in rideshare, delivery or professional driving helps, as do clear reporting skills and comfort with technology.

steps: Education

Most ramp, operations and scheduling jobs require a high school diploma or GED. Many airline and airport operations roles prefer a degree in aviation management, aviation science or business. Courses in weather, aircraft performance and airport operations are useful.
Airport security badge

Anyone who works in secure areas of an airport needs a badge, which requires a fingerprint-based criminal history check and a TSA security threat assessment. Many roles also need a driver’s license and training to drive on the airfield.
First job

Common first jobs are ramp agent, operations agent, customer service agent, crew scheduler or airport operations specialist. These teach how flights are turned, loaded and dispatched, and how delays, weather and crew limits affect the schedule.
Dispatcher certificate

Airline dispatchers need an FAA Aircraft Dispatcher Certificate. You must be at least 23 to hold it, pass the FAA knowledge test, complete an FAA-approved course or qualify through experience, and pass a practical test. Dispatchers are also subject to drug and alcohol testing.
Airport credentials

Airport operations staff learn FAA Part 139 airport certification rules, wildlife hazards and airfield safety. Many earn the ACE (Airport Certified Employee) from the American Association of Airport Executives, and later pursue the C.M. or A.A.E. for management roles.
Time it takes

You can start as a ramp or operations agent within weeks, once your badge is approved. An aircraft dispatcher course usually takes several weeks of full-time study. Moving to operations controller or airport operations manager typically takes several years.
qa: How do you become an aircraft dispatcher?

You need an FAA Aircraft Dispatcher Certificate. Most people complete an FAA-approved dispatcher course of several weeks, pass the FAA knowledge test and then a practical test with an examiner. You must be at least 23 to hold the certificate. Many dispatchers first work as operations agents or crew schedulers to gain airline experience.
Can you get into aviation operations without experience?

Yes. Ramp agent, operations agent and customer service agent jobs are common entry points, and airlines and airports train new hires. You must pass a fingerprint-based background check and a TSA security threat assessment to get an airport badge, and some roles require drug testing. Many people move into scheduling, dispatch or airport operations from these jobs.

steps: Engineering degree

Most avionics engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in electrical, computer or aerospace engineering, ideally from an ABET-accredited program. Key courses include circuits, signals and systems, embedded systems, control theory and electromagnetics. Some go on to a master’s degree to specialize in guidance, navigation and control or flight software.
Internships and projects

Students build hands-on experience through internships or co-ops with aircraft, space or defense employers, and on student teams that build drones, rockets or small satellites. Practice with microcontrollers, circuit board design, C or C++, and lab tools like oscilloscopes makes a resume stand out.
Industry standards

No license or certification is required to do this work. Employers do expect you to learn the standards used to certify flight systems, such as DO-178C for airborne software, DO-254 for airborne electronic hardware and DO-160 for environmental testing. Most people learn these on the job.
Citizenship and clearance

Much avionics work is covered by export rules such as ITAR, so many employers hire only US citizens or permanent residents. Defense and space programs often require a security clearance, which the employer sponsors after you are hired.
Optional PE license

A Professional Engineer license is optional because most aerospace employers fall under the industrial exemption. Some engineers pass the FE exam near graduation and later the PE exam after about four years of qualifying experience. Requirements vary by state.
First job

Most people start as entry-level electrical, systems, test or embedded software engineers working on one part of the aircraft, such as a flight computer, sensor or radio. Expect about four years of school, then several years on the job before leading full avionics design work.
qa: Do you need a license to be an avionics engineer?

No. Most avionics engineers work without a license because aerospace and defense employers are generally exempt from state Professional Engineer rules. A PE license is optional, and requirements vary by state. Many employers do require US citizenship or permanent residency for export-controlled work, and defense projects often require a security clearance.
How long does it take to become an avionics engineer?

It usually takes about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in electrical, computer or aerospace engineering and land an entry-level engineering job. Becoming an independent designer who leads certification work under standards like DO-178C or DO-254 typically takes several more years of experience. A master’s degree adds about one to two years.

steps: Education

Most backend engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field, which usually takes four years. Some enter through self-study or a coding bootcamp instead. Either way, employers expect core knowledge of data structures, algorithms, networking and how databases work.
Core backend skills

Learn one server-side language well, such as Java, Python, Go, C# or JavaScript with Node.js. Add SQL and a relational database, building REST APIs, Git for version control, basic Linux, and writing automated tests. Knowing how to keep data correct and secure matters as much as the language.
Portfolio projects

Build a few working projects that run on a server: an API with user login, a database behind it, and tests. Put the code in a public repository and deploy at least one project to a cloud host. This matters most for people without a degree or internship.
No license required

No state license, registration or exam is required to work as a backend engineer anywhere in the US. Cloud and database certifications exist and can help show your skills, but employers rarely require them for entry-level roles.
First job

Most people start as a software engineering intern, then a junior or associate software engineer. Others move over from related roles such as QA tester, IT support or front-end developer. Hiring usually includes coding interviews plus questions about databases and API design.
Time it takes

Expect about four years through a degree, or one to two years of steady self-study for career changers. Reaching a mid-level backend role usually takes another two to four years of work on live production systems.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a backend engineer?

No law requires a degree, and no license or exam is needed. Many employers still list a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field. People without one get hired by showing strong skills through deployed projects, open source work, or experience in a related tech role such as QA or IT support.
How long does it take to become a backend engineer?

Through a computer science degree it usually takes about four years, often with an internship along the way. Career changers who study on their own or in a bootcamp often need one to two years before landing a junior role. Becoming a solid mid-level backend engineer usually takes another two to four years on the job.

steps: Education

There is no license for banking operations or partner bank management. Most people hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, business or economics. What employers value most is a working knowledge of how money moves: accounts, ACH, wires, card settlement and reconciliation.
First job

Common ways in are operations roles at a bank, such as deposit operations, wire processing or treasury management support, or payment operations at a fintech. Compliance roles in BSA/AML or KYC are another route, since partner banks focus heavily on those controls.
Rules to learn

Partner bank work runs on rules. Learn the Nacha Operating Rules for ACH, how Fedwire transfers settle, Regulation E for consumer transfers, and the Bank Secrecy Act duties that banks pass to their fintech partners through due diligence and oversight.
Certification

Certifications are optional but valued. Options include the Accredited ACH Professional (AAP) from Nacha, the Certified Treasury Professional (CTP) from the Association for Financial Professionals, and the Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialist (CAMS) from ACAMS for roles close to compliance.
Time it takes

Entry-level payment operations analyst roles are open to new graduates and are a common starting point. Managing a company’s partner bank relationships usually takes several years of experience in bank operations, payments or compliance.
qa: What certification helps in banking operations?

No certification is required. Useful ones include the Accredited ACH Professional (AAP) from Nacha for ACH payments, the Certified Treasury Professional (CTP) from the Association for Financial Professionals for cash and treasury work, and the Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialist (CAMS) from ACAMS for roles close to compliance.
Can you get into banking operations without experience?

Yes, at the entry level. Banks hire new graduates and career changers into operations roles such as deposit operations, wire processing and account servicing, and fintechs hire payment operations analysts. Managing a company’s partner bank relationships usually takes several years of experience in payments, bank operations or compliance.

steps: Education

No degree is required. Most cafés hire people with or without a high school diploma, and many baristas are students. Some employers set a minimum age, which can vary by state labor rules. Friendly service, cash handling and the ability to work fast during rushes matter more than schooling.
Food handler card

There is no barista license. Some states and counties require food workers to hold a food handler card, earned through a short course and test. Requirements vary by state and locality, so check local health department rules. Employers often help new hires complete it soon after starting.
On-the-job training

Most baristas learn at work. Training usually covers espresso extraction, milk steaming, the drink menu, cleaning the machines and food safety. New hires often shadow experienced staff for several shifts before working the bar alone.
Optional certification

Certification is not required, but some baristas take the Specialty Coffee Association (SCA) Coffee Skills Program courses in barista skills, brewing or sensory skills. These can help when applying to specialty coffee shops or moving toward roles like trainer or head barista.
Time it takes

You can usually start working within days of being hired. Becoming comfortable with the full menu and busy shifts often takes a few weeks. Developing strong latte art and espresso dialing skills can take several months of steady practice.
First job
Many people start as a barista trainee at a chain or local café. Others begin as a cashier, counter attendant or food service worker and move onto the espresso bar once they learn the basics.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a barista?

No. Baristas do not need a license or certification to work in the US. Some states and counties do require a food handler card for anyone handling food or drinks. Optional courses, such as those from the Specialty Coffee Association (SCA), can help with specialty café jobs but are not required.
How long does it take to become a barista?

Most people can start as a barista with no prior experience and learn on the job. Basic training often lasts a few days to a couple of weeks. Becoming confident on busy shifts, pulling consistent espresso shots and pouring good latte art usually takes a few months of regular practice.

steps: Education

Most battery engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in chemical engineering, materials science, electrical engineering or mechanical engineering. Cell work leans on electrochemistry and materials courses. Pack and system work leans on circuits, power electronics, thermal management and controls.
Hands-on experience

Employers look for real lab or build time. Students get it through internships, co-ops, university research labs that test cells, and student teams that build electric or solar vehicles. Experience with cyclers, test chambers, battery management systems and data analysis helps most.
Graduate degree, often

Many cell design, chemistry and research roles ask for a master’s degree or PhD focused on electrochemistry or materials. Manufacturing, pack design and test roles more often hire people with a bachelor’s degree and relevant experience.
Safety standards

No license is required for this work. Instead, employers expect you to learn battery safety and testing standards such as UN 38.3 for shipping, UL 2580 for electric vehicle batteries and UL 9540 for energy storage systems. A PE license is optional and rarely required.
First job

Common entry roles are battery test engineer, validation engineer, process engineer on a cell production line, or battery management system engineer. Some people start as lab or test technicians and move into engineering roles after finishing a degree.
Time it takes

Usually about four years for a bachelor’s degree, about six years with a master’s, and eight to ten years with a PhD. Gaining enough experience to lead cell or pack design often takes several more years on the job.
qa: Do you need a license to be a battery engineer?

No. Battery engineers in the US do not need a state license for most jobs. Employers care more about your degree, lab experience and knowledge of safety standards such as UN 38.3 and UL 2580. A Professional Engineer license is optional and only matters in a few roles, such as some grid or utility projects.
How long does it take to become a battery engineer?

Usually four years for a bachelor’s degree in chemical, materials, electrical or mechanical engineering, plus internships along the way. Many research and cell design jobs want a master’s degree or PhD, which adds about two to six years. Manufacturing and test roles often hire straight out of a bachelor’s program.

steps: Education

Most benefits specialists have a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business, finance or a related field. Some start with an associate degree or high school diploma and work their way up. Courses in HR, accounting and employment law are the most useful.
First job

Common first jobs are HR assistant, benefits assistant or benefits coordinator, where you process enrollments, update records and answer employee questions. Others start in customer service at an insurer or at a firm that administers benefit plans for employers.
Benefits law

The job requires a working knowledge of ERISA, COBRA, HIPAA, the Affordable Care Act and the Family and Medical Leave Act, plus state leave laws. Most people learn these on the job, guided by benefits brokers, legal counsel and industry courses.
Certification

No license is required for in-house benefits work. Many specialists earn the CEBS (Certified Employee Benefit Specialist) from the International Foundation of Employee Benefit Plans or the CBP (Certified Benefits Professional) from WorldatWork. General HR credentials such as the SHRM-CP or PHR also help.
Insurance license

Benefits specialists who work for an employer usually do not need a license. People who sell or advise on health or life insurance for a broker or agency must hold a state insurance producer license, which means passing a state exam, often after a prelicensing course.
Time it takes

Most people reach a benefits specialist role after one to three years as an HR or benefits assistant. The CEBS is earned through self-paced courses and exams taken while working. Benefits manager roles often require five or more years of experience.
qa: What certification is best for a benefits specialist?

There is no required certification, but two are widely known. The CEBS (Certified Employee Benefit Specialist) comes from the International Foundation of Employee Benefit Plans, and the CBP (Certified Benefits Professional) comes from WorldatWork. Many specialists also hold a general HR credential, such as the SHRM-CP or the PHR.
Do you need a license to be a benefits specialist?

Not if you work in house for an employer. Benefits specialists who run a company’s own plans need no state license. If you sell, solicit or negotiate health or life insurance for a broker or agency, you need a state insurance producer license, which means passing a state exam, and some states require a prelicensing course.

steps: Education

Most BI developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information systems, statistics, business analytics or a related field. Some come from business or finance degrees and add technical skills on their own. Employers care most that you can write SQL and understand how data is stored and joined.
Core technical skills

Learn SQL well, then data modeling, star schemas and basic ETL. Get hands-on with at least one dashboard tool, usually Power BI or Tableau. Learning DAX for Power BI, plus some Excel and Python, makes you more useful on real reporting projects.
Portfolio

Build a few dashboards from public datasets and publish them, for example on Tableau Public. Show the data model, the business question each dashboard answers and how you cleaned the data. A portfolio helps most when you lack direct work experience.
Optional certifications

No license is required to work as a BI developer in the US. Vendor certifications such as Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate (exam PL-300) or Tableau Certified Data Analyst are optional, but some employers list them as a plus.
First job

Most people start as a data analyst, reporting analyst or business analyst, building reports and writing queries. Others move in from database or IT support roles. After handling data models and dashboards for the business, they move into a BI developer title.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then usually one to three years in an analyst or reporting role. Career changers with strong SQL and tool skills can sometimes make the move faster through an internal transfer.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a BI developer?

No. There is no required license or certification for BI developers in the US. Certifications such as Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate or Tableau Certified Data Analyst can help your résumé stand out. Still, employers usually weigh SQL skills, a solid portfolio and work experience with real business data more heavily.
How long does it take to become a BI developer?

For most people it takes about five to seven years. That includes a four-year degree plus one to three years as a data analyst or reporting analyst. People who already work with data in another role can often move into BI development sooner by learning SQL, data modeling and a tool like Power BI or Tableau.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Classes in bookkeeping, business math, spreadsheets and customer service help. Some people take a short certificate or an associate degree in accounting or business, which can make it easier to get hired.
Software and office skills

Learn spreadsheets and the basics of accounting or billing software. Billing work means reading invoices, matching payments to accounts, spotting errors and keeping clear records. Accurate data entry and careful attention to detail matter as much as any formal training.
First job

Many people start as a customer service representative, accounts receivable clerk, data entry clerk or office assistant. These roles teach how accounts, payments and customer questions work. That experience often leads to a billing role inside the same company.
Optional certification

No license is required. People who bill for doctors, hospitals or clinics often earn a credential such as the AAPC’s Certified Professional Biller (CPB) or the NHA’s Certified Billing and Coding Specialist (CBCS). Employers in other industries rarely ask for one.
Time it takes

Getting in usually takes a few months to two years. Someone with office or customer service experience can move into billing quickly. A certificate or associate degree program adds time but may help with a first billing job.
qa: Do you need a license to be a billing specialist?

No. There is no state or federal license for billing specialists in the US. Most employers want a high school diploma and some office or customer service experience. In medical billing, a voluntary certification such as the CPB or CBCS is common and can help, but it is not required by law.
How long does it take to become a billing specialist?

It usually takes a few months to two years. Some people are hired with only a diploma and learn on the job. Others first complete a short certificate or an associate degree in accounting or business. Starting in customer service or accounts receivable is a common way to move into billing.

steps: Education

Most bioinformatics scientists study bioinformatics, computational biology, biology, genetics, computer science or statistics. A mix of biology and programming matters most. Master’s degrees open analyst and engineer jobs, while scientist titles at drug companies and research institutes usually go to people with a PhD.
Core skills

You need to program in Python or R, work on the Linux command line and use statistics. Many jobs involve analyzing DNA and RNA sequencing data, single-cell data or protein structures, building data pipelines and running jobs on computing clusters or the cloud.
Research experience

There is no license or required certification. Experience comes from undergraduate research, a graduate thesis or a postdoc in a lab or core facility. Publications and a public code portfolio showing real analyses help employers judge your work.
First job

Typical first jobs are bioinformatics analyst, research associate in a computational group, bioinformatics engineer or postdoctoral researcher. Hospitals, sequencing core facilities, universities, startups and drug companies all hire for these roles. Many lab biologists switch over by learning programming on the job.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree and one to two more for a master’s. A PhD usually adds five to six years, and many scientists also complete a postdoc of one to three years before an industry or senior academic role.
qa: How long does it take to become a bioinformatics scientist?

Analyst roles are open after a bachelor’s or master’s degree, so four to six years after high school. A bioinformatics scientist title in industry usually requires a PhD, which adds about five to six years after the bachelor’s degree, sometimes followed by a postdoc. People switching from lab biology often retrain in one to two years.
Is there a certification for bioinformatics?

There is no license and no standard certification that employers require. They judge candidates by their degree, publications and code. Graduate certificates and online courses can help biologists learn programming or programmers learn biology, but a portfolio of real analyses, such as sequencing pipelines shared publicly, usually matters more.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most biologists start with a four-year bachelor’s degree in biology or a related field such as molecular biology, microbiology or ecology. Coursework usually includes chemistry, physics, statistics and lab classes. Federal biologist jobs set specific coursework requirements in the biological sciences, so check those if you want government work.
Undergraduate lab experience

Hands-on research matters as much as grades. Students join a professor’s lab, take part in summer research programs or work as lab aides. This is where you learn techniques like cell culture, PCR and microscopy, and earn the references that graduate programs and employers ask for.
First job

The usual first job is research assistant, lab technician or field technician in a university, government or industry lab. These roles involve running experiments, keeping records and maintaining equipment. Many people work one to three years in such a role before or instead of graduate school.
Graduate degree

A master’s degree opens more advanced lab and field roles. Leading independent research or running a lab usually requires a PhD, which typically takes five to six years. Many PhD holders then complete a postdoctoral position, often two to four years, before a permanent research job.
Licenses and certifications

There is no general license to work as a biologist. Employers expect lab safety training, and work with animals, human samples or hazardous materials requires institution-specific training. Some specialties offer optional credentials, such as Certified Wildlife Biologist from The Wildlife Society for wildlife work.
Time it takes

With a bachelor’s degree you can work as a lab or field technician in about four years. Reaching an independent research biologist role with a PhD and postdoctoral training usually takes ten years or more after high school.
qa: Do you need a license to be a biologist?

No. There is no general state or federal license for biologists in the US. Employers look at your degree, research experience and lab skills instead. You will need workplace safety training, and some specialties offer optional certifications, such as Certified Wildlife Biologist from The Wildlife Society, which can help in wildlife and conservation work.
How long does it take to become a biologist?

Entry-level lab or field technician jobs usually need a four-year bachelor’s degree. A master’s degree adds about two years and opens more advanced roles. Leading your own research typically requires a PhD, which takes five to six years, often followed by two to four years of postdoctoral work, so the full path can take ten years or more.

steps: Education

Most blockchain engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering, math, or a related field. Some are self-taught. Useful coursework includes data structures, algorithms, distributed systems, networking, and cryptography, since blockchains combine all of these.
Software engineering base

Become a solid general programmer first. Common languages are Solidity for Ethereum and EVM-compatible chains, Rust for chains such as Solana, Go for node software, and TypeScript or JavaScript for apps and tooling that talk to smart contracts.
Security skills

Smart contracts often hold real money and are hard to change once deployed. Learn common flaws such as reentrancy and access control bugs, write thorough tests, use fuzzing, and study public audit reports to see how real contracts fail.
Portfolio

There is no license and no required certification. Employers judge public work: smart contracts on GitHub, apps deployed to testnets, contributions to open source protocols, hackathon projects, and findings from audit contests or bug bounty programs.
Time it takes

A typical path is a four-year degree plus one to three years of software experience. Developers who already work in software can often move into blockchain roles after several months to a year of focused study and project work.
First job

Common first jobs are software engineer, backend developer, or junior smart contract developer on a protocol, wallet, or exchange team. Some start as junior security auditors or in testing roles and move into building contracts later.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a blockchain engineer?

No. No US license or certification is required, and most employers do not ask for one. They look for strong programming skills, knowledge of a language like Solidity or Rust, and proof of work such as deployed smart contracts, open source contributions, or security findings. A computer science degree helps but is not always required.
How long does it take to become a blockchain engineer?

It usually takes about four years for a related degree plus one to three years of software development experience. An experienced software engineer can often switch in several months to a year by learning smart contract languages, studying security, and building a public portfolio of projects deployed to testnets.

steps: Education

Bookkeepers usually need a high school diploma, and many take a certificate or associate degree program in accounting or bookkeeping. General ledger accountant roles more often ask for a bachelor’s degree in accounting. Courses in double-entry accounting and spreadsheets matter most.
First job

Common ways in are accounts payable clerk, accounts receivable clerk, billing clerk or accounting assistant. These jobs teach how invoices, payments and bank activity reach the general ledger. Many small business bookkeepers start in an office manager or administrative role.
Software

Most bookkeeping is done in accounting software, so learn at least one small business package, and an ERP system if you want to work at larger companies. Some software makers offer free user certifications. Spreadsheet skills, including lookups and pivot tables, help with reconciliations.
Certification

No license is required. The American Institute of Professional Bookkeepers (AIPB) offers the Certified Bookkeeper (CB) credential, which requires passing exams and some bookkeeping experience. It is optional, but it can help self-employed bookkeepers and career changers show their skills.
Close and reconciliation

To move toward general ledger accountant, learn journal entries, accruals, account reconciliations and the month-end close. GL accountants prepare trial balances and support the financial statements, so many earn a bachelor’s degree in accounting while working.
Time it takes

A bookkeeping certificate usually takes a few months to a year, and an associate degree about two years. Many people start in entry-level roles right away and learn on the job. Moving up to general ledger accountant often takes a few years or a bachelor’s degree.
qa: Do you need a license to be a bookkeeper?

No. Bookkeepers do not need a state license in the US, since licensing applies to CPAs who perform audits and similar work. Optional credentials, such as the Certified Bookkeeper (CB) from the American Institute of Professional Bookkeepers, can show your skills. Bookkeepers who prepare federal tax returns for pay need an IRS Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN).
How long does it take to become a bookkeeper?

It can take only a few months. Many bookkeepers start in entry-level roles such as accounts payable clerk or accounting assistant with a high school diploma and learn on the job. A bookkeeping certificate usually takes a few months to a year, and an associate degree about two years. Certification takes longer because it requires experience.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. Most roles ask for a high school diploma or less. A college degree in marketing or communications can help for campus programs or longer contracts, but outgoing energy and reliability matter more to most hiring managers.
Build customer-facing experience

Employers look for time spent talking with the public. Retail sales, restaurant service, hospitality, or event staffing all count. Practice opening conversations with strangers, explaining a product in a sentence or two, and handling a quick no without losing your energy.
Permits for sampling

No license covers brand ambassador work itself. If you hand out alcohol samples, many states require responsible beverage service or alcohol server training. Food sampling may require a food handler card, depending on your state or county. Requirements vary by state, so check before you accept those gigs.
Join staffing agencies

Much of this work runs through promotional and event staffing agencies. Create profiles with several, add a clear headshot, list your availability, and note any permits you hold. Students can apply directly to campus ambassador programs run by brands.
First job

The usual entry point is a short in-store demo or a single event shift, often part-time or gig-based. Showing up on time, hitting sampling numbers, and sending clean reports leads to repeat bookings, team lead roles, and longer tours or field marketing jobs.
Time it takes

Most people can start within a few days to a few weeks. Once your agency profiles are approved and any needed permits are done, gigs can begin right away. Moving into lead or full-time field marketing roles usually takes a year or more of steady work.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a brand ambassador?

No. Most brand ambassador jobs do not require a college degree, and many accept a high school diploma or less. Employers care more about friendly communication, reliability, and a professional appearance. A marketing or communications degree can help for campus programs or for moving later into field marketing or event management roles.
Do brand ambassadors need a license or certification?

There is no license for the job itself. If you serve alcohol samples, many states require responsible beverage service or alcohol server training, and food sampling may require a food handler card in some states or counties. Rules vary by state, so check local requirements before taking sampling gigs with alcohol or food.

steps: Education

Most brand designers earn a bachelor’s degree in graphic design, visual communication or a related art field. Classes cover typography, color theory, layout, logo design and tools such as Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop, InDesign and Figma. Some people are self-taught or take shorter courses, but many employers ask for a degree.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam to work as a brand designer in the US. Optional software certifications exist, such as Adobe Certified Professional, but hiring managers judge you mainly on your portfolio and experience.
Build a portfolio

Your portfolio is the main way in. Show a handful of strong identity projects: logo, color palette, type choices and how the system works on packaging, websites, signage and social media. Explain your process, from the brief and research to sketches and final brand guidelines.
Internship

An internship at a design studio, branding agency or in-house marketing team gives you real client work, feedback from senior designers and references. Many students complete one or two internships before or right after graduating.
First job

Most people start as a junior graphic designer, production designer or design assistant. In these roles you create ads, social posts and presentations that follow an existing brand’s guidelines. This teaches you how identity systems hold up in daily use.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then usually two to five years of design work before landing a brand designer title. Senior brand designer or brand lead roles typically take several more years of experience.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a brand designer?

No law requires a degree, and there is no license for brand designers in the US. Still, many employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in graphic design or a related field. A strong portfolio of identity work can make up for a missing degree, especially at smaller studios and startups.
How long does it take to become a brand designer?

It usually takes about four years to finish a design degree, plus two to five years working as a junior or graphic designer. During that time you build a portfolio of logos, color systems and brand guidelines that shows you can create and manage a full visual identity.

steps: Education

Most employers expect a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications, advertising or a related field. Useful courses include consumer behavior, market research, advertising, statistics and writing. Brand marketing has no license, registration or required exam.
Internships and early work

Marketing internships during school matter a lot. Work at a company’s marketing team, an advertising or PR agency, or a campus brand program shows you can plan campaigns, write clear messages and read basic data. Keep samples of campaigns, social posts and results you helped deliver.
First job

The usual way in is an entry-level role such as marketing coordinator, marketing assistant, brand associate or agency account coordinator. At large consumer goods companies, the first step is often assistant brand manager. These roles teach budgets, agency briefs, launch timelines and reporting.
Build brand experience

Next, take ownership of campaigns, product launches, partnerships and brand guidelines. Learn to set positioning, manage creative agencies, track brand awareness and sales data, and present results to leaders. Strong results usually lead to promotion to brand manager or brand marketing manager.
Optional MBA or certificates

An MBA is common, though not required, for brand roles at large consumer goods companies, which often hire assistant brand managers from MBA programs. Optional certificates, such as the American Marketing Association’s Professional Certified Marketer, can add credibility but rarely replace experience.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually three to seven years in marketing roles before reaching brand marketing manager. People who move up from assistant brand manager after an MBA may get there faster, while those switching from other fields often take longer.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a brand marketing manager?

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications or a related field. There is no license or required exam. Some people without a degree get in through strong agency, social media or sales experience, but a degree plus internships is the most common path. Large consumer goods companies often prefer an MBA.
How long does it take to become a brand marketing manager?

It usually takes several years. After a four-year bachelor’s degree, most people spend about three to seven years in roles like marketing coordinator or assistant brand manager before managing a brand. The pace depends on the company, the results you deliver and whether you earn an MBA along the way.

steps: Education

Most browser engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, computer engineering or a related field. Useful courses include data structures, operating systems, compilers, computer networks, graphics and security. Some people get in self-taught, but they need to show the same depth through real code.
Core technical skills

Major browser engines are written mostly in C++, with Rust used more and more. You also need a solid grasp of JavaScript, HTML, CSS, the DOM and web standards from WHATWG and W3C, plus skill at debugging, profiling and reading very large codebases.
Open-source contributions

The main engines, such as Chromium, Gecko and WebKit, are open source and accept outside patches. Fixing small bugs, adding tests to web-platform-tests and going through code review is the most common way people prove they can do this work.
No license required

There is no license, state registration or required exam for browser engineers. Employers judge your code, your contribution history and technical interviews. Those aiming at browser security often build a record of reported vulnerabilities through bug bounty programs.
First job

Few people start on a browser team. Common first roles are general software engineer, systems or C++ developer, or front-end developer focused on performance. Internships on browser, compiler or graphics teams are another way in.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then usually a few more years of systems programming or steady open-source work before landing a browser engineering role. Strong contributors to an engine can sometimes move in sooner.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a browser engineer?

A degree in computer science or a related field is the usual path, and many employers list it. It is not legally required, though. Some browser engineers are self-taught and got hired after making accepted contributions to open-source engines such as Chromium, Gecko or WebKit, which show they can work in a large C++ codebase.
What programming languages do browser engineers use?

C++ is the main language of the major browser engines, and Rust is increasingly used for new and security-sensitive parts. Browser engineers also work with JavaScript, HTML and CSS, since they implement and test these web standards. Python and shell scripting often appear in build and test tooling.

steps: Education

Most business analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in business, finance, economics, information systems, computer science or a related field. Useful courses include statistics, accounting, database basics and operations. No single major is required, and some employers accept equivalent work experience instead of a degree.
Core skills

Learn spreadsheets well, basic SQL for pulling data, and a data visualization tool. Practice mapping a process step by step, writing clear requirements and user stories, and presenting findings to managers. Short online courses or self-study projects using public data can show these skills to employers.
First job

Common entry points are junior or associate business analyst, data analyst, operations analyst or reporting analyst roles. Many people move in from inside a company, from finance, customer support, quality assurance or operations, because they already know how the business runs.
Optional certification

No license or state registration is required. Some people earn certifications from the International Institute of Business Analysis (IIBA): the ECBA for beginners, then the CCBA or CBAP, which require documented business analysis experience. Agile or Scrum certificates are also sometimes requested in software teams.
Time it takes

A typical path is a four-year degree followed by one to three years in a junior analyst or related role before holding a full business analyst title. People who switch from another role inside their company can often move over faster.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a business analyst?

No. Business analysis has no license, and certification is not required to get hired. Some employers value IIBA credentials such as the ECBA for newcomers or the CCBA and CBAP for experienced analysts. Most hiring decisions still rest on your degree, your experience with data and processes, and how clearly you communicate findings.
Can you become a business analyst without a degree?

Yes, though it is less common. Many employers list a bachelor’s degree, but some accept equivalent experience. People without a degree often get in by working first in operations, customer support, finance or quality assurance, learning spreadsheets and SQL, and then moving into an analyst role within the same company where their knowledge of the business is already proven.

steps: Education

Most people in this field have a bachelor’s degree in emergency management, homeland security, business, public administration or information technology. Some earn a master’s degree in emergency management. Courses in risk management, project management and IT disaster recovery help most.
Free federal training

Many start with free online independent study courses from FEMA’s Emergency Management Institute, such as IS-100 and IS-700, which cover the Incident Command System and the National Incident Management System. Employers in emergency management often expect these basics.
First job

Common ways in are business continuity analyst, emergency management coordinator, risk analyst or IT disaster recovery support roles. Many people come from the military, fire service, police, healthcare or IT operations, where they already handled incidents and drills.
Certification

No license is required. Employers often ask for the CBCP (Certified Business Continuity Professional) from DRI International or the CBCI from the Business Continuity Institute. Emergency managers may pursue the CEM (Certified Emergency Manager) from the International Association of Emergency Managers. Higher levels require documented experience.
Standards and plans

The work follows standards such as ISO 22301 for business continuity management. You learn to run business impact analyses, write recovery plans, set recovery time objectives and lead tabletop exercises and drills with teams across the company.
Time it takes

With a related degree, you can start as an analyst right away. Most professionals spend two to five years building experience before earning the CBCP and leading a program. Senior roles that run continuity for a large company usually need many more years.
qa: What certification do you need for business continuity?

No certification is legally required, but employers often ask for one. The most common are the CBCP (Certified Business Continuity Professional) from DRI International and the CBCI from the Business Continuity Institute. People in public emergency management often earn the CEM (Certified Emergency Manager) from the International Association of Emergency Managers. Higher levels require documented experience.
How long does it take to become a business continuity manager?

Usually five years or more. Most people start as a business continuity analyst, emergency management coordinator or IT disaster recovery specialist after a related degree or military service. After a few years of writing plans and running exercises, they earn a credential such as the CBCP and move into managing a program.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing, economics or a field tied to the industry, such as engineering or computer science for software partnerships. No specific major is required. Some companies hire on a strong record of sales or partner results alone.
First job

Most people start in a sales or customer-facing role, such as sales development representative, account executive, account manager or channel sales coordinator. These jobs teach prospecting, pipeline tracking, negotiation and how deals actually close.
Product and industry knowledge

Partner deals depend on knowing the product and how partners make money. For integrations, time in solutions engineering, product or customer success helps. For reseller and joint offers, you need to understand pricing, margins and contract terms in your industry.
No license required

Business development has no state license, registration or required exam. Some people take negotiation courses or training from a vendor’s partner program. Employers weigh a record of closed deals, partner revenue and working relationships far more than any certificate.
Time it takes

It usually takes three to five years of sales, account management or partner experience before landing a manager title. Senior or director roles that own a whole partner program usually ask for more years and a track record of signed deals.
Move into the role

Many get in by taking on partner work in their current job, such as handling a reseller account or helping close an integration deal. A few signed partnerships with clear results often lead to promotion or a hire as business development manager.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a business development manager?

Most job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in business, marketing or a field related to the industry. It is not legally required, though. People with several years of strong sales or partner results can get hired without one, especially at smaller companies and startups that care more about deals closed than credentials.
How long does it take to become a business development manager?

After college, it usually takes three to five years. Most people spend that time in sales development, account executive or account manager roles, learning to find prospects and close deals. Taking on partner or reseller work along the way can shorten the path, since it gives direct proof you can negotiate and manage partnerships.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in business, economics, finance, engineering, or another quantitative field. Courses in statistics, accounting, and financial modeling matter most, because the job runs on numbers, forecasts, and clear written arguments.
First analyst job

The usual way in is two to four years as an analyst. Common starting roles include management consulting analyst, investment banking analyst, corporate finance analyst, business analyst, or operations analyst. These jobs build spreadsheet modeling, SQL, data analysis, and slide writing skills.
No license required

There is no license, registration, or required exam for this work. Some people in operations-heavy roles earn the PMP from the Project Management Institute or a Lean Six Sigma belt, but employers rarely require them. A track record of solved problems counts for more.
MBA or internal move

Many people move up after an MBA, often recruited into strategy and operations or corporate strategy roles at larger companies. Others skip the MBA and get promoted from analyst or associate jobs inside a company, especially at startups and tech firms.
Time it takes

Reaching a strategy and operations manager title usually takes five to eight years after a bachelor’s degree. That typically covers several years of analyst work plus either an MBA or one or two internal promotions through associate or senior associate roles.
qa: Do you need an MBA to be a strategy and operations manager?

No, an MBA is not required. Many strategy and operations managers have one, especially at large companies that recruit from business schools. Plenty of others get there through consulting, finance, or analyst roles and internal promotion. Strong analytical skills, clear writing, and proof that you improved a business result often matter more than the degree itself.
How long does it take to become a strategy and operations manager?

It usually takes five to eight years after finishing a bachelor’s degree. Most people spend two to four years in an analyst role, such as consulting, banking, or business analysis, then either complete an MBA or earn promotions through associate roles before reaching the manager level. Fast-growing startups sometimes move people up sooner.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in information systems, business, computer science, accounting or a related field. A degree is not legally required, and many analysts come from finance, HR or sales roles where they learned the business process first.
Learn one platform hands-on

Pick the system used in the work you want, such as Salesforce for sales, NetSuite or SAP for finance and operations, or Workday for HR. Salesforce and some other vendors offer free practice environments and online training, so you can build real configuration skills before you are hired.
Vendor certifications

There is no license for this work. Employers often value vendor certifications, such as the Salesforce Administrator certification, SAP certifications or NetSuite certifications. Workday training is usually available only through an employer or partner. The IIBA’s ECBA and CBAP are optional business analysis credentials.
First job

Common ways in are help desk or application support roles, a junior system administrator job, or being the go-to power user in finance, HR or sales operations. Associate consultant roles at firms that implement these systems are another frequent entry point.
Time it takes

After a degree or related work, it usually takes two to five years of hands-on work with business software to land the analyst title. You grow by gathering requirements, mapping processes, configuring workflows, testing changes and learning basic SQL and reporting.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a business systems analyst?

No license or certification is required by law. Many employers still prefer a vendor certification for the system they run, such as a Salesforce Administrator, SAP or NetSuite certification. Hands-on experience configuring the software often counts as much as the certificate itself, so pairing a certification with real project work makes you a stronger candidate.
How long does it take to become a business systems analyst?

Most people need a bachelor’s degree plus about two to five years of related work. That work is often in application support, system administration or a business role like finance or HR where they used the software heavily. People who already know one platform well and hold its certification can sometimes move in faster.

steps: Education

Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, supply chain management, economics, or a related field. Some hire people with a high school diploma or associate degree and train them on the job, especially for entry-level purchasing roles. Classes in negotiation, contracts, accounting, and spreadsheets are useful.
First job

Many people start as a purchasing assistant, procurement clerk, expediter, or assistant buyer. The work involves entering purchase orders, requesting quotes, tracking shipments, and following up on late deliveries. It teaches how suppliers, pricing, and company ordering systems work.
On-the-job training

No state license is required to be a buyer. New hires usually learn under a senior buyer or purchasing manager. They learn the company’s purchasing software, approval rules, supplier vetting, and how to compare bids and negotiate price and delivery terms.
Optional certification

Certification is voluntary but valued. Common options include the CPSM from ISM and the CPIM or CSCP from ASCM. Buyers in state or local government often pursue the CPPB or CPPO from UPPCC. Most require some work experience plus an exam.
Time it takes

A bachelor’s degree usually takes about four years. After that, people often spend one to three years in an assistant or junior role before working as a full buyer. Those who start without a degree may need more years of experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a buyer or purchasing agent?

No. There is no state license for buyers and purchasing agents. Employers look at education and experience instead. Voluntary certifications such as the CPSM from ISM, the CPIM or CSCP from ASCM, or the CPPB for public purchasing can help show skill. Federal contracting jobs have their own government certification programs, which differ between civilian agencies and the Department of Defense.
How long does it take to become a purchasing agent?

It often takes about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree, then one to three years in an entry role such as purchasing assistant or assistant buyer. Some people start right after high school as clerks and work their way up, which usually takes longer. Certification, if pursued, typically comes after a few years of experience.

steps: Education

Most drafters complete a certificate or a two-year associate degree in drafting, CAD or engineering technology at a community college or technical school. Courses cover technical drawing, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T), blueprint reading, materials and basic math. Some people start through high school drafting classes or a related engineering degree.
Learn the software

Employers expect real skill in the CAD tools used in their field. Mechanical and manufacturing work often uses SOLIDWORKS, Inventor or Creo. Architecture and construction use AutoCAD and Revit. Civil and survey work often uses Civil 3D. Learn the drawing standards that go with each field, not just the commands.
Build a portfolio

Keep a portfolio of your best models and drawings: part and assembly drawings, floor plans, site plans or detail sheets with clean dimensions and title blocks. Hiring managers often ask to see sample work or give a short drawing test, so show accuracy and neat, standard-following sheets.
Optional certification

No license is required to work as a drafter. Some people earn voluntary credentials to show skill, such as the ADDA Certified Drafter exam, Autodesk Certified Professional exams, or the SOLIDWORKS CSWA and CSWP. These can help a newcomer stand out but are rarely a strict requirement.
First job

The usual way in is a junior drafter, CAD technician or detailer role, redlining and updating drawings under a senior drafter or engineer. With experience you take on full models and drawing sets, and some move into design, checking or engineering technician roles.
Time it takes

A certificate can take under a year and an associate degree usually takes about two years. Most people then spend two to four years in entry-level roles before working independently as a CAD designer on complex projects.
qa: Do you need a license to be a drafter?

No. Drafters and CAD designers do not need a state license in the US. Licensed engineers or architects usually review and sign the final drawings. Voluntary certifications such as the ADDA Certified Drafter exam, Autodesk certifications or the SOLIDWORKS CSWA can help show your skills to employers.
How long does it take to become a CAD designer?

Most people take one to two years of training, through a drafting certificate or an associate degree, then start as a junior drafter or CAD technician. Moving up to a CAD designer role that handles full models and complex drawing sets usually takes another two to four years of on-the-job experience.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. A college degree is not needed for most entry-level roles. Classes in communication, business, or a second language help, and bilingual reps, especially Spanish speakers, are often in demand.
Customer service experience

Work in retail, food service, hospitality, or reception counts. Employers look for people who stay calm with upset customers, speak clearly, and type accurately while talking. Basic computer skills matter, since you’ll often use several systems at once.
Employer training

New hires usually go through paid training that lasts one to several weeks. It covers the company’s products, policies, call software, and scripts. Many centers follow it with a nesting period, where you take live calls with extra support and close monitoring before working alone.
Licenses for some roles

There is no general license for call center work. Some roles need one. Reps who sell or quote insurance usually need a state insurance producer license, and brokerage reps may need FINRA exams such as the SIE and Series 7. Employers often sponsor these after hire.
Time it takes

With a diploma and some customer-facing experience, many people get hired within a few weeks. Training and nesting usually take two to eight weeks. Becoming fully comfortable and meeting targets for handle time and customer satisfaction often takes a few months.
First job

The usual entry point is an inbound customer service or tech support rep, often through seasonal hiring or outsourcing firms. From there, people move into tier 2 support, quality assurance, training, workforce planning, or team lead roles.
qa: Do you need a degree to work in a call center?

No. Most call center jobs ask only for a high school diploma or GED. Employers care more about clear speaking, patience, typing speed, and basic computer skills. Prior work in retail, food service, or another customer-facing job helps. A degree can help later if you want to move into management, training, or analytics.
How long is call center training?

Most companies run paid training that lasts one to several weeks, followed by a nesting period of live calls with extra support. Simple customer service roles train faster. Technical support, healthcare, and financial roles take longer. Jobs that need a state insurance license or FINRA exams add time for study and testing.

steps: Education

Many care coordinator jobs accept a high school diploma or associate degree plus healthcare experience. Others ask for a bachelor’s in social work, nursing, public health, psychology or a related field. Hospital case manager roles usually call for a registered nurse or a social worker.
Nursing license route

Nurse case managers need a state RN license. You earn it by finishing an associate or bachelor’s nursing program and passing the NCLEX-RN. Many employers also want a few years of hands-on nursing before you move into case management.
Social work license route

Social work case managers often need a state license. Most states use ASWB exams, but whether a BSW can be licensed or an MSW is required varies by state. Hospital roles often ask for an MSW, and clinical licensure such as the LCSW adds post-degree supervised hours.
Certification

Certification is usually optional but valued by employers. Common options are the CCM, the ACM from the American Case Management Association, and the ANCC nursing case management credential for RNs. Each requires a qualifying license or degree plus case management work experience before you can sit for the exam.
Time it takes

Non-clinical care coordinator roles can be reached after months to a few years of related work. The RN route usually means two to four years of school plus clinical experience. The MSW route is about six years of school, and clinical licensure often adds about two years of supervised practice, depending on the state.
First job

Many people start as medical assistants, patient service representatives, community health workers or social services assistants. Nurses often move over from hospital or home health work, and social workers often come from discharge planning or community agencies.
qa: Do you need a license to be a care coordinator?

Not always. Many non-clinical care coordinator and patient navigator jobs have no license requirement. Case manager roles filled by nurses require a state RN license, and social work case manager roles often require a state social work license. Rules for social work licensure vary by state. Certifications such as the CCM are usually optional but can help.
How long does it take to become a case manager?

It depends on the path. Nurse case managers usually spend two to four years in nursing school, pass the NCLEX-RN, and often work a few years in clinical care first. Social work case managers in hospitals often need an MSW, about six years of school, and clinical licensure can add supervised practice that varies by state.

steps: Age and background

Casino floor jobs usually require you to be at least 21, though some states and tribal casinos allow 18. Expect a background check, fingerprints and often drug testing. A criminal record, especially for theft or fraud, can block a gaming license.
Gaming license

Most states require casino employees to hold a gaming license or work permit from the state gaming regulator, or from a tribal gaming commission at tribal casinos. Managers and key employees face deeper checks. In states with legal sports betting, operator staff often need an occupational license too. Rules vary by state.
Dealer school

Dealers usually learn games such as blackjack, roulette, craps and poker at a dealer school or a casino’s own training program. Courses often take a few weeks to a few months per game. Most casinos then hold an audition before hiring.
Betting and trading

Sports betting traders, odds compilers and risk analysts usually have a degree in mathematics, statistics, economics or finance, plus deep sports knowledge. Skills in Excel, SQL or Python and probability help. Many start in customer support or risk operations and move into trading.
Compliance

Casinos and betting operators follow anti-money laundering rules under the Bank Secrecy Act, state gaming rules and responsible gaming programs. Compliance and support staff learn identity checks, age and location verification, and how to handle problem gambling cases.
First job and timeline

Common first jobs are dealer, slot attendant, cage cashier, security officer, customer support agent or junior trading analyst. Entry roles can start within weeks or a few months. Moving to floor supervisor, pit manager or trader usually takes several years.
qa: Do you need a license to work in a casino?

In most states, yes. Casino employees usually need a gaming license, registration or work permit from the state gaming regulator, or from a tribal gaming commission at tribal casinos. Applying involves a background check and fingerprints. Managers and key employees face stricter checks. Rules and license levels vary by state.
How long does it take to become a casino dealer?

Usually a few weeks to a few months. Dealer schools and casino training programs teach one game at a time, and blackjack is often the quickest to learn. After training, most casinos hold an audition, and new dealers must get a gaming license or work permit before starting.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most CFOs start with a bachelor’s degree in accounting, finance or economics. An accounting major is the most flexible choice because it covers the coursework most state boards require before you can sit for the CPA exam.
First finance job

The usual first job is staff accountant or auditor at a public accounting firm, or financial analyst in a company’s planning and analysis team. Some future CFOs start in investment banking, where they learn deal work and fundraising.
CPA license

No license is legally required to be a CFO, but many employers expect a CPA. You pass the Uniform CPA Examination and meet your state board’s education and supervised experience rules, which vary by state.
Graduate study

Many CFOs add an MBA or a master’s in accounting or finance, often while working. People headed for investment-heavy companies sometimes earn the CFA charter, which requires passing three exam levels and documented work experience.
Climbing the ladder

Typical steps are senior accountant or analyst, finance manager, controller, then director or vice president of finance. Along the way you need experience in financial reporting, budgeting, cash and treasury, audits, and working with banks, investors and the board.
Time it takes

Reaching CFO usually takes 15 years or more after college. At small companies and startups people sometimes get the title sooner, while public company CFO roles usually require long experience with SEC reporting and Sarbanes-Oxley controls.
qa: Do you need to be a CPA to become a CFO?

No. There is no license required to hold the CFO title, and many CFOs come from finance or banking without one. Still, a CPA is common and often preferred, especially for roles that oversee accounting, audits and public company reporting. Getting it means passing the CPA exam and meeting state board rules, which vary by state.
How long does it take to become a CFO?

It usually takes 15 years or more. Most people spend four years on a bachelor’s degree, then move from accountant or analyst to manager, controller and vice president of finance. Startups and small firms may hire CFOs with less experience, while large public companies usually want long leadership experience.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in business, human resources, organizational psychology, communications, or a related field. Some later add a master’s degree such as an MBA or a degree in organizational development, but it is not required for most roles.
First job

There is no single entry route. Common starting roles are business analyst, project coordinator, HR generalist, corporate trainer, internal communications specialist, or junior consultant. These jobs teach you how projects run and how employees react when systems and processes change.
Hands-on change work

Next, people take on change work inside projects, often as a change analyst or change coordinator. Typical tasks include stakeholder analysis, training plans, communication plans, and tracking whether people actually adopt a new system or process.
Certification

No license is required. Many employers like to see a change management credential, such as the Certified Change Management Professional (CCMP) from the Association of Change Management Professionals (ACMP). Because this work overlaps with projects, some people also earn the PMP from the Project Management Institute (PMI).
Time it takes

Reaching a change manager title usually takes about five to ten years after a bachelor’s degree. Most people get there through several roles in projects, HR, training, or consulting. Transformation manager roles that lead large, company-wide programs often expect even more experience.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a change manager?

No license or certification is legally required to work in change management in the US. Many employers still list a credential as preferred, most often the CCMP from the Association of Change Management Professionals. Proven experience leading people through new systems or reorganizations usually matters more than any certificate.
How long does it take to become a change and transformation manager?

Most people need about five to ten years of work experience after a bachelor’s degree. They usually start in analyst, project, HR, training, or consulting roles. Then they move into change analyst or specialist jobs before managing change and transformation programs themselves.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing, communications or a related field. In technology channels, some IT coursework helps you talk with technical partners. No degree is legally required, and a strong sales record can stand in for one at many companies.
First sales job

Most people start in direct B2B sales as a sales development representative, inside sales rep or account executive. You learn prospecting, pipeline management, forecasting and CRM habits, and you build a track record of hitting quota that channel hiring managers look for.
Partner-facing role

The usual next step is partner account manager, channel account manager or a sales job at a reseller, distributor or consultancy. Here you learn partner programs, deal registration, margins and discounts, co-marketing funds and how to build joint business plans with partners.
Product training

There is no license, registration or state exam for this work. Many vendors expect channel staff to complete the same product and sales certifications their partners take. In technology, a vendor’s technical certification can add credibility with partner engineers.
Time it takes

It usually takes three to seven years of B2B sales experience to reach a channel sales manager title. Employers often want at least one to two years of that spent working directly with resellers, distributors or other partners.
First manager job

A first channel sales manager role usually means owning a set of partners in one region or industry. You recruit new partners, train and enable existing ones, plan joint campaigns and are measured on the revenue those partners bring in.
qa: Do you need a license to be a channel sales manager?

No. Channel sales has no license, state registration or required exam in the US. Employers judge candidates on sales results and partner experience. Many vendors do ask channel staff to finish their own product and partner program certifications, and some regulated industries such as insurance or financial products have separate licensing rules for selling those products.
How long does it take to become a channel sales manager?

Most people need three to seven years after college. They usually spend a few years in direct B2B sales, then one to two years in a partner account or channel account role before moving up. People who start at a reseller or distributor sometimes move faster because they already understand how partners make money.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. A college degree is rarely required. There is no license, registration or state exam for this work in any US state. Some college or coursework in English or communication can help you stand out.
Writing and typing skills

Practice writing short, clear, friendly replies with correct grammar and spelling. Build a steady typing speed, since you may handle several chats at once. Many employers give typing, grammar and sample-reply tests during hiring, so practice these before you apply.
Customer-facing experience

Prior work dealing with the public helps a lot. Retail, food service, front desk and phone support jobs all count. They show you can stay calm with upset customers, follow policies and solve problems without passing every case to a manager.
Employer training

New agents usually go through paid training run by the employer. It often lasts one to four weeks and covers the product, company policies, the ticketing or help desk software, saved replies and how to escalate problems you cannot solve yourself.
Time it takes

If you already write well and type quickly, you can usually be hired and working within a few weeks to a few months. Most of the real learning happens on the job during your first months answering live tickets.
First job

The usual entry point is a tier 1 support agent role, often remote and sometimes with an outsourcing firm or on contract. From there, people move into tier 2 support, quality review, team lead or customer success roles.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a chat support agent?

No. Most chat and email support jobs only ask for a high school diploma or GED. Employers care more about clear writing, good grammar, typing speed and experience with customers. A degree can help later if you want to move into management, training or customer success roles.
Do you need a certification to work in chat or email support?

No license or certification is required in the US. Some private customer service certifications exist, but most employers do not ask for them. Passing the company’s own typing, grammar and writing tests, then completing its paid training, is what usually gets you into the job.

steps: Training

No degree or license is required to cook. Many cooks learn on the job, starting in a kitchen with no training. Others take a culinary arts certificate or associate degree, which usually lasts one to two years and covers knife skills, cooking methods, baking, sanitation and kitchen costs.
First job

Most people start as dishwasher, prep cook or line cook in a restaurant, hotel, cafeteria or catering kitchen. You learn stations, speed and kitchen routines under a sous chef or chef. Moving through stations, such as grill, sauté and pantry, builds your skills.
Food safety

Many states and counties require food handlers to earn a food handler card soon after starting. Most kitchens also need at least one certified food protection manager on staff, which means passing an accredited exam. Requirements vary by state and local health department.
Apprenticeship

Some cooks join a registered culinary apprenticeship, which combines paid kitchen work with classroom study, often over two to three years. The American Culinary Federation offers apprenticeships and certifications such as Certified Culinarian, Certified Sous Chef and Certified Executive Chef.
Time it takes

A new cook can start working within days. Becoming a sous chef usually takes several years of kitchen experience, and executive chef roles take many more. Culinary school can speed up early learning but does not replace time on the line.
qa: Do you need a license to be a chef?

No license is needed to work as a cook or chef. Many states and local health departments, however, require a food handler card for kitchen staff, and most food businesses need at least one certified food protection manager. Requirements vary by state. Certification from the American Culinary Federation is optional.
Can you become a chef without culinary school?

Yes. Many chefs never attend culinary school and learn by working up from dishwasher or prep cook to line cook, sous chef and chef. Culinary school can teach basics faster and help with first jobs, but employers mainly value speed, consistency and experience. A registered apprenticeship is another way to train while being paid.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most chemists start with a bachelor’s degree in chemistry or biochemistry. Programs approved by the American Chemical Society (ACS) cover analytical, organic, inorganic and physical chemistry with lab work. Coursework in math, physics and some programming also helps.
Lab experience

Employers value hands-on time with instruments such as HPLC, GC, mass spectrometry and NMR. Undergraduate research, summer research programs, co-ops and internships give this experience. Lab safety training and careful record-keeping in lab notebooks are expected from the start.
Rules and training

There is no general license for chemists. Jobs in drug, food and environmental labs require training in Good Laboratory Practice or Good Manufacturing Practice, OSHA safety rules and hazardous waste handling. Some clinical and forensic lab roles have their own licensing or certification.
First job

Common first jobs are laboratory technician, quality control chemist, analytical chemist or research associate in manufacturing, pharmaceutical, environmental, food or materials labs. Computational chemists usually need graduate training in modeling and programming.
Graduate degree

A master’s degree helps for senior lab roles. Leading independent research in industry or academia usually requires a PhD, which takes about five to six years and is often funded. Many PhD chemists then complete a postdoc of one to three years.
Time it takes

You can start working as a lab chemist after a four-year bachelor’s degree. Moving to senior analytical roles usually takes several years of experience. A research scientist path with a PhD and postdoc often takes ten or more years after high school.
qa: Do you need a license to be a chemist?

No general license is required to work as a chemist in the US. Employers rely on your degree, lab skills and training in safety and quality rules such as Good Manufacturing Practice. Some related jobs, such as clinical laboratory scientist in certain states, require a separate license or certification.
How long does it take to become a chemist?

You can work as a chemist after a four-year bachelor’s degree in chemistry, usually starting as a lab technician or quality control chemist. A master’s degree takes about two more years. A research chemist leading projects usually has a PhD, which takes about five to six years after the bachelor’s, often followed by a postdoc.

steps: Education

Most chiefs of staff hold a bachelor’s degree in business, economics, political science, public policy or a related field. Many corporate roles favor candidates with an MBA, but no specific degree is required to enter this work.
No license or exam
