There is no license or required degree. Many .NET developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science or software engineering, while others learn through community college courses, coding bootcamps or self-study. Learn C#, object-oriented design, SQL and how web applications work.
Core skills

Build skills in modern .NET, ASP.NET Core for web APIs, Entity Framework Core for data access, and a relational database such as SQL Server. Git, unit testing and cloud basics, often on Azure, are common requirements.
Portfolio

Show your work with two or three complete projects, such as a web API with a database and user login, published with clean code in a public repository. Employers hiring juniors want proof you can build, test and deploy an application, not only follow tutorials.
Certifications

Certifications are optional. Microsoft offers role-based certifications, such as for Azure developers, that some employers and consulting firms value. Most hiring decisions still rest on coding interviews, technical tests and real projects.
First job

The usual first job is junior .NET developer or junior software engineer, often at a large company, government contractor, bank or consulting firm that runs Microsoft systems. Some move in from help desk, QA testing or IT support roles inside a company that uses .NET.
Time it takes

A computer science degree takes about four years. Self-taught developers and career changers often need one to two years of steady study and projects before landing a first job. Reaching senior level usually takes about five or more years.
qa: How long does it take to become a .NET developer?

Through a computer science degree, about four years. Career changers learning C# and .NET on their own or in a bootcamp often need one to two years of steady study and project work before a first junior role. Moving from junior to senior .NET developer usually takes about five or more years of professional experience.
What certification is good for a .NET developer?

No certification is required to work as a .NET developer. Microsoft offers role-based certifications, including ones for Azure developers, which can help with employers and consulting firms that build on Microsoft cloud services. Most employers still judge candidates mainly on coding interviews, technical tests and real projects.

steps: Driver’s license and record

Start with a valid state driver’s license and a clean driving record. Employers usually run a background check and review your motor vehicle record. Many ask for a few years of licensed driving. Federal rules require drivers to be at least 21 to drive commercial vehicles across state lines.
Chauffeur or for-hire permit

Some states issue a separate chauffeur license or classification for driving people for pay. Many cities, counties and airports also require a for-hire or limousine permit, often with fingerprinting. Requirements vary by state and locality, so check with your state licensing agency and local authorities.
When a CDL applies

You need a commercial driver’s license for vehicles with a gross vehicle weight rating of 26,001 pounds or more, vehicles designed to carry 16 or more people including the driver, or vehicles hauling placarded hazardous materials. Passenger work needs a P endorsement. School buses also need an S endorsement.
Permit and training

Pass your state’s knowledge tests to get a commercial learner’s permit. First-time Class A or B applicants, upgrades, and first-time P, S or H endorsements also need Entry-Level Driver Training from a provider on the FMCSA Training Provider Registry. Behind-the-wheel training requires the permit, and training must be finished before the skills test.
Medical and drug tests

CDL drivers need a DOT medical exam from an examiner on the National Registry of Certified Medical Examiners. Employers of CDL drivers must run a pre-employment drug test and a query of the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse. Many non-CDL employers also drug test.
First job and timing

Common first jobs are delivery, courier, shuttle or rideshare driving, which may take only weeks to start. Drivers then move into chauffeur, transit or bus work. CDL training often takes a few weeks to a few months. Some transit and school bus employers train new hires for the CDL.
qa: Do you need a CDL to be a bus driver?

Yes, for buses designed to carry 16 or more people including the driver. You need a CDL with a P endorsement, plus an S endorsement for school buses. You first get a commercial learner’s permit, complete Entry-Level Driver Training, then pass the skills test. Some transit and school bus employers provide this training to new hires.
How long does it take to become a chauffeur?

For a sedan or small van, you can often start within a few weeks once you hold a driver’s license, pass the employer’s background check and get any local for-hire permit your area requires. If the job uses larger passenger vehicles that need a CDL, add a few weeks to a few months for training and testing.

steps: Education

Drone engineers usually have a bachelor’s degree in aerospace, mechanical, electrical or computer engineering, or computer science. Controls, embedded systems and robotics courses matter most. Drone pilots do not need a degree, though some take college or technical programs in uncrewed aircraft systems.
Part 107 certificate

Anyone who flies a drone for work in the US needs an FAA Remote Pilot Certificate under Part 107. You must be at least 16, pass the FAA knowledge test at an approved testing center and pass a TSA security check. Recurrent online training is required every 24 months.
Registration and airspace

Drones that weigh more than 0.55 pounds must be registered with the FAA. Flights beyond visual line of sight, or other operations Part 107 does not allow, need an FAA waiver. Many commercial jobs also require getting airspace authorization near airports.
First job

Pilots often start with inspection, mapping, surveying, construction, real estate or agriculture work. Engineers usually start as junior design, test or flight test engineers. Military experience with uncrewed aircraft is another common way in, especially for defense work.
Defense and security

Jobs on military drones usually require US citizenship and often a security clearance, which employers sponsor after hiring. Export control rules under ITAR limit who can work on many defense systems, so companies often hire only US persons.
Time it takes

Most people can study for and earn a Part 107 certificate within a few weeks. Becoming a skilled commercial pilot takes months of practice. Drone engineers spend four years on a degree, then often two to five years before leading designs.
qa: Do you need a license to fly a drone for work?

Yes. In the US, flying a drone for any business purpose requires an FAA Remote Pilot Certificate under Part 107. You must be at least 16, pass the FAA knowledge test and clear a TSA security check, then complete free recurrent online training every 24 months. Drones over 0.55 pounds must also be registered.
How long does it take to become a drone pilot?

Most people can earn the FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate within a few weeks of study. Building the flying skill and experience that employers want, such as for inspections or mapping, usually takes several months to a year. Drone engineers take longer, since most need a four-year engineering degree.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing, or a related field, though no law requires one. Courses in digital marketing, statistics, merchandising, and supply chain are the most useful. Some people get in without a degree by showing results from a store they ran.
No license required

There is no license, registration, or required exam for this work in any state. Optional certificates in web analytics, online advertising, or specific store platforms can show your skills, but employers rarely require them and value proven sales results more.
First job

Most people start as an e-commerce coordinator, e-commerce assistant, marketplace specialist, or merchandising assistant. Typical tasks include uploading product listings, writing product copy, updating prices, checking stock levels, and pulling weekly sales reports. Some move over from retail buying, digital marketing, or customer service roles.
Skills built on the job

In those early roles you learn listing optimization, pricing and promotions, conversion rates, site analytics, and paid ads on search and marketplaces. You also learn to work with inventory, fulfillment, and design teams. Running a small online store of your own is another way to build and prove these skills.
Time it takes

It usually takes three to five years of hands-on experience to reach an e-commerce manager title. Smaller companies may promote faster, while large retailers often want a record of growing online sales and managing a budget or a small team first.
qa: Do you need a license to be an e-commerce manager?

No. There is no license, registration, or required exam for e-commerce managers in the US. Most employers look for a bachelor’s degree in business or marketing and several years of experience running product listings, pricing, and online sales. Optional analytics or advertising certificates can help a resume but are rarely required.
How long does it take to become an e-commerce manager?

Most people need a four-year degree plus about three to five years of work in entry roles such as e-commerce coordinator or marketplace specialist. People who can show strong sales results, for example from running their own online store, can sometimes move up faster, especially at smaller companies.

steps: Education

Most economist jobs require a master’s degree or PhD in economics, and academic and many government research roles require a PhD. A bachelor’s degree in economics, mathematics or statistics prepares you. Key subjects are microeconomics, macroeconomics, econometrics, calculus and linear algebra.
Research skills

Learn econometrics and statistical software such as Stata, R or Python, and practice working with large data sets. Economists must also write clearly, explaining what a policy or price change will do and how sure they are.
Research assistant

Many future economists work one to two years as a research assistant after college, at a central bank, government agency, think tank or university. These jobs build data skills and lead to strong recommendation letters for PhD programs.
Graduate school

A PhD in economics usually takes five to six years, including coursework, field exams and a dissertation. Master’s programs take one to two years and lead to roles in consulting, government, finance and industry. Doctoral graduates then enter the job market for faculty, government or industry roles.
First job

Common first jobs are research assistant, economic analyst or junior economist at a government agency, consulting firm, bank or think tank. Federal economist jobs require a set amount of economics coursework. No license or certification is required.
Time it takes

With a master’s degree, most economists start working about five to six years after high school. With a PhD, it usually takes ten years or more, often including a year or two as a research assistant before graduate school.
qa: How long does it take to become an economist?

With a master’s degree, about five to six years after high school: four years for a bachelor’s degree and one to two for a master’s. Research economists usually need a PhD, which takes five to six more years, so the full path often takes ten years or more, sometimes with a research assistant job in between.
Do you need a license to be an economist?

No. There is no license or required certification for economists in the US. Employers judge candidates by their degree, research, writing and skill with data and econometrics. Federal economist jobs do require a set amount of college coursework in economics, and some economists in finance pursue optional credentials such as the CFA.

steps: Education

Public school teachers need at least a bachelor’s degree and must complete a state-approved teacher preparation program, either within the degree or after it. Many states also offer alternative routes for people who already hold a degree in another field. Instructional designers often study education or instructional design.
Student teaching

Teacher preparation programs include supervised classroom practice, usually a semester or more of student teaching under an experienced teacher. Alternative route programs often let you teach on a provisional license while you complete training and work with a mentor.
State teaching license

Every state requires a license or certificate to teach in public K-12 schools. Most require passing exams on basic skills, subject knowledge or teaching, such as the Praxis tests used in many states, plus a background check. Private schools, colleges and online course providers usually do not require one.
Online course design

For online courses and education products, roles like instructional designer, curriculum writer and learning experience designer need no license. Employers look for a portfolio of lessons or course modules, teaching experience and skill with authoring tools and learning management systems. Many move into this work after classroom teaching.
First job

The usual first jobs are classroom teacher, substitute teacher, teacher’s aide or tutor. Substitute teaching rules vary by state, and some states allow it without a full license. For online education, many start as a tutor, course assistant or junior instructional designer.
Time it takes

Becoming a licensed public school teacher usually takes about four years through a bachelor’s degree with a built-in preparation program. Alternative routes can put degree holders in a classroom within a year. Most states also require continuing education to renew a license.
qa: Do you need a license to be a teacher?

To teach in a US public K-12 school, yes. Every state requires a teaching license or certificate, usually earned with a bachelor’s degree, a state-approved preparation program, student teaching, state exams and a background check. Private schools, colleges, tutoring and online course providers usually do not require a state license, though they may prefer one.
How long does it take to become a teacher?

Usually about four years. Most teachers earn a bachelor’s degree that includes a state-approved preparation program and a semester or more of student teaching, then pass state exams. People who already hold a degree can often use an alternative route and start teaching on a provisional license within a year while finishing training.

steps: Education

Most education program managers have a bachelor’s degree in education, communications, psychology or the program’s subject. A master’s in education, instructional design or nonprofit management helps for senior roles. There is no license for the job itself.
First job

Common starting roles are teacher, trainer, program coordinator, instructional designer, outreach coordinator or customer education specialist. These roles teach how learners behave, how programs run day to day and how to work with schools, partners or customers.
Key skills

Managers plan curricula and schedules, recruit learners and instructors, manage budgets and measure results. Learning management systems, survey and data tools, and instructional design models such as ADDIE are common requirements. Programs for minors also require background checks and child safety training.
Certification

Certification is optional. Options include the Project Management Professional (PMP) from the Project Management Institute and the Certified Professional in Talent Development (CPTD) from the Association for Talent Development. Programs run in public schools may prefer candidates with a state teaching license.
Time it takes

Most people spend two to five years as a teacher, trainer or coordinator before managing a program. Former teachers with experience leading projects or departments often move into program management sooner.
qa: How do you become an education program manager?

Most people start in teaching, training or program coordination and take on more planning and partner work over two to five years. A bachelor’s degree is the usual minimum, and a master’s in education or instructional design helps. Experience with budgets, data and learning platforms makes the move to manager easier.
Can teachers become education program managers?

Yes, it is one of the most common paths. Teachers bring curriculum, classroom and assessment skills. To make the move, they often lead school projects, coordinate after-school or summer programs, or take a training or customer education role first. Skills in project management, budgets and reporting help close the gap.

steps: Education

Most safety engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in occupational safety and health, safety engineering, industrial hygiene, environmental science, or an engineering field. Useful courses include chemistry, toxicology, ergonomics, fire protection, and OSHA and EPA regulations. Some people come from operations or the military and complete a degree later.
Early training

Employers expect working knowledge of OSHA standards. Many new hires complete OSHA 30-hour outreach training, and roles involving hazardous waste or cleanup sites often require 40-hour HAZWOPER training. First aid, CPR, confined space, and lockout/tagout training are also common in the first year.
First job

The usual way in is a role as an EHS coordinator, safety specialist, safety technician, or environmental technician, often after an internship. You run inspections, track training, keep injury logs, help with permits and reports, and investigate incidents under a senior EHS manager.
Certification

No state license is required for most EHS work. Employers often ask for the Certified Safety Professional (CSP) from BCSP. It requires a bachelor’s degree, about four years of safety experience, a qualifying credential such as the ASP or GSP, and passing the CSP exam. Industrial hygiene roles may call for the CIH.
Engineering license

A Professional Engineer (PE) license is optional for most safety roles but helps in design, consulting, and fire protection work. It means passing the NCEES FE exam, gaining supervised engineering experience, usually about four years, and passing a PE exam. Requirements vary by state.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, then roughly four more years of safety work before you qualify for the CSP. Many people reach a full safety engineer or EHS manager title about five to eight years after starting college.
qa: Do you need a license to be a safety engineer?

Usually not. Most EHS and safety engineer jobs require no state license. Employers often prefer the Certified Safety Professional (CSP) credential from BCSP, plus OSHA training. A Professional Engineer (PE) license is only needed if you sign engineering designs or offer engineering services to the public, and those rules vary by state.
How long does it take to become a safety engineer?

Most people spend four years earning a bachelor’s degree in safety, environmental science, or engineering, then start as an EHS coordinator or safety specialist. After about four years of safety experience they can sit for the CSP exam. Reaching a safety engineer or EHS manager role typically takes five to eight years in total.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most electrical engineers earn a four-year bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering. Choose an ABET-accredited program, because most state licensing boards and many employers expect it. Coursework covers circuits, electronics, signals, electromagnetics, power systems and programming, built on calculus and physics.
Internships and co-ops

Many students complete one or more summer internships or co-op terms while in school. These give hands-on work in design, testing or field service, and they often lead straight to a full-time offer after graduation.
FE exam

Near or after graduation, many take the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam in electrical and computer engineering. Passing it lets you register with your state as an Engineer in Training (EIT) or Engineer Intern, the first step toward a license.
First job

The usual entry point is a role such as junior electrical engineer, design engineer or test engineer. You work under experienced engineers on tasks like circuit layout, power distribution drawings, battery systems or RF testing, depending on the industry.
PE license

A Professional Engineer (PE) license is needed to sign and seal drawings or offer engineering services to the public. Most states require about four years of supervised experience after the degree, then passing the NCEES PE Electrical and Computer exam. Requirements vary by state.
Time it takes

Expect four years to earn the degree and start working as an entry-level engineer. Reaching a PE license usually takes about eight years in total. A master’s degree is optional but common for research, RF and advanced design roles.
qa: Do you need a license to be an electrical engineer?

Not always. Many electrical engineers in manufacturing, electronics and tech companies work without a license under industry exemptions in most states. A Professional Engineer (PE) license is required if you sign and seal plans, work for the public as a consultant or approve building and utility designs. Utilities and consulting firms often expect a PE for senior roles. Requirements vary by state.
How long does it take to become an electrical engineer?

It usually takes four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and get hired as an entry-level engineer. If you pursue a PE license, plan on roughly four more years of supervised work experience plus passing the FE and PE exams, so about eight years in total. A master’s degree adds one to two years.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Many technicians also earn a one-year certificate or two-year associate degree in electronics or electrical engineering technology from a community college or technical school. Military electronics training is also widely accepted.
Hands-on bench skills

Training should cover reading schematics and wiring diagrams, soldering through-hole and surface-mount parts, and crimping and terminating wire. You also need to use multimeters, oscilloscopes and power supplies to test and troubleshoot circuits. Employers value this practical work more than theory alone.
Industry certifications

No state license is required for this bench work. Many employers, especially in aerospace, defense and medical devices, expect IPC certifications such as IPC J-STD-001 for soldering, IPC-A-610 for inspecting assemblies, and IPC/WHMA-A-620 for cables and wire harnesses. Employers often pay for this training, and the certifications must be renewed periodically.
First job

A common way in is a job as an electronics assembler, wire harness assembler or production technician. In these roles you build and solder assemblies to set standards. You learn the employer’s procedures and gain the experience needed to move into testing and repair.
Time it takes

Expect anywhere from a few months to about two years of school, depending on whether you take a short certificate or an associate degree. Moving from assembler to a full technician role that includes troubleshooting usually takes another one to three years of on-the-job experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be an electronics technician?

Usually not. Building, soldering and testing electronic assemblies in a shop or factory needs no state license. This is different from electricians who wire buildings, who must be licensed in most states. Many employers do require IPC certifications for soldering and inspection, and some technicians add voluntary certifications from ETA International to show their skills.
How long does it take to become an electronics technician?

Most people take between several months and two years. A certificate program can be finished in under a year, while an associate degree usually takes two years. Some people start as assemblers with only a high school diploma and on-the-job training, then move up to technician work after one to three years of experience.

steps: Education

Most apprenticeship programs require a high school diploma or GED, a minimum age of 18, and a passing score on a basic algebra and reading aptitude test. Math, physics and shop classes help. Some people take a trade school or pre-apprenticeship program first, which may count toward later training.
First job

Most people start as an apprentice electrician or electrician’s helper, pulling wire, bending conduit and handling materials under a licensed electrician. Many states require apprentices to register with the state licensing board before they can work on job sites.
Apprenticeship

Most electricians train through a paid apprenticeship of four to five years. Union programs run by the IBEW and NECA and nonunion programs through groups like IEC and ABC combine about 8,000 hours of supervised work with classroom study of the National Electrical Code, blueprints and safety.
Journeyman license

Most states require a journeyman license to work without direct supervision. After the required hours, you usually pass an exam on the National Electrical Code, local codes and electrical theory. In some states cities or counties handle licensing instead, so requirements vary by location.
Time it takes

It usually takes four to five years to go from new apprentice to licensed journeyman electrician. Many states also require continuing education, often on National Electrical Code updates, to renew the license.
Master electrician

After more years as a journeyman, often two or more, many states let you take a master electrician exam. A master license allows you to pull permits and supervise others. Running your own business may also require a separate state contractor’s license.
qa: Do you need a license to be an electrician?

In most states, yes. Electricians usually need a journeyman license to work without direct supervision, earned by completing supervised hours and passing an exam based on the National Electrical Code. Apprentices often must register with the state. Some states leave licensing to cities or counties, so requirements vary by location.
How long does it take to become an electrician?

Usually four to five years. Most people complete a paid apprenticeship with about 8,000 hours of on-the-job training plus classroom study, then pass a journeyman licensing exam. Trade school can sometimes shorten the apprenticeship. Becoming a master electrician typically takes several more years of experience and another exam.

steps: Education

Most embedded engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer engineering, electrical engineering, or computer science. Courses that matter most cover C programming, digital logic, computer architecture, operating systems, and basic circuits. A degree usually takes four years. Some people move in from electronics technician work, but employers commonly expect a degree.
Hands-on projects

Build real projects on microcontroller boards. Write C or C++ that reads sensors, drives motors, and talks over buses like I2C, SPI, and UART. Learn to use a debugger, an oscilloscope, and a logic analyzer. Put the code on a public repository so employers can see your work.
Internships

Internships at device, automotive, or electronics makers are a common way in. They teach you how firmware is tested, reviewed, and shipped on real hardware. Many entry-level offers go to people who interned with the same team, so start applying in your second or third year of school.
No license required

There is no state license or required exam to write embedded software. Professional Engineer licensure is rarely needed for this work. Some defense and aerospace jobs require a security clearance, which the employer sponsors and which only U.S. citizens can usually hold.
First job

The usual first role is junior or associate firmware engineer, embedded software engineer, or test engineer working on hardware. You will fix bugs, write drivers, and test boards. In cars, medical devices, or aircraft, you also learn safety standards such as ISO 26262, IEC 62304, or DO-178C on the job.
Time it takes

Counting a four-year degree, most people land their first embedded role in about four to five years. Working independently on full products, such as bringing up a new board or designing a real-time system, usually takes another two to four years of experience.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an embedded engineer?

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer engineering, electrical engineering, or computer science. Some people get in without one by building strong microcontroller projects, working as electronics technicians or test engineers, and moving into firmware roles. Without a degree, a solid portfolio showing C code running on real hardware is the main thing that gets interviews.
Is there a certification for embedded engineers?

No single certification is required or expected for embedded engineers in the US, and there is no license. Employers mostly judge your C and C++ skills, your knowledge of microcontrollers and real-time systems, and your hardware debugging ability. In regulated fields like automotive or medical devices, familiarity with safety standards matters more than any certificate.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business, psychology, communications or a related field. Courses in organizational behavior, survey design and data analysis help, since much of the job is measuring how employees feel and acting on the results.
First job

Most people start as an HR coordinator, people operations coordinator, office or workplace coordinator, or event coordinator. These roles teach onboarding logistics, HR systems, vendor management and how to plan events and programs for staff.
Own employee programs

Volunteer to run projects such as new hire orientation, an engagement survey, culture events or an office refresh. Employers want proof you can plan a program, measure results with survey data, work with leaders and improve things based on feedback.
Optional certification

No license is required for this work. Some people earn the SHRM-CP from the Society for Human Resource Management or the PHR from HRCI to show broad HR knowledge. These are optional, but they can help when moving from coordinator to manager.
Time it takes

It usually takes about three to six years after a degree. Most manager postings ask for several years in HR, people operations, workplace or event roles, plus a record of running employee programs from start to finish.
qa: Do you need a certification to be an employee experience manager?

No. There is no license or required certification for this work. Some people earn the SHRM-CP or PHR to show HR knowledge, and employers may see them as a plus. Experience running onboarding, engagement surveys, culture programs and events usually matters more than any credential.
How long does it take to become an employee experience manager?

Most people need a bachelor’s degree and then about three to six years of related work. A common path is starting as an HR, people operations, office or event coordinator, taking on employee programs, and moving into a manager role once you can show results from projects you led.

steps: Education

Most employee relations specialists hold a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business, psychology, labor relations or a related field. Courses in employment law, communication and conflict resolution help most. Some people come from a legal background, such as paralegal work or a law degree.
First job

The usual way in is an HR assistant, HR coordinator or HR generalist role, where you handle employee questions, policies and records. Some start in recruiting or payroll. Generalists who take on complaints and discipline cases often move into employee relations.
Employment law

The work rests on federal laws such as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act and the National Labor Relations Act, plus state laws. Most specialists learn them on the job and through employment law training.
Investigation training

Employers expect fair, well-documented workplace investigations. Many specialists take training from groups such as the Association of Workplace Investigators. In some states, outside investigators who are not attorneys need a private investigator license, but in-house HR staff usually do not.
HR certification

No license is required for in-house employee relations work. Many employers prefer an HR certification such as the SHRM-CP or SHRM-SCP from the Society for Human Resource Management, or the PHR or SPHR from the HR Certification Institute.
Time it takes

Most people spend about three to five years in general HR roles before becoming an employee relations specialist. Senior roles, such as managing investigations across a large company, often take several more years and deep knowledge of employment law.
qa: Do you need a certification to work in employee relations?

No certification is legally required. Many employers prefer one, most often the SHRM-CP or SHRM-SCP from the Society for Human Resource Management, or the PHR or SPHR from the HR Certification Institute. Training in workplace investigations also helps, since running fair investigations is a core part of the job.
How long does it take to become an employee relations specialist?

Usually about three to five years after a bachelor’s degree. Most people first work as an HR assistant, coordinator or generalist, handling policies, complaints and discipline. Once they have run investigations and know employment law well, they can move into a dedicated employee relations role. Larger employers may ask for more experience.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Start with a bachelor’s degree in any field. No major is required, but courses in writing, political science, economics, psychology or human resources help. Most law schools use the LSAT for admission, and some also accept the GRE.
Law school

Most employment lawyers earn a Juris Doctor (JD) from an ABA-accredited law school, usually three years full time. Take employment law, labor law, employment discrimination and contracts. Look for clinics or summer jobs with firms, legal aid groups or agencies that handle workplace claims.
Bar admission

Requirements vary by state. Most states require a bar exam, often the Uniform Bar Exam, and many also require the MPRE ethics exam and a character and fitness review. Wisconsin admits its own law graduates through diploma privilege. Experienced lawyers can often be admitted on motion or by transferring a UBE score.
First job

Most start as associates at law firms with labor and employment practices, representing employers or workers. Others begin at agencies such as the EEOC, the U.S. Department of Labor or state labor departments, or in judicial clerkships. In-house employment counsel roles usually go to lawyers with several years of experience.
Time it takes

Expect about seven years after high school: four years of college and three of law school, then the bar exam where your state requires one. Advising on staff in many countries usually takes several more years of practice and close work with local counsel abroad.
Optional certification

A few states, including Texas and Florida, offer board certification in labor and employment law for experienced lawyers. It is not required to practice, but it signals deep expertise to clients and employers.
qa: Do you need a law degree to be an employment lawyer?

Almost always. Most employment lawyers earn a JD from an ABA-accredited law school. A few states, including California, Virginia, Vermont and Washington, allow bar admission after supervised law-office study instead, but that path is rare. HR professionals can advise on workplace policy without a law degree, but they cannot give legal advice or represent clients.
How long does it take to become an employment lawyer?

Usually about seven years after high school: a four-year bachelor’s degree, three years of law school, and then bar admission, which in most states means passing a bar exam. Handling employment matters on your own, or advising on staff in many countries, typically takes several more years of practice.

steps: Education

Many employers ask for an associate or bachelor’s degree in information technology, computer science or a related field. Plenty of people get in without one by showing hands-on experience and certifications instead. There is no license for this work in any state.
Entry certifications

Most people start with CompTIA A+ to prove they can support hardware and operating systems. CompTIA Network+ and CompTIA Security+ often follow, since endpoint work touches networking, encryption and security policy.
First job

The usual way in is a help desk, desktop support or IT support technician role. There you image laptops, set up phones, reset accounts and learn how staff actually use their devices. Ask to help with device rollouts and patching to build relevant experience.
Platform skills

Next, learn a device management platform in depth, along with scripting such as PowerShell or shell scripts. Vendor certifications like Microsoft 365 Certified: Endpoint Administrator Associate are widely recognized. Employers often value proof that you have managed real devices at scale over any single credential.
Time it takes

Moving from a first support job to an endpoint or device management engineer role usually takes two to five years. Many people pass through a systems administrator or desktop engineer role along the way.
qa: Do you need a certification to become an endpoint engineer?

No certification is legally required, and there is no state license for this work. Still, many employers look for CompTIA A+ or Security+ and a vendor certification such as Microsoft 365 Certified: Endpoint Administrator Associate. Certifications help most early on, before you have a long record of managing devices at scale.
How long does it take to become an endpoint engineer?

Most people take two to five years. They usually start in help desk or desktop support, move into systems administration or desktop engineering, and then specialize in device management. A degree can shorten the path slightly, but hands-on experience rolling out, securing and patching company devices matters most to employers.

steps: Education

Most engagement managers hold a bachelor’s degree in business, economics, engineering, computer science or a field tied to the clients they serve. At large strategy consultancies, many also have an MBA, often earned after a few years of work experience.
First job

People usually start as an analyst, consultant, associate or project coordinator at a consultancy, agency or software vendor. Others come from account management, implementation or client services roles where they already work directly with customers.
Building client experience

Over several years you take on larger pieces of client work. You lead a workstream, guide junior staff, run client meetings and help shape proposals. Firms promote you once you can own scope, budget, timeline and the client relationship on your own.
Optional certification

No license, registration or exam is required for this work. Some engagement managers earn the PMP from the Project Management Institute (PMI), which requires documented project experience and an exam. Scrum or Agile certifications are common at software and IT services firms.
Time it takes

It usually takes five to ten years after a bachelor’s degree. At large strategy consultancies, people hired after an MBA often reach engagement manager in about two to three years. At vendors and agencies, promotion depends on client results more than on a set timeline.
qa: Do you need a certification to be an engagement manager?

No. There is no license or required exam for engagement managers in the US. Employers hire based on client delivery experience and a record of leading projects. Some people add the PMP from the Project Management Institute or an Agile certification to show project skills, but these are optional and more valued at IT and software firms than at strategy consultancies.
How long does it take to become an engagement manager?

Most people need five to ten years of work after a bachelor’s degree. They usually start as an analyst, consultant or project coordinator and move up by leading bigger parts of client projects. At large consulting firms, people who join after an MBA often reach engagement manager in about two to three years.

steps: Engineering degree program

Enroll in a bachelor’s program in an engineering field such as mechanical, electrical, civil, chemical or computer engineering. Many employers prefer programs accredited by ABET. Most internships require you to be a current student, so enrollment is the real entry ticket.
Core courses and projects

Finish the first one or two years of math, physics and intro engineering courses. Join a student design team, research lab or hands-on club. These projects give you something concrete to put on a resume before you have work experience.
Applying early

Many companies recruit in the fall for the following summer, often through campus career fairs and online portals. Prepare a one-page resume, list your GPA and projects, and practice technical interviews. Some schools also run formal co-op programs that alternate semesters of study and paid work.
Work authorization

No license or exam is required to be an engineering intern. You do need to be allowed to work in the US. International students on F-1 visas usually use CPT through their school. Some defense and government roles require US citizenship or a security clearance.
Time it takes

Most students land a first internship after their sophomore or junior year, so usually one to three years into college. Some get one after freshman year, especially with strong project experience. Many students complete two or three internships or co-op terms before graduating.
After the internship

A good internship often leads to a return offer for another term or a full-time job. After graduating, engineers in many fields take the FE exam to become an Engineer in Training, an early step toward a state PE license.
qa: Do you need a license to be an engineering intern?

No. Engineering interns work under the supervision of experienced engineers, so no license or certification is required. Employers mainly look for enrollment in an engineering degree program, relevant coursework and projects. A state PE license comes much later in a career and usually requires a degree, the FE and PE exams, and several years of supervised work.
When should you start applying for engineering internships?

Start in the fall of the school year before the summer you want to work. Many larger companies fill summer spots through fall career fairs and online applications, while smaller firms may hire into spring. Most students get their first internship after sophomore or junior year, but applying earlier builds interview practice and contacts.

steps: Education

Most engineering managers hold a bachelor’s degree in an engineering field or computer science, which usually takes four years. Some later earn a master’s degree in engineering management or an MBA, but employers rarely require one for a first management role.
Engineering experience

You first work as an engineer. Most people move into management after about five to ten years of hands-on engineering work. Teams want a manager who understands the technical work, can judge design choices, and has earned the trust of other engineers.
Leadership practice

Before the title, most people take on leadership tasks as a senior engineer or tech lead. They mentor newer engineers, run projects, help interview candidates, and plan work with other teams. This record is what employers look for when promoting or hiring a manager.
License or certification

There is no license to be an engineering manager. In fields like civil engineering, where engineering work for the public must be approved by a licensed engineer, a Professional Engineer (PE) license is often expected for senior roles. Rules for the PE license vary by state.
First job

The usual first role is a team lead or first-line engineering manager over a small team, often on the same team where you worked as an engineer. Internal promotion is more common than being hired from outside into a first management job.
qa: How long does it take to become an engineering manager?

Most people spend four years on a bachelor’s degree, then about five to ten years working as an engineer before their first management role. That adds up to roughly nine to fourteen years from the start of college. A career changer who still needs an engineering degree should expect the longer end of that range or more.
Do you need a license to be an engineering manager?

No license is required to manage engineers in most fields, including software. In some fields, such as civil engineering, employers often expect senior engineers and managers to hold a Professional Engineer (PE) license, because certain work must be approved by a licensed engineer. PE requirements vary by state.

steps: Education

No specific degree is required, but most employers prefer a bachelor’s degree. Common majors are business, marketing, communications and economics. A technical background helps when selling software, cloud or engineering products to IT and technical buyers.
First sales job

Most people start as a sales development representative (SDR) or business development representative (BDR). You book meetings through cold calls, email and social outreach. This role usually lasts one to two years and teaches prospecting, qualifying leads and handling rejection.
Closing smaller deals

Next comes an account executive role selling to small or mid-market companies. You own a quota, run demos, write proposals, negotiate and close. A steady record of hitting quota over several years is what enterprise hiring managers check first.
Sales training

There is no general license or exam. Many companies train reps in methods such as MEDDIC, MEDDPICC or Challenger and expect daily use of a CRM. Selling regulated products such as insurance or securities may require a state license or FINRA exams.
Time it takes

Reaching an enterprise role usually takes five or more years in sales. That typically includes one to two years in an SDR or BDR role and several years closing deals with smaller or mid-market customers.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an enterprise account executive?

A degree is not legally required, but most employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, communications or a related field. In practice, a proven record of meeting quota matters more than the major. Some people without degrees reach enterprise roles by starting as SDRs and moving up through strong results.
How long does it take to become an enterprise account executive?

It usually takes five or more years. Most people spend one to two years booking meetings as an SDR or BDR, then several years closing deals with small or mid-market companies. Enterprise roles go to reps who have consistently hit quota and can manage long deals with many decision makers.

steps: Education

Most enterprise architects hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information systems, engineering or business, and some add a master’s degree or MBA. No license is required. What matters most is broad knowledge of applications, data, infrastructure, security and how the business runs.
Technical career

Nobody starts as an enterprise architect. Most spend years as a software developer, systems analyst, infrastructure engineer or business analyst, learning how many systems work and connect. This hands-on experience is what makes their later plans realistic.
Solution architect

The usual step before enterprise architecture is a solution architect, technical architect or domain architect role, designing one system or area at a time. Here you learn to write architecture documents, compare options, estimate costs and win support from business leaders.
TOGAF and frameworks

Many employers ask for TOGAF certification from The Open Group, the best-known enterprise architecture framework. Some also value cloud architect certifications or knowledge of the Zachman Framework and ArchiMate modeling. Certification helps, but experience counts more.
Time it takes

Enterprise architects usually have ten or more years of experience across development, infrastructure or business analysis, including several years in architecture roles. The first TOGAF level can be passed after a few weeks of study, but the role itself comes only with experience.
qa: What certification do you need to be an enterprise architect?

No certification is legally required. The best known is TOGAF certification from The Open Group, which tests knowledge of the most widely used enterprise architecture framework, and many employers ask for it. Cloud architect certifications can also help. Employers still weigh experience most, usually ten or more years across development, infrastructure and architecture roles.
How long does it take to become an enterprise architect?

Usually ten years or more. Most enterprise architects first work as developers, systems analysts or infrastructure engineers, then spend several years as solution or technical architects before taking on the whole company’s systems. A four-year degree in computer science, information systems or business is the usual starting point, and TOGAF certification is common along the way.

steps: Education

Most engineers earn a bachelor’s degree in environmental, civil or chemical engineering, ideally from an ABET-accredited program. Scientists usually study environmental science, chemistry, biology or geology. A master’s degree helps for research, modeling and senior technical roles, but it is not required to start.
FE exam

Engineering students often take the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam near graduation. Passing it lets you register with your state as an engineer in training (EIT) or engineer intern. This is the first formal step toward a professional license.
Safety training

Jobs on contaminated or hazardous waste sites usually require 40-hour HAZWOPER training under OSHA rules, plus an 8-hour refresher each year. Employers often provide it after hiring. Field roles also call for comfort with sampling gear and long days outdoors.
First job

Most people start as a staff engineer, staff scientist or field technician at a consulting firm, utility or government agency. Early work includes collecting soil and water samples, logging data, drafting permit applications and helping design treatment systems under a licensed engineer.
PE license

To sign plans and lead projects, engineers seek a state Professional Engineer (PE) license. Most states require about four years of qualifying work under a PE, then passing the NCEES PE Environmental exam. Requirements vary by state. Scientists have no single license, though some states license geologists.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree and about four more years of supervised experience before a PE license, so roughly eight years in total. Scientists can work right after the degree and usually gain independence over two to five years.
qa: Do you need a license to be an environmental engineer?

You can start working without one, under the supervision of a licensed engineer. To approve designs, sign permit documents or offer services to the public, you need a state Professional Engineer (PE) license. Most states require a degree, the FE exam, about four years of experience and the PE Environmental exam. Rules vary by state.
How long does it take to become an environmental engineer?

An entry-level job usually follows a four-year bachelor’s degree in environmental, civil or chemical engineering. Becoming a licensed Professional Engineer typically takes about four more years of supervised work plus passing the FE and PE exams. In total, most people reach full licensure about eight years after starting college.

steps: Education

Most ERP specialists hold a bachelor’s degree in accounting, finance, information systems or business. Employers care most that you understand how accounting, purchasing, orders and inventory fit together. A degree is common but not strictly required if you can show strong hands-on system experience.
First job

Many people start in a role that uses the ERP every day, such as staff accountant, accounts payable or receivable clerk, inventory or supply chain analyst, or IT help desk. Becoming the team’s go-to power user for NetSuite or Oracle is a common way in.
Learn the system

Build skills in configuration, user roles and permissions, saved searches and reports, workflows, data imports and month-end close processes. Some specialists also learn SQL, and NetSuite admins often pick up SuiteScript, which is based on JavaScript, to handle customizations and integrations.
Vendor certification

No license is required for this work. Certifications are optional but valued. Oracle NetSuite offers exams such as SuiteFoundation, NetSuite Administrator and NetSuite ERP Consultant. Oracle also offers certifications for its Cloud ERP applications. Most people earn them after some real system experience.
Time it takes

Moving from a user role into a dedicated ERP administrator, analyst or specialist job usually takes two to four years. Taking part in an implementation, upgrade or system migration often speeds this up, because it shows you can handle setup, testing and training.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a NetSuite administrator?

No. There is no required license, and many admins learn on the job. Still, Oracle NetSuite certifications such as SuiteFoundation and NetSuite Administrator can help you stand out, especially without years of direct experience. Employers usually weigh hands-on work, like configuring roles, building saved searches and supporting month-end close, more heavily than a certificate alone.
How long does it take to become an ERP specialist?

It usually takes two to four years after starting in a related role. Most people first spend time in accounting, operations or IT using the ERP daily, then take on admin tasks and projects. Those with a degree in accounting or information systems, plus experience on an implementation project, often move into a specialist role faster.

steps: Education

A high school diploma or equivalent is usually enough. Some employers, especially banks, insurers and health plans, prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree in business, communications or a related field. No specific degree is required, and experience usually counts for more than schooling.
First job

Most people start as a customer service representative, call center agent, help desk agent or member services representative. Frontline work teaches you the products, the policies and the systems that complaint cases depend on. Escalations roles are rarely entry level.
Build a track record

Ask to take difficult calls, volunteer for tier 2 or team lead duties, and keep clean case notes in the ticketing or CRM system. Supervisors promote people who calm upset customers, follow cases to a fix and write clear summaries others can act on.
Learn the complaint rules

In regulated fields such as banking, insurance, health plans and utilities, formal complaints and grievances must follow set procedures, documentation standards and response deadlines. Rules differ by industry and often by state, so learn the ones your employer must meet. There is no license for this work itself.
Optional training

Short courses in de-escalation, conflict resolution and business writing help. Later in a career, some people earn the CCXP from the Customer Experience Professionals Association. These are optional, and most employers hire on proven experience instead.
Time it takes

Most people move into an escalations or complaints role after one to three years of frontline customer service. Those with strong results, good writing and knowledge of industry rules can move up faster, often through an internal promotion.
qa: Do you need a license or certification to be an escalations specialist?

No. There is no license for escalations or complaints work in the US, and no certification is required. Employers look for frontline customer service experience, calm handling of difficult cases and clear writing. In regulated industries like banking, insurance and health plans, you must follow complaint rules and deadlines, which you usually learn on the job.
How long does it take to become a complaints specialist?

It usually takes one to three years. Most people first work as customer service or call center representatives, then get promoted after showing they can resolve hard cases and document them well. Some employers hire directly into complaints roles when a candidate already has relevant experience in the same industry.

steps: Education

Most cost estimators have a bachelor’s degree in construction management, civil or mechanical engineering, quantity surveying or a related field. Project controls roles also hire from finance and business. Some estimators come up from the trades, using years of field experience instead of a degree.
First job

Common first jobs are assistant estimator, junior estimator, quantity takeoff technician, project engineer or project controls analyst. You start by measuring quantities from drawings, pricing materials and labor, and updating cost reports under a senior estimator.
Skills and tools

Estimators learn to read drawings and specifications, run quantity takeoffs, build cost databases and price risk. Project controls staff learn scheduling, earned value management and change order tracking. Most of this comes from on-the-job training with estimating and scheduling software.
Certification

No license is required. AACE International offers the CCP (Certified Cost Professional), CEP (Certified Estimating Professional) and PSP (Planning and Scheduling Professional). The American Society of Professional Estimators offers the CPE. The PMI-SP and PMP from the Project Management Institute are also common.
Government work

Estimators on federal and defense programs work with federal acquisition rules and earned value requirements. The International Cost Estimating and Analysis Association offers the CCEA for this field. Some defense roles also require US citizenship and a security clearance.
Time it takes

With a degree, most people start as an assistant estimator and become a full estimator in about two to five years. Chief estimator and project controls manager roles usually take eight or more years. Certifications such as the CCP require years of experience.
qa: What certification is best for a cost estimator?

No certification is required, but several are respected. AACE International offers the CCP (Certified Cost Professional) and CEP (Certified Estimating Professional). The American Society of Professional Estimators offers the CPE. Schedulers often earn the PSP from AACE or the PMI-SP from the Project Management Institute. Most of these require work experience before the exam.
How long does it take to become a cost estimator?

Usually two to five years after starting as an assistant estimator or project engineer. Most estimators first earn a bachelor’s degree in construction management or engineering, though some move up from the trades. Senior estimator and project controls manager roles typically take eight or more years of experience.

steps: Education

Installers usually start with a high school diploma and an electrical apprenticeship or trade school. Field service technicians often have an associate degree or certificate in electrical or electronics technology. Engineers who design charging sites usually hold a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering.
Electrician license

Installing chargers is electrical work, so most states and cities require a licensed electrician and a permit. Becoming a journeyman electrician usually means a four- to five-year apprenticeship and an exam on the National Electrical Code, which has an article on EV charging equipment.
EVITP certification

The Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Training Program offers EVITP certification for licensed electricians. Under federal NEVI program rules, electricians installing or maintaining chargers paid for with those funds need EVITP certification or training through a registered apprenticeship that covers EV chargers.
First job

Common ways in are electrician’s apprentice, EV charger field service technician, commissioning technician or project coordinator at an installer or charging network. Field technicians troubleshoot chargers, swap parts and work with network support teams.
Safety and network skills

Technicians train in electrical safety under NFPA 70E, lockout and tagout, and work on high-voltage DC fast chargers. Many learn how chargers talk to networks through OCPP, the Open Charge Point Protocol. Engineers who stamp site designs need a state PE license.
Time it takes

A field service technician can often start within months after a technical certificate. Becoming a licensed electrician who can install chargers takes four to five years. Electrical engineers need four years for a degree, and about four more years of experience for a PE license.
qa: Do you need a license to install EV chargers?

In most places, yes. Hardwired chargers are electrical work, so most states and cities require a licensed electrician and a permit. Chargers paid for with federal NEVI funds must be installed by electricians with EVITP certification or registered apprenticeship training that covers EV chargers. Rules vary by state, so check local licensing requirements.
What certification do you need for EV charging work?

The best-known one is EVITP certification from the Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Training Program, which is open to licensed electricians and required on federally funded NEVI projects unless the electrician trained through a qualifying registered apprenticeship. Technicians also take electrical safety training under NFPA 70E. Engineers who design sites may need a state PE license.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in hospitality, event management, marketing, communications or business. No single degree is required. A related degree plus hands-on event work counts for more than the major itself.
Hands-on experience

Build experience early by volunteering at conferences, helping run campus or nonprofit events, or working at a hotel or venue. Employers look for proof that you have handled budgets, vendors, schedules, registration and on-site problems.
First job

The usual way in is as an event coordinator, event assistant, or meeting planner assistant. Others start in hotel catering or conference sales, exhibitor services, or marketing roles that support trade shows.
Time it takes
There is no license or required apprenticeship. Moving from coordinator to events manager usually takes about three to five years of steady work running larger events and more of the budget.
Optional certification

Certification is voluntary but valued. The Certified Meeting Professional (CMP) from the Events Industry Council requires several years of industry work before you can sit the exam. Trade-show staff may pursue the Certified in Exhibition Management (CEM) from IAEE.
qa: Do you need a license to be an events manager?

No. Events managers in the US do not need a state license. Some venues or events may need permits, such as for alcohol or large gatherings, but those are usually handled per event. Many managers earn the voluntary CMP credential to show experience and stand out to employers.
How long does it take to become an events manager?

Most people spend four years on a bachelor’s degree, then about three to five years as an event coordinator or assistant before moving up to manager. People who start in hotel sales, catering or marketing can move over sooner if they already handle event budgets and vendors.

steps: Background

There is no standard degree or license for exchange operations. People come from finance, economics, computer science, business or other fields. What matters is understanding how crypto moves on chain, how payments settle and how trading venues work. Expect a background check, since exchanges hold customer money.
First job

Common first jobs are customer support agent, KYC analyst, operations analyst, payments operations specialist or transaction monitoring analyst at an exchange, broker or payments firm. Experience in bank operations, payments or anti-money laundering work also carries over.
Rules to learn

Exchanges serving US customers register with FinCEN as money services businesses and hold state money transmitter licenses, plus a BitLicense or trust charter in New York. Staff learn the Bank Secrecy Act, KYC, OFAC sanctions screening and the Travel Rule. Individual employees do not need a license.
Certification

Certification is optional but valued in compliance work. The Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialist (CAMS) from ACAMS is the most common. Fraud teams may earn the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential. Blockchain analytics vendors also offer product certifications, usually paid for by the employer.
Time it takes

Entry roles can start within weeks. Moving from support or KYC into listings, market surveillance or treasury operations usually takes one to three years. Senior roles expect deep knowledge of wallets, chains and settlement, and experience handling incidents.
qa: Do you need a license to work at a crypto exchange?

Individual employees usually do not need a license. The exchange itself must register with FinCEN as a money services business and hold state money transmitter licenses, plus a BitLicense or trust charter in New York. Employees are usually screened with background checks and trained in anti-money laundering and sanctions rules.
Can you work in crypto exchange operations without experience?

Yes. Many people start in customer support, KYC review or operations analyst roles, which train new hires on the job. Knowing how wallets, blockchain transactions and trading work helps a lot. Experience in banking, payments or anti-money laundering compliance also transfers well, and the CAMS certification can strengthen a compliance application.

steps: Education

A high school diploma is the usual minimum for administrative assistant jobs. Many people take business or office administration courses at a community college. Executive assistant roles supporting senior leaders often prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree, commonly in business, communications or a related field.
Office and software skills

Learn fast, accurate typing, professional email writing, and calendar and travel booking. Get comfortable with Microsoft Office or Google Workspace, especially Word, Excel and Outlook. The Microsoft Office Specialist (MOS) certification is an optional way to prove these skills to employers.
First job

Most people start as a receptionist, office assistant, front desk coordinator or entry-level administrative assistant. These roles teach phones, scheduling, filing and handling visitors. Temporary staffing work is another common way in and can lead to a permanent offer.
Optional certification

No state license is required to work as an administrative or executive assistant. The International Association of Administrative Professionals (IAAP) offers the Certified Administrative Professional (CAP), which requires work experience and passing an exam. It is optional, but some employers value it for senior roles.
Time it takes

An entry-level administrative job can be reached within a few months of building basic office skills. Moving up to executive assistant usually takes three to five years of experience supporting managers, showing discretion with confidential information and handling complex calendars.
Executive assistant role

Many first support one manager or a small team, then move to supporting a director or executive. At this level the work adds managing priorities, preparing meeting materials, coordinating travel across time zones and acting as the executive’s main point of contact.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an executive assistant?

Not always. Many administrative assistant jobs ask only for a high school diploma plus office skills. Executive assistant roles supporting senior leaders often prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree, but several years of strong administrative experience can substitute at many employers. No license is required in any state.
How long does it take to become an executive assistant?

Most people spend about three to five years in administrative roles before becoming an executive assistant. They usually start as a receptionist, office assistant or administrative assistant, then take on more scheduling, travel and confidential work. Optional credentials such as the IAAP’s Certified Administrative Professional (CAP) can help when applying for senior roles.

steps: Education

Most executive and business recruiters hold a bachelor’s degree, often in business, human resources, psychology or communications. No single major is required. Firms that fill finance, legal or sales roles also value a degree or work history in that field, because it helps you judge candidates and talk credibly with hiring leaders.
First job

The usual way in is a research associate, sourcer or recruiting coordinator role at a search firm, or a contingency recruiter job at a staffing agency. You build candidate lists, screen résumés, schedule interviews and learn to cold call. Some people instead switch in after years in sales, finance or law.
Licensing

Individual recruiters generally need no license. A few states regulate employment agencies, especially those charging fees to job seekers, so requirements vary by state. Since most executive search firms are paid by the employer, recruiters there rarely need any state license of their own.
Optional certifications

Certifications are optional but can help early on. Options include the Certified Personnel Consultant (CPC) from the National Association of Personnel Services, and SHRM-CP or PHR credentials for those working closer to human resources. Most employers care more about your placement record than about any credential.
Moving into executive search

After proving you can source, assess and close candidates, you move up to associate, then principal or senior recruiter. Leading searches for directors, vice presidents and C-suite roles depends on a network of senior contacts and a record of completed placements in one industry or function.
Time it takes

Getting a first recruiting job can take a few months after school. Running business-level searches usually takes one to three years. Leading true executive searches on your own often takes five or more years of combined recruiting and industry experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be an executive recruiter?

Usually not. Individual recruiters do not need a personal license in most of the US. A few states regulate employment agencies, mainly those that charge fees to job seekers, so rules vary by state. Executive search firms are normally paid by the hiring company. Optional credentials such as the CPC exist, but employers mostly judge you on your placements.
How do you become an executive recruiter with no experience?

Start in an entry-level role such as sourcer, research associate or recruiting coordinator at a search firm or staffing agency. Learn to build candidate lists, screen people and handle cold calls. Sales experience helps because the work involves selling to clients and candidates. After a few years of steady placements, you can move into leading senior-level searches.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in statistics, economics, data science, mathematics, computer science or quantitative psychology. Larger tech employers often prefer a master’s or PhD for senior roles, especially in economics or statistics, because the work leans on causal inference and experimental design.
Statistics and tools

Learn hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, power analysis and sample size, multiple comparisons, and common pitfalls like peeking and novelty effects. Build working skill in SQL plus Python or R. Methods for when randomizing is not possible, such as difference-in-differences, also help.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in the US. Some testing software vendors offer their own certificates, but employers mainly judge candidates on statistical skill, coding tests and how well they explain a past experiment.
Portfolio of tests

Show a few analyses from start to finish. Write a hypothesis, choose a metric, calculate sample size, analyze the results and explain whether the change caused the effect. Public datasets, class projects or tests run on a small website all work.
First job

The usual way in is a related analyst role, such as data analyst, product analyst, marketing analyst or conversion rate optimization analyst. People take on A/B test analysis there, then move into a dedicated experimentation or causal inference role.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually one to three years in an analyst role before being hired mainly to run experiments. A graduate degree can shorten the work experience needed but adds one to six years of study.
qa: Do you need a license to run A/B tests?

No. There is no license, certification or state requirement to run A/B tests or work as an experimentation specialist in the US. Employers look for a quantitative degree, solid statistics, SQL and Python or R skills, and proof that you can design a test and explain its results clearly.
How long does it take to become an experimentation specialist?

Most people need about five to seven years in total. That usually means a four-year degree in a quantitative field, then one to three years as a data, product or marketing analyst analyzing tests. Those with a master’s or PhD in statistics or economics sometimes move straight into experimentation roles.

steps: High school basics

Most employers want a high school diploma or equivalent. Shop classes, math, geometry and blueprint reading help most. You should be comfortable with a tape measure, fractions and basic shop safety before you apply.
Technical training

Many people take a welding or metal fabrication certificate at a community college or technical school. This often takes several months to a year. An associate degree takes about two years. Others skip school and learn on the job from a helper role.
Apprenticeship option

Some people enter through a registered apprenticeship as a welder, ironworker or sheet metal worker. You earn pay while you learn and take classroom hours alongside shop work. Length varies by trade and program. Sheet metal worker apprenticeships commonly run four to five years.
Certifications and local rules

Employers often ask for welding certifications tested to a code such as AWS D1.1 for structural steel. Most states have no fabricator license, but some places regulate welders. Oklahoma licenses welders, and cities such as New York and Los Angeles require local certification for structural welding. Check your state and city rules.
First job

The usual first job is fabrication helper, shop helper or production welder. You run saws, shears, press brakes and grinders and prep parts for welding. With experience you move up to layout, fitting and building full assemblies from drawings.
Time it takes

Many people work as entry-level fabricators within a year of starting training. Becoming a skilled, independent fabrication technician who reads complex drawings and handles several processes usually takes a few years of shop experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a fabrication technician?

In most of the US, no license is needed to work in a fabrication shop. Some places do regulate welding. Oklahoma licenses welders, and cities such as New York and Los Angeles require local welder certification for structural welding. Employers also commonly expect welding certifications tested to codes like AWS D1.1. Requirements vary by state and city, so check local rules.
How long does it take to become a fabrication technician?

A welding or fabrication certificate often takes several months to a year, and an associate degree about two years. Many people start as helpers and learn on the job instead. Registered apprenticeships take longer, and sheet metal worker programs commonly run four to five years. Reaching a skilled, independent level usually takes a few years of shop work.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. Many facilities managers hold a bachelor’s degree in facility management, business, construction management or engineering. Others start in a skilled trade such as HVAC, electrical or general maintenance and move into management after years on the job.
First job

Common ways in are facilities coordinator, assistant facilities manager, maintenance technician, building engineer or office services roles. These jobs teach work orders, vendor management, preventive maintenance, safety rules and handling office moves.
No state license

Facilities managers generally do not need a state license. Specific tasks may require credentialed workers, such as technicians who hold EPA Section 608 certification for refrigerant work or licensed electricians. Managers usually hire and oversee these people rather than hold the credentials themselves.
Professional certifications

Certifications are optional but many employers value them. IFMA offers the Facility Management Professional (FMP), the Certified Facility Manager (CFM), which requires work experience, and the Sustainability Facility Professional (SFP). BOMI International offers the Facilities Management Administrator (FMA) designation.
Time it takes

Most people spend several years in coordinator, technician or assistant roles before managing a building or site on their own. A move into a full facilities manager role often takes three to five years or more, depending on prior trade or degree experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a facilities manager?

Usually not. There is no general state license for facilities managers. Some work they oversee, such as electrical, plumbing or refrigerant work, must be done by people with the right license or certification, and rules vary by state and city. Many managers earn voluntary certifications such as IFMA’s FMP or CFM to show their skills.
How long does it take to become a facilities manager?

It usually takes several years. People often start as a facilities coordinator, maintenance technician or building engineer and learn budgets, vendors and safety on the job. With a related bachelor’s degree or a strong trade background, many reach a facilities manager role in about three to five years, though larger sites often expect more experience.

steps: Education
