Most fellowships require at least a bachelor’s degree. Public service and policy fellowships often target recent graduates or graduate students. Research fellowships, such as postdoctoral positions, usually require a completed PhD, MD or similar doctoral degree in the field.
Relevant experience

Programs look for proof you can do the work. Build a record through internships, research assistant roles, volunteering, campus leadership or published work. A strong writing sample or research record often matters as much as grades.
Application package

Expect to submit a résumé or CV, a personal statement, letters of recommendation and sometimes a writing sample or research proposal. Deadlines often fall six to twelve months before the start date, and finalists usually interview.
Eligibility checks

There is no license or national exam for fellows. Each program sets its own rules instead. Some require US citizenship, a degree earned within a set number of years, or the ability to pass a background check or security clearance for government work.
Time it takes

Getting ready usually takes the length of your degree plus one application cycle of about a year. The fellowship itself is fixed-term, most often one to two years, though some research fellowships run up to three years.
First job

The fellowship is often the first real job in the field. Many fellows came in from an internship or assistant role, and many move afterward into a full-time staff, research or government position, sometimes with the host organization.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a fellow?

Almost always. Most public service and policy fellowships ask for at least a bachelor’s degree, and many favor recent graduates or graduate students. Research fellowships, such as postdoctoral positions, usually require a doctoral degree. A few community or arts fellowships weigh experience over degrees, so check each program’s eligibility rules.
How long does a fellowship last?

Most fellowships last one to two years, and some research fellowships run up to three years. The end date is set when you start. Applying usually takes several months, because deadlines often come six to twelve months before the program begins, so plan for about a year from application to start.

steps: Education

Most fiber and telecom technician jobs require a high school diploma or GED and a valid driver’s license. Some people take a community college or technical school program in telecommunications, electronics or network cabling, which can take a few months to two years.
First job

Common first jobs are installer helper, cable installer, fiber splicer trainee or tower ground hand. You pull cable, place conduit, mount equipment and learn to splice, terminate and test fiber under an experienced technician.
Certification

No national license is required, but many employers value certifications. The Fiber Optic Association offers the CFOT (Certified Fiber Optic Technician), ETA International offers fiber optics installer certifications, and BICSI offers installer and technician credentials for structured cabling.
Tower and safety training

Tower climbers complete fall protection and climber rescue training before climbing, and many also train in RF radiation safety. Technicians working near power lines, in trenches or in confined spaces get OSHA safety training. Some employers require an OSHA 10-hour card.
State and local rules

Some states and cities require a low-voltage or limited-energy license for cabling work, and rules vary widely. Technicians who drive large bucket or splicing trucks may need a commercial driver’s license. Work on government networks may require a background check.
Time it takes

You can usually start as a helper within weeks. Becoming a skilled fiber splicer or tower technician typically takes one to three years of on-the-job training. Senior roles, such as lead technician or BICSI RCDD designer, take several more years.
qa: Can you become a fiber technician without experience?

Yes. Many employers hire helpers and trainees with a high school diploma, a clean driving record and comfort working outdoors and at heights, then train them on the job. A short fiber optics course and a certification such as the CFOT from the Fiber Optic Association can help you get hired faster.
What certification do you need to be a fiber optic technician?

No single certification is required nationally. Common choices are the CFOT (Certified Fiber Optic Technician) from the Fiber Optic Association, fiber optics installer certifications from ETA International, and installer credentials from BICSI. Some states and cities also require a low-voltage license for cabling work, and tower climbers need fall protection and rescue training.

steps: Education

Most field marketing managers hold a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications or a related field. Coursework in consumer behavior, digital marketing, analytics and public speaking helps. Some people come from sales or event backgrounds without a marketing degree and learn on the job.
First job

The usual way in is an entry-level role such as marketing coordinator, event coordinator, field marketing specialist or sales development representative. These jobs teach event logistics, lead follow-up, budgeting and how to work alongside account executives in a territory.
Build field experience

Employers want proof you can plan and run local events, trade shows and regional campaigns, then show results in pipeline or sales. Learn the CRM and marketing automation tools sales teams use, and track the leads and revenue your programs produce.
Optional certifications

No license or exam is required. Some people add the Certified Meeting Professional (CMP) from the Events Industry Council or the American Marketing Association’s Professional Certified Marketer (PCM) to show event or marketing knowledge, but employers rarely require either.
Time it takes

Most people reach a field marketing manager title after about three to six years of marketing, events or sales experience following college. Moving up from specialist to manager usually depends on owning a region’s program budget and showing measurable results.
qa: Do you need a license to be a field marketing manager?

No. There is no state or federal license for field marketing work in the US. Employers look for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business or communications plus several years of event, campaign or sales support experience. Optional credentials like the CMP or the AMA’s PCM can help, but they are not required.
How long does it take to become a field marketing manager?

Usually about seven to ten years in total: four years for a bachelor’s degree, then three to six years in roles like marketing coordinator, event coordinator or field marketing specialist. People who start in sales development and move into marketing can sometimes move faster if they already know a territory and its customers.

steps: Education

Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing, communications or a field tied to the product, such as biology for medical sales. Others hire with a high school diploma plus a solid record in retail, customer service or route sales, especially for home services and consumer products.
Driver’s license and vehicle

Most field sales jobs require a valid driver’s license and a clean driving record, because you spend much of the day driving between customers. Employers often check your motor vehicle record. Some also expect you to use your own reliable car and carry auto insurance.
Product licenses if needed

Most field sales work needs no license. The exceptions depend on what you sell. Insurance sales require a state producer license. Selling securities requires FINRA exams such as the SIE and Series 6 or Series 7. Door-to-door sellers may need a local solicitor permit, and rules vary by city and state.
First job

Many people start in inside sales, as a sales development representative, in retail sales or in customer service. These roles teach prospecting, handling objections and tracking deals in a CRM, which hiring managers want to see before trusting you with your own territory.
Company training

Once hired, expect company training on the product, pricing and sales process, often followed by ride-alongs with an experienced rep. Medical device reps may also need hospital vendor credentialing, such as background checks and proof of vaccinations, before they can visit facilities.
Time it takes

With a degree or prior sales experience, you can often land a field role right away. Coming from an unrelated job, people usually spend one to two years in inside sales or retail first. New reps typically need several months to a year to build a steady pipeline.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a field sales representative?

Not always. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree, and technical or medical sales often expect one. Plenty of companies, especially in home services, consumer goods and route sales, hire people with a high school diploma who can show strong results in retail, customer service or inside sales.
Do you need a license to be a field sales representative?

Usually not. Most field sales jobs only require a valid driver’s license. You need a state producer license to sell insurance and must pass FINRA exams, such as the SIE and Series 6 or 7, to sell securities. Some cities and states also require permits for door-to-door selling, so check local rules.

steps: Education

Most employers want a high school diploma plus technical training. Common routes are a certificate or associate degree in electronics, electromechanical technology, industrial maintenance, HVAC or a similar field. Military training on equipment repair is also widely accepted.
First job

Many people start as a bench technician, installer, maintenance technician or helper to a senior field tech. This is where you learn troubleshooting, reading schematics and working safely around electrical, mechanical and pressurized systems.
Factory training

Once hired, you usually go through the manufacturer’s or employer’s own training on the specific equipment you will service. This often mixes classroom sessions with supervised visits alongside an experienced technician before you handle customer sites alone.
Licenses and certifications

There is no single license for field service work. Some equipment brings its own rules. Handling refrigerants requires EPA Section 608 certification, and some electrical work requires a state or local license, which varies by state. A valid driver’s license and clean driving record are usually expected.
Time it takes

Expect about one to two years of school or equivalent training. Then plan on another one to three years of hands-on experience before you work independently on complex equipment and travel to customer sites on your own.
qa: Do you need a license to be a field service technician?

Usually not for the job itself. The license depends on the equipment. Working with refrigerants requires EPA Section 608 certification, and some electrical or HVAC work needs a state or local license, which varies by state. Most employers also require a valid driver’s license, since the work means driving to customer sites.
How long does it take to become a field service technician?

Most people take one to two years for a certificate, an associate degree or military technical training. After that, it usually takes another one to three years in a related role, such as bench technician or installer, plus employer training on specific equipment, before working independently in the field.

steps: Education

Most finance managers hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting, economics or business administration. Useful courses include financial accounting, corporate finance, statistics and spreadsheet modeling. Employers rarely hire into this role without a four-year degree.
First job

People usually start as a financial analyst, staff accountant, budget analyst or junior auditor. These roles teach how to build budgets, prepare forecasts, close the books, explain variances and write reports for managers.
Optional certifications

No license is required to work as a finance manager. Many people still earn a credential to stand out. Common choices are the CPA, licensed by each state with requirements that vary by state, the CMA from the IMA, and the CFA from the CFA Institute.
Graduate degree
An MBA or a master’s degree in finance or accounting is not required, but larger employers often prefer it for management roles. Many people earn one part time while they keep working.
Moving into management

After several years, analysts move up to senior analyst, FP&A lead or accounting supervisor. Owning a full budget cycle, presenting to leadership and supervising a small team are the usual steps before a finance manager title.
Time it takes

Plan on four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually five or more years of finance or accounting work. That adds up to about nine years or longer. People at small companies sometimes move up sooner.
qa: Do you need a license to be a finance manager?

No. There is no state license for finance managers in the US. A CPA license is only required for certain public accounting work, such as signing audit opinions, and its rules vary by state. Many finance managers still choose to earn the CPA, CMA or CFA because employers value them.
How long does it take to become a finance manager?

Most people spend four years earning a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting or a related field, then work usually five or more years as an analyst or accountant. That makes about nine years or longer in total. A graduate degree can add time, while smaller companies may promote people faster.

steps: Education

Most FP&A analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting, economics or business. Employers look for coursework in financial accounting, corporate finance and statistics. A degree in a related field such as math or engineering can also work if you add accounting and finance classes.
Skills to build

Learn Excel well: formulas, pivot tables and building a three-statement financial model. Practice budgeting, forecasting and variance analysis, which means explaining why actual results differ from the plan. Many teams also use SQL, business intelligence tools or planning software.
Internship

A finance or accounting internship during college is the most common way to get an entry-level offer. Internships give you real budgeting and reporting work to point to, and many companies hire their interns into full-time analyst roles.
First job

The usual entry point is a junior or entry-level financial analyst role, a corporate finance rotational program, or a staff accountant job. Many people move into FP&A after a year or two in accounting, audit or a related finance role.
Certifications

No license is required for FP&A work. Optional credentials can help with promotion: the Certified Corporate FP&A Professional (FPAC) from the Association for Financial Professionals, the Certified Management Accountant (CMA) from the IMA, or a CPA for those coming from accounting. The CFA fits investment roles more than budgeting.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then an entry-level analyst job right after graduation. Moving up to senior analyst usually takes two to four years. Some people later earn an MBA to move into FP&A manager or finance leadership roles.
qa: Do you need a license to be a financial analyst?

No license is needed for corporate FP&A work like budgeting and forecasting. FINRA licenses such as the Series 7 apply to people who sell securities or publish investment research, not to in-house planning roles. Many analysts choose optional certifications like the FPAC, CMA or CPA to strengthen their resume and qualify for promotion.
How long does it take to become a financial analyst?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting or economics, then start as an entry-level analyst right after graduating. An internship during college makes that first job much easier to land. Reaching a senior analyst title usually takes another two to four years of experience.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in accounting. Key courses include intermediate and advanced accounting, auditing and tax. Many students add a master’s in accounting or extra credits to reach the education hours most states require for a CPA license.
CPA exam

Employers in this field strongly prefer a CPA. The Uniform CPA Exam has three core sections, including Financial Accounting and Reporting, plus one discipline section. You must pass all four within a set window. Each state board of accountancy sets its own eligibility rules.
Supervised experience

Most states require one to two years of accounting experience verified by a licensed CPA before granting the license. Many states also require an ethics exam. Education and experience rules vary by state, and some now accept 120 credit hours paired with more work experience.
First job

Many people start as staff auditors at a public accounting firm, reviewing other companies’ financial statements. Others start as staff accountants handling month-end close. Audit experience is especially valued because it builds deep knowledge of US GAAP and how statements are tested.
Move into reporting

After a few years, people move into financial reporting, SEC reporting or technical accounting roles. The work means applying US GAAP through the FASB Accounting Standards Codification, writing memos on unusual transactions and, at public companies, preparing 10-K and 10-Q filings.
Time it takes

Expect about four to five years of college, then usually two to four years in audit or general accounting before a dedicated financial reporting role. Earning the CPA along the way often shortens that path.
qa: Do you need a CPA to be a financial reporting accountant?

No law requires a CPA license to prepare a company’s own financial statements. A license is only required for public accounting work such as signing audit opinions. Still, many employers list the CPA as required or preferred for financial reporting, SEC reporting and technical accounting roles, and it often speeds promotion to manager and controller levels.
How long does it take to become a financial reporting accountant?

It usually takes six to nine years in total. That includes four to five years of college to earn an accounting degree and meet CPA education hours, then two to four years of work, often in public accounting audit, before moving into a dedicated financial reporting role. Passing the CPA exam during this time is common.

steps: Education

Firefighters and emergency responders usually need a high school diploma or GED and a valid driver’s license. Fire alarm and sprinkler technicians often take technical courses. Fire protection engineers earn a bachelor’s degree in fire protection, mechanical or civil engineering.
EMT and firefighter certification

Most fire departments and industrial emergency teams require EMT certification, often through the National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians exam, and state Firefighter I and II certification, often accredited by IFSAC or the Pro Board. Hiring usually includes a physical ability test such as the CPAT.
Fire academy

Career firefighters complete a fire academy, which usually lasts several months and covers firefighting, rescue, hazardous materials and medical response. Industrial emergency teams train to OSHA rules for fire brigades and for hazardous waste operations and emergency response.
Technician certification

Fire alarm and sprinkler inspection technicians often earn NICET certification in fire alarm systems or water-based systems, which has four levels. Some states and cities require contractors to employ NICET-certified staff. Sprinkler fitters typically complete a four- to five-year apprenticeship.
Inspector and engineer

Fire inspectors often earn certification from NFPA or the International Code Council. Fire protection engineers can take the NCEES PE Fire Protection exam after passing the FE exam and gaining experience, and need a state PE license to sign designs.
Time it takes

Career firefighters usually spend six months to two years earning EMT and firefighter certifications and getting through a hiring process. Alarm and sprinkler technicians reach NICET Level II in a few years. Engineers usually need about four years after their degree for a PE license.
qa: How long does it take to become a firefighter?

Usually six months to two years. Most candidates earn EMT certification, which takes a few months, then pass written and physical ability tests and a background check. Once hired, they attend a fire academy lasting several months and earn state Firefighter I and II certification. Competitive departments may take longer to hire.
What certification do you need for fire alarm and sprinkler work?

Many employers and some states expect NICET certification, which has four levels in areas such as fire alarm systems and inspection and testing of water-based systems. Licensing for fire alarm and sprinkler contractors varies by state. Sprinkler fitters usually complete a four- to five-year apprenticeship, and fire protection engineers need a state PE license to sign designs.

steps: Education

Most firmware engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer engineering, electrical engineering, or computer science. Useful courses cover C programming, digital logic, computer architecture, operating systems, and circuits. Some employers accept an electronics technology degree plus strong hands-on experience, but a four-year engineering degree is the usual route.
Hands-on projects

Build projects on microcontroller boards. Write drivers for sensors, use timers and interrupts, and talk to chips over I2C, SPI, and UART. Learn to debug with a JTAG probe, logic analyzer, and oscilloscope. A public code repository showing this work helps when you apply.
Internships

Many people land a co-op or internship in embedded software, hardware testing, or electronics during college. Employers value time spent bringing up real boards and fixing bugs on hardware, and an internship often turns into a full-time offer.
No license required

There is no state license or required exam for firmware engineers. Work in regulated fields asks you to follow standards such as DO-178C for avionics, ISO 26262 for cars, or IEC 62304 for medical devices. Defense jobs may require a US security clearance, which the employer sponsors.
First job

The usual first role is junior or associate firmware engineer, or embedded software engineer. Some start as test engineers, hardware validation engineers, or electronics technicians and move into firmware after learning the product and showing they can write reliable low-level code.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, often with one or more internships along the way. Moving from entry level to working independently on board bring-up, bootloaders, and drivers usually takes another two to four years on the job.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a firmware engineer?

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer engineering, electrical engineering, or computer science. A few hire people without one if they show strong skills in C, microcontrollers, and hardware debugging through projects or past work. Starting as a test or electronics technician and moving into firmware is another path some people take.
How long does it take to become a firmware engineer?

Usually about four years to finish a related bachelor’s degree, which qualifies you for entry-level firmware or embedded software jobs. Internships during school make the first job easier to get. Becoming a fully independent firmware engineer who can bring up new boards and own a product’s code typically takes another two to four years.

steps: Education

Many employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, logistics, supply chain management or a related field. Others hire without a degree when a person has years of hands-on experience as a vehicle technician, driver or dispatcher. Automotive technology training or an associate degree can also help.
First job

Most people start as a fleet coordinator, dispatcher, fleet analyst, transportation coordinator or vehicle maintenance technician. These roles teach maintenance scheduling, vehicle records, fuel tracking, working with vendors and the fleet software companies use to manage their vehicles.
Safety and compliance

No license is required to work as a fleet manager. If the fleet includes commercial vehicles, you must learn FMCSA rules on driver qualification, hours of service, drug and alcohol testing and vehicle inspections. Some employers prefer a manager who holds or once held a CDL.
Optional certification

Certification is not required but is valued by many employers. NAFA Fleet Management Association offers the Certified Automotive Fleet Manager (CAFM) and Certified Automotive Fleet Specialist (CAFS). Both involve passing exams in areas such as asset management, maintenance, finance and risk.
Time it takes

With a bachelor’s degree, plan on about four years of school and then usually two to five years in coordinator, analyst or technician roles before managing a fleet. Without a degree, the climb from technician or driver often takes longer. Small fleets may promote sooner.
qa: Do you need a license to be a fleet manager?

No state or federal license is required to be a fleet manager. You only need a CDL if you personally drive certain commercial vehicles. Employers with commercial fleets do expect you to know FMCSA safety rules. Voluntary certifications such as NAFA’s CAFM or CAFS can help you stand out.
How long does it take to become a fleet manager?

For most people it takes several years. A bachelor’s degree usually takes four years, and graduates then typically spend two to five years as a fleet coordinator, dispatcher or analyst before moving up. People who start as technicians or drivers without a degree often need more years of experience before being promoted.

steps: Education

Most flight software engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, computer engineering, electrical engineering or aerospace engineering. Useful courses include embedded systems, operating systems, control theory, digital logic and real-time programming. A master’s degree helps for guidance, navigation and control work but is not required for most roles.
Embedded skills and projects

Learn C and C++ well, plus real-time operating systems, microcontrollers, serial buses and Linux. Student rocketry, CubeSat and drone autopilot teams give hands-on flight code experience. Employers often ask about these projects in interviews.
Internships

Internships or co-ops at aerospace, defense, space or drone companies are a common way in. Many entry-level hires come from intern pools, so applying during school, often starting junior year or earlier, matters.
Citizenship and clearance

Because of ITAR export rules, many flight software jobs are open only to US persons, such as citizens and permanent residents. Defense and some government programs also require a security clearance, which the employer sponsors after hiring and which requires US citizenship.
Standards on the job

There is no license for this work. Instead, you learn the process standards your project follows, such as DO-178C for software on FAA-certified aircraft or NASA’s NPR 7150.2 for NASA missions. Code reviews, requirements tracing and heavy testing are part of daily work.
First job

Typical first jobs are embedded software engineer, flight software test engineer or hardware-in-the-loop test engineer. With a four-year degree and a few years of experience, engineers usually move to owning flight code for a subsystem.
qa: Do you need a license to be a flight software engineer?

No. There is no state or federal license for flight software engineers. Employers look for a relevant engineering or computer science degree and embedded programming skills. Work on certified aircraft must follow DO-178C, and NASA projects follow NPR 7150.2, but these are process standards you learn on the job, not personal licenses. Many roles do require US person status or a security clearance.
How long does it take to become a flight software engineer?

Usually about four years for a bachelor’s degree, often with one or more internships along the way. Many graduates are hired straight into entry-level flight software or test roles. Taking real responsibility for flight code on a subsystem typically comes after two to five years of experience, depending on the employer and the program.

steps: Requirements

Food service jobs usually need no diploma or experience. Many employers hire teens, though federal and state child labor laws limit the hours and tasks of younger workers. Being reliable, able to stand for long shifts and able to lift supplies matters most.
Food handler card

Many states and counties require food handlers to get a food handler card soon after starting, usually after a short course and test on hygiene, temperatures and cross-contamination. Requirements vary by state and local health department. Some states also require allergen awareness training.
On-the-job training

Most training happens on the job, often over a few days to a few weeks. You learn food safety, cleaning and sanitizing, portion sizes, register use and how to run a dish machine. Schools and hospitals may add training on special diets.
First job

Typical first jobs are dishwasher, cafeteria server, counter attendant, busser, prep worker or catering helper in schools, hospitals, offices, stadiums and restaurants. Workers who serve alcohol may need responsible beverage service training, which some states require.
Moving up

With experience, workers move up to cook, shift lead and food service supervisor. Supervisors and managers often need a certified food protection manager credential, earned by passing an accredited exam. Some take a culinary or hospitality program to advance.
Time it takes
You can usually start within days of being hired. Earning a food handler card takes a few hours. Reaching shift lead or supervisor often takes one to three years, depending on the employer.
qa: Do you need a food handler card to work in food service?

It depends on where you work. Several states and many counties require food handler cards for workers who prepare or serve food, usually within a set number of days after hire. The training is short and ends with a test. Where no card is required, employers still train staff in food safety.
Can you get a food service job without experience?

Yes. Most food service jobs, such as dishwasher, cafeteria server or counter attendant, are entry level and come with on-the-job training. Employers look for reliability, teamwork and a willingness to follow food safety rules. A food handler card, if your state or county requires one, can make you ready to start sooner.

steps: Education

Most forward deployed engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering, math or another technical field. Some come from data science, physics or engineering. Courses in data structures, databases and systems design matter most, because the job means writing real code against a customer’s data.
Build hands-on coding skills

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work. Employers judge you on what you can build. Get fluent in a language such as Python, Java or TypeScript, plus SQL. Practice building small end-to-end tools that pull in messy data and present it to a user.
Customer-facing practice

Learn to explain technical tradeoffs to people who are not engineers. Internships, consulting projects, hackathons with real users, or support roles all help. Interviews often include a case where you break down a vague customer problem and decide what to build first.
Security clearance

Roles serving defense, intelligence or other federal customers often require U.S. citizenship and a government security clearance. You cannot apply for a clearance on your own. The employer sponsors it after hiring, and the background investigation can take several months.
First job

Some employers hire forward deployed engineers straight out of college. More often, people move in after working as a software engineer, data engineer, solutions engineer or technical consultant, where they learned to ship code and work directly with clients.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then anywhere from no experience to a few years in a related role. Many of these jobs also expect travel or on-site weeks at customer locations, so plan for that from the start.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a forward deployed engineer?

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer science or another technical field, but it is not a legal requirement. There is no license or required certification. People without a degree can get in by showing strong coding skills, a portfolio of working projects, and experience solving problems directly for users or clients.
How long does it take to become a forward deployed engineer?

Usually about four to seven years. That covers a four-year technical degree plus, in many cases, one to three years as a software engineer, data engineer or solutions engineer. Some companies hire new graduates directly into the role. Jobs with government customers may add months of waiting for a security clearance.

steps: Education

A bachelor’s degree in business, economics, engineering or a related field is common, but no specific major is required. Some people later add an MBA. Most founders hire for a track record of getting things done over credentials.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in any state. Certifications are optional. Employers judge you on results you can show, such as projects you ran, analyses you built and teams you coordinated.
Build structured experience

Many people enter after two to four years in management consulting, investment banking, venture capital or startup operations. These jobs teach you to break down messy problems, build financial models, write clear memos and keep projects on deadline across teams.
First job

Common first roles are business analyst, operations associate, strategy associate or executive assistant to a senior leader at a startup. Early-stage companies often hand strong generalists cross-functional projects quickly, and that work becomes the proof founders look for.
Time it takes

Most people reach a special projects or founder’s office role about two to five years after college. Hiring often runs through referrals, so building relationships with founders, investors and startup communities can shorten the path.
qa: Do you need an MBA to be a special projects manager?

No. An MBA can help, especially for people switching from an unrelated field, but it is not required. Many special projects managers come straight from consulting, banking or startup operations with only a bachelor’s degree. Founders mostly look for proof that you can own a messy project, work fast and communicate clearly.
How do you get a job in a founder’s office?

Most people get in by building two to four years of experience in consulting, banking, venture capital or startup operations, then moving to a growing company. Roles are often filled through referrals and networks. Showing specific projects you led, like a launch, a hiring push or a fundraising process, makes you a stronger candidate.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering or computer engineering. Key courses include digital logic, computer architecture, signals and systems, and embedded systems. Some people come from physics or computer science and fill the gaps with digital design courses.
Learn HDL and tools

Learn VHDL or Verilog, plus SystemVerilog for verification. Practice simulation, synthesis, timing constraints and timing closure in vendor design tools. Low-cost FPGA development boards let you build real projects, such as a UART, a video controller or a simple processor.
Internships and projects

Internships with defense, aerospace, telecom or semiconductor employers are a common way in. A senior design project built on an FPGA, shared code and a clear write-up of what you built help when you have no work history.
Clearance, not license

No state license or required certification exists for this work, and a PE license is rarely asked for. Many defense and space roles require US citizenship and the ability to obtain a government security clearance, which the employer sponsors after hiring.
Graduate degree, optional
A master’s degree is not required. It is common for roles in digital signal processing, wireless systems or low-latency trading hardware. Some people earn it part time while working.
First job

Common first roles are entry-level FPGA engineer, digital design engineer, verification engineer or hardware test engineer. Expect about four years for the degree, then usually two to five years before you lead complex designs on your own.
qa: Do you need a license to be an FPGA engineer?

No. There is no state license or required certification for FPGA engineers in the US. Employers look for a degree in electrical or computer engineering and proven skill in VHDL or Verilog. Many defense and aerospace jobs require US citizenship and eligibility for a security clearance, which the employer arranges.
How long does it take to become an FPGA engineer?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree in electrical or computer engineering, often with an internship along the way. That leads to an entry-level role. Working on your own on complex designs, including timing closure and high-speed interfaces, usually takes another two to five years of experience.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting, criminal justice, business or data analytics. Some banks and payment companies hire without a degree if you have related work experience. Courses in statistics, Excel and SQL help a lot, since much of the job is digging through transaction data.
No license required

No state or federal license is needed to work as a fraud analyst. Employers usually run a background check and a credit check, because you will see customer accounts, card numbers and personal data. A clean record matters more than any credential at the start.
First job

Many people start as a fraud specialist, chargeback or dispute analyst, KYC analyst, trust and safety agent, or call center rep in a bank’s fraud department. These roles teach you how stolen cards, fake accounts and scams look in real cases before you move into analyst work.
Build analysis skills

Analysts review alerts, spot patterns and write rules to block fraud. Learning SQL, advanced Excel and the basics of fraud detection tools makes you stand out. Some move on to Python or machine learning to work with risk models at larger companies.
Optional certifications

Certifications are not required but some employers value them. The Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential from the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE) requires passing an exam plus education and work experience. In banking, the CAMS credential from ACAMS is common for anti-money laundering work.
Time it takes

With a related degree, you can often land an entry-level fraud role right after school. Moving from a support or dispute role into an analyst title usually takes one to two years. Senior or lead analyst roles typically come after three to five years.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a fraud analyst?

No. There is no required license or certification for fraud analysts in the US. Many people are hired on the strength of a degree or related experience. Later, some earn the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential from the ACFE, or CAMS from ACAMS if they work in anti-money laundering, to move up.
Can you become a fraud analyst without a degree?

Yes, it is possible. Many analysts start in a bank call center, a dispute or chargeback team, or a trust and safety role, then move up after showing they can spot fraud patterns. Learning Excel and SQL on your own helps. Larger banks and some employers still list a bachelor’s degree as a requirement.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting, economics, statistics, data analytics, or a related field. Some fraud roles also accept criminal justice. Courses in statistics, accounting, and databases help most, since the daily work means reading transaction data and spotting patterns.
Data skills

Learn SQL and spreadsheets well, and ideally some Python or R. Analysts pull transaction records, build reports, and test fraud rules against past data. Knowing how payments, cards, lending, or insurance claims work in practice makes your analysis far more useful.
First job

Many people start in fraud operations, chargebacks and disputes, transaction monitoring, KYC review, or claims investigation. These roles teach you how real fraud looks case by case. After a year or two, people often move into analyst roles that set rules and measure losses.
Certifications

No license is required. Many analysts later earn the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential from the ACFE. Those in anti-money laundering often earn CAMS from ACAMS. Those focused on financial risk may pursue the FRM from GARP. Each has its own exam and experience requirements.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually one to three years in an entry-level fraud, compliance, or operations role before landing a full fraud or risk analyst job. Senior roles that build models or own rule strategy typically take several more years.
qa: Do you need a license to be a fraud analyst?

No. There is no state or federal license for fraud or risk analysts in the US. Employers mainly look for a relevant degree, data skills, and hands-on experience. Optional certifications such as the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE), CAMS for anti-money laundering work, or the FRM for financial risk can help you stand out and advance.
How long does it take to become a fraud and risk analyst?

Most people take about five to seven years in total. That usually means a four-year bachelor’s degree, followed by one to three years in a starting role such as fraud operations, disputes, or transaction monitoring. People with strong SQL and analytics skills sometimes move into analyst roles faster.

steps: Education

Many employers hire with a high school diploma, but an associate or bachelor’s degree in logistics, supply chain management or international business helps. Useful coursework covers trade documents, Incoterms, geography, customs basics and spreadsheets. A second language helps on international lanes.
First job

Most people start as an import or export coordinator, documentation clerk, or customer service rep at a forwarder, carrier or customs broker. You prepare bills of lading, commercial invoices and booking requests, track shipments and learn how ocean, air and truck freight connect.
Required safety training

There is no personal license to work as a forwarder. Staff who handle hazardous materials need DOT hazmat training under federal rules, and air shipments of dangerous goods require training to IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations. Staff at companies that ship air cargo on passenger planes need TSA security training.
Optional certifications

Credentials are optional but valued. Common choices are IATA training courses in cargo and forwarding, trade association certificates in export or customs compliance, and the Customs Broker License Exam if you also want to clear goods through U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
Time it takes

Expect about one to three years of on-the-job work before you quote rates, book carriers and manage complex door-to-door moves on your own. Taking a degree first adds two to four years. Learning customs rules and carrier contracts continues throughout a career.
Company license

If you later open your own firm, ocean forwarding and NVOCC businesses need an Ocean Transportation Intermediary license from the Federal Maritime Commission. The license is held by the company, which must name a qualifying individual with several years of shipping experience. Air cargo firms face separate TSA requirements.
qa: Do you need a license to be a freight forwarder?

Individual employees do not need a personal license. Companies that forward ocean freight must hold an Ocean Transportation Intermediary license from the Federal Maritime Commission. Workers who handle hazardous materials need DOT hazmat training, and air cargo staff often need TSA security training. A customs broker license is separate and optional for forwarders.
How long does it take to become a freight forwarder?

You can get an entry-level coordinator job right after high school or college. It usually takes one to three years of on-the-job experience to handle shipments independently, quote rates and manage door-to-door moves. Earning a degree in logistics or supply chain management first adds two to four years but can speed later promotion.

steps: Learn the core languages

Start with HTML for page structure, CSS for layout and styling, and JavaScript for behavior. Many people learn these through online courses, books or college classes. Practice building small pages that work on both phones and desktop screens.
Education

Many frontend engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field, which usually takes four years. A degree is common but not always required. Others come in through a coding bootcamp or self-study. There is no license, required exam or standard certification for this work.
Frameworks and tools

Employers usually expect skill in at least one JavaScript framework such as React, Angular or Vue, plus TypeScript, Git version control, browser developer tools and testing. Learn responsive design and web accessibility, including the WCAG guidelines, since many teams must meet accessibility standards.
Build a portfolio

Because there is no license, your work is your proof. Build several real projects, such as an interactive app or a redesigned site, and publish the code in a public repository. Write clear notes on what you built and why. Hiring managers often review this before an interview.
First job

Most people start as a junior frontend developer, web developer or software engineering intern. Some move in from related roles like web design, UX design, QA testing or technical support. Expect coding exercises or take-home projects during interviews.
Time it takes

It usually takes one to four years to land a first frontend role. A degree takes about four years. Focused self-study or a bootcamp plus portfolio work often takes one to two years. Reaching a mid-level engineer title typically takes a few more years on the job.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a frontend engineer?

No. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field, but plenty hire people who are self-taught or trained through a bootcamp. There is no license or required certification. What matters most is showing you can build working, accessible interfaces, usually through a portfolio of projects and a coding interview.
How long does it take to become a frontend engineer?

Most people need one to four years. A computer science degree takes about four years, often with an internship along the way. Career changers who study steadily and build a portfolio commonly reach a junior role in one to two years. Advancing from junior to mid-level usually takes a few more years of professional work.

steps: Education

Most full-stack engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. No degree is legally required, and many people enter through self-study or a coding bootcamp, but employers often prefer a degree for entry-level roles.
Core skills
You learn front-end basics like HTML, CSS and JavaScript, plus a framework such as React. On the back end you learn a server language, databases and SQL, APIs, Git and basic cloud deployment.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam for this work. Cloud or vendor certifications exist and can help, but most employers judge you on projects, coding interviews and work history instead.
Portfolio and internships

Build a few complete applications with a working front end, back end and database, and publish the code. Internships, open-source contributions and freelance projects give you real experience that hiring managers look for.
Time it takes
A degree path usually takes about four years. Career changers who study intensively often become job-ready in one to two years, though finding the first role can take longer in a tight market.
First job
Many start as junior software developers, junior web developers or front-end or back-end developers. After working on both sides of a product for a few years, they move into full-stack roles.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a full-stack engineer?

No law requires a degree, and many working full-stack engineers are self-taught or came from bootcamps. Still, many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field, especially for entry-level jobs. Without one, a strong portfolio of complete projects and solid coding interview skills matter even more.
How long does it take to become a full-stack engineer?

It usually takes about four years through a computer science degree, or one to two years of focused self-study or training for career changers. Many people then work a few years as junior developers on the front end or back end before taking a role with full-stack responsibilities.

steps: Education

Most fund accountants hold a bachelor’s degree in accounting or finance. Courses in financial accounting, investments and securities help most. Employers also test spreadsheet skills, since much of the work is reconciling trades, cash and positions and checking prices.
First job

The usual first job is fund accountant or fund accounting associate at a fund administrator, custodian bank or asset manager. New hires often start with daily reconciliations and pricing checks before calculating a fund’s net asset value (NAV) themselves.
Fund types

Work differs by fund type. Mutual fund and ETF accountants calculate a NAV every business day under SEC rules. Hedge fund accountants handle monthly NAVs and investor allocations, and private equity accountants handle capital calls, distributions and waterfall calculations.
Standards and credentials

There is no license for fund accounting. The work follows US GAAP for investment companies, ASC 946. Many senior fund accountants and controllers earn a CPA license, and some on the investment side pursue the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) designation, though neither is needed to start.
Time it takes

Entry-level roles are open to new graduates. Moving to senior fund accountant usually takes a few years, and to fund controller or manager several more. Audit experience with asset management clients is another common route into senior roles.
qa: Can you become a fund accountant without experience?

Yes. Fund administrators and custodian banks hire many new graduates with a degree in accounting or finance into entry-level fund accountant roles and train them on the job. Internships, strong spreadsheet skills and coursework in investments help. Some people also move in from audit or banking operations roles.
Do you need a CPA to be a fund accountant?

No. Entry-level and mid-level fund accountants do not need a CPA license, and many never get one. A CPA becomes more useful for senior roles such as fund controller or financial reporting manager, where you prepare audited fund financial statements. Some on the investment side pursue the CFA designation instead.

steps: Education

Most fundraisers and grant writers have a bachelor’s degree, often in communications, English, marketing, public relations or nonprofit management. Strong writing matters more than the major. Some later earn a master’s degree in nonprofit management or philanthropic studies.
First job

Common first jobs are development assistant, development coordinator, annual fund associate, events coordinator or grants assistant. Many people start by volunteering, interning or helping a small nonprofit write its first grant proposals.
Core skills

The work involves donor research, writing proposals and appeal letters, managing a donor database, planning events and reporting results to funders. Grant writers learn to read funder guidelines, build budgets and use federal grant registration and application systems.
State registration

Fundraisers themselves usually need no license. Many states require charities that ask the public for donations, and outside fundraising firms and counsel, to register, usually with the attorney general or secretary of state. Development staff help keep these filings current.
Certification

No certification is required. After a few years, many fundraisers earn the CFRE (Certified Fund Raising Executive) from CFRE International, which requires fundraising experience and an exam. Grant writers can earn the GPC (Grant Professional Certified) from the Grant Professionals Certification Institute.
Time it takes

With a degree, you can often start as a development assistant right away. Moving to a gift officer, grants manager or development director role usually takes three to seven years. Major gifts roles often require a proven record of closing large gifts.
qa: How long does it take to become a grant writer?

Some people start writing grants within months, especially at small nonprofits. Most grant writers spend one to three years as a development assistant or coordinator first, learning proposals, budgets and reports. A full-time grants manager role usually takes several years of experience and a record of funded proposals.
What certification helps in fundraising?

No certification is required. The best-known fundraising credential is the CFRE (Certified Fund Raising Executive) from CFRE International, which requires professional fundraising experience and an exam. Grant writers can earn the GPC (Grant Professional Certified) from the Grant Professionals Certification Institute. Many employers value a record of money raised more than any credential.

steps: Art fundamentals

Start with drawing, anatomy, perspective, color, light and composition. Concept artists are judged on these basics more than on any tool, so most people practice daily from life and reference long before they apply for work.
Education

Many artists earn a bachelor’s degree in illustration, fine art, animation or game art, usually over four years. A degree is common but not required. Some learn through community college programs, online courses and self-study instead.
Software skills

Learn the tools studios use, such as Photoshop for painting and concept work, and 3D programs like Blender, Maya, ZBrush or Substance Painter for modeling and texturing. There is no license or required certification for this work.
Portfolio

The portfolio is what gets you hired. Build a focused online portfolio of finished pieces that match the job you want, such as character, environment or prop design, and show process sketches, variations and turnarounds.
Time it takes

Reaching a hireable portfolio usually takes two to four years of steady study and practice. Dedicated concept artist roles often expect several years of professional experience, so many people start in related art jobs first.
First job

Common first jobs are junior or associate artist, art intern, 3D or texture artist at an outsourcing studio, or freelance illustration. Some people enter a studio through quality assurance testing and move into the art team later.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a game artist?

No. There is no license or required degree for game or concept art in the US. Many artists hold a bachelor’s degree in illustration, animation or game art, but studios hire mainly on the strength of the portfolio. Self-taught artists with strong fundamentals and polished, relevant work can get hired.
How long does it take to become a concept artist?

Building a portfolio good enough for an entry-level art job usually takes two to four years of study and practice. Concept artist positions are competitive, and many studios want several years of professional experience, so people often start as junior, 3D or freelance artists and move into concept work over time.

steps: Education

Most game designers hold a bachelor’s degree, often in game design, computer science, or a related field such as interactive media. A degree is not legally required, and some studios hire self-taught designers with strong work. Classes in programming, math, writing and psychology all help.
Tools and skills

Learn a game engine such as Unity or Unreal Engine, plus basic scripting. Practice writing design documents, building spreadsheets to model game economies, and tuning balance. Paper prototypes and board games are a cheap way to test rules and systems.
Portfolio

Studios hire mainly on a portfolio. Build small playable games, levels or mods, and explain your design thinking: the goal, what playtesting showed, and what you changed. Game jams are a common way to finish short projects and work alongside artists and programmers.
No license needed

There is no license, registration or required exam for game designers in any state. No certification is standard across the industry. Employers judge your skill through your portfolio, design tests and interviews instead.
First job

Many people start as a QA tester, junior or associate designer, or level designer. Others move over from programming, writing or art roles inside a studio. Small independent teams and mobile game studios are also common ways in.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then months to a few years of portfolio work and entry-level jobs before holding a full designer title. Self-taught paths vary widely and depend on the quality of finished projects.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a game designer?

No law requires a degree, and there is no license for game designers. Many studios list a bachelor’s degree in game design, computer science or a related field, but a strong portfolio of playable games, levels or mods often matters more. Some designers are self-taught or move in from QA testing, programming or writing roles.
How long does it take to become a game designer?

It usually takes several years. A bachelor’s degree takes about four years, and many people then spend months to a few years building a portfolio or working as a QA tester or junior designer. Self-taught designers may move faster or slower, depending on how many finished, polished projects they can show.

steps: Education

Most game developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering, game design or digital art. Programmers need strong math and coding skills, often in C++ or C#. Artists usually study illustration, animation or 3D modeling. A degree helps with hiring, but no law requires one.
Learn a game engine

Studios build most games in engines such as Unity, which uses C#, and Unreal Engine, which uses C++ and Blueprints. Learn one deeply. Also learn version control tools such as Git or Perforce, since teams use them every day.
Build a portfolio

Studios hire mostly on proof of work. Finish small, playable games, join game jams and contribute to mods or open projects. Keep a portfolio site with playable builds, code samples or art, and explain your exact role on each team project.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam to work as a game developer in the US. Engine makers offer optional certifications, such as Unity’s certification exams, but most employers care far more about your portfolio and shipped games.
Time it takes

The usual path takes about four years, matching a bachelor’s degree, with portfolio work done along the way. Self-taught developers often need two to four years of steady practice before they have games strong enough to land a first role.
First job

Common first jobs include QA tester, junior or associate programmer, junior artist and technical support roles at studios. Some people start in general software jobs or release small independent games first, then move into larger studios with that experience.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a game developer?

No law requires a degree, and some developers are self-taught. Still, many studios prefer a bachelor’s degree in computer science, game design or digital art, especially for programming roles. A strong portfolio of finished, playable games often matters as much as the degree, and it can open doors for people without one.
How long does it take to become a game developer?

It usually takes two to four years. Many people spend four years earning a related bachelor’s degree while building a portfolio. Self-taught developers often need two to four years of regular practice with an engine like Unity or Unreal Engine. Many then start as QA testers or junior developers before moving into larger roles.

steps: Education

Most game programmers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. Some colleges offer game development degrees. Math matters: linear algebra, physics and algorithms come up daily in gameplay and engine work. Self-taught programmers do get hired when their work is strong.
Languages and engines

Learn C++, the main language of most console and PC game engines, and C# for Unity. Get comfortable with Unreal Engine or Unity, version control such as Git, and debugging and profiling tools. Specialties like graphics, networking or game AI need deeper study.
Portfolio

Studios hire on proof of skill. Build small finished games, gameplay prototypes or engine features, and share code and playable builds online. Game jams, mods and team student projects show you can finish work and collaborate. There is no license, registration or required certification for this work.
First job

Common first jobs are junior or associate gameplay programmer, tools programmer, or programming intern at a game studio. Some people start in QA testing or general software development and move over later. Expect technical interviews with coding tests, often in C++, plus math and problem-solving questions.
Time it takes

It usually takes about four years to earn a degree while building a portfolio. Many people land their first game programming job within a year or two after graduating. Reaching senior roles typically takes several more years and a few shipped titles.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a game programmer?

No law or license requires a degree to program games. Still, many studios ask for a bachelor’s in computer science or a related field, or equivalent experience. Self-taught programmers can get hired with a strong portfolio of finished games, solid C++ or C# skills, and the ability to pass a technical interview.
How long does it take to become a game programmer?

Most people take about four years to earn a computer science or related degree, building games and a portfolio along the way. Landing the first job often takes another few months to two years. Self-taught paths vary widely and depend on how quickly you can show finished, working game projects.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Earn a four-year bachelor’s degree in any field. Law schools do not require a specific major, but courses in writing, business, economics or political science help. Strong grades and an LSAT score matter for law school admission.
Law degree

Most future general counsel complete a three-year Juris Doctor (JD), usually at an ABA-accredited law school. Most states require this degree for bar admission, though a few, such as California, Virginia, Vermont and Washington, allow supervised law office study instead.
Bar admission

Get admitted to practice in at least one state. Most states require passing a bar exam, and most also require the MPRE ethics exam and a character and fitness review. Rules vary by state. Many states also let in-house lawyers licensed elsewhere register as in-house counsel.
First job

Most start as associates at law firms, often in corporate, securities, litigation or regulatory practice. Others join a company as junior in-house counsel or work in government. These early years build the legal judgment and business knowledge companies expect from their top lawyer.
Move in-house and lead

Lawyers usually move in-house as counsel or senior counsel, then rise to deputy or associate general counsel. Managing other lawyers, outside firms and budgets, and advising executives directly, prepares you for the top legal role.
Time it takes

Expect about seven years of school after high school, then often a decade or more of legal practice. Smaller companies and startups sometimes hire general counsel with less experience than large public companies do.
qa: Do you need to be a lawyer to be a general counsel?

In practice, yes. Companies expect their general counsel to be an attorney admitted to practice in at least one state. Most lawyers get there with a JD and a state bar exam, but rules vary by state. Wisconsin offers diploma privilege, and a few states allow law office study instead of law school.
How long does it take to become a general counsel?

It usually takes many years. Most people spend four years on a bachelor’s degree and three years in law school, then pass the bar. After that, they often practice for ten or more years at a law firm or in-house before leading a company’s legal team. Startups may hire sooner.

steps: Education

Most general managers hold a bachelor’s degree in business administration, management, finance, economics or a field tied to their industry, such as engineering or hospitality. For division or country roles at large companies, many employers prefer an MBA. Some people rise without a degree, especially in retail and restaurants.
First job

The usual way in is a starting role with people or numbers to manage: assistant manager, management trainee, shift or department supervisor, or a sales, operations or financial analyst. These jobs teach scheduling, budgets, customer issues and how the business makes money.
Build P&L experience

Employers want proof that you have run something and owned its results. People move up through roles like department head, store or plant manager, operations manager, district manager or product line leader. Each step adds budget control, hiring decisions and accountability for revenue and costs.
Industry credentials

The general manager title has no license of its own, but some industries add rules. Many states and localities require food service managers to hold a Certified Food Protection Manager credential, and some states require manager permits for places that serve alcohol. Requirements vary by state and industry, so check local rules.
Time it takes

Timelines vary widely. Running a single store, restaurant or hotel can come after several years of management experience. Leading a business unit or a country for a larger company usually takes ten years or more of progressively bigger roles, often across different functions.
qa: Do you need a license to be a general manager?

There is no general license for the job title itself. Some industries do have requirements. Many states and localities require food service managers to hold a Certified Food Protection Manager credential, and some states require a manager permit for businesses that serve alcohol. Rules vary by state and industry, so check what applies where you plan to work.
How long does it take to become a general manager?

It depends on the size of the operation. Someone can become general manager of a single store, restaurant or hotel after several years in supervisor and assistant manager roles. General managers of a business unit or country usually have ten years or more of experience, including running budgets and teams and answering for profit and loss.

steps: Education

Geologists need a bachelor’s degree in geology or geoscience, and many earn a master’s, which is common in exploration and consulting. Mining engineers usually earn a bachelor’s degree in mining engineering from an ABET-accredited program. Geology students usually complete a summer field camp.
Mine safety training

Anyone working at a US mine must complete MSHA training before starting. New miners at surface mines get at least 24 hours of training, new underground miners at least 40 hours, and everyone takes annual refresher training of at least 8 hours.
First job

Geologists often start as field or staff geologists in exploration, mining, environmental or engineering consulting, logging core and mapping rock. Mining engineers usually start as junior or rotational engineers at a mine, planning blasts, haul roads and ventilation.
Geologist license

Many states license geologists, though not all. Most require a degree, several years of supervised experience and passing the ASBOG exams: the Fundamentals of Geology exam and the Practice of Geology exam. Passing the first exam early often earns a geologist-in-training title.
Mining engineer license

Mining engineers can take the FE exam near graduation, then the NCEES PE Mining and Mineral Processing exam after about four years of experience. A state PE license is needed to sign certain designs and plans. Many also join the Society for Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, and two more for a master’s if you take one. Licensed geologists and mining engineers usually need about four to five years of experience after the degree before getting their license, depending on the state.
qa: Do you need a license to be a geologist?

It depends on the state. Many states require a Professional Geologist license for geologists who offer services to the public or sign geologic reports. Licensing usually needs a geology degree, several years of supervised experience and passing the ASBOG Fundamentals of Geology and Practice of Geology exams. In states without licensing, geologists can work without one.
How long does it take to become a mining engineer?

Usually four years for a bachelor’s degree in mining engineering, often with summer work at a mine. New engineers then train on site, including required MSHA safety training. Earning a PE license usually takes about four more years of experience and passing the FE exam and the PE Mining and Mineral Processing exam.

steps: Education

Most people earn a bachelor’s degree in geography, GIS, geomatics, environmental science, urban planning or computer science. Coursework should cover cartography, spatial analysis, remote sensing and databases. Career changers who already hold a degree often add a graduate GIS certificate, which usually takes one year or less.
Technical skills

Employers expect hands-on skill with desktop GIS software, both commercial and open source. Many postings also ask for SQL, spatial databases and Python scripting. Work for logistics, navigation or self-driving cars leans more on programming, GPS data, lidar and large datasets.
Portfolio and internship

A portfolio of real maps and analysis projects helps you stand out. Internships with city or county governments, utilities, planning offices or environmental agencies give practical experience. Many students land their first job through these placements.
First job

The usual first job is GIS technician, mapping technician or junior GIS analyst. Typical tasks include data entry, digitizing, cleaning location data and making routine maps. Some start in map data editing or annotation roles for navigation and autonomous vehicle teams.
Optional certification

No license is required for most GIS work. After several years of experience, many professionals earn the voluntary GISP credential from the GIS Certification Institute. ASPRS also offers certifications in mapping and photogrammetry. Work that legally defines property boundaries requires a state land surveyor’s license.
Time it takes

Reaching an entry-level GIS job usually takes about four years, the length of a bachelor’s degree. With a related degree already in hand, a certificate can shorten this to one year. Moving up to analyst or developer roles typically takes two to five more years.
qa: Do you need a license to be a GIS specialist?

No. Most GIS and mapping jobs in the US require no state license. Employers look for a relevant degree, software skills and a portfolio. The GISP credential is voluntary but respected. The exception is work that legally establishes property boundaries, which falls under land surveying and requires a state license. Rules on surveying and photogrammetry vary by state.
How long does it take to become a GIS analyst?

Most people take about four years to finish a bachelor’s degree in geography, GIS or a related field. They then often spend one to three years as a GIS technician before moving into an analyst role. Someone who already has a related degree can add a GIS certificate in about a year and enter at the technician level.

steps: Education

Most GNC engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in aerospace, mechanical or electrical engineering. Core courses include linear algebra, differential equations, dynamics, feedback control and probability. Pick electives in control systems, flight or orbital mechanics, and estimation when you can.
Graduate study

Many employers prefer a master’s degree for GNC roles, and research-heavy teams often hire PhDs. Graduate work usually covers state estimation and Kalman filtering, optimal and robust control, and navigation with inertial sensors and GPS.
Hands-on projects

Internships, co-ops and student rocketry, drone, robotics or satellite teams show you can turn theory into working code. Build skills in MATLAB and Simulink, C or C++, and Python. Get practice with simulation and hardware-in-the-loop testing.
Clearance and citizenship

There is no license or required exam for this work, and a Professional Engineer license is rarely needed. Many defense and space jobs fall under export control rules or need a security clearance, so they are often open only to US citizens. The employer sponsors the clearance after an offer.
First job

Most people start as an entry-level GNC, controls or flight software engineer. Early work is often simulation, analysis and testing under senior engineers. Some move in from related roles such as systems, test or robotics engineering.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, plus one to two years if you earn a master’s. Leading the design of a full GNC system usually takes several more years of experience on real flight or vehicle programs.
qa: What degree do you need to become a GNC engineer?

Most GNC engineers have a bachelor’s degree in aerospace, mechanical or electrical engineering, with strong coursework in control systems, dynamics and estimation. Many employers prefer a master’s degree, and some research and advanced design roles look for a PhD. No license is required to do the work.
Do GNC engineers need a security clearance?

Not always, but many do. A large share of GNC jobs are in defense and space programs that require a security clearance or fall under export control rules. These jobs are often open only to US citizens. Employers usually sponsor the clearance after hiring, and commercial drone, automotive and robotics roles often need no clearance.

steps: Education

Most Go developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. No degree is legally required. Some people get in through self-study or a coding program, but many employers still ask for a degree or equivalent work experience.
Learn Go and backend basics

Learn the core of Go: goroutines, channels, interfaces, error handling and the standard library. Pair it with backend skills employers expect, such as HTTP and REST APIs, SQL databases, Linux, Git, and writing tests with Go’s built-in testing tools.
Cloud and infrastructure tools

Much Go work sits in cloud infrastructure. Get comfortable with Docker, Kubernetes, gRPC and at least one major cloud platform. Docker and Kubernetes are themselves written in Go, so reading their code is useful practice.
Portfolio instead of license

There is no license or required exam for this work. Show your skill with public projects, such as a REST or gRPC service, a command-line tool, or fixes merged into open-source Go projects. Optional certifications like the CNCF’s CKAD can help but are not required.
First job

Few entry-level postings ask for Go alone. Many people start as a junior backend or software engineer using another language, such as Python or Java. They then pick up Go on the job or move into a Go-focused role after a year or two.
Time it takes

A degree usually takes four years. Programmers who already know another language can often become productive in Go within a few months. Roles titled Go developer or Golang engineer usually expect two or more years of backend experience.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a Go developer?

No. There is no license, required exam or official Go certification for this work in the US. Employers judge you on your code, past projects and technical interviews. Some people add optional cloud certifications, such as the CNCF’s Kubernetes exams, to show infrastructure skills, but a strong portfolio and backend experience matter more.
How long does it take to become a Go developer?

Starting from zero, most people spend about four years on a degree or two to three years of serious self-study and junior work. If you already program in another language, you can learn Go well enough to be useful in a few months. Most Go-specific roles still ask for around two years of backend experience.

steps: Education

Most government contracts specialists hold a bachelor’s degree in business, contract management, supply chain, finance or prelaw. Federal contract specialist jobs in the GS-1102 series have their own education rules, usually a bachelor’s degree or a set amount of business coursework.
First job

Common first jobs are contracts administrator, subcontracts administrator or proposal coordinator at a contractor, or contract specialist trainee at a federal agency. Many company specialists started in government, where they learned the process from the buying side.
Rules to learn

The core is the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), plus agency supplements such as the DFARS for defense work. Learn contract types, small business rules, the Truthful Cost or Pricing Data rules, Cost Accounting Standards and how DCAA audits contractors, and follow ongoing FAR revisions.
Certification

Certification is optional for company staff. The National Contract Management Association (NCMA) offers the Certified Federal Contracts Manager (CFCM) and Certified Professional Contracts Manager (CPCM). Federal contracting staff earn the Federal Acquisition Certification in Contracting (FAC-C) through their agency.
Security clearance
