No. No license, exam, or certification is required to work as a field CTO or industry specialist. Employers hire based on deep industry experience, technical depth, and skill with customers. Vendor cloud certifications or security credentials can strengthen a resume, but credibility with executives in the industry counts for more.
How long does it take to become an industry specialist in tech sales?

It usually takes about ten to fifteen years. Most people first spend years working in the industry they will cover, then move into a customer-facing role such as sales engineer or solutions architect. The specialist or field CTO title comes once they can speak to customers as true peers.

steps: Education

Most inference engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, computer engineering or electrical engineering. Many also have a master’s or PhD focused on machine learning systems, compilers or high-performance computing. Useful courses include operating systems, computer architecture, parallel programming and linear algebra.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in the US. Some vendors and cloud providers offer certificates, but employers rarely ask for them. Hiring teams judge you on the code you write and on systems you have made faster.
Core technical skills

Learn Python and C++, GPU programming with CUDA and a deep learning framework such as PyTorch. Study how transformer models run, then practice quantization, batching, KV caching, model parallelism and profiling latency and memory use on real hardware.
Public proof of work

Many people get noticed by contributing to open-source model serving, compiler or GPU kernel projects. Others publish benchmarks or write-ups showing how they cut latency or cost for a model. This work often matters more than certificates.
First job

Few people start as inference engineers. The usual first job is software engineer on a backend or infrastructure team, machine learning engineer, or GPU performance engineer. Some move over from research engineering or high-performance computing roles.
Time it takes

Expect a four-year degree plus, often, two to five years of software or machine learning systems experience before landing an inference role. A graduate degree or strong open-source work can shorten the path.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an inference engineer?

Most inference engineers have a degree in computer science, computer engineering or a related field, and many have a master’s or PhD. It is not legally required. Some people without degrees get hired by showing strong GPU, systems and open-source work, but the competition for these roles makes a degree the common path.
How long does it take to become an inference engineer?

It usually takes several years. Most people finish a four-year degree, then spend two to five years as a software, infrastructure or machine learning engineer before moving into inference work. There is no license or exam, so the time depends on how fast you build real experience making models run faster and cheaper.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, communications, public relations, journalism or business. No single major is required. Courses in digital marketing, social media, consumer behavior, copywriting and basic analytics are the most useful.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in any state. Short certificates in social media or digital marketing exist, but they are optional. Employers care far more about the campaigns you have actually run.
Learn disclosure rules

Study the FTC’s Endorsement Guides, which require creators to clearly disclose paid partnerships, free products and other material connections. Managers are expected to put these rules into creator contracts and check that posts are labeled properly.
First job

Most people start as a social media coordinator, influencer marketing coordinator or specialist, PR assistant, or marketing assistant at a brand or agency. The work includes building creator lists, sending outreach, shipping products, tracking posts and reporting results.
Build a track record

Keep a record of every campaign you help run: creators recruited, budgets, reach, engagement and sales. A portfolio with real results, plus solid contacts with creators and talent agencies, is what gets people promoted or hired as managers.
Time it takes

Expect roughly two to five years in coordinator or specialist roles before a manager title. Counting a four-year degree, the path usually takes about six to eight years, though fast-growing brands and startups sometimes promote sooner.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an influencer marketing manager?

Most job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree, usually in marketing, communications, public relations or business. It is not a legal requirement, and there is no license. People without a degree can get in through social media or creator work, but they usually need a strong portfolio of campaigns with measurable results.
How long does it take to become an influencer marketing manager?

After a bachelor’s degree, most people spend about two to five years as a social media or influencer marketing coordinator or specialist before becoming a manager. Those who already work in PR, social media or talent management can sometimes move up faster if they can show results from creator campaigns.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in cybersecurity, computer science, information technology or a related field. Some people enter with an associate degree or military training, backed by certifications and hands-on IT experience. Coursework in networking, operating systems and scripting is useful.
Related IT experience

Many analysts first spend one to several years in general IT work, such as help desk, systems administration or network administration. This teaches how real networks, servers and user accounts work, which is what you later protect and investigate during incidents.
Entry certifications

No state license is required. Employers often expect an entry certification such as CompTIA Security+, and some also value CompTIA Network+ or a GIAC certification. Some government and defense contractor roles ask for specific certifications or a security clearance, so check each posting.
Advanced certifications

With experience, many analysts earn the CISSP from ISC2, which needs five years of paid work in at least two of its eight domains; a four-year degree or approved credential can count for one year. Those still short can pass the exam and become an Associate of ISC2. ISACA’s CISM and CISA suit management and audit paths.
Time it takes

Becoming an information security analyst usually takes four to six years: a four-year degree plus one or more years in IT or a junior security role. Career changers with IT experience can move faster by adding certifications and lab practice.
First job

A common first security job is a tier 1 analyst in a security operations center (SOC), monitoring alerts and escalating incidents. Others start as a junior security analyst, IT auditor or IT support technician with security duties, then move into a full analyst role.
qa: Do you need a license to be an information security analyst?

No. There is no state license for information security analysts in the US. Instead, employers often look for certifications such as CompTIA Security+ for entry roles and CISSP or CISM for senior roles. Some government and defense contractor jobs also require a security clearance or specific certifications listed in the posting.
How long does it take to become an information security analyst?

It usually takes four to six years. Most people complete a four-year degree in cybersecurity, computer science or IT, then gain one or more years of experience in help desk, network or junior security work. People already working in IT can often move into a security analyst role sooner by earning certifications such as CompTIA Security+.

steps: Education

Most entry jobs ask for a high school diploma. Many employers, especially in software and business-to-business sales, prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing or communications. A degree is often not required if you can show strong phone and writing skills.
Related experience

Customer service, call center, retail or hospitality work helps. These jobs build the skills inside sales uses daily: talking with strangers, handling objections, staying organized and working toward targets.
First job

The usual way in is an entry-level role such as sales development representative (SDR), business development representative or inside sales associate. You make outbound calls and emails, qualify leads and book meetings for more senior sellers.
On-the-job training
Employers train new hires on the product, the sales process and CRM software. Training usually runs a few weeks to a few months, often with call shadowing, scripts and coaching on recorded calls.
License if required

Most inside sales jobs need no license. Some products do. Selling insurance requires a state insurance producer license, and rules vary by state. Selling securities usually requires FINRA exams; anyone 18 or older can take the SIE, but the Series 7 requires sponsorship by a FINRA member firm.
Time it takes

You can often be hired with no sales experience and start within weeks. Moving from an SDR role to an account executive role that closes deals commonly takes about one to two years of meeting targets.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an inside sales representative?

No, not always. Many inside sales jobs accept a high school diploma plus customer service or call center experience. Some employers, especially in technology and business-to-business sales, prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing or communications. Strong communication skills and a record of meeting goals often matter as much as a degree.
Do you need a license to work in inside sales?

Most inside sales jobs need no license. It depends on what you sell. Insurance sales require a state insurance producer license, and requirements vary by state. Securities sales usually require FINRA exams; the SIE is open to anyone 18 or older, while the Series 7 requires a sponsoring FINRA member firm. Real estate also requires a state license.

steps: Education

Most instructional designers hold a bachelor’s degree, often in education, English, communications or psychology. Many employers prefer a master’s in instructional design, educational technology or learning design, especially in higher education. A graduate certificate in instructional design is a common shorter option for career changers.
Learn the methods and tools

Learn a design model such as ADDIE, how to write learning objectives, and how to build assessments that test them. Most corporate roles also expect skill with e-learning authoring tools such as Articulate Storyline or Adobe Captivate, plus a learning management system.
Build a portfolio

There is no license for this work, so a portfolio does much of the convincing. Include a few short e-learning modules, a course outline, a storyboard and an assessment. Show your design reasoning, not just finished slides. Volunteer projects and redesigns of existing training count.
Optional certification

No certification is required. Some designers later earn a credential from the Association for Talent Development, such as the APTD or CPTD, to show broader training knowledge. Employers usually weigh a strong portfolio and relevant experience more heavily than any certificate.
Time it takes

The path usually takes one to three years for someone with a related degree. Former teachers and trainers often move in faster, since they already plan lessons and assessments. Starting from scratch with a bachelor’s and master’s can take five to six years.
First job

Common first roles include e-learning developer, instructional design assistant, training coordinator or curriculum developer. Many people also move in from classroom teaching, corporate training or subject expert roles, picking up design work inside their current organization before taking the title.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an instructional designer?

Most postings ask for a bachelor’s degree, and many, especially at colleges and universities, prefer a master’s in instructional design or educational technology. Some corporate employers hire without a specific degree if you have a strong portfolio and experience in teaching or training. There is no license, so proof of your work matters a great deal.
Can a teacher become an instructional designer?

Yes. Teaching is one of the most common routes into instructional design. Teachers already write objectives, plan lessons and assess learning. To make the switch, most learn adult learning principles and authoring tools such as Articulate Storyline, then build a portfolio of e-learning samples. Some also complete a graduate certificate to show focused training.

steps: Education

Most employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, finance, economics, risk management or a related field, especially for underwriting. Some claims roles accept a high school diploma plus relevant experience. Courses in math, statistics and writing help, since the work means pricing risk and documenting decisions clearly.
Adjuster license

Many states require claims adjusters to hold a state adjuster license. You usually take a prelicensing course, pass a state exam and clear a background check. Requirements vary by state and by type of adjuster. Underwriters generally do not need a state license.
Employer training

Most new hires join a trainee program at an insurer or claims firm. Underwriting trainees learn rating guidelines under a senior underwriter. Claims trainees handle simple claims under supervision before taking on complex losses. Training usually lasts several months to a year.
Professional designations

Many specialists later earn industry designations such as the CPCU (Chartered Property Casualty Underwriter) or the AIC (Associate in Claims) from The Institutes. These are not required by law, but employers often value them for promotion. Licensed adjusters must also complete continuing education to renew.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, plus a few weeks to a few months to prepare for an adjuster exam if your state requires one. Handling large accounts or complex claims on your own usually takes two to five years of experience.
First job

Common entry points are claims trainee, underwriting assistant, underwriting trainee or customer service roles at an insurance carrier or agency. Some people move in from related work such as banking, auto repair, construction or nursing, which helps with certain claim types.
qa: Do you need a license to be an insurance claims adjuster?

In many states, yes. Most states license independent and public adjusters, and many also license staff adjusters who work for an insurer. You usually pass a state exam and a background check. Adjusters who live in a state without adjuster licensing often get a designated home state license so they can work in other states. Rules vary by state.
Do insurance underwriters need a license?

Insurance underwriters usually do not need a state license. Employers look for a degree, strong analytical skills and on-the-job training under senior underwriters. Many underwriters build credibility with voluntary designations such as the CPCU from The Institutes, which covers insurance law, risk and underwriting topics and can support promotion to senior roles.

steps: Basic requirements

A college degree is not required for a license. Most states require you to be at least 18 and pass a background check, often with fingerprints. Some agents study business, finance or risk management, and agencies often hire for sales and customer service skills.
Pre-licensing course

Many states require a pre-licensing course for each line of insurance you plan to sell, such as life, accident and health, property, or casualty. Hours and rules vary by state, and some states have dropped the course requirement but still require the exam.
State exam and license

You pass a state licensing exam for each line of authority, then apply to the state department of insurance for a producer license. Agents who sell in other states add nonresident licenses, often filed through the National Insurance Producer Registry (NIPR).
Appointment and first job

Most new agents start at an agency or insurer as a licensed sales agent, account manager or customer service representative. In most states an insurer must also appoint you before you can sell its policies. Captive agents sell for one company; independent agents represent several.
Extra licenses

Selling variable annuities or variable life insurance also requires FINRA registration, usually the SIE plus the Series 6 or Series 7, and the Series 63 in most states. Many states also require special training before you sell annuities or long-term care insurance.
Time it takes

Getting licensed usually takes a few weeks. Most states require continuing education, usually every two years, to renew. Experienced agents may earn designations such as the CPCU, CIC, CLU or ChFC, which take months to years of study.
qa: Do you need a license to sell insurance?

Yes. Every state requires a producer license from its department of insurance to sell insurance. You usually take a pre-licensing course, pass a state exam for each line of insurance, such as life and health or property and casualty, and pass a background check. Variable products also require FINRA securities registration.
How long does it take to become an insurance agent?

Usually a few weeks to two months. Pre-licensing study takes days to a few weeks depending on your state and the lines you choose, and exams can often be scheduled quickly. After you pass, the state issues your license and an insurer appoints you. Building a full book of clients takes much longer.

steps: Education

Patent work usually starts with a bachelor’s degree in engineering, a physical or life science, or computer science, since the USPTO requires technical training to register. Trademark, copyright and brand protection roles accept a wider range of degrees, and some people start with a paralegal certificate.
Patent bar exam

To prepare and file patent applications for clients, you must pass the USPTO registration examination, often called the patent bar. It is a federal exam, so it is the same in every state. You must first show a qualifying science or engineering degree or equivalent coursework.
Law school and state bar

Passing the patent bar alone makes you a patent agent. To become a patent attorney, handle trademark matters for clients before the USPTO, or take infringement cases to court, you need a law degree and admission to a state bar. Bar rules vary by state.
First job

Common ways in are patent paralegal, IP docketing specialist, technical specialist at a law firm, patent examiner at the USPTO, or brand protection analyst at a company. Brand protection and docketing roles need no license and often hire people with a related degree and strong attention to detail.
Time it takes

Plan on about four years for a technical degree plus a few months to prepare for the patent bar to become a patent agent. A patent attorney usually needs about seven years: a four-year degree and three years of law school, then the bar exam.
qa: Do you need a law degree to be a patent agent?

No. A patent agent needs a qualifying science or engineering background and must pass the USPTO registration exam, often called the patent bar. Agents can prepare and prosecute patent applications before the USPTO. They cannot give general legal advice, represent clients in court, or handle trademark matters for clients. Those tasks require a law degree and state bar admission.
How long does it take to become a patent attorney?

It usually takes about seven years after high school. Most people earn a four-year degree in engineering or science, then complete three years of law school. They must pass a state bar exam and the USPTO registration exam. Some take the patent bar during or before law school and work as patent agents first.

steps: Education

Most intelligence analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in international relations, political science, history, security studies, area studies, criminal justice or computer science. Foreign language skills and knowledge of a region are valued. Many federal analysts also hold a master’s degree.
Security clearance

Government and defense intelligence jobs require US citizenship and a security clearance, usually Top Secret with access to sensitive compartmented information (TS/SCI). Some agencies also require a polygraph. The employer sponsors the clearance, and the process can take many months to over a year.
Military path

Many analysts start in the military. The Army’s 35F Intelligence Analyst specialty and similar roles in other branches train enlisted members in analysis after basic training. Veterans leave with experience and often an active clearance, which defense contractors value highly.
Analytic skills

Analysts must collect information, judge sources, spot patterns and write short, clear assessments with stated confidence. Structured analytic techniques, briefing skills and tools for mapping, link analysis and data are central. Writing samples are often part of hiring.
First job

Common first jobs are intelligence analyst at a federal agency, military intelligence analyst, crime analyst at a police department, or threat intelligence analyst at a company. Federal internships and student programs are a common way in for college graduates.
Time it takes

With a bachelor’s degree, you can apply right after graduation, but federal hiring and the clearance process often take six months to over a year. The military path includes basic training and then several months of intelligence training before a first assignment.
qa: How long does it take to become an intelligence analyst?

Usually four years for a bachelor’s degree, plus the hiring and security clearance process, which often takes six months to more than a year for federal and defense jobs. Military analysts complete basic training and then several months of intelligence training. Private sector threat intelligence and crime analyst roles can be faster because many do not require a clearance.
Can you become an intelligence analyst without a clearance?

Yes. You cannot apply for a clearance yourself, so most people get one when an agency, military branch or contractor hires them and sponsors the investigation. You must be a US citizen and able to pass a background check. Corporate threat intelligence and police crime analyst jobs often require no federal clearance.

steps: Enrollment

Most internships require you to be enrolled in a college, university or community college program, or to have graduated recently. New grad roles usually ask for a bachelor’s or associate degree finished within the past year or so. Some employers ask for a specific major or a minimum GPA.
Resume and early experience

Build a one-page resume with relevant coursework, class projects, campus jobs, volunteer work and student organizations. For technical, design or writing roles, a small portfolio or project list helps. No license, certification or exam is required to become an intern or new grad hire.
Applications and timing

Many large employers recruit in the fall for the following summer, often nine to twelve months ahead. Smaller employers hire closer to the start date. Use your school’s career center, career fairs, faculty contacts and online postings. International students on F-1 visas usually need CPT or OPT authorization before working.
Interviews

Expect a screening call, then one or more interviews about your coursework, projects and teamwork. Technical fields often add a skills test or case exercise. Some programs give for-credit placements and require approval from your school before you start.
The internship

Most internships last 10 to 12 weeks in summer, or a full semester for co-op programs. You work under a supervisor, receive on-the-job training and often finish a final project. Under federal labor rules, unpaid internships at for-profit employers are allowed only in limited cases.
First job

A strong internship often leads to a return offer for another internship or a full-time new grad role after graduation. Otherwise, new grads apply to entry-level jobs, rotational programs or associate positions, listing internship work as experience.
qa: Do you have to be a student to get an internship?

Usually yes. Most internships are for current students in college or graduate school, and some are open to high school students. A smaller number accept recent graduates. After graduation, most people apply for new grad or entry-level roles instead, which offer similar training but are permanent jobs rather than fixed-term placements.
When should you apply for a summer internship?

Start in the fall of the school year before the summer you want to work. Many large employers open applications in August or September and fill most spots by winter. Smaller companies, nonprofits and government offices often hire in spring. Applying early and to many places gives you the best chance.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in communications, public relations, journalism, English or marketing. Coursework in writing, editing, organizational behavior and media helps. Some employers accept a degree in another field if you can show strong writing samples.
No license required

There is no state license or required exam for internal communications in the US. Optional credentials exist, such as the APR from the Universal Accreditation Board or the CMP from the Global Communication Certification Council, but most employers hire on experience and writing ability.
First job

The usual way in is an entry role such as communications coordinator, communications specialist, HR or employee communications assistant, or a public relations or agency assistant. Former reporters and editors also move into this work. Early tasks include drafting newsletters, updating the intranet and helping plan all-hands meetings.
Build a portfolio

Keep samples of your work: staff newsletters, leadership emails, change announcements, intranet pages, event plans and survey results. Show how you shaped messages for different audiences and measured whether employees read and understood them. Hiring managers often ask to see these.
Time it takes

Moving from an entry role to internal communications manager usually takes about five to eight years. Along the way, people take on bigger projects such as mergers, reorganizations or policy rollouts, and start advising executives on what to say and when.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an internal communications manager?

Most employers expect a bachelor’s degree, usually in communications, public relations, journalism, English or marketing. It is not a legal requirement, though. People with degrees in other fields get hired when they have strong writing samples and several years of communications experience, often from journalism, HR or agency work.
Is there a certification for internal communications?

There is no required certification. Some professionals earn optional credentials such as the Accreditation in Public Relations (APR) or the Communication Management Professional (CMP). These can help show experience and judgment, but most hiring decisions rest on your portfolio, your track record with leadership messages and your years in communications roles.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in accounting, finance or business. Courses in auditing, financial accounting and accounting information systems matter most. A degree in information systems also works for those aiming at IT general controls testing.
First job

The usual entry point is a staff auditor role in a public accounting firm’s audit or risk advisory group. Others start as an internal audit associate or staff accountant at a public company, where they help document processes and test controls.
Learn the frameworks

On the job you learn SOX Section 404, the COSO Internal Control Integrated Framework and, if you work for an outside auditor, PCAOB standards. You practice walkthroughs, control design reviews, sample testing and writing up deficiencies.
Certifications

No license is required to do this work. Employers often prefer a CPA, a state license earned by passing the CPA exam, with education and experience rules that vary by state. The CIA from The Institute of Internal Auditors and the CISA from ISACA are also common.
Time it takes

After a four-year degree, most people spend two to four years in audit or accounting before holding a SOX or internal controls specialist title. Senior and manager roles usually follow after several more years of testing and leading compliance cycles.
qa: Do you need to be a CPA to work in SOX compliance?

No. There is no license required to design or test internal controls. Many employers still prefer or ask for a CPA, especially in public accounting. The CIA from The Institute of Internal Auditors is a common alternative for internal audit roles, and the CISA from ISACA is valued for IT controls work.
How long does it take to become a SOX specialist?

Most people need a four-year degree in accounting or a related field, then two to four years as a staff auditor, internal audit associate or staff accountant. That puts the usual path at about six to eight years from starting college, depending on the employer and any certifications earned along the way.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Coursework in math, basic accounting or computers helps. Some people earn an associate degree or certificate in supply chain management, logistics or business, but it is not required for most entry-level inventory roles.
First job

Many inventory specialists start as warehouse associates, stock clerks, receiving clerks or order pickers. These jobs teach how goods arrive, get stored and ship out, and how scanners and stock records work. Retail stockroom work is another common way in.
On-the-job training

Training is usually done at work. New hires learn cycle counting, receiving checks, reconciling counts with system records and finding the cause of shortages. Most also learn the company’s inventory or ERP software, handheld RF scanners and spreadsheet tools like Excel.
Forklift training

There is no state license for inventory work. If the job involves driving a forklift or other powered industrial truck, OSHA requires the employer to train and evaluate the operator before they drive. Many warehouse postings list forklift experience as a plus.
Optional certifications

Certifications are not required but can help with promotion. Options include the MSSC Certified Logistics Associate and Certified Logistics Technician for warehouse work, and the ASCM (formerly APICS) CPIM for people moving toward inventory planning or control roles.
Time it takes

Moving from a warehouse or stock clerk job into an inventory specialist role usually takes six months to two years. Accurate counting, attention to detail and comfort with inventory software are what usually earn the move.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an inventory specialist?

No. Most inventory specialist jobs require only a high school diploma or GED plus experience in a warehouse, stockroom or receiving area. An associate or bachelor’s degree in supply chain or business can help you move into inventory control, planning or management roles later, but employers mainly look for accuracy and software skills.
Is there a certification for inventory specialists?

There is no required license or certification. Optional credentials include the MSSC Certified Logistics Associate and Certified Logistics Technician, which cover warehouse and logistics basics, and the ASCM CPIM, which focuses on production and inventory planning. If you will drive a forklift, OSHA requires your employer to train and evaluate you first.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree. Common fields are criminal justice, accounting, finance, business or law. Accounting helps for financial fraud work, while criminal justice or law suits misconduct and abuse cases. Courses in interviewing, evidence and report writing are useful in any field.
Related first job

Few people start as investigators. Common ways in are fraud analyst, insurance claims adjuster, compliance analyst, auditor, loss prevention officer, HR generalist or police officer. Military police and federal agency work also lead here. These jobs teach evidence handling, interviewing and clear written reports.
State license

Most states require a private investigator license for people who investigate for hire through an agency. Rules usually include a background check, an exam and documented experience. In-house investigators who work only for their own employer are often exempt. Requirements vary by state, so check your state’s licensing board.
Professional certification

Certification is not legally required, but many employers value it. The Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) from the ACFE is the best known for fraud work. ASIS International offers the Professional Certified Investigator (PCI). Both require passing an exam and having relevant work experience.
Time it takes

Expect usually two to five years after a bachelor’s degree. That time goes to a related first job where you build case experience. Certification and any state license often come during or after those years, since both usually require proof of experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be an investigations specialist?

It depends on who you work for. Most states require a private investigator license if you investigate for clients through an agency. If you work in-house for one company, such as in compliance, HR or a fraud team, you usually do not need a state license. Rules vary by state, so check with your state’s licensing board.
How long does it take to become a fraud investigator?

Most people take about two to five years after a bachelor’s degree. They usually start in a related role, such as fraud analyst, auditor, claims adjuster or police officer, and build case experience there. Many then earn the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential, which requires passing an exam and showing relevant work experience.

steps: Education

Most employers want a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, accounting, or a related field. Math, statistics, and engineering majors also get hired if they learn accounting and valuation. Focus on reading financial statements, building spreadsheet models, and writing clear summaries of a company or market.
Internships

Many analyst jobs are filled from summer internships taken before the final year of college. Investment banks, asset managers, and research firms often make full-time offers to their interns. Finance clubs, investment competitions, and networking with alumni help you get noticed.
First job

The usual entry point is a junior analyst role at an investment bank, asset manager, research firm, or a company’s finance team. You build financial models, value companies, research industries, and prepare reports and pitch materials for senior staff who make the final decisions.
Licensing exams

There is no state license for the analyst title itself. Roles at broker-dealers usually need FINRA registration. Anyone 18 or older can take the SIE alone, but exams such as the Series 7 or Series 86 and 87 need firm sponsorship. Some roles also need state-law exams like the NASAA Series 63 or 65, depending on the job and state.
CFA charter

The CFA charter from CFA Institute is not required by law but is widely respected, especially in asset management and research. You must pass three levels of exams and complete qualifying work experience. Many analysts study for it while working, and the full process usually takes several years.
Time it takes

Expect about four years of college, then two to three years as an analyst before promotion to associate. Moving into private equity, portfolio management, or investor relations often takes several more years, and some people complete an MBA along the way.
qa: Do you need a license to be an investment analyst?

Not always. Many analysts at asset managers or in corporate finance need no license. Analysts at broker-dealers often must register with FINRA, which can mean the SIE plus exams like the Series 7 or Series 86 and 87. Some roles also require state-law exams such as the Series 63 or 65. Your employer will tell you which ones apply.
Do you need a CFA to become an investment analyst?

No. The CFA charter is optional, and many people get analyst jobs with only a bachelor’s degree. It is valued by employers, especially in asset management and equity research, and can help with promotions. Earning it means passing three exam levels from CFA Institute and completing qualifying work experience, so most people pursue it after they start working.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most analysts hold a bachelor’s degree, often in finance, economics, accounting or business. Banks also hire math, engineering and other majors with strong grades. Courses in corporate finance, accounting and valuation help, and many students teach themselves Excel financial modeling before recruiting starts.
Summer analyst internship

The main way in is a summer analyst internship, usually after junior year. Recruiting often starts a year or more ahead, through networking, applications and technical interviews on accounting, valuation and deal concepts. Many full-time analyst offers go to former summer interns.
FINRA exams

Analysts who work on securities deals must be registered with FINRA through their firm. That usually means passing the SIE exam, which anyone can take, and the Series 79, which requires firm sponsorship. Some firms also require the Series 63. Firms typically schedule these exams soon after hiring.
Firm training

New analysts usually begin with several weeks of firm training on financial modeling, accounting and deal processes. After that, learning happens on live deals, building models, pitch books and due diligence materials under associates and vice presidents. Long hours are common.
Time it takes

Expect about four years of college, including the internship, before starting as a full-time analyst. The analyst role itself typically lasts two to three years before promotion to associate, a move to private equity or corporate finance, or graduate school such as an MBA.
First job

For most people, the full-time analyst job is the first job out of college. Career changers often come from accounting firm transaction advisory work, corporate finance or consulting, or enter later as an associate after earning an MBA.
qa: Do you need a license to be an investment banking analyst?

There is no state license, but analysts who work on securities transactions must be registered with FINRA through their firm. Most pass the SIE exam and the Series 79, and some firms also require the Series 63. The Series 79 needs firm sponsorship, so you usually take it after you are hired.
Can you become an investment banking analyst without a finance degree?

Yes. Banks hire majors in economics, math, engineering, accounting and the liberal arts. What matters most is strong grades, a relevant internship, and the ability to answer technical questions on accounting, valuation and financial modeling. Non-finance majors usually close the gap with extra coursework, self-study and networking.

steps: Education

Most investor relations professionals hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting, economics or communications, and many add an MBA. The job needs both sides: reading financial statements and valuation models, and writing clear earnings releases, call scripts and presentations.
First job

Few people start in investor relations. Common ways in are sell-side equity research, buy-side analysis, financial planning and analysis, corporate finance, investment banking or financial communications. Some public companies and IR agencies hire IR analysts or associates early in their careers.
Rules to learn

IR teams work within SEC rules. Learn Regulation FD, which bars sharing material nonpublic information with selected investors or analysts before the public, plus the main filings such as the 10-K, 10-Q and 8-K, insider trading rules, quiet periods and how earnings guidance works.
Certification

There is no license for investor relations. The National Investor Relations Institute (NIRI) offers the Investor Relations Charter (IRC), an optional credential earned by passing an exam. Some IR professionals also hold the CFA charter, which helps when talking with analysts.
Time it takes

Most IR managers have several years in finance, research or communications before taking the role, often with some time as an IR analyst or associate. Heading IR at a public company usually takes longer and close work with the CFO.
qa: How do you get into investor relations?

Most people move in after several years in a related field, such as equity research, corporate finance, financial planning and analysis, investment banking or financial communications. Some start as IR analysts or associates at public companies or IR agencies. Knowing SEC rules like Regulation FD and explaining financial results clearly matter most.
What certification is there for investor relations?

The main one is the Investor Relations Charter (IRC) from the National Investor Relations Institute (NIRI), earned by passing an exam. It is optional, and there is no license for investor relations work. Some IR professionals also hold the CFA charter, which builds credibility with analysts and portfolio managers.

steps: Education

Many iOS developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field, which usually takes four years. A degree is common but not required. Employers mostly care whether you can build and ship working apps.
Learn Swift and Xcode

Learn Swift, Xcode and Apple’s frameworks such as SwiftUI and UIKit. Study data storage, networking, testing and Apple’s App Store Review Guidelines. Apple’s free documentation, tutorials and sample code are the standard starting point.
Build a portfolio

Build two or three complete apps and publish at least one on the App Store through the Apple Developer Program. Share your code on GitHub. A shipped app proves you can take a project from idea to release.
No license required

There is no state license, exam or required certification for iOS developers in the US. Hiring is based on your portfolio, technical interviews and coding exercises, which often include Swift questions and a small take-home app.
Time it takes

Most people need one to two years of focused study and practice to become hireable without a degree. Graduates with a computer science degree usually add several months of iOS projects. Internships during school can shorten the path.
First job

The usual first role is junior iOS developer, mobile developer or software engineering intern. Some people start in QA testing, web development or app support, then move onto an iOS team once they show Swift skills.
qa: Do you need a degree to be an iOS developer?

No. Many iOS developers have a computer science or related degree, but it is not required and there is no license. Self-taught developers get hired when they can show published App Store apps, clean Swift code on GitHub and pass technical interviews. Some larger employers still list a bachelor’s degree as preferred.
How long does it take to become an iOS developer?

Most people take one to two years of steady study and project work to land a first iOS job without a degree. A four-year computer science degree plus a few months of iOS projects is another common path. Shipping a real app and doing an internship usually speeds things up.

steps: Education

Most IT managers hold a bachelor’s degree in information technology, computer science, information systems or a related field. Some employers accept an associate degree or strong experience instead. A degree in business with technical coursework also works, and some managers later add a master’s degree such as an MBA.
First job

Most people start in a hands-on role such as help desk technician, IT support specialist or desktop support technician. There you learn to manage laptops, user accounts, password resets, software installs and basic networking while working tickets for real users.
Technical experience

The next step is usually a role like systems administrator, network administrator or IT specialist. You take ownership of servers, cloud accounts, backups, security settings and vendor software. Leading small projects or training newer staff shows you are ready to supervise.
Certifications

No license is required, but many employers value certifications. Common ones are CompTIA A+, Network+ and Security+, Microsoft or cloud provider certifications, ITIL 4 Foundation for IT service management, and PMP for project management. Security-focused managers may pursue CISSP, which requires several years of experience.
Management skills

Moving up means learning budgeting, vendor contracts, software license tracking, hiring and staff scheduling. Many people gain this as a team lead or IT supervisor before taking a full manager title. Clear writing and explaining technology to non-technical leaders matter as much as technical skill.
Time it takes

Expect a four-year degree followed by usually five or more years of IT work before reaching manager. At small companies a strong generalist may step up sooner. Larger organizations often expect more years and prior supervisory experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be an IT manager?

No. There is no state or federal license for IT managers in the US. Employers instead look for a relevant degree, several years of hands-on IT experience and often certifications such as CompTIA Security+, ITIL 4 Foundation or PMP. Some government or defense jobs require specific security certifications or a security clearance.
How long does it take to become an IT manager?

Most people need about eight to ten years in total. That usually means a four-year bachelor’s degree plus five or more years in roles like help desk, desktop support or systems administration. Experience leading projects or supervising staff can shorten the path, especially at smaller companies with lean IT teams.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in information technology, computer science, information systems or business. A degree is not legally required, and some people move up from technical roles without one, but many postings list it as a baseline.
First job in IT

Few people start as IT project managers. The usual way in is a technical or support role such as help desk, systems administrator, developer, business analyst or project coordinator, where you learn how systems, rollouts and migrations actually work.
Entry certifications

No state license exists for this work. Early on, many people earn the CAPM from PMI or CompTIA Project+ to show they know project basics. Agile credentials such as Certified ScrumMaster are also common on software projects.
PMP certification

The PMP from PMI is the credential employers ask for most. It requires 36 months of experience leading projects in the past eight years with a four-year degree, or 60 months without one, plus 35 hours of project management education and a passing exam score.
Time it takes

Expect several years. A degree usually takes four years, and most people then spend a few years in IT or coordinator roles before leading projects on their own. Earning the PMP adds at least three more years of project experience.
First project manager job

A common first step is project coordinator or junior project manager, often handling smaller internal projects such as a software upgrade. Many people get promoted inside the company where they already work, after taking on parts of projects informally.
qa: Do you need a certification to be an IT project manager?

No license or certification is legally required. Many employers still prefer or require one, most often the PMP from PMI. People earlier in their careers often start with the CAPM or CompTIA Project+, and agile roles may ask for Certified ScrumMaster or a similar Scrum credential.
How long does it take to become an IT project manager?

It usually takes several years. Most people earn a degree, then work a few years in IT support, development, analysis or coordination before managing projects. The PMP requires 36 months of project leadership experience with a four-year degree, or 60 months without one, so senior roles often come later.

steps: Education

Many employers hire with a high school diploma plus proven skills. Others prefer a certificate or associate degree in information technology or computer support. A bachelor’s degree in IT or computer science helps with later promotion but is rarely required for entry-level support.
Certifications

No state license exists for this work. Employers often ask for CompTIA A+, which covers hardware, operating systems, troubleshooting and basic security over two exams. CompTIA Network+ and Security+ are common next steps. ITIL 4 Foundation shows you understand service desk processes.
Hands-on practice

Build a small home lab. Set up a PC, install Windows and Linux, configure a router, and practice managing user accounts and permissions. Volunteering, campus tech jobs or internships give you real support tickets to describe on a resume.
First job

Most people start as a help desk or Tier 1 support technician. You answer calls and tickets, reset passwords, set up laptops and printers, and escalate harder problems. Desktop support technician is another common way in.
Time it takes

A beginner can usually prepare for CompTIA A+ in one to three months. A certificate or associate degree takes six months to two years. Moving from help desk into a full IT support specialist role often takes one to two years on the job.
qa: Do you need a degree to become an IT support specialist?

No. Many entry-level IT support jobs accept a high school diploma when you can show skills through certifications like CompTIA A+ and hands-on experience. Some employers prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree in IT, and a degree can help later when you move toward system administration or management.
What certification should you get first for IT support?

CompTIA A+ is the most common first certification for IT support. It covers hardware, operating systems, networking basics, security and troubleshooting, and it requires passing two exams. Many people add CompTIA Network+ or Security+ after landing a help desk job to move into higher support roles.

steps: Education

No license is required. Many ITSM professionals hold a degree in information technology, information systems or business, but plenty start without one and learn on the job. Knowing how IT support, change control and service catalogs work matters most.
First job

Most people start at the IT service desk or help desk, handling tickets and following incident and request processes. From there they move into roles such as incident manager, problem manager, change coordinator or ServiceNow administrator.
ITIL certification

ITIL is the most widely used framework for IT service management. The ITIL 4 Foundation certification is the usual first step, and many employers ask for it. More advanced ITIL modules cover topics such as service design, operations and strategy.
Platform skills

Much ITSM work runs in ServiceNow, which offers its own certifications, such as Certified System Administrator and Certified Implementation Specialist. Jira Service Management is another common tool. Learning workflows, reporting and basic scripting helps you configure them.
Process ownership

With experience, people take on process ownership: designing how incidents, changes, problems and requests flow, setting service level agreements and running reports. Some move into ITSM consulting or platform development, building and configuring the ticket system for other teams.
Time it takes

Help desk jobs often require basic IT skills and sometimes an entry certification such as CompTIA A+. ITIL 4 Foundation usually takes a few weeks of study. Moving into a process manager or ServiceNow administrator role usually takes one to three years.
qa: What certification do you need for IT service management?

No certification is legally required, but ITIL 4 Foundation is the one employers ask for most in ITSM roles. People who configure the ticket system often add ServiceNow certifications, such as Certified System Administrator. Experienced process managers may take advanced ITIL modules. Most start at a help desk, where they learn incident and request handling first.
How long does it take to get into ITSM?

Many people start at an IT help desk with no prior experience and learn incident and request handling there. With ITIL 4 Foundation, which usually takes a few weeks to study for, and one to three years of service desk work, they often move into roles such as incident manager, change coordinator or ServiceNow administrator.

steps: Education

No diploma is required for most janitor and cleaner jobs, though some employers prefer a high school diploma or GED. Reliability, attention to detail and the physical ability to stand, lift and move equipment for a full shift matter most.
First job

Most people start as a janitor, custodian, housekeeper, porter or cleaning crew member with a contract cleaning firm, school, hospital, hotel or building owner. Night and early morning shifts are common, which makes these jobs easier to fit around school or family.
On-the-job training

Training usually takes a few days to a few weeks. You learn cleaning chemicals and safe dilution, floor care machines, restroom and trash routines, and building security. Employers must train you on chemical hazards and safety data sheets under OSHA’s Hazard Communication Standard.
Healthcare and special cleaning

Cleaners in hospitals and clinics learn infection control and, if exposed to blood, receive OSHA bloodborne pathogens training. Environmental services workers can later earn the CHESP from the Association for the Health Care Environment. Carpet and restoration technicians often earn IICRC certifications.
Licensing and business

There is no state license for janitors or cleaners. Some jobs at schools, airports or government buildings require a background check. People who start their own cleaning business usually need a local business license, insurance and often a bond.
Time it takes

You can usually start within days of applying. Moving up to lead cleaner or supervisor often takes one to three years. Optional industry certificates, such as those offered by ISSA, can help with supervisor and manager roles.
qa: Can you become a janitor without experience?

Yes. Most janitor and cleaner jobs are entry level, and employers train new staff on the job within days or weeks. They look for reliability, attention to detail and the ability to do physical work for a full shift. Some jobs require a background check, and employers must train you on chemical safety.
Do you need a license to be a janitor or cleaner?

No. There is no state license for janitors or cleaners. Employers must give OSHA chemical hazard training, and hospital cleaners exposed to blood receive bloodborne pathogens training. If you run your own cleaning business, you usually need a local business license, liability insurance and often a bond. Optional certificates from industry groups can help with promotion.

steps: Education

Many Java developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. Employers often list a degree, but some hire people who learned through community college courses, bootcamps or self-study if they can show strong coding skills.
Core Java skills

Learn Java itself: object-oriented design, collections, exceptions, concurrency and testing with JUnit. Then learn the server tools employers expect, such as the Spring framework, SQL databases, REST APIs, Maven or Gradle, and Git for version control.
Portfolio projects

Build a few working server applications, such as a REST API backed by a database, and publish the code in a public repository. Hiring managers use these projects to judge your skills, especially if you have no degree or prior job.
Optional certification

No license or certification is required to work as a Java developer in the US. Some people take Oracle’s Java SE certification exams, such as Oracle Certified Professional: Java SE Developer, to show their knowledge, but employers rarely demand it.
Time it takes

Most people need two to four years to become job ready. That includes a four-year degree for many, or one to two years of focused self-study and project work for career changers who already have some technical background.
First job

The usual entry point is a junior or associate software developer role, often on a team maintaining existing Java systems. Internships, QA or test automation roles, and support engineering jobs are also common ways in.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a Java developer?

No law requires a degree, and there is no license for this work. Many employers, especially banks and large companies, prefer a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field. Others will hire candidates without one if they show solid Java skills through projects, internships or prior work in a related technical role.
How long does it take to become a Java developer?

It usually takes two to four years. Students often finish a four-year computer science degree with internship experience. Career changers who study full time and build portfolio projects can sometimes reach a junior role in one to two years. Becoming a senior developer typically takes several more years of on-the-job experience.

steps: Education

No license or specific degree is required. Some JavaScript developers hold a computer science degree, while many learned through bootcamps, community college courses or self-study. Start with programming basics, HTML and CSS, then JavaScript and TypeScript.
Language skills

Learn modern JavaScript in depth: scope, closures, the event loop, promises, async/await and modules. Then add TypeScript’s type system, which many professional teams now use. Git, testing, package managers and browser developer tools are everyday skills.
Choose a focus

JavaScript runs both in the browser and on servers. Pick a focus: front end with a framework such as React, Angular or Vue, back end with Node.js, or full stack with both. Each path adds its own tools, databases or design skills.
Portfolio

Build and deploy several complete projects that show both clean code and a working product, and publish the code publicly. Small open-source contributions, such as fixing a bug in a library you use, show you can work in someone else’s codebase.
First job

Common first jobs are junior front-end developer, junior web developer, junior full-stack developer or junior software engineer. Some people move in from web design, QA testing, technical support or content management roles where they already edited websites.
Time it takes

Self-taught developers and career changers often land a first job after one to two years of steady practice. A computer science degree takes about four years. Reaching mid-level usually takes two to four more years of professional work.
qa: How long does it take to become a JavaScript developer?

Most career changers need one to two years of steady study and project work to get a first junior JavaScript job. A computer science degree takes about four years. You can learn the basics of the language in a few months, but employers expect solid TypeScript, a framework and a portfolio of deployed projects.
What certification helps a JavaScript developer?

No certification is required, and most US employers do not ask for one. Hiring is based on coding interviews, take-home projects and your public code. Some optional certificates exist from course providers, but a portfolio of deployed apps and contributions to real codebases usually carries far more weight with employers.

steps: Education

Most junior engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. Others come from a different degree, an intensive coding program or self-study. Employers mainly want proof you can program, use data structures and algorithms, and work with tools like Git.
No license required

Software engineering has no state license, registration or required exam in the US. Vendor certifications, such as cloud platform credentials, are optional and rarely required for entry-level roles. Your skills, projects and interview performance matter far more than any credential.
Portfolio and internships

Build a few real projects you can show on a public code repository, and contribute to open-source work if you can. Internships, co-op programs and part-time coding work are the strongest signal for employers and often lead directly to a full-time offer.
Technical interviews

Hiring usually includes coding challenges, live problem-solving and questions about your past projects. Many candidates spend several weeks to a few months practicing algorithm problems and explaining their reasoning out loud before applying widely.
Time it takes

A computer science degree usually takes four years. Career changers often need six months to two years of focused study and project work. The job search itself can take several months, especially when entry-level openings are scarce.
First job

Common first titles include junior software engineer, associate developer and software engineer I. Some people start in related roles such as QA tester, technical support or IT, then move into development. Expect a mentor, code reviews and smaller tasks at first.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a junior software engineer?

No law requires one, but many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field. People without a degree do get hired, usually by showing strong projects, open-source contributions, internship experience or work in a related technical role. Without a degree, expect your portfolio and interviews to carry more weight.
How long does it take to become a junior software engineer?

Through a computer science degree, it usually takes about four years, often with one or more internships along the way. Self-taught learners and career changers commonly take six months to two years to build enough skill and projects. Add time for the job search, which can stretch several months.

steps: Education

Most kernel engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, computer engineering or electrical engineering. Courses in operating systems, computer architecture, compilers and concurrency matter most. Some virtualization and research teams prefer a master’s degree, but it is rarely required.
Core systems skills

Learn C deeply, plus enough assembly to read what the compiler produces. Study memory management, scheduling, interrupts and locking. Practice with a debugger, kernel tracing tools and a virtual machine such as QEMU, so a crash does not take down your own computer.
Open source patches

There is no license, exam or required certification for this work. Employers look at code instead. Many people get in by sending small fixes to the Linux kernel or another open source operating system and learning to work through public code review on mailing lists.
First job

Few people are hired straight into core kernel work. Common first jobs are embedded or firmware engineer, device driver developer, systems software engineer, or a test and validation role on a hardware or platform team. These roles build the low-level debugging habits kernel teams expect.
Time it takes

Expect a four-year degree, then usually two to five years in related systems roles before working mainly on kernel, driver or hypervisor code. A strong record of accepted open source patches can shorten that path.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a kernel engineer?

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer science, computer engineering or a related field. It is not legally required, and some engineers get in through embedded work and accepted open source patches instead. Without a degree, a public record of kernel or driver contributions is usually what convinces a hiring team.
Is there a certification for kernel and operating systems engineers?

No standard license or certification exists for kernel or operating systems engineering in the US. Common Linux certifications cover system administration, not kernel development, so they carry little weight for these roles. Employers judge candidates on C skill, knowledge of operating system internals, and code they can review, such as merged patches.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing, communications or a field tied to the product, such as engineering or life sciences for technical sales. No law requires a degree, and some companies accept a strong sales record instead.
First job in sales

Almost no one starts as a key account manager. The usual way in is an entry-level sales or customer role, such as sales development representative, inside sales representative, account coordinator or customer success associate, where you learn the product, the pipeline and the customers.
Smaller accounts first

Next comes a role as account executive or account manager handling a larger book of smaller or mid-size customers. Here you build the record employers look for: renewals kept, revenue grown, contracts negotiated and relationships held over several years.
Industry licenses

Key account management has no license of its own. Some industries add one. Selling insurance needs a state insurance producer license, and selling securities usually requires FINRA registration exams such as the SIE and Series 7. Requirements vary by state and product.
Skills and training

Certifications are optional. What helps more is training in negotiation, account planning and CRM software, plus deep knowledge of the industry you sell into. Many companies train new key account managers on their own process and largest customers after hiring.
Time it takes

Most people reach a key account manager title after three to seven years in sales or account management. Moving up within one company, where you already know the customers and products, is often faster than being hired into the role from outside.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a key account manager?

No law requires one, but most employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing or a field related to the product. Many companies will hire people without a degree if they have several years of proven sales results, especially when they are promoted from within after handling smaller accounts well.
How long does it take to become a key account manager?

It usually takes three to seven years. Most people spend one to three years in an entry-level sales or customer role, then a few years managing a book of smaller accounts. Once they show they can keep and grow important customers, they move up to key accounts.

steps: Education

No license or specific degree is required. Many Kotlin developers studied computer science, and many others came from Java or learned on their own. Learn programming fundamentals, object-oriented and functional ideas, and Kotlin features such as null safety, data classes and coroutines.
Android or server path

Most Kotlin work is Android apps, built with the Android SDK, Jetpack Compose and Android Studio. The other path is back-end services on the Java Virtual Machine, using frameworks such as Spring Boot or Ktor. Pick one path first and go deep.
Portfolio

For Android, build and publish one or two apps to the Play Store, with networking, local storage and tests. For back-end work, build and deploy a service with a database and API. Share the code publicly so employers can review it.
Moving from Java

Many Kotlin developers start as Java developers and switch, since Kotlin runs on the same platform and works with Java code. Knowing Java helps with older Android codebases and many back-end systems, and employers often list both languages together.
First job

The usual first job is junior Android developer, junior mobile developer or junior back-end engineer. Some start in QA testing for mobile apps or as Java developers on a team moving to Kotlin, then take on Kotlin work.
Time it takes

A computer science degree takes about four years. Career changers often need one to two years of steady study and app building to land a first Android job. Experienced Java developers can usually become productive in Kotlin within a few months.
qa: How long does it take to become a Kotlin developer?

Starting from zero, plan on one to two years of steady study and project work to land a junior Android or back-end role, or about four years through a computer science degree. If you already know Java, you can usually become productive in Kotlin within a few months, since both run on the same platform.
Is there a certification for Kotlin or Android developers?

No certification is required for Kotlin or Android jobs in the US. Employers judge candidates on published apps, public code, take-home projects and technical interviews. Cloud certifications can help for back-end Kotlin roles, but a working app in the Play Store usually says more to a hiring manager than any certificate.

steps: Education

No license or set degree is required. Many people hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information technology or a related field. Employers also hire people who learned through self-study or on the job. What matters most is solid skill with Linux, networking and scripting.
First job

Few people start as Kubernetes engineers. The usual way in is a role such as Linux system administrator, IT support, software developer or junior DevOps engineer. There you learn servers, networking, build pipelines and how production systems break.
Hands-on practice

Build your own clusters on a laptop or in a cloud account. Learn to package applications into container images, write deployment manifests, use Helm, and set up monitoring and CI/CD pipelines. A public code repository showing this work helps prove your skills.
Certifications

Certifications are optional but widely recognized. The CNCF offers the CKA (Certified Kubernetes Administrator) for running clusters, the CKAD (Certified Kubernetes Application Developer) for deploying applications, and the CKS for security. These are hands-on, performance-based exams taken online.
Time it takes

Expect several years. People often move into a Kubernetes-focused role after two to five years in operations or development work. The move can be faster if your current job already has you running containers in production.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a Kubernetes engineer?

No. There is no license or required certification. Employers mainly look for hands-on experience running workloads in production. Still, the CNCF’s CKA, which covers cluster administration and troubleshooting, and the CKAD, which covers designing and deploying applications on Kubernetes, are well known. They can help your resume stand out, especially early in your career.
How long does it take to become a Kubernetes engineer?

Most people take several years. A common path is two to five years as a system administrator, developer or DevOps engineer, followed by a move into Kubernetes work. Preparing for a certification such as the CKA usually takes a few weeks to a few months on top of that, depending on your Linux background.

steps: Education

Most research labs ask for a bachelor’s degree in biology, chemistry, biochemistry or a related science. Some technician roles accept an associate degree in biotechnology or laboratory science. Research associate roles often prefer a bachelor’s with lab experience or a master’s degree.
Hands-on lab experience

Employers want proof you can work at the bench. Undergraduate research, lab courses, internships, co-ops and work-study jobs in campus labs all count. Learn pipetting, solution prep, sterile technique, basic instruments and careful notebook records.
Safety training

There is no general license for research lab work. Employers train new hires in chemical hygiene under the OSHA Laboratory Standard, bloodborne pathogens, biosafety and waste handling. Shipping samples may require dangerous goods training. Animal work often adds AALAS certification such as ALAT or LAT.
Clinical lab exception

Labs that test patient samples are different. Some states, including California and New York, license clinical laboratory personnel, and many employers expect ASCP certification such as MLT or MLS. Requirements vary by state, so check before moving into clinical work.
First job

The usual way in is a lab assistant, lab technician or research technician job, often in a university, hospital research lab or biotech company. You prepare reagents, maintain equipment, track samples and run routine assays under a scientist’s supervision.
Time it takes

Expect about two to four years of schooling for an entry technician role. Moving up to research associate usually takes one to three more years of lab experience, or a master’s degree, plus skill with specific methods your field uses.
qa: Do you need a license to be a lab technician?

For research labs, no. There is no general license for research technicians or research associates, and employers train you in safety on the job. Clinical labs that test patient samples are different. Some states license clinical laboratory personnel, and many employers expect ASCP certification. Requirements vary by state.
How long does it take to become a research associate?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree in a life or physical science. Many then work one to three years as a lab or research technician before taking a research associate title. A master’s degree can shorten that path, since some employers accept it in place of extra experience.

steps: Engineering degree

Most launch engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in aerospace, mechanical or electrical engineering, often from an ABET-accredited program. Courses in fluid systems, thermodynamics, controls and instrumentation help most. Some launch technicians enter with an associate degree or military experience in place of an engineering degree.
Hands-on rocket work

Employers look for people who have built and tested real hardware. Students join rocketry or satellite teams, take internships or co-ops on test stands and launch sites, and learn to wire sensors, read piping diagrams and write test procedures.
Export rules and clearance

Many roles fall under ITAR export rules, so employers often require applicants to be US persons. That category includes citizens, lawful permanent residents and certain protected individuals such as refugees and asylees. Some defense or government missions also require a security clearance, which the employer sponsors.
No license, employer training

No state license is required for this work, and a PE license is rarely expected. Instead, employers train and certify new hires on their own procedures, including high-pressure systems, cryogenic and hazardous propellants, and specific console positions used during countdown.
First job

People usually start as test engineers, ground support equipment engineers, propulsion or fluids engineers, or launch technicians. They work on vehicle processing, propellant loading and recovery operations before moving to a console seat in the launch control room.
Time it takes
Expect about four years for the degree. After that, it often takes several more years of test and launch campaigns before someone leads a console position or becomes a launch conductor.
qa: Do you need a license to be a launch engineer?

No. There is no state license for launch engineering, and most employers do not require a PE license. Instead, companies certify workers on their own procedures and console positions. Many jobs do require being a US person under ITAR export rules, and some government or defense missions require a security clearance.
How long does it take to become a launch engineer?

Most people spend about four years earning an engineering degree, often with internships or student rocketry along the way. They then start in a test, fluids or ground support role. Reaching a lead console position or launch conductor role usually takes several more years of hands-on campaign experience.

steps: Basic requirements

Most police departments require US citizenship, a minimum age of 21 (some accept 18 or 19), a high school diploma or GED, a valid driver’s license and a clean record. Many agencies prefer some college, and some require a two-year or four-year degree, often in criminal justice.
Hiring process

Applicants usually pass a written exam, a physical fitness test, a background investigation, an oral board interview, a psychological evaluation and a medical exam. Many agencies add a polygraph. The whole process often takes several months, so many people apply to more than one agency.
Police academy

New hires attend a state-approved police academy, which usually lasts about four to six months. Training covers state law, use of force, firearms, defensive tactics, emergency driving and first aid. In some states people can pay their own way through an academy before being hired.
State certification

Each state sets officer standards through a board often called Peace Officer Standards and Training, or POST. In most states, academy graduates must pass a state exam to be certified as a sworn officer, and yearly in-service training keeps the certification. Requirements vary by state.
Field training

After the academy, new officers usually spend several months riding with an experienced field training officer, then serve a probation period that often lasts one year. Federal agents follow separate federal hiring rules and train at federal academies instead of state ones.
Company and civilian roles

Company roles that answer police requests, subpoenas and court orders need no police certification. Employers often hire former officers, investigators, paralegals or compliance staff, and expect knowledge of warrants, subpoenas, privacy laws and how evidence must be handled for court.
qa: How long does it take to become a police officer?

Usually about six months to a year from application to working alone on patrol. The hiring process often takes a few months, the academy usually four to six months, and field training several more months. Most new officers then serve a probation period, often one year, before the job becomes permanent.
What is POST certification for police officers?

POST stands for Peace Officer Standards and Training. Each state has a board or commission, often called POST, that sets minimum hiring and training standards, approves academies and certifies officers. You usually complete an approved academy and, in most states, pass a state exam. Officers keep certification through in-service training, and rules vary by state.

steps: Bachelor’s degree
