Law schools accept any major. Common choices include political science, history, English, economics and business. Strong grades and clear writing matter more than the subject. A bachelor’s degree usually takes four years of full-time study.
Law school

Most applicants take the LSAT, though some ABA-approved law schools also accept the GRE. You then earn a Juris Doctor (JD), usually in three years of full-time study. Courses in contracts, business associations and regulation, plus legal clinics or summer internships, prepare you for advising a company.
Bar exam and license

You must pass the bar exam in the state where you will practice. Many states use the Uniform Bar Exam (UBE). Nearly all states also require the MPRE ethics exam and a character and fitness review. Requirements vary by state, and most states require continuing legal education to keep the license.
First job

Most in-house lawyers start as associates at law firms, often in corporate, commercial, litigation or regulatory practice. Others begin as attorneys in government agencies. Some companies hire new law graduates directly, but most legal counsel postings ask for prior practice experience.
Time it takes

Expect about seven years of school after high school, plus several months to prepare for and pass the bar. Most people then spend two to five years in practice before moving into a legal counsel role at a company.
qa: Do you need to be a lawyer to be legal counsel?

Yes. Legal counsel gives legal advice, so you must be a licensed attorney in good standing. That means a JD and passing a state bar exam. Many states let lawyers licensed in another state work in-house for one employer through registered in-house counsel rules. Requirements vary by state.
How long does it take to become legal counsel?

Usually about seven years after high school: four years for a bachelor’s degree and three for a JD, followed by the bar exam. Most companies then want two to five years of experience, often at a law firm or government agency, before hiring someone as legal counsel.

steps: College and LSAT

Law school requires a bachelor’s degree in any major. Most applicants take the Law School Admission Test (LSAT), and many schools also accept the GRE. Strong grades, writing and reasoning skills matter more than the major itself.
Law school

Most lawyers earn a Juris Doctor (JD) from an ABA-accredited law school, which takes three years full time or about four years part time. Legal writing courses, clinics and journals build the skills employers look for in interns.
Internships

Law students usually intern after the first year with judges, government agencies, public interest groups or companies. After the second year, many work as summer associates at law firms, which often leads to a job offer. Many states let supervised students appear in court under student practice rules.
Bar exam

To practice, you must pass a state bar exam, which in many states is the Uniform Bar Exam. Nearly all states also require the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination (MPRE) on legal ethics and a character and fitness review.
First job

New lawyers usually start as junior associates at law firms, as judicial law clerks, or in government and public interest roles. Few go straight in-house; most corporate legal teams hire lawyers after a few years at a firm, though some run trainee or fellowship programs.
Time it takes

Expect about seven years after high school: four years of college, three years of law school, then a bar exam a few months after graduation. A few states, such as California and Virginia, let people qualify through supervised study in a law office instead of law school.
qa: How long does it take to become a lawyer?

Usually about seven years after high school. That means a four-year bachelor’s degree, three years of full-time law school for a Juris Doctor (JD), and passing a state bar exam, usually taken a few months after graduating. Part-time law school takes about four years, which adds a year.
Can law students practice law as interns?

Only under supervision. Most states have student practice rules that let law students, usually after finishing part of law school, represent clients in court or before agencies under a licensed lawyer’s supervision. Without that certification, legal interns can research, draft and assist, but cannot give legal advice or appear in court on their own.

steps: Education

Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in finance, business, economics or accounting, especially for commercial lending. Some banks and mortgage companies hire people with a high school diploma and sales or customer service experience, then train them on the job.
First job

Many people start as a bank teller, loan processor, loan officer assistant or credit analyst. These roles teach loan documents, underwriting basics and how lenders judge credit, income and collateral before you handle your own borrowers.
Pre-licensing education

Mortgage loan originators who work for nonbank lenders must complete at least 20 hours of NMLS-approved pre-licensing education under the federal SAFE Act. The course covers federal law, ethics and nontraditional mortgage lending. Some states add their own required hours.
Exam and state license

Next comes the SAFE Mortgage Loan Originator Test, a national exam with uniform state content. You then apply for a license in each state where you will originate loans, with fingerprints, a background check and a credit report. Licensed originators complete continuing education every year.
Bank registration

Mortgage originators employed by banks and credit unions register through the NMLS instead of getting a state license. Commercial, consumer and auto loan officers usually need no license at all. Employers train them in credit analysis and lending policy instead.
Time it takes

A new mortgage loan originator can often finish education, pass the exam and get licensed within a few months. Commercial loan officers usually spend two to four years after a degree in credit analyst or training roles before managing their own loans.
qa: Do you need a license to be a loan officer?

It depends on the loan type. Mortgage loan originators at nonbank lenders need a state license through the NMLS, which requires pre-licensing education, the SAFE MLO Test and a background check. Mortgage originators at banks and credit unions register with the NMLS instead. Commercial, consumer and auto loan officers usually need no license.
How long does it take to become a mortgage loan officer?

Many people finish the 20 hours of required education, pass the SAFE Mortgage Loan Originator Test and receive a state license within a few months. Timing depends on state rules, background check processing and whether you already work at a lender. Building a steady base of borrowers usually takes longer.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in biology, chemistry, biochemistry, physics or a related science. Lab courses, statistics and math matter. Hands-on undergraduate research in a faculty lab is often what gets you your first hire.
First job

The usual way in is a role as a research assistant, lab technician or research associate. You prepare samples, run experiments, keep careful lab notebooks and follow safety and quality rules under a senior scientist.
Graduate degree

To lead your own projects, most employers expect a master’s degree or a PhD. A PhD usually takes five to six years and includes original research and a dissertation. A master’s often takes about two years.
Postdoctoral training

PhD holders aiming for academic or senior industry research often spend two to five years as postdoctoral researchers. They build publications, grant experience and specialized skills before applying for scientist or faculty positions.
Licenses and certificates

Research scientists generally need no state license. Clinical laboratory work is different. Some states license clinical laboratory scientists, and employers often expect ASCP certification. Lab safety training is standard, and AALAS certification is common for work with research animals.
Time it takes
A bench role takes about four years of college. A scientist title with a master’s takes about six. Independent research with a PhD and a postdoc often takes ten years or more after high school.
qa: Do you need a PhD to be a life scientist?

No. Many lab jobs, such as research assistant or lab technician, need only a bachelor’s degree in a science. A master’s can lead to research associate or scientist roles in industry. A PhD is usually required to run your own research program, lead a team or work as a university professor.
How long does it take to become a life scientist?

You can start working in a lab after a four-year bachelor’s degree. Becoming an independent research scientist usually takes longer. A PhD typically adds five to six years, and many people then spend two to five years as postdoctoral researchers. In total, that path often takes ten or more years after high school.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications or a related field. Some will hire without one if you can show results. Classes in statistics, consumer behavior and writing help, because the job mixes copywriting, data and testing.
Core skills

Learn how email, push and in-app messages are built, targeted and sent. Employers often ask for basic HTML for email, SQL for pulling customer segments, and A/B testing. Learn the CAN-SPAM Act for email and the TCPA for text messages, since these sending rules are legal requirements.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in the US. Some people earn optional certifications from the email and customer engagement platforms they use. These can help at companies that run that platform, but hands-on campaign experience counts more.
First job

Most people start as an email marketing coordinator or specialist, a CRM coordinator, or a marketing operations associate. You build and test campaigns, manage lists and report on opens, clicks and conversions. Others move in from customer success, analytics or general digital marketing roles.
Time it takes

Reaching a lifecycle or CRM manager title usually takes three to six years after entry level. You move up by owning automated journeys such as onboarding, win-back and renewal, and by showing measured gains in retention or revenue.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a lifecycle marketing manager?

Most job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications or a related field. It is not a legal requirement, and there is no license for this work. People without a degree can get in by showing past campaign results, testing experience and skills with email tools and SQL.
How long does it take to become a CRM marketing manager?

It usually takes three to six years after a first job in email or CRM marketing. Most people start as a coordinator or specialist, build and test campaigns, then take ownership of automated journeys. Moving up depends on showing measurable gains in customer retention, repeat purchases or revenue.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Earn a four-year bachelor’s degree in any field. No specific major is required, but courses that build writing, research and argument skills, such as history, political science, English or economics, help with law school and later with court filings.
Law school admission
Take the LSAT, the standard law school admission test. Some law schools also accept the GRE. Schools weigh your test score, grades, personal statement and recommendations when deciding on admission.
Juris Doctor degree

Complete a Juris Doctor (JD), usually three years of full-time study at an ABA-accredited law school. Future litigators take civil procedure, evidence and trial advocacy, and often join moot court, mock trial or a litigation clinic.
Bar exam and admission

Pass the bar exam in the state where you will practice. Many states use the Uniform Bar Exam. Nearly all states also require the MPRE ethics exam and a character and fitness review. Requirements vary by state.
First job

Most new litigators start as junior associates at a law firm, or as judicial law clerks, government attorneys or public defenders. They draft motions, handle discovery and take depositions before running cases on their own.
Moving in-house

Roles that manage outside law firms and settle disputes for a company usually go to lawyers with several years of firm litigation experience. Counting college and law school, reaching a licensed litigation job usually takes about seven years after high school.
qa: Do you need a law license to be a litigation lawyer?

Yes. To represent clients or a company in court, you must be admitted to the bar in at least one state. That usually means a JD from an ABA-accredited law school, passing the state bar exam and the MPRE, and clearing a character and fitness review. Rules vary by state, and some states allow in-house lawyers a limited registration.
How long does it take to become a litigation lawyer?

It usually takes about seven years after high school: four years for a bachelor’s degree and three years of law school, followed by the bar exam. In-house litigation roles that oversee outside counsel and settlements often ask for several more years of experience at a law firm or in government practice first.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in computer science, mathematics, statistics, physics or electrical engineering. The coursework that matters most is linear algebra, probability, calculus, optimization and programming, especially in Python. Taking machine learning and natural language processing classes early helps.
Graduate study

Most research scientist roles ask for a PhD in machine learning, natural language processing or a related field, which usually takes five to six years in the US. A master’s degree plus strong engineering skills can lead to research engineer roles that also work on training models.
Research record

Employers judge candidates mainly on published work. That means papers at venues such as NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL or EMNLP, plus public code. Reproducing known results, training small models and contributing to open-source projects show you can do the work.
No license required

There is no license, registration or standard certification for this work. Instead, hiring teams look for hands-on skill with deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch, experience training on GPUs, distributed training, and a clear understanding of transformer models and how they are evaluated.
Internships and first job

Research internships during graduate school are the most common way in, and many lead to full-time offers. Without a PhD, people usually start as machine learning engineers or research engineers, or join a one-year AI residency program, then move toward research over time.
Time it takes

Counting college and a PhD, the path usually takes nine to ten years. The engineering route, with a bachelor’s or master’s degree and several years building and training models, can take five to seven years, but research roles reached this way are more competitive.
qa: Do you need a PhD to be an LLM researcher?

Not always, but most research scientist job postings ask for one. People without a PhD often get in as research engineers or machine learning engineers and build a record through published papers, open-source work and experience training large models. Strong results and code can matter as much as the degree.
How long does it take to become an LLM researcher?

Usually nine to ten years if you count a four-year bachelor’s degree and a five to six year PhD. Some people move faster through a master’s degree and a few years as a machine learning or research engineer, often five to seven years in total. There is no license or exam step.

steps: Education

Most localization specialists hold a bachelor’s degree in translation, a foreign language, linguistics, international studies or a related field. Some add a master’s degree in translation or localization management. Native or near-native skill in at least two languages, plus a solid grasp of the target country’s culture, is the core requirement.
Tools and technical skills

Learn computer-assisted translation (CAT) tools, translation memory, terminology management and translation management systems. Basic knowledge of file formats such as XML, JSON and HTML, along with software strings, Unicode and date or currency formats, helps when adapting apps, websites, documents and games.
Optional certification

No license is required in the US. Some translators earn ATA certification from the American Translators Association, a voluntary exam for specific language pairs. Employers mostly judge applicants by language tests, sample translations and tool experience rather than formal credentials.
First job

Common entry roles are freelance or in-house translator, linguistic quality assurance tester, localization coordinator or project coordinator at a language services provider. These roles teach review workflows, style guides, deadlines and how to work with engineers, designers and outside vendors.
Time it takes

It usually takes four years for a bachelor’s degree, then one to three years in an entry role before moving into a localization specialist title. People who already speak two languages fluently and work in translation or software testing can often move faster.
qa: Do you need a certification to work in localization?

No. There is no license or required certification for localization work in the US. Employers look for fluency in your language pairs, translation samples and experience with CAT tools. ATA certification from the American Translators Association is a voluntary credential that some translators earn to show their skill in a specific language pair.
How long does it take to become a localization specialist?

Most people spend about four years on a bachelor’s degree in languages, translation or a related field, then one to three years as a translator, linguistic tester or localization coordinator. Those who already speak two languages fluently and have software or translation experience can often make the move sooner.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for at least a high school diploma. Many prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree in supply chain management, logistics, business or a related field. Courses in transportation, inventory, spreadsheets and basic accounting help, as does comfort with shipping and tracking software.
First job

Many people start as a shipping and receiving clerk, logistics clerk, dispatcher, warehouse associate or customer service rep at a carrier or freight forwarder. These roles teach bills of lading, carrier booking, shipment tracking and how delays get solved.
On-the-job training

There is no apprenticeship or required supervised hours. New coordinators usually learn the employer’s transportation management system, carrier rules, freight terms such as Incoterms and shipping paperwork on the job, often over several months alongside an experienced coordinator.
Required training

No license is needed to work as a logistics coordinator. If you prepare hazardous materials shipments, federal DOT rules require hazmat training, repeated at least every three years. A customs broker license is needed only to conduct customs business on behalf of others, which most coordinators do not do.
Optional certifications

Certifications can help but are rarely required for entry roles. Common choices include the CLTD (Certified in Logistics, Transportation and Distribution) and CSCP from ASCM, and the SCPro from CSCMP. Many people earn them after gaining some work experience.
Time it takes

With a high school diploma, moving from a clerk or dispatcher job into a coordinator role usually takes one to three years. With a relevant bachelor’s degree, some people are hired as coordinators right after school or after an internship.
qa: Do you need a license to be a logistics coordinator?

No. No state or federal license is required to work as a logistics coordinator. Coordinators who prepare hazardous materials shipments must complete DOT hazmat training. A customs broker license from U.S. Customs and Border Protection is needed only to conduct customs business on behalf of others, and coordinators handling imports often work with a licensed broker instead.
Can you become a logistics coordinator without a degree?

Yes. Many logistics coordinators start with a high school diploma and work their way up from jobs like shipping clerk, dispatcher or warehouse associate. A degree in supply chain management or business can speed things up, and some employers prefer one, but hands-on experience with carriers, tracking and shipping paperwork often counts just as much.

steps: Education

Most machine learning engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, data science, math, statistics or electrical engineering. Many employers prefer a master’s degree, and research-heavy roles often ask for a PhD. Core subjects are programming, linear algebra, probability, statistics and algorithms.
Programming and ML skills

You need strong Python and solid software engineering habits, including version control, testing and writing clean code. Learn common ML libraries, how to train and evaluate models, SQL, and the basics of cloud platforms, containers and data pipelines.
Projects and portfolio

There is no license or required exam for this work. Employers judge you by what you have built. A portfolio of end-to-end projects helps: train a model, deploy it behind an API, and monitor it. Public code, open-source work or competition results add proof.
Optional certifications

Cloud provider machine learning certifications are optional. Some employers like them as a sign you can deploy models on their platform, but they do not replace a degree, real projects or work experience. Treat them as a supplement, not a requirement.
First job

Few people start as machine learning engineers. Common first jobs are software engineer, data scientist, data engineer or data analyst. Many move into ML work after they help build or ship models on their team. Internships during school are another common way in.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, plus one to two years for a master’s if you take one. Most people then spend two to five years in a related software or data role before holding the machine learning engineer title.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a machine learning engineer?

Most employers expect at least a bachelor’s degree in computer science, data science, math or a related field, and many prefer a master’s. Some people get in without a degree through strong software experience and a portfolio of deployed ML projects. That path is harder, and it usually starts with a software or data job first.
How long does it take to become a machine learning engineer?

It usually takes six to ten years in total. That covers a four-year bachelor’s degree, often a one- to two-year master’s, and a few years in a related role such as software engineer or data scientist. Someone already working as a software engineer can sometimes move into ML work within one to two years.

steps: High school basics

Most employers want a high school diploma or GED. Classes in algebra, geometry, trigonometry, shop, drafting and computer skills help, because machinists read engineering drawings, calculate dimensions and work to tolerances measured in thousandths of an inch.
Training program

Many people take a certificate or associate degree in machine tool technology or CNC machining at a community college or vocational school. These usually take one to two years and cover blueprint reading, measuring tools, lathes, mills, CNC programming and shop safety.
Apprenticeship

Another common path is a registered apprenticeship through an employer or union, approved by the US Department of Labor or a state apprenticeship agency. It usually lasts about four years and combines paid on-the-job training under experienced machinists with related classroom instruction.
Optional certification

No state license is required to work as a machinist. Some workers earn credentials from NIMS (National Institute for Metalworking Skills) to show skills in areas like CNC operation or measurement. They are voluntary, but some employers value them when hiring or promoting.
First job

The usual way in is a job as a CNC machine operator, machinist trainee or machine shop helper. Early work often means loading parts, running set programs and checking dimensions, then moving on to setups, editing programs and running manual machines.
Time it takes

You can start as a CNC operator within a few months with basic training. Becoming a fully skilled, journey-level machinist who can set up and run many machines on your own usually takes about four years of combined training and work.
qa: Do you need a license to be a machinist?

No. Machinists in the US do not need a state license. Employers look for training, shop experience and the ability to read drawings and use measuring tools. Some workers earn voluntary NIMS credentials or a journeyworker certificate from a registered apprenticeship to prove their skills.
How long does it take to become a machinist?

Entry-level CNC operator jobs can start after a few months of training or even on the job. A full machinist usually needs about four years, through a registered apprenticeship or a one to two year school program followed by several years of shop experience.

steps: High school or GED

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Classes in math, shop, electronics and auto or building trades help, because the job mixes basic electrical, mechanical and plumbing work with reading manuals and diagrams.
Trade school training

Many people take a certificate or associate degree program in industrial maintenance, mechatronics, HVAC or electrical technology at a community or technical college. Programs usually last one to two years and cover motors, controls, hydraulics, pneumatics, welding and safety.
Apprenticeship or on-the-job training

Others learn on the job. Factories and large employers often run industrial maintenance mechanic apprenticeships, some registered with the state or the U.S. Department of Labor, that usually take up to four years of paid work plus classroom hours.
Certifications and licenses

There is no general license for maintenance technicians. Anyone who works on refrigerant systems needs EPA Section 608 certification. Some states or cities license electrical, HVAC or boiler work. Optional credentials include CMRT from SMRP and, for apartment work, CAMT.
First job

Common entry points are maintenance helper, general maintenance worker, apartment make-ready or porter roles, and production jobs in a plant. Helpers assist senior technicians with preventive maintenance and simple repairs, then take on troubleshooting as their skills grow.
Time it takes

Most people work independently as a maintenance technician after about two to four years of combined training and experience. Moving into industrial or multi-craft roles with controls and PLC work usually takes longer.
qa: Do you need a license to be a maintenance technician?

No general license is required. However, you need EPA Section 608 certification to handle refrigerants in HVAC and appliance work. Some states and cities also require licenses for electrical, plumbing, HVAC or boiler work beyond minor repairs, so requirements vary by state and by the tasks you do.
How long does it take to become a maintenance technician?

Many people start as helpers right after high school and become full technicians in about two to four years. A one- to two-year trade school program can shorten the path. Industrial apprenticeships usually last up to four years and combine paid work with classroom training.

steps: Education

Most employers want a bachelor’s degree in manufacturing, industrial or mechanical engineering, usually from an ABET-accredited program. Coursework in materials, statistics, process design and quality control matters most. Some people start with an engineering technology degree and move up through experience on the shop floor.
Co-op or internship

Plant internships and co-op terms during school are the usual way in. You learn how production lines run, how parts are inspected, and how engineers work with operators and supervisors. Many first offers come from the company where a student did a co-op.
First job

The usual first role is associate or junior production engineer, process engineer or manufacturing engineer. You support an experienced engineer, fix line problems, write work instructions, and help bring new products into production. Some start as quality technicians or line supervisors before moving into engineering.
Certifications

No certification is required, but employers often value them. Common choices are SME’s Certified Manufacturing Engineer (CMfgE), ASQ’s Certified Quality Engineer (CQE), and Lean or Six Sigma belts. These show you can improve processes and keep each part built to specification.
Optional PE license

Most production engineers in factories never need a license. Some take the FE exam after graduating, and later the PE exam after about four years of supervised work, if they want to sign off on designs or move into consulting. Requirements vary by state.
Time it takes

Plan on four years for the degree, often a bit longer with co-op terms. After that, it usually takes two to five years on the job to work on your own and lead production launches or line improvements.
qa: Do you need a license to be a production engineer?

Usually not. Most production engineers work for manufacturers, and companies rarely require a Professional Engineer (PE) license for plant work. Some engineers earn one anyway by passing the FE exam, gaining supervised experience, and passing the PE exam. Rules vary by state. Certifications such as SME’s CMfgE or ASQ’s CQE are more common in this field.
How long does it take to become a production engineer?

Most people need about four years to finish a bachelor’s degree in manufacturing, industrial or mechanical engineering, sometimes five with co-op terms. You can be hired as a junior production engineer right after graduating. Expect two to five more years of experience before you lead launches, run your own lines, or supervise other engineers.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most employers expect a four-year bachelor’s degree in manufacturing, mechanical, industrial or a closely related engineering field. ABET-accredited programs are preferred. Useful coursework includes materials, statics, manufacturing processes, CAD, statistics and quality control.
Internship or co-op

Many students complete one or more internships or co-op terms in a plant during school. Time on a real production floor working on line layouts, tooling or process changes often leads straight to a full-time offer.
First job

The usual entry role is associate or entry-level manufacturing engineer, process engineer or production engineer. Some people move up from manufacturing technician or quality technician jobs, often after earning an associate degree and then finishing a bachelor’s degree.
Optional certifications

No license is required for most manufacturing engineering jobs. Many engineers add certifications employers recognize, such as SME’s Certified Manufacturing Technologist (CMfgT) or Certified Manufacturing Engineer (CMfgE), or a Lean or Six Sigma belt such as ASQ’s Certified Six Sigma Green Belt.
Professional Engineer license
A PE license is optional for most roles in industry. Those who want it pass the FE exam, gain about four years of qualifying experience, then pass the PE exam. Requirements vary by state.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for the degree, then usually two to five years of plant experience before taking on senior work such as leading new product launches, designing full production lines or running improvement programs.
qa: Do you need a license to be a manufacturing engineer?

Usually no. Most manufacturing engineers work in industry, where a Professional Engineer license is not required. Some earn a PE to sign off on certain designs or advance into consulting, which means passing the FE exam, gaining qualifying experience and passing the PE exam. Requirements vary by state. Certifications like SME’s CMfgE or a Six Sigma belt are more common.
How long does it take to become a manufacturing engineer?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in manufacturing, mechanical or industrial engineering, and they can start as an entry-level manufacturing engineer right after graduating. Reaching a senior or lead role usually takes another two to five years of hands-on experience improving processes on the production floor.

steps: Education

Most market makers study mathematics, statistics, computer science, physics, engineering or economics. Strong probability, mental math and programming in Python or C++ matter more than the field. Many firms recruit directly from universities through summer internships.
Hiring tests

Trading firms test candidates with probability puzzles, mental math, market-making games and coding exercises. Practicing these, along with poker or other strategy games, is part of preparing. Quant roles may also ask about statistics and machine learning.
Registration

In US securities markets, traders at FINRA member firms usually must pass the Securities Industry Essentials (SIE) exam and the Series 57 Securities Trader exam, sponsored by the firm. Futures roles may require NFA registration. Crypto market makers generally need no individual license, though rules continue to develop.
First job

The usual first job is junior trader, trading assistant, quantitative analyst or trading operations analyst at a proprietary trading firm, bank, exchange or crypto liquidity provider. New hires usually go through a training program before trading with real risk limits.
Time it takes

Most junior traders train for several months, then trade small risk limits under supervision. Becoming an independent trader often takes one to three years. Managing a desk or liquidity across many exchanges usually comes after several years of steady results.
qa: Do you need a license to be a market maker?

It depends on the market. Traders at FINRA member firms in US securities usually must pass the SIE and the Series 57 Securities Trader exam, with firm sponsorship. Futures work may require NFA registration. Crypto market makers generally need no individual license, though their firms may face registration rules that vary by state and continue to change.
How long does it take to become a trader at a market maker?

Graduates usually join as junior traders after an internship and an intensive interview process. Training programs often last a few months, followed by trading small risk limits under supervision. Most traders take about one to three years to trade independently, and running a desk usually takes several more years.

steps: Education

Most marketing analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, economics, statistics or a related field. Coursework in statistics, consumer behavior and research methods matters most. A bachelor’s degree usually takes four years. Some people later add a master’s in marketing analytics or business analytics, but it is not required to start.
Analytical skills

Employers expect you to work with data directly. Learn spreadsheets, SQL, basic statistics and a dashboard or visualization tool. Learn web analytics, A/B testing and attribution, which is how credit for a sale is split across channels. Some analysts also use Python or R for deeper modeling.
Internships and portfolio

Internships in marketing, sales operations or research give you real campaign data to analyze. Since there is no license, a short portfolio helps. Include projects that measure campaign results, compare channels or suggest where a budget should go, with your method and conclusions explained in plain language.
Optional certifications

No license, registration or exam is required to work as a marketing analyst in the US. Some people earn vendor certificates in web analytics or advertising platforms to show tool skills. These can help an entry-level application but rarely replace a degree or hands-on experience.
First job

Common first jobs are marketing coordinator, junior or associate marketing analyst, data analyst, or digital marketing specialist. In these roles you pull reports, track campaign results and build dashboards. That work leads to owning analysis of channels, budgets and return on spending.
Time it takes
The usual path is a four-year bachelor’s degree followed by one to two years in an entry role. That makes about five to six years in total before most people hold a full marketing analyst title.
qa: Do you need a license to be a marketing analyst?

No. There is no state or federal license, registration or required exam for marketing analysts in the US. Employers usually look for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, statistics or a related field, plus skills in spreadsheets, SQL and analytics tools. Optional vendor certificates can show tool knowledge, but experience matters more.
How long does it take to become a marketing analyst?

Most people take about five to six years. That is usually four years for a bachelor’s degree, then one to two years in an entry role such as marketing coordinator, junior analyst or data analyst. Strong internships during school can help you move into a full analyst title sooner.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, communications, business or a related field. Useful courses cover marketing principles, writing, consumer behavior, digital marketing and basic statistics. A degree is common but not legally required, so some people get in through related work and a strong record of results.
Internships and hands-on work

Internships matter a lot in this field. Many coordinators first schedule social posts, draft emails or help run events as interns, student club officers or volunteers. Keep samples of posts, newsletters, event plans and campaign results to show employers in a simple portfolio.
Tools and optional certificates

There is no license or required exam. Employers often want comfort with email platforms, social media schedulers, spreadsheets and analytics. Optional credentials such as Google Analytics certification, HubSpot Academy courses or the American Marketing Association’s Professional Certified Marketer can help a resume but are rarely required.
First job

Common entry points are marketing assistant, marketing intern, social media assistant or junior coordinator roles. Some people move over from sales support, administrative work, customer service or event staffing inside a company, picking up marketing tasks before taking the coordinator title.
Time it takes

The usual path is a four-year degree plus one or more internships. Graduates with internship experience often land coordinator roles right away. People coming from an assistant or related role usually move up within one to two years.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a marketing coordinator?

Most job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, communications, business or a similar field. It is not legally required, though. People without a degree can get in by showing a portfolio of real work, such as social posts, email campaigns or events they ran, often after starting as a marketing assistant or in a related support role.
Do you need a certification to become a marketing coordinator?

No license or certification is required to work as a marketing coordinator in the US. Optional credentials, like Google Analytics certification, HubSpot Academy certificates or the American Marketing Association’s Professional Certified Marketer, can show skills to employers. Internship experience and work samples usually count for more than certificates when hiring for entry-level roles.

steps: Education

Most marketing managers hold a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications or a related field. Useful coursework covers consumer behavior, market research, statistics, digital advertising and writing. Some people add an MBA later, which can help for senior roles at larger employers, but it is rarely required to start.
First job

Almost no one starts as a manager. The usual entry points are marketing coordinator, marketing assistant, marketing specialist, digital marketing associate or a related role in sales, advertising or public relations. These jobs teach you how campaigns are planned, launched, measured and adjusted.
Build hands-on skills

Employers look for proof you can run campaigns that bring in customers. Gain experience with email marketing, paid search and social ads, content planning, web analytics and budget tracking. Keep a record of results, such as leads generated or sales lift, to show in interviews.
Optional certification

There is no license or required exam for this work in the US. Some people earn voluntary credentials, such as the American Marketing Association’s Professional Certified Marketer (PCM), or platform certificates in advertising and analytics tools, to show current skills.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree plus usually three to five years in marketing roles before moving into a manager position. People who lead projects, manage small budgets or supervise interns early often move up faster.
qa: Do you need a license to be a marketing manager?

No. Marketing managers in the US do not need a state license or any required exam. Employers mainly look for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business or a related field and several years of marketing experience. Voluntary certifications, such as the American Marketing Association’s PCM, can strengthen a resume but are not required.
How long does it take to become a marketing manager?

It usually takes seven to nine years in total. That includes about four years for a bachelor’s degree and then three to five years in entry-level roles such as marketing coordinator or specialist. Strong campaign results, leadership on projects and experience managing budgets can shorten the time it takes to be promoted.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications, information systems or a related field. No specific major is required. Courses in statistics, data analysis and spreadsheets help, since much of the job is reporting and working with lead data.
Learn the tools

Build hands-on skill with marketing automation platforms, CRM systems, web analytics and tag management. Learn basic HTML for email templates and enough SQL or spreadsheet work to clean and join data. Many people practice by running email or tracking for a small business, nonprofit or campus group.
First job

Common entry roles are marketing coordinator, email marketing specialist, marketing automation specialist or CRM administrator. In these jobs you build campaigns, set up forms and lead scoring, clean contact data and pull reports. That is the core of marketing operations, and it leads directly to the manager role.
Certifications

There is no license and no required exam for this work. Many employers value vendor certifications for the specific marketing automation platform or CRM they use. These are optional, but they show you can run the system without much training.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then usually three to five years in coordinator or specialist roles before a manager title. People can move faster at small companies, where one person often owns all the marketing systems early on.
qa: Do you need a certification to become a marketing operations manager?

No. There is no license or required exam for marketing operations in the US. Many employers do like to see vendor certifications for the marketing automation platform or CRM they use, because it shows you can manage the system. Real experience running campaigns, lead scoring and reports usually matters more than any certificate.
How long does it take to become a marketing operations manager?

It usually takes about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then three to five years of work in roles like marketing coordinator, email specialist or marketing automation specialist. Some people reach the manager title sooner at small companies, where they run the email platform, tracking and reporting on their own from the start.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in materials science and engineering. Degrees in metallurgical, chemical or mechanical engineering are also common ways in. ABET-accredited programs are the usual expectation. Coursework covers thermodynamics, phase diagrams, mechanical testing, polymers, ceramics, metals and manufacturing processes.
Internships and co-ops

Students often complete one or more internships or co-op terms in a plant, test lab or research group. This hands-on time with heat treating, casting, molding, coatings or failure analysis is what hiring managers look for on an entry-level resume.
FE exam

Many students take the NCEES FE exam near graduation to earn engineer-in-training or engineer-intern status. It is optional for most industry jobs, but it is the first step toward a PE license if a role later needs one.
First job

The usual first job is an entry-level materials, process, manufacturing or quality engineer. New hires run tests, support production lines, review supplier materials and investigate defects under a senior engineer before owning material choices and process designs.
Further credentials

A PE license is rarely required in manufacturing, where many states exempt company engineering work. It generally takes passing the FE and PE exams plus about four years of experience, and rules vary by state. Some engineers add a master’s degree or quality certifications such as ASQ’s Certified Quality Engineer.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for the bachelor’s degree, sometimes five with co-op terms. A master’s degree adds one to two years. Most engineers work several years before leading material selection or process development on their own.
qa: Do you need a license to be a materials engineer?

Usually not. Most materials and process engineers work in manufacturing or research, where many states exempt company engineering work from licensing. A PE license matters mainly for consulting or work offered to the public. Earning one generally means passing the NCEES FE and PE exams and gaining about four years of experience, and the exact rules vary by state.
How long does it take to become a materials engineer?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in materials science and engineering or a related field, sometimes longer with co-op terms. They can then start as entry-level engineers. A master’s degree adds one to two years, and leading material and process decisions on your own typically takes several more years of work.

steps: Education

Most employers want a high school diploma. Many mechanics then complete a postsecondary program in automotive or diesel technology at a community college or trade school. Certificates usually take six months to a year, and associate degrees take about two years. High school auto shop, math and electronics classes help.
First job

Most people start as a lube technician, tire technician, shop helper or entry-level trainee. You change oil, rotate tires and assist senior technicians while learning diagnostics. Some dealerships and fleet operators run paid apprenticeship or manufacturer training programs. Many shops expect you to build your own tool set over time.
EPA Section 609

Federal rules require EPA Section 609 certification to service motor vehicle air conditioning systems. It is an open-book test offered through EPA-approved training programs and does not expire. Many employers expect new technicians to get it early, since A/C work is common in car and truck shops.
ASE certification

ASE certification is voluntary but widely expected. You pass ASE tests in areas such as brakes, engine repair or electrical systems, plus hands-on work experience, usually two years, with formal training able to replace part of it. Diesel technicians take the Medium/Heavy Truck tests. Certifications must be renewed periodically.
State rules and CDL

Most states do not license individual mechanics, but a few, such as Michigan, require state certification for certain repairs. Emissions or safety inspection work often needs a separate state license. Diesel employers may ask for a commercial driver’s license (CDL) so you can road test trucks.
Time it takes

Expect about two to five years to become a fully qualified technician, counting school and on-the-job training. Reaching master technician status, by passing a full series of ASE tests, usually takes longer and comes with more experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a mechanic?

In most states, no. Individual mechanics usually do not need a state license, though a few states, such as Michigan, require state certification for certain repairs. Federal rules require EPA Section 609 certification to work on vehicle air conditioning. Emissions inspection work often needs a state license, and most employers prefer ASE certification.
How long does it take to become a diesel mechanic?

It usually takes two to five years. Many people complete a diesel technology certificate or associate degree, which takes six months to two years, then gain hands-on experience in a shop or fleet. After about two years of work experience, they can earn ASE Medium/Heavy Truck certifications. Some employers also want a CDL.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering, ideally from an ABET-accredited program. Core courses include statics, mechanics of materials, machine design and manufacturing processes. Some people start as drafters with an associate degree and move up later.
CAD and drawing skills

Learn at least one major 3D CAD package well, plus 2D drawings and GD&T under ASME Y14.5. Software vendor certifications are optional but can help a new graduate stand out. Basic FEA and tolerance stack-ups are also expected.
Internships and projects

Co-op terms, internships and student design competitions give you real parts that went through prototyping and testing. Employers often hire their own interns. A portfolio of models, drawings and test results helps in interviews.
FE exam

The NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam is optional for most product design jobs, but many students take it near graduation. Passing it lets you register as an Engineer in Training (EIT) or Engineer Intern, the first step toward a PE license.
First job

The usual first role is entry-level or junior mechanical design engineer, sometimes titled associate engineer or CAD designer. You model parts, release drawings, work with machinists and suppliers on prototypes, and run tests under a senior engineer.
Time it takes

Plan on four to five years for the degree, including any co-op terms. Then expect a few years of work before you design whole assemblies on your own. A PE license, if you want one, usually takes about four years of qualifying experience after the degree.
qa: Do you need a license to be a mechanical design engineer?

Usually not. Most mechanical design engineers work for manufacturers, and state laws generally exempt engineers who design their employer’s own products. A Professional Engineer (PE) license is needed when you offer engineering services to the public or seal drawings, such as for building systems. Requirements vary by state.
How long does it take to become a mechanical design engineer?

Most people spend about four years on a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering, sometimes five with co-op terms. After that, expect a few years in a junior role before you lead designs on your own. A PE license, optional for most design jobs, typically adds about four years of experience and two exams.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering, which usually takes four years. Choose an ABET-accredited program, since accreditation matters for licensure later. Core courses include statics, dynamics, thermodynamics, heat transfer, fluid mechanics, materials and machine design.
CAD and drawing skills

Product design work runs on 3D CAD. Learn to model parts and assemblies, make production drawings and apply GD&T per ASME Y14.5. Also learn design for manufacturing for molded plastic, sheet metal and machined parts, plus basic stress and thermal analysis.
Internships or co-ops

Most students complete one or more internships or co-op terms before graduating. Hands-on experience building prototypes, testing parts or working with suppliers is what hiring managers look for when filling entry-level product design roles.
FE exam

Many graduates take the Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam from NCEES near or soon after graduation. Passing it lets you register as an Engineer in Training (EIT) or Engineer Intern in most states. It is optional for most product design jobs but keeps the PE path open.
First job

The usual first job is entry-level mechanical engineer, design engineer or product development engineer, working under a senior engineer on housings, brackets, mechanisms or cooling. Some people start as test engineers, manufacturing engineers or CAD designers and move into design later.
PE license if needed

Most product design roles do not require a Professional Engineer (PE) license because of industrial exemptions. It matters in consulting, HVAC and public work. Most states require the FE, about four years of qualifying experience and passing the PE Mechanical exam. Rules vary by state.
qa: Do you need a license to be a mechanical engineer?

Not for most product design jobs. Industrial exemptions in most states let engineers design products for their employer without a PE license. A PE license is required to offer engineering services to the public or to sign and seal drawings, which is common in HVAC and building systems work. Requirements vary by state.
How long does it take to become a mechanical engineer?

It usually takes about four years to earn an accredited bachelor’s degree, sometimes five with co-op terms. Most graduates start working as entry-level engineers right away. Becoming a licensed PE usually takes about four more years of qualifying experience, plus passing the FE and PE exams.

steps: High school basics

Start with a high school diploma or GED. Classes in algebra, trigonometry, physics, shop and drafting help most, because the work depends on reading drawings, taking precise measurements and understanding how parts fit and move together.
Technical education

Most employers prefer an associate degree in mechanical engineering technology or a certificate from a community college or technical school. Programs usually take one to two years and cover blueprint reading, GD&T, CAD, machining, hand and power tools, and measuring instruments. Military mechanical training is another common route.
Licenses and certifications

No state license is required to work as a mechanical technician. Certifications are optional but can help, such as ASME’s GD&T Professional certification or SME’s Certified Manufacturing Technologist. Some aerospace and defense employers also require US citizenship or the ability to get a security clearance.
On-the-job training

New technicians train under experienced techs or engineers for several months. They learn the employer’s assembly procedures, torque and fit specifications, test rigs, inspection steps and documentation rules. Safety training, such as OSHA 10-hour courses, is common in shops and plants.
First job

The usual way in is an entry role such as mechanical assembler, technician trainee, test technician or Technician I in a manufacturing, aerospace, energy or research setting. Some people move up from machinist, maintenance or production roles after showing they can work from drawings.
Time it takes

Most people are ready for an entry-level mechanical technician job in about one to two years after high school. Working independently on complex assemblies and tests usually takes another two to four years of experience.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a mechanical technician?

A degree is not legally required, but many employers prefer an associate degree in mechanical engineering technology or a related technical certificate. People without one can still get in through military training or by moving up from assembler, machinist or maintenance jobs, as long as they can read drawings and use precision measuring tools.
How long does it take to become a mechanical technician?

Most people take one to two years, usually through a certificate or associate degree program, before landing an entry-level job. After hiring, expect several months of supervised training. Becoming a senior technician who handles complex builds and testing on your own typically takes a few more years of hands-on experience.

steps: Training

Most coders take a certificate or associate degree program in medical coding, billing or health information management. Certificate programs usually take several months to a year. Key subjects are anatomy, medical terminology, ICD-10-CM, CPT and HCPCS Level II codes, and insurance rules.
Certification

There is no state license, but employers expect certification. Common choices are the Certified Professional Coder (CPC) from AAPC and the Certified Coding Associate (CCA) or Certified Coding Specialist (CCS) from AHIMA. Billers often earn AAPC’s Certified Professional Biller (CPB).
Apprentice status

New CPC holders without enough work experience receive the CPC-A, an apprentice designation. AAPC removes it once you show the required coding experience or complete approved practical training. Some job ads ask for coders without the apprentice designation, which makes the first job the hardest step.
First job

Many coders start in related roles such as medical records clerk, charge entry, payment posting, billing specialist or patient registration at a hospital or physician practice. These jobs teach claim workflows and give the experience coding employers want.
Specialty credentials

With experience, coders add specialty credentials in areas such as risk adjustment, inpatient hospital coding or auditing. AAPC’s Certified Risk Adjustment Coder (CRC) and AHIMA’s CCS are common for hospital and health plan roles. Certified coders complete continuing education to keep their credentials.
Time it takes

Expect about one year to finish training and pass a certification exam, or two years with an associate degree. Moving from a first coding job to remote or specialty coding usually takes one to three more years of experience.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a medical coder?

No law requires one, but most employers expect it. The most common are the CPC from AAPC and the CCA or CCS from AHIMA. New CPC holders without work experience start with the apprentice designation CPC-A, which AAPC removes after they document coding experience or approved training. Billers often hold AAPC’s CPB.
How long does it take to become a medical coder?

Usually several months to two years. Certificate programs often take less than a year, and associate degrees in health information take about two years. After training you pass an exam such as the CPC or CCA. Many new coders spend another year or two in billing, records or entry-level coding before working remotely or in a specialty.

steps: Bachelor’s and medical school
Earn a bachelor’s degree with premed science courses and take the MCAT. Then complete four years of medical school to earn a Doctor of Medicine (MD) or Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO) degree.
Licensing exams
MD students and graduates pass USMLE Steps 1, 2 and 3. DO students usually take the COMLEX-USA series, and many also take the USMLE. Passing these exams is required for a state medical license.
Residency and state license

Complete a residency in a specialty, usually three to seven years. Then apply for a license from a state medical board. Requirements vary by state, and most employers want an active, unrestricted license.
Board certification

Most employers expect board certification from an ABMS member board or an AOA specialty board. Some physicians later add an MBA, MPH or physician leadership training, which helps for executive roles but is rarely required.
First job

Most people practice as attending physicians for several years first. Common next steps are associate medical director, physician advisor or, in biotech and pharma, medical monitor or clinical research physician, before moving up to medical director or chief medical officer.
Time it takes

Expect about 11 to 15 years of education and training after high school, plus several more years of clinical, research or management experience. Chief medical officer roles usually go to physicians with long leadership track records.
qa: Do you need to be a doctor to be a medical director?

Yes. Medical directors and chief medical officers are physicians with an MD or DO degree. Most positions also require an active state medical license and board certification in a specialty. Many roles, especially at hospitals and health plans, ask for years of hands-on clinical practice before any leadership duties.
How long does it take to become a chief medical officer?

It usually takes 15 years or more. That includes four years of college, four years of medical school, three to seven years of residency, and then several years as a practicing physician and in roles like associate medical director. Leadership experience matters as much as clinical training for this top role.

steps: Doctoral degree

Most medical science liaisons hold a doctoral degree, usually a PharmD, PhD, MD or DO. Some employers also hire nurse practitioners or physician assistants. Depth in a therapeutic area, such as oncology or immunology, matters because MSLs discuss complex data with leading specialists.
Clinical or research experience

Employers usually want clinical, research or industry experience after the degree. Pharmacists may work in clinical practice or complete a residency, and PhDs often complete a postdoc. Publications, presentations and experience reading clinical trial data all help.
Industry fellowship

Many PharmD graduates enter through a one- to two-year postdoctoral fellowship in medical affairs run by a drug company, often in partnership with a pharmacy school. Others move from medical information, clinical research or medical education roles into the MSL job.
Rules and training

There is no license specific to MSLs, though clinicians often keep their own professional license. New MSLs train in FDA rules that bar off-label promotion, company compliance policies and the evidence behind each product. Optional certification exists, such as the Board Certified Medical Affairs Specialist (BCMAS).
First MSL job

The first role is usually medical science liaison or associate MSL covering a region, with frequent travel to meet doctors and researchers. Some start in an internal medical affairs role first. Without industry experience, networking and a fellowship are the most common way in.
Time it takes

Expect four to six years for a doctoral degree after college, then often one to three years of clinical, research or fellowship experience. Senior MSL and field team leader roles usually follow after several years in the field.
qa: Can you become a medical science liaison without experience?

It is hard but possible. Most employers want a doctorate plus clinical, research or industry experience. New PharmD graduates often get in through a one- to two-year medical affairs fellowship. PhDs and physicians with deep knowledge of a therapeutic area sometimes land associate MSL roles directly, especially after networking with current MSLs.
Do you need a license to be a medical science liaison?

No license is required for the MSL role itself. Clinicians such as pharmacists or physicians often keep their professional license active, and some employers prefer it. MSLs must follow FDA rules and company compliance policies on scientific exchange and off-label information. Certification, such as the BCMAS, is optional.

steps: Education

Most medical writers have a degree in life sciences, pharmacy, nursing or medicine, and many hold a PhD, PharmD or MD. Some come from English or journalism with strong science coursework. Regulatory writing jobs usually expect an advanced science degree.
Writing samples

There is no license or required credential, so a portfolio matters most. Published papers, a thesis, grant applications, patient materials or health articles show your skill. Many employers also give a writing or editing test during hiring.
Learn the standards

Medical writing follows set formats. Regulatory writers use ICH guidelines such as ICH E3 for clinical study reports. Publication writers follow ICMJE recommendations and reporting guidelines such as CONSORT. Knowing AMA style and how to read statistics is expected in most roles.
Certification

Certification is optional. The American Medical Writers Association (AMWA) offers the Medical Writer Certified (MWC) credential for writers with experience. Editors may earn the ELS credential from the Board of Editors in the Life Sciences. Many writers also take short courses in regulatory or publication writing.
First job

The usual first job is associate medical writer at a contract research organization, a medical communications agency or a drug or device company. Others start as medical editors, quality reviewers, regulatory coordinators or freelance writers of patient education and continuing medical education.
Time it takes

Scientists often move in right after graduate school or a postdoc. People without an advanced degree usually build skills for one to three years in an editing or communications role. Reaching senior writer typically takes several years of experience.
qa: Can you become a medical writer without experience?

Yes, but you need proof of skill. Many new writers come from graduate school, research, pharmacy or nursing and use papers, theses or sample documents as a portfolio. Entry roles such as associate medical writer, medical editor or quality reviewer take people with little writing experience, often after a writing test.
What certification do medical writers need?

None is required. The Medical Writer Certified (MWC) credential from the American Medical Writers Association shows experience and knowledge, but it is meant for people already working in the field. Editors may earn the ELS from the Board of Editors in the Life Sciences. Employers usually care more about your degree and writing samples.

steps: Education

Licensed therapists usually need a master’s degree in clinical mental health counseling, marriage and family therapy or social work. Psychologists need a doctorate, a PhD or PsyD, in clinical or counseling psychology. Psychiatrists are medical doctors who complete a psychiatry residency. Programs include supervised practicum and internship hours.
Supervised practice

After graduating, counselors, marriage and family therapists and clinical social workers must work under a licensed supervisor before full licensure. Most states require at least two years and several thousand hours of supervised clinical work. Exact hours vary by state and license.
Licensing exams

Each license has its own exam. Counselors usually take the National Counselor Examination (NCE) or the National Clinical Mental Health Counseling Examination (NCMHCE), social workers the ASWB clinical exam, marriage and family therapists the AMFTRB national exam, and psychologists the EPPP. Which exam a state uses varies.
State license

You need a license in every state where your clients are located, including for online therapy. Titles include LPC, LMHC, LMFT, LCSW and licensed psychologist. Interstate compacts, such as PSYPACT for psychologists, make practicing across participating states easier.
First job

Most new graduates start under a provisional or associate license at a community mental health agency, hospital, school or group practice, seeing clients under supervision. Before graduate school, some work as a mental health technician, case manager or crisis line counselor.
Time it takes

Becoming a fully licensed counselor, marriage and family therapist or clinical social worker usually takes six to eight years after high school: a bachelor’s degree, two to three years of graduate school, then about two years of supervised practice. Psychologists usually need longer.
qa: Do you need a license to be a therapist?

Yes. To provide therapy in the US you need a state license, such as LPC, LMHC, LMFT, LCSW or licensed psychologist. Licensing usually requires a graduate degree, supervised clinical hours and a national exam. For online therapy you must be licensed in the state where the client is located, though compacts like PSYPACT help psychologists.
How long does it take to become a therapist?

Usually six to eight years after high school. That covers a bachelor’s degree, a two to three year master’s degree in counseling, marriage and family therapy or social work, and about two years of supervised practice before full licensure. Psychologists need a doctorate, which usually adds several more years.

steps: Entry roles

Many people start as mental health technicians, behavioral health technicians or residential counselors. These jobs usually need a high school diploma or an associate degree, plus CPR and crisis de-escalation training. A few states, such as California, license psychiatric technicians, which requires a formal program and an exam.
Bachelor’s degree

A bachelor’s degree in psychology, social work or human services opens case manager and counselor assistant jobs. Many states also certify addiction counselors and peer support specialists, sometimes without a bachelor’s degree, after supervised hours and a state or IC&RC exam.
Master’s degree

To become a licensed counselor you need a master’s degree in clinical mental health counseling or a related field, which usually takes two to three years. Programs accredited by CACREP are preferred, and some states require one. Training includes a supervised practicum and internship.
Supervised hours

After graduating, you work under a licensed supervisor with an associate or provisional license. Most states require about two to three years of post-degree supervised practice, often around 3,000 hours. The exact hours and supervision rules vary by state.
Licensing exam

Most states require the National Clinical Mental Health Counseling Examination (NCMHCE) or the National Counselor Examination (NCE), both from the National Board for Certified Counselors. The license title varies by state, such as LPC, LMHC or LPCC. Some states add a law exam.
Time it takes

Technician jobs can start within weeks. A licensed counselor usually needs about eight to ten years after high school: four for a bachelor’s degree, two to three for a master’s, and two to three of supervised work.
qa: Do you need a license to be a mental health counselor?

To provide counseling on your own, yes. Every state licenses professional counselors, under titles such as LPC, LMHC or LPCC. You need a master’s degree, supervised post-degree hours and a passing score on a national exam such as the NCMHCE. Mental health technicians and peer support staff work under licensed staff, with lighter rules that vary by state.
Can you become a mental health technician without experience?

Yes. Many hospitals, residential programs and crisis centers hire mental health technicians with a high school diploma and no experience, then train them on the job in safety, crisis de-escalation and patient care. CPR certification is often required. Volunteer work, such as on a crisis line, and courses in psychology help applicants stand out.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Some prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree in business, communications or a related field, but a degree is rarely required. There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in the US.
Customer service experience

Employers usually want six months to two years of customer-facing work. Common sources are call centers, retail, restaurants, banking or help desk roles. Experience helping business customers, handling payments or resolving disputes counts for the most.
Build practical skills

Learn to work in ticketing and chat systems, write clear emails, and handle phone, chat and email at the same time. Basic spreadsheet skills, comfort with online payments and refunds, and the ability to explain account settings to small business owners all help. Speaking a second language, often Spanish, is a plus.
First job

Many people start as a customer support representative or consumer support agent on a platform. Once there, they move to the merchant, partner or driver support team. Others are hired directly into merchant support from a call center or small business background.
On-the-job training

New hires usually get two to six weeks of paid training on the platform’s tools, policies and fraud rules. After that comes a period of closer review of tickets and calls. Optional customer service certificates exist, but employers seldom require them.
Time it takes

Getting in usually takes a few months to two years, depending on prior experience. With strong ratings, people can move up to senior specialist, account management, onboarding or team lead roles in about one to three years.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a merchant support specialist?

Usually not. Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED plus some customer service experience. A degree in business or communications can help you stand out or move into account management later. Clear writing, patience and comfort with online tools matter more to most hiring teams than formal education.
Is there a certification for merchant support?

There is no license or required certification for merchant support work in the US. Some people take general customer service certificate courses, but employers rarely ask for them. Platforms train new hires on their own tools and policies. Proven experience solving customer or business account problems is what employers look for most.

steps: Education

Most employers prefer a bachelor’s degree, often in business, marketing, communications or a related field. The major matters less than proof you can sell. Some companies hire people without a degree when they bring strong results from a quota-carrying role or customer-facing work.
First job

Most people start as a sales development representative (SDR) or business development representative (BDR). You prospect through cold calls, emails and social outreach, qualify leads and book meetings for account executives. This is where you learn prospecting, handling objections and keeping records in a CRM system.
Small business AE

Many SDRs are promoted to a small business (SMB) account executive role. Here you run the full sales cycle on smaller, faster deals: discovery, demos, proposals and closing. Hitting quota consistently at this level is usually what employers want to see before moving you to mid-market.
Licenses and training

No license or certification is required for most mid-market sales jobs, including software sales. Exceptions exist: selling insurance requires a state insurance producer license, and selling securities requires FINRA registration and exams. Sales methodology courses and product training are optional but common, and employers often provide them.
Time it takes

Moving from a first sales job to mid-market account executive usually takes two to four years. A common path is about a year or more as an SDR or BDR, then a year or more as an SMB account executive, depending on performance and how fast the company grows.
Mid-market role

Your first mid-market role brings larger deals, longer sales cycles and more decision makers at each customer. You manage your own pipeline, work with finance and leadership contacts, and negotiate pricing and contract terms. Success here can lead to enterprise account executive or sales management roles.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a mid-market account executive?

No license or specific degree is legally required. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, communications or a related field, but a proven sales record often matters more. People without a degree commonly get in by succeeding as an SDR or BDR, then as a small business account executive, and showing consistent quota attainment.
How long does it take to become a mid-market account executive?

It usually takes two to four years. Most people spend about a year or more as a sales development representative, then a year or more as a small business account executive before promotion. Strong performers at fast-growing companies can move faster, while people switching from unrelated fields may take longer to build a sales track record.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in aerospace, electrical, or mechanical engineering, physics, or computer science. Courses in orbital mechanics, control systems, and communications help most. Student satellite projects, rocketry clubs, and internships give the hands-on experience hiring teams look for.
Work eligibility

Many spacecraft jobs fall under ITAR export rules, so employers often require US person status, such as US citizenship or permanent residency. Defense and some government missions also need a security clearance, which requires US citizenship.
First job

People often start as a satellite operator, flight controller, ground systems engineer, or spacecraft operations analyst. Some come in from military space operations roles. Entry work means watching telemetry, running pass plans, sending routine commands, and logging anomalies.
Console certification

There is no state license for this work. Each mission trains and certifies its own operators through procedure study, fault simulations, and supervised shifts on console. Certifying for a position usually takes several months, and shift work and on-call duty are common.
Time it takes

Counting a four-year degree and console training, most people are flying spacecraft within about four to five years. Moving up to roles such as flight director or mission operations lead usually takes several more years of hands-on operations experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a mission operations engineer?

No. There is no state or national license for mission operations work. Instead, each employer or mission trains and certifies its own operators through simulations and supervised console shifts. Some roles do require a security clearance or US person status because of export rules, but that is a job requirement, not a license.
Do you need to be a US citizen to work in spacecraft operations?

Not always. Many roles fall under ITAR, which limits access to US persons. That group includes US citizens, lawful permanent residents, and certain protected individuals such as refugees and asylees. Jobs that need a security clearance do require US citizenship. Some commercial missions without export limits can hire more broadly.

steps: Education
