Yes. Every state requires physician assistants to hold a state license, usually issued by the state medical board. To qualify, you must graduate from an ARC-PA accredited program and pass the PANCE from the NCCPA. PAs also work under supervision or collaboration rules that vary by state, and need DEA registration to prescribe controlled substances.

steps: Education

Most platform engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. A degree is common but not required. Some people enter after self-study or an associate degree, backed by strong coding and systems skills they can show in projects or past work.
Core technical skills

Learn Linux, networking basics, scripting in a language like Python or Go, and Git. Then build skills in containers, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code tools such as Terraform, CI/CD pipelines, and at least one major cloud provider. Building and running your own small projects helps a lot.
First job

Very few people start as platform engineers. The usual way in is a first role as a software engineer, systems administrator, DevOps engineer, site reliability engineer or cloud support engineer. These jobs teach how production systems run, fail and get deployed.
Optional certifications

No license or certification is required. Some employers value the Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) from the Linux Foundation and CNCF, cloud certifications from AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud, or the HashiCorp Terraform Associate. These can help when switching from a nearby role, but hands-on experience usually counts more.
Time it takes

Expect about two to five years of related engineering or operations work before landing a platform engineer title. Many people move over internally after building shared tools, deployment pipelines or infrastructure that other teams at their company start to rely on.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a platform engineer?

No. Many platform engineers have a computer science or related degree, and many employers list one, but it is not a legal requirement. People without a degree get hired by showing solid experience in Linux, cloud, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code and coding, usually gained in earlier roles like systems administrator, DevOps engineer or software engineer.
Is there a certification or license for platform engineers?

There is no license for platform engineering in the US, and no single required certification. Some people earn the Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), cloud provider certifications from AWS, Azure or Google Cloud, or the HashiCorp Terraform Associate to show their skills. Employers usually weigh real work running production infrastructure more heavily than any certificate.

steps: Education

Most apprenticeship programs require a high school diploma or GED, a minimum age of 18 and a passing score on an aptitude test in math and reading. Algebra, shop and drafting classes help. Some people complete a trade school or pre-apprenticeship program first.
First job

Most people start as an apprentice or plumber’s helper, carrying materials, cutting and threading pipe and digging trenches under a licensed plumber. Many states require apprentices to register with the state licensing board or apprenticeship agency.
Apprenticeship

Most plumbers and pipefitters train through a paid apprenticeship of four to five years. Union programs run by the United Association and nonunion programs through groups such as ABC and PHCC combine on-the-job training with classroom study of codes, math, blueprints and safety.
Journeyman license

Most states, or their cities and counties, require plumbers to hold a journeyman license to work without direct supervision. After the required hours, you pass an exam based on the code your state uses, usually the International Plumbing Code or the Uniform Plumbing Code. Pipefitter licensing varies more by state.
Special certifications

Pipefitters and steamfitters often need welding qualifications under ASME Section IX for pressure piping. Backflow testers, medical gas installers and gas fitters may need extra certificates or state licenses, such as ASSE certifications for backflow testing and medical gas work.
Time it takes

It usually takes four to five years to go from apprentice to licensed journeyman. After more years as a journeyman, often two or more, many states let you take a master plumber exam, which is needed to pull permits or run a plumbing business.
qa: Do you need a license to be a plumber?

In most states, yes. Plumbers usually need a journeyman license to work without supervision, earned through an apprenticeship and an exam based on the International Plumbing Code or the Uniform Plumbing Code. Some states leave licensing to cities or counties. Pipefitters are licensed in some states but not others, and welding certifications are common.
How long does it take to become a plumber?

Usually four to five years. Most plumbers complete a paid apprenticeship that combines thousands of hours of on-the-job training with classroom study, then pass a journeyman licensing exam. Trade school can sometimes shorten the apprenticeship. Becoming a master plumber, who can pull permits and run a business, typically takes several more years.

steps: Education

Most policy managers hold a bachelor’s degree in political science, public policy, economics, or a field tied to their industry. Many add a Master of Public Policy, a law degree, or another graduate degree, which helps in heavily regulated sectors such as energy, health care, finance, or technology.
First job in government

A common way in is working as a legislative aide or staffer for an elected official, or as staff at a federal or state agency. Others start as policy analysts at think tanks or trade associations, or as coordinators on a company’s government affairs team.
Build subject expertise

Employers want people who know how bills move, how agencies write rules, and how public comment periods work. You also need deep knowledge of one sector’s laws. Writing policy memos, comment letters, and briefings is a core skill to practice early.
Lobbying registration

There is no license for this work. If your contacts with federal officials meet the thresholds in the Lobbying Disclosure Act, you or your employer must register and file reports with the Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Senate. Most states have their own lobbyist registration rules, which vary by state.
Time it takes

Reaching a manager title usually takes about five or more years of policy, legislative, or regulatory experience after a bachelor’s degree. A graduate degree or time spent working inside government can shorten the climb, because companies value people who already know regulators and lawmakers.
qa: Do you need a license to be a policy manager?

No license is required. However, if your work includes lobbying federal officials above certain thresholds, you or your employer must register under the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Most states also require lobbyists to register, and rules vary by state. Former government employees may face cooling-off limits on contacting their old offices.
What degree do you need to work in public policy for a company?

Most people have a bachelor’s degree in political science, public policy, economics, or a subject related to the company’s industry. Many policy managers also earn a Master of Public Policy or a law degree. Real experience, such as working for a legislator or a regulatory agency, often matters as much as the degree itself.

steps: Education

Most policy analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in public policy, political science, economics or a related field. Many add a master’s in public policy (MPP) or public administration (MPA), or a law degree. Research methods, statistics and clear writing are the core skills.
First job

Common first jobs are legislative aide or staffer, research assistant at a think tank or trade association, analyst at a government agency, or junior associate at a public affairs or consulting firm. Work in Congress or a state legislature teaches how laws are made.
Skills

Analysts read bills and proposed rules, follow the rulemaking process, including notice and comment, and write memos, comment letters and position papers. Learn to find rules in the Federal Register and to estimate a rule’s cost and impact with data.
Lobbying rules

There is no license for policy analysis. If your work includes contacting officials to influence laws or rules, federal and state lobbying laws may apply. Under the federal Lobbying Disclosure Act, employers register and report lobbying once thresholds are met, and state rules vary.
Time it takes

Entry-level analyst jobs are open to new graduates, often after internships. A master’s degree usually takes two years full time. Senior roles on a company’s public policy team usually ask for several years in government, a think tank or a regulated industry.
qa: How do you become a policy analyst?

Most policy analysts earn a bachelor’s degree in political science, economics or public policy, then gain experience through internships or entry-level jobs in a legislature, government agency, think tank or trade association. Many later earn a master’s in public policy or a law degree. Strong research, data and writing samples matter most when applying.
Do policy analysts need to register as lobbyists?

Not usually, since research and writing alone are not lobbying. If you contact lawmakers or officials to influence legislation or rules, federal or state lobbying laws may require registration. Under the federal Lobbying Disclosure Act, registration depends on time spent lobbying and money involved, and states set their own rules.

steps: Education

Most portfolio managers hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, accounting, mathematics or a related field. Many later earn an MBA or a master’s in finance. Coursework in valuation, financial statements, statistics and economics forms the base of investment work.
First job

The usual way in is an analyst role: investment analyst, equity or credit research analyst, or portfolio analyst at an asset manager, bank, insurer, pension fund or wealth firm. Analysts research securities, build models and recommend trades. Internships are the main path to these jobs.
CFA charter

The Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) charter from CFA Institute is the most common credential. Candidates pass three exam levels and need 4,000 hours of relevant work experience over at least 36 months. Many take about four years or longer to finish.
Licenses

Requirements depend on the firm and its clients. Managers who advise individual clients usually register as investment adviser representatives, which in most states means passing the Series 65, or the Series 66 with the Series 7. Those at broker-dealers need FINRA registration. Many institutional managers need no individual license.
Time it takes

Most portfolio managers spend about five to ten years as analysts or associate portfolio managers before managing money on their own. Firms look for a long record of sound research and investment calls, and often a CFA charter or MBA.
qa: How long does it take to become a portfolio manager?

Usually about five to ten years after a bachelor’s degree. Most people start as investment or research analysts, then become associate or co-portfolio managers before running money on their own. Many earn the CFA charter along the way, which requires passing three exam levels and 4,000 hours of relevant work experience over at least 36 months.
Do you need a license to be a portfolio manager?

It depends on the role. Portfolio managers who advise individual clients usually register as investment adviser representatives, which typically means passing the Series 65, or the Series 66 with the Series 7. Those working through a broker-dealer need FINRA registration. Many managers at institutional funds need no individual license, though employers often expect a CFA charter.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, usually from an ABET-accredited program. Useful courses include circuit analysis, semiconductor devices, power electronics, control systems, electromagnetics and signals. A degree in electrical and computer engineering also works if you choose power and analog electives.
Hands-on experience

Employers look for real hardware work. Internships, co-ops and student projects such as solar cars, robotics or motor drives help a lot. Learn to use oscilloscopes, build and debug prototype boards, and work with circuit simulation and PCB layout tools.
Graduate degree

A master’s degree is common in this field, though not required. It often focuses on converter topologies, magnetics design, wide-bandgap devices like silicon carbide and gallium nitride, and digital control. Research and advanced design roles sometimes ask for a PhD.
Licensing

No license is required for most product design jobs, since many states exempt engineers working for manufacturers. A Professional Engineer (PE) license matters more for utility, grid or public work. It means passing the NCEES FE exam, gaining supervised experience, then passing the PE exam. Requirements vary by state.
First job

Graduates usually start as a junior hardware engineer, power electronics design engineer, test engineer or applications engineer. Early work includes testing converters, checking thermal performance, debugging boards and supporting senior engineers on new designs for chargers, drives or power supplies.
Time it takes

A bachelor’s degree usually takes four years, and a master’s adds one to two more. Working independently on full converter designs typically takes another three to five years of experience after your first job.
qa: Do you need a license to be a power electronics engineer?

Usually not. Most power electronics engineers design products for manufacturers, and many states exempt that work from licensing. A Professional Engineer (PE) license is mainly needed for engineers who approve public or utility projects. Getting one involves the NCEES FE exam, several years of supervised experience and the PE exam. Requirements vary by state.
How long does it take to become a power electronics engineer?

It usually takes four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, which is enough for many entry-level jobs. Many people add a one to two year master’s degree focused on power electronics. After that, it typically takes several more years of work experience to lead full converter or power supply designs on your own.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or equivalent with solid math and science. Some prefer an associate degree or vocational certificate in power plant technology, process technology, or electrical or mechanical work. Military experience, especially Navy nuclear training, is a common way in.
Employer aptitude tests

Many utilities screen applicants with written aptitude tests before hiring. A common one is the Edison Electric Institute’s POSS test, which checks mechanical understanding, reading, and math. Some employers also require a physical exam, drug screening, and a background check, especially at nuclear plants.
Apprenticeship and training

New hires learn mostly on the job. Many start in a formal apprenticeship or company training program that mixes classroom work with supervised shifts. Trainees learn plant systems, safety rules, and control room procedures while working under experienced operators, often moving up through several qualification levels.
Licenses and certification

Nuclear plant reactor operators must hold a Reactor Operator or Senior Reactor Operator license from the NRC. Grid and system operators often need NERC System Operator Certification. Some states and cities also require a stationary engineer or boiler operator license. Requirements vary by state and plant type.
Time it takes

Becoming a fully qualified operator usually takes several years of on-the-job training. Reaching control room operator often takes three to five years. Nuclear operators typically need years of plant experience plus extensive training before they can sit for NRC license exams.
First job

The usual first job is auxiliary operator, equipment operator, plant helper, or apprentice operator. These roles involve walking the plant, checking gauges, and doing routine equipment work. With experience and passed qualifications, people move into control room operator and later shift supervisor roles.
qa: Do you need a license to be a power plant operator?

It depends on the plant and state. Nuclear reactor operators must be licensed by the NRC. System operators who control the grid often need NERC System Operator Certification. Some states and cities require a stationary engineer or boiler operator license for fossil fuel plants. Many other operators qualify through their employer’s own training and testing program.
How long does it take to become a power plant operator?

You can get hired as an entry level or auxiliary operator with a high school diploma and a passing aptitude test. Becoming a fully qualified control room operator usually takes several years of on-the-job training, often three to five. Nuclear plant operators generally need longer because of NRC licensing requirements.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most power systems engineers earn a four-year bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from an ABET-accredited program. Take electives in power systems, electric machines, power electronics and protection. A degree from an ABET-accredited program is the simplest route to a state engineering license later.
FE exam

Many students take the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam, Electrical and Computer, in their final year or soon after graduating. Passing it lets you apply to your state board for Engineer in Training (EIT) or Engineer Intern (EI) status, which many employers expect from new hires.
First job

The usual first job is junior or entry-level electrical engineer at a utility, a consulting engineering firm or an equipment maker. Early work often includes substation layouts, protection and relay settings, load flow and short-circuit studies, and drafting one-line diagrams under a senior engineer.
Supervised experience

Most states require about four years of progressive engineering experience, usually under a licensed Professional Engineer, before you can earn a PE license. Keep records of your projects and supervisors, since the state board will ask for references and a description of your work.
PE license

After the required experience, take the NCEES PE Electrical and Computer: Power exam and apply to your state board. A PE is needed to seal drawings and offer engineering services to the public. Some utility roles do not require it, and rules vary by state.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for the degree and roughly four more years of experience before earning a PE, so usually around eight years in total. You can start doing paid power systems work right after graduation as an engineer in training.
qa: Do you need a license to be a power systems engineer?

Not always. You can work as a power systems engineer under a licensed engineer’s supervision without one. But a state Professional Engineer (PE) license is needed to seal drawings and offer services to the public, and many consulting firms expect it for senior roles. Getting one usually means passing the FE exam, gaining about four years of experience and passing the PE Power exam.
How long does it take to become a power systems engineer?

You can start working in entry-level power systems roles after a four-year electrical engineering degree. Becoming a licensed Professional Engineer usually takes about four more years of supervised experience plus passing the FE and PE exams. In total, most people reach full licensure in around eight years, though requirements vary by state.

steps: Background

There is no standard degree or license. Trading and pricing roles favor math, statistics, economics, computer science or finance. Market creation and event resolution roles value research and writing skills from journalism, law, policy or data analysis. Strong knowledge of politics, sports or economics helps.
Rules to learn

In the US, regulated prediction markets operate as exchanges overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which treats their products as event contracts. Staff learn the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC rules on market surveillance and fair trading. Some contracts, especially on sports, face legal challenges from states.
Registration

Most exchange employees need no individual license. People who solicit customers or handle orders at futures brokers usually register with the National Futures Association (NFA) and pass the Series 3 exam. Compliance staff learn NFA and CFTC reporting rules.
First job

Common first jobs are market operations analyst, market surveillance analyst, customer support agent, junior trader, market researcher or data analyst. Some people come from sports betting trading, futures brokers, crypto exchanges or political and economic research jobs.
Time it takes

Entry roles can start right after a degree or a related first job. Moving into market creation, trading or surveillance leadership usually takes a few years. Since the industry is young and rules change, keeping up with CFTC and state decisions is part of the job.
qa: Do you need a license to work at a prediction market?

Usually not. In the US, the exchange itself is regulated by the CFTC, but most staff need no individual license. People who solicit or handle customer orders at a futures broker typically register with the National Futures Association and pass the Series 3 exam. Rules for sports and political contracts are still contested, so the field changes quickly.
Can you work in prediction markets without experience?

Yes, especially in operations, research and support roles. Employers value deep knowledge of politics, sports, economics or weather, careful writing for contract rules, and comfort with data. For trading roles, a strong math or statistics background and experience in sports betting, futures or crypto trading help. A record of your own forecasts can show skill.

steps: Education

Most pricing analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in economics, finance, statistics, mathematics or business. Courses in statistics, microeconomics, accounting and data analysis matter most. A master’s degree is not required, though some take one for senior or strategy roles.
Data and tool skills

Employers expect strong Excel skills and, more and more, SQL. Many also want experience with a BI tool or with Python or R. People build these through coursework, online classes and their own projects that analyze margins, discounts or price changes.
No license required

There is no state license or required exam for pricing work. Some people earn the Certified Pricing Professional (CPP) credential from the Professional Pricing Society, but employers rarely require it. Insurance pricing roles may ask for progress on SOA or CAS actuarial exams.
First job

Many start as a data analyst, financial analyst, business analyst or sales operations analyst. Some enter directly as a junior pricing analyst after an internship. These roles teach margin analysis, sales data, discounting and how to explain numbers to sales and finance teams.
Time it takes

It usually takes about four years for a degree. Many then spend one to three years in a related analyst job before moving into a dedicated pricing role. Strong graduates with internships sometimes start in pricing right away.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a pricing analyst?

No. No license or certification is required to work as a pricing analyst in the US. Employers mostly look for a relevant degree, Excel and SQL skills, and analytical experience. The Certified Pricing Professional (CPP) credential from the Professional Pricing Society is optional and can help show commitment to the field, but few job postings require it.
How long does it take to become a pricing analyst?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in economics, finance, statistics or business. Some land an entry-level pricing job right after graduating, often after an internship. Others first spend one to three years as a data, financial or business analyst, then move into pricing once they have solid analysis experience.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Earn a four-year bachelor’s degree in any field. Political science, history, economics and computer science are common choices. Technical coursework helps later when you advise on how data actually moves. Take the LSAT, which most law schools use for admission.
Law school

Complete a Juris Doctor (JD) at an ABA-accredited law school, usually three years full time. Take courses in privacy law, cybersecurity, technology law and administrative law. Clinics, journal work and summer jobs in privacy or data security practices give you useful experience.
Bar admission

Pass the bar exam in the state where you plan to practice. Most states also require the MPRE, an ethics exam, and a character and fitness review. Many states use the Uniform Bar Exam, but requirements vary by state.
Privacy certification

No law requires a privacy certification, but many employers expect one. The CIPP/US from the IAPP is the most common for US privacy law. Lawyers handling European data often add the CIPP/E, and some add the CIPM for privacy program work.
First job

Most start as associates at law firms with privacy and data security practices, or in government, regulatory or compliance roles. After several years advising on breaches, data laws and vendor contracts, many move in-house to a company’s legal team with the title privacy counsel.
Time it takes

Expect about seven years of school after high school: four for a bachelor’s degree and three for law school. Employers usually want several years of legal practice in privacy or a related area, so reaching a privacy counsel role often takes ten years or more in total.
qa: Do you need to be a lawyer to be a privacy counsel?

Yes. The title counsel means a licensed attorney, so you need a JD and admission to a state bar. People without a law degree can still work in privacy as privacy analysts, privacy program managers or compliance specialists, but they cannot give legal advice or hold a counsel role.
Is the CIPP/US required to work as a privacy counsel?

No law requires it, and your bar license is what allows you to practice. Still, the CIPP/US from the IAPP is widely listed in job postings and helps show focused privacy knowledge. Many lawyers earn it early in their privacy careers, and some add the CIPP/E for European data protection work.

steps: Education

Most process development scientists study chemical engineering, chemistry, biochemistry, bioengineering or biology. Bachelor’s and master’s graduates usually start as associate scientists or engineers, while senior scientist roles often go to people with a PhD or several years of industry experience.
Core skills

The work centers on scale-up: moving a process from lab glassware or small bioreactors to pilot plant and manufacturing equipment. You learn design of experiments, process analytics, purification methods, mass and heat transfer, and how to write development reports and technology transfer documents.
Regulations

There is no license, but drug and biologic work follows FDA current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) rules and ICH guidelines such as Q8 on pharmaceutical development and Q11 on drug substances. Process validation and quality by design are central. A Professional Engineer license is rarely required.
First job

Common first jobs are associate scientist or research associate in process development, manufacturing sciences and technology (MSAT), or manufacturing technician on a GMP production floor. Internships and co-ops at drug, biotech or chemical companies are a frequent way in.
Time it takes

With a bachelor’s degree, people often reach scientist level after about four to six years of industry work. A PhD usually takes five to six years and can lead directly to a scientist title. Leading process development for a product usually takes several more years.
qa: How long does it take to become a process development scientist?

With a bachelor’s degree, you can start as an associate scientist right away and usually reach scientist level in four to six years. With a master’s, it may take a few years less. A PhD, which usually takes five to six years, often leads straight to a scientist title.
Can you become a process development scientist without experience?

You can enter at associate or research associate level right after a degree, especially with internship or co-op experience at a drug, biotech or chemical company. Lab skills, knowledge of cGMP and experience with bioreactors, chromatography or reactors help. Moving over from a manufacturing technician or quality control role is another common way in.

steps: Education

There is no license. Most people hold a bachelor’s degree in industrial engineering, business, operations management or a related field. Coursework in statistics, operations and data analysis is the most useful, since Six Sigma relies on measuring variation and testing changes.
First job

Most enter from inside operations: a production supervisor, quality technician, operations analyst, industrial engineer or supply chain analyst who starts leading small improvement projects. Hospitals, banks and logistics companies also promote people from their own operations staff.
Belt training

Lean Six Sigma training is ranked by belts: Yellow Belt for basics, Green Belt for leading small projects part time, Black Belt for leading larger projects full time and coaching others, and Master Black Belt for running a whole program. Many employers train their own staff.
Certification

No single body controls the belts, so quality varies by provider. Widely recognized options include the Certified Six Sigma Green Belt (CSSGB) and Certified Six Sigma Black Belt (CSSBB) from ASQ, and exams from IASSC. ASQ’s Black Belt requires proof of completed projects.
Projects

Employers care most about completed projects with measured results. Running projects with the DMAIC method (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) and Lean tools such as value stream mapping, 5S and kaizen builds the record hiring managers ask about.
Time it takes

A Green Belt usually takes a few weeks of training plus one project over a few months. Reaching Black Belt level often takes a few years of project work. Continuous improvement manager roles usually ask for a Black Belt and several years of experience.
qa: What certification do you need for process improvement jobs?

No license is required, but many postings ask for a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt or Black Belt. Belts come from many providers, so employers favor recognized ones, such as ASQ’s Certified Six Sigma Green Belt (CSSGB) and Certified Six Sigma Black Belt (CSSBB), or IASSC exams, along with proof of completed projects.
How long does it take to get a Six Sigma Black Belt?

Black Belt training itself usually runs several weeks, often spread over a few months, but most Black Belts first gain experience as a Green Belt. ASQ’s Black Belt exam also requires proof of completed projects. Counting project work, reaching Black Belt usually takes a few years from your first improvement project.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, supply chain management, finance or economics. Some hire with an associate degree plus purchasing experience. Courses in negotiation, contract basics, accounting and spreadsheets help most, along with experience using ERP or purchasing software.
First job

Many people start as a purchasing assistant, procurement coordinator, junior buyer or inventory clerk. These roles involve processing purchase orders, chasing deliveries, comparing quotes and keeping supplier records. Some move in from accounts payable, logistics or warehouse roles where they already work with vendors.
Buyer experience

After a year or two, people usually take on their own spend categories as a buyer. They run requests for quotes, negotiate price and terms, and track supplier performance. This hands-on negotiation record is what employers look for when hiring procurement specialists.
Optional certification

No license is required. Many specialists add a certification to stand out, such as the CPSM from the Institute for Supply Management or ASCM’s CPIM or CSCP. In government purchasing, the CPPB and CPPO are common, and federal contracting staff follow the FAC-C program.
Time it takes

Counting a four-year degree, reaching a specialist title usually takes about five to seven years. Someone already holding a degree often gets there in two to three years of buyer or coordinator work. Certifications typically require some years of experience before you qualify.
qa: Do you need a certification to work in procurement?

No. There is no license or required exam for private-sector procurement in the US. Certifications such as the CPSM, CPIM or CPPB are optional, but some employers prefer them for senior or public-sector roles. Most people get hired on a degree and purchasing experience, then certify later to move up.
Can you get into procurement without a degree?

Yes, though it is harder. Some people start as a purchasing clerk, inventory assistant or receiving coordinator and work up to buyer by learning the company’s suppliers and systems. Many specialist postings still ask for a bachelor’s degree, so experience and a supply management certification help make up the gap.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, supply chain management, finance or a related field. Some roles accept an associate degree or a high school diploma plus solid office or purchasing experience. Courses in accounting, contracts and data analysis help most.
System and spreadsheet skills

The daily work runs through procurement software and ERP systems. Learn how requisitions, approval workflows, purchase orders and invoice matching work. Strong spreadsheet skills matter, since you will track spend, open orders and vendor records. Many people learn specific systems on the job.
First job

People usually start as a purchasing assistant, procurement coordinator, junior buyer or accounts payable clerk. These roles teach how orders move from request to payment, how to handle vendor questions and how to follow company purchasing policy.
Optional certification

No license is required. Some people add a certification after gaining experience, such as the CPSM from the Institute for Supply Management. In government purchasing, the CPPB is common and some agencies prefer it. Each has its own experience and exam requirements.
Time it takes

With a degree, moving into a procurement operations specialist role usually takes one to three years of related work. Without a degree, it often takes longer and depends on showing reliable experience with purchasing systems and processes.
qa: Do you need a certification to work in procurement operations?

No. There is no license or required certification for this work in the US. Employers mostly look for a related degree and hands-on experience with purchase orders and procurement systems. Certifications such as the CPSM, or the CPPB in public sector purchasing, can help you stand out but are usually earned after a few years in the field.
How long does it take to become a procurement operations specialist?

Most people take about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then one to three years in an entry role such as purchasing assistant, procurement coordinator or accounts payable clerk. People without a degree can still get in, but it usually takes more years of related office or purchasing experience first.

steps: Education

Most producers hold a bachelor’s degree in film, media, communications, business or game design, but no specific degree is required. Classes in budgeting, scheduling and team management help. Many also learn by running student films, game jams or their own podcasts or video channels.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam to work as a producer in the US. Some game and tech studios value agile or project management training, such as Certified ScrumMaster or the PMP from the Project Management Institute, but these are optional and rarely required for entry.
First job

Most people start as a production assistant or production coordinator. In games, many also start as QA testers. These roles teach schedules, call sheets, task tracking and how departments work together, and they build the contacts that lead to later work.
Associate producer

The usual next step is associate producer or assistant producer. You own parts of the schedule, track tasks and budget lines, and run meetings with artists, engineers, editors or hosts while a senior producer oversees the whole project.
Time it takes

Moving from an entry role to a producer title usually takes three to seven years. Hiring managers weigh shipped games, aired episodes, published shows and strong references more than formal credentials, so building a record of finished projects matters most.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a producer?

No degree is strictly required, but most producers have a bachelor’s degree in film, media, communications, business or game design. Employers care more about finished projects and experience coordinating teams. Many producers start as production assistants, coordinators or QA testers and work their way up through associate producer roles.
How long does it take to become a producer?

It usually takes three to seven years after entering the field. Most people spend a few years as a production assistant, coordinator or QA tester, then move to associate producer before earning the producer title. The pace depends on the projects you finish, the size of the studio or network, and your references.

steps: Education

Most product analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in a field like statistics, economics, mathematics, computer science or business. No single major is required. What matters is coursework in statistics, data analysis and some exposure to how software products are built and measured.
Core skills

Learn SQL well, since most of the job is pulling and shaping data on user behavior. Add spreadsheets, a dashboard tool, basic statistics and A/B testing. Some Python or R helps. You also need to explain findings clearly to product managers, designers and engineers.
Portfolio projects

Because there is no license or standard credential, a portfolio carries weight. Analyze public app or website data, build a funnel or retention analysis, or write up a mock experiment. Show the question, the method and the product change you would recommend.
Optional certificates

There is no required license, registration or exam for this work. Some people take online certificates in data analytics or SQL to show skills, but employers usually care more about practical ability shown in interviews, take-home tasks and past projects.
First job

Many people start as a data analyst, business analyst, marketing analyst or operations analyst, often at a company with a digital product. Others move over from customer support, quality assurance or product operations roles after learning SQL and taking on analysis work.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually one to three years in a related analyst role before landing a product analyst title. Career changers with strong SQL skills and a solid portfolio can sometimes move in faster.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a product analyst?

No. There is no license, state registration or required exam for product analysts in the US. Some people earn online certificates in data analytics or SQL, but hiring usually depends on technical interviews, take-home assignments and a portfolio that shows you can turn user data into clear product recommendations.
How long does it take to become a product analyst?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree, then one to three years working as a data, business or marketing analyst before moving into a product analyst role. Someone switching careers with strong SQL and analytics skills may get there sooner, especially by moving internally at a company with a digital product.

steps: Education

There is no required degree or license. Many product designers hold a bachelor’s degree in graphic design, interaction design, human-computer interaction, psychology or computer science. Others come from related fields and learn design through short courses or self-study.
Core skills and tools

Learn user research, wireframing, prototyping, visual design and usability testing. Get comfortable in a common design tool such as Figma. Basic knowledge of how web and mobile apps are built helps you work well with engineers.
Portfolio

Employers hire mainly on your portfolio. Build three to five case studies that show the problem, your research, sketches, the screens you designed and what changed as a result. Redesigns of real apps or volunteer projects count when you explain your thinking.
Internship or first job

Common ways in are a design internship, a junior product designer or UX designer role, or a visual or web designer job. Some people move over from front-end development, research or customer support inside a tech company.
Time it takes

With a related degree, many people land a first design role soon after graduating. Career changers usually spend about one to two years building skills and a portfolio. Reaching a mid-level product designer role typically takes two to four more years.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a product designer?

No. There is no license or required degree for product design in the US. Many designers studied graphic design, interaction design or human-computer interaction, but employers mostly judge your portfolio. Strong case studies that show research, problem solving and finished screens can get you hired without a design degree, though some larger companies still prefer a bachelor’s degree.
How long does it take to become a product designer?

It usually takes one to four years. Students in a related bachelor’s program can start in a junior role right after graduating. People changing careers often need about one to two years of focused learning, practice projects and portfolio work before landing a first job as a junior product designer, UX designer or design intern.

steps: Know which role you mean

This section covers the software sense of the title. In manufacturing and hardware companies, “product engineer” usually means a mechanical, electrical or manufacturing engineer who designs physical products. Those roles normally require a bachelor’s degree in engineering, often from an ABET-accredited program, and follow a different path.
Education

Many software product engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field. Some employers also hire people who learned through self-study or short courses and can show strong work. Either way, you need a frontend framework, a backend language, databases, APIs and deployment.
Product skills

Learn what sets this role apart from pure coding. Practice talking to users, reading analytics, writing short specs, and working with designers and product managers. Employers want someone who can decide what to build, ship it, and check whether it helped users.
Portfolio of shipped work

Build and release at least one complete product that real people use, from the idea to the launch. Show the problem, your choices, the code and what you learned after release. This matters most if you have no degree or no prior engineering job.
First job

Few people start with this title. The usual way in is a role as a software engineer, full-stack developer or frontend developer, often at a startup or small team where engineers talk to users. Many move into product engineering after a few years of that work.
Time it takes

There is no license, required exam or standard certification for software product engineers. The path usually takes several years: a degree or equivalent self-study, then often two to four years building features as a software engineer before people hold the product engineer title.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a product engineer?

It depends on which kind. For software product engineers, many employers prefer a computer science or related degree, but some hire based on shipped work and experience. For hardware or manufacturing product engineers, who design physical products, employers normally require a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, electrical or another engineering field.
Do you need a license to be a product engineer?

Software product engineers need no state license and no standard certification. Hiring depends on skills, shipped work and experience. Engineers who design physical products sometimes earn a Professional Engineer (PE) license from a state board, but whether it is needed varies by state, employer and the type of work.

steps: Education

Most product managers hold a bachelor’s degree, often in computer science, engineering, business, economics or design. No specific major is required. Technical coursework helps in software product roles. Some people later earn an MBA, which some employers value for strategy-heavy or consumer product teams.
No required license

There is no state license, registration or required exam for product managers. Optional credentials exist, such as the Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) from Scrum Alliance. Employers mostly judge you on products you helped ship, your judgment and how clearly you communicate.
Related role first

Most people move in from a nearby role such as software engineering, UX design, data analysis, marketing, consulting or customer support. In that job, volunteer to write requirements, interview users, run small experiments and work closely with the product team.
Build evidence

Keep a record of product decisions you shaped: the user problem, what you learned, what you chose not to build and the result. Side projects, a launched app or written product teardowns help when you lack the title. Interviews usually test product sense and prioritization.
First job

The usual entry titles are associate product manager (APM) or junior product manager. Some larger companies run APM programs for new graduates. Internal transfers are also common, since your employer already knows how you work with its engineers and customers.
Time it takes

Expect a four-year degree plus usually two to five years in a related role before earning a product manager title. Graduates hired into APM roles often reach full product manager in about two years. Career changers with deep industry knowledge sometimes move faster.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a product manager?

No. Product management has no required license, exam or certification in the US. Credentials like the Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) can show interest and teach basic agile practice, but hiring managers care far more about real experience. Showing that you understood users, made tradeoffs and shipped results matters most.
How long does it take to become a product manager?

For most people it takes a bachelor’s degree plus two to five years of experience in a related role, such as engineering, design, analytics or marketing. Some new graduates start right away as associate product managers and move up in about two years. There is no fixed timeline because no formal training path exists.

steps: Education

Most product marketing managers hold a bachelor’s degree in marketing, business, communications, economics or a related field. For software, medical or engineering products, a technical degree or strong technical knowledge helps. Some larger employers prefer an MBA, but it is not required for most roles.
No license required

There is no license, state registration or required exam for this work. Private certificate courses in product marketing exist and can show interest, but employers mostly judge candidates on past launches, writing samples and knowledge of the product’s market.
First job

Few people start in product marketing. Common first jobs are marketing coordinator, content marketer, marketing associate, sales development representative or customer success associate. Others move over from sales engineering, product management or market research after learning the product and its buyers.
Build core skills

While in that first role, people practice the core of the job: interviewing customers, studying competitors, writing positioning and messaging, building sales decks and comparison sheets, and helping run product launches. Keeping samples of this work makes it easier to show readiness for a product marketing role.
Time it takes

The usual path is a four-year bachelor’s degree followed by three to five years of experience in marketing, sales or a related role. That makes about seven to nine years in total after high school. Career changers who already know an industry well can sometimes move in faster.
Entry product marketing role

The first title in the field is often associate product marketing manager, or product marketing manager at a smaller company. From there, people take on larger products or launches and can move up to senior product marketing manager and director roles.
qa: Do you need a license to be a product marketing manager?

No. Product marketing has no license, state registration or required exam in the US. Optional certificate courses are available from private providers, but employers focus on a bachelor’s degree, relevant experience in marketing, sales or product roles, and proof of past work such as launch plans, messaging and sales materials.
How long does it take to become a product marketing manager?

It usually takes about seven to nine years in total. That includes a four-year bachelor’s degree plus three to five years of experience in a related role such as marketing coordinator, content marketer or sales. People who switch over from product management or sales engineering may get there faster because they already know the product and its buyers.

steps: Education

Most product operations managers hold a bachelor’s degree, often in business, information systems, computer science, engineering or economics. No single major is required. Coursework in data analysis, statistics and project management helps, since much of the job is tracking launches, reading usage data and organizing customer feedback.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for product operations work in any state. Some people earn the PMP from the Project Management Institute or a Scrum certification, but employers rarely require them. Proof that you have run processes and tools for a product team counts for more.
First job

People usually enter from a nearby role. Common starting points are customer support, customer success, business analyst, program or project coordinator, sales operations and associate product manager. In these jobs you learn how products ship, how support tickets and customer requests flow, and how teams use tools like issue trackers and analytics dashboards.
Build ops experience

Volunteer to own operational work in your current job. Examples include running release checklists, setting up a feedback intake process, cleaning up a ticketing workflow, building reports on product usage, or writing launch documentation. Keep concrete examples, because hiring managers ask how you improved a process and what changed as a result.
Time it takes

Most people move into a product operations manager title after about three to five years of related work following a degree. Some start as a product operations analyst or specialist first and are promoted to manager after one to three years in that role.
qa: Do you need a certification to become a product operations manager?

No. No license or certification is required to work in product operations in the US. Some people add a PMP or a Scrum certification to show process skills, but most employers care more about hands-on experience running launches, managing product tools and turning customer and support feedback into clear input for product teams.
How long does it take to become a product operations manager?

It usually takes about three to five years after a bachelor’s degree. Most people first work in customer support, customer success, business analysis, program coordination or a junior product role. Many then spend one to three years as a product operations analyst or specialist before moving up to a manager title.

steps: Education

There is no license and no required degree. Many product owners hold a bachelor’s degree in business, computer science, information systems or engineering. What matters more is understanding how software gets built and how to turn business needs into clear, testable work.
First job

Most people move in from a related role on a software team, such as business analyst, QA tester, developer, project coordinator, scrum master or support lead. Working daily with an agile team teaches backlogs, sprints and how developers estimate work.
Agile skills

Product owners write user stories with acceptance criteria, order the product backlog by value, and take part in sprint planning and reviews. Studying the Scrum Guide and practicing story writing and backlog ordering on real projects builds the core skill.
Certification

Certification is optional but common in job ads. The main ones are the Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) from Scrum Alliance, earned through a course, the Professional Scrum Product Owner I (PSPO I) from Scrum.org, earned by passing an online assessment, and SAFe Product Owner/Product Manager (POPM) from Scaled Agile.
Time it takes

Most product owners take the title after a few years in a related role. A certification course takes only a few days, but employers usually look for experience owning a backlog and working with stakeholders, not the certificate alone.
Next steps

From product owner, people often move to senior product owner, product manager or group product manager. Some move toward agile coaching or portfolio roles in companies that use scaled agile frameworks.
qa: What certification do you need to be a product owner?

None is legally required, but many job ads ask for one. The most common are the Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) from Scrum Alliance, the Professional Scrum Product Owner I (PSPO I) from Scrum.org, and SAFe Product Owner/Product Manager (POPM) from Scaled Agile. Employers still weigh hands-on backlog experience more than any certificate.
Can you become a product owner without experience?

It is rare to be hired as a product owner with no work experience. Most people first work as a business analyst, developer, tester, project coordinator or scrum master on an agile team. Some companies give the role to a subject expert from the business side, such as operations or customer support.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in supply chain management, operations management, industrial engineering or business. Some hire people with an associate degree or a high school diploma who have years of shop floor or warehouse experience instead.
Planning software skills

Planners work daily in ERP and MRP systems and in spreadsheets. Learning how material requirements planning works, plus strong Excel skills, makes you far more hireable. Many people pick this up in class, through online courses or on the job.
First job

Common ways in are roles as a production scheduler, material planner, inventory analyst, buyer, expediter or production coordinator. People also move up from machine operator, team lead or warehouse jobs once they know how the plant runs.
Optional certification

No license is required. Many planners later earn the CPIM (Certified in Planning and Inventory Management) from ASCM, formerly APICS. Some employers prefer or pay for it, and it helps when moving to senior planner or supply chain roles.
Time it takes

With a four-year degree, people usually work one to three years in a scheduling, inventory or buying role before taking a full production planner job. Coming up from the shop floor often takes longer but is a well-worn path.
qa: Do you need a license or certification to be a production planner?

No. There is no state license for production planners. Certification is optional. The best known is the CPIM from ASCM, which covers planning, scheduling and inventory. Some employers list it as preferred, and it can help with promotions, but many planners are hired on experience and ERP skills alone.
How long does it take to become a production planner?

Most people take about five to seven years in total. That is usually a four-year degree in supply chain, operations or industrial engineering, then one to three years in a related job such as scheduler, buyer or inventory analyst. People who start on the shop floor without a degree can also get there, usually after several years.

steps: Education

A high school diploma is the minimum. Many employers prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree in industrial engineering, manufacturing technology, operations management or business. Plant manager roles usually expect a bachelor’s degree, and some larger plants favor an engineering background or an MBA.
Experience on the floor

Most supervisors start on the production floor as operators, assemblers or technicians. You learn the equipment, the product, quality checks and safety rules firsthand. Graduates sometimes skip this through supervisor trainee or management development programs that rotate them through departments.
Lead role

The usual next step is team lead or line lead. You train new workers, cover breaks, track output and fill in for the supervisor. This is where you show you can handle people, schedules and problems on your own.
Optional certifications

There is no license to supervise production. Employers often value an OSHA 30-hour General Industry card, Lean or Six Sigma training such as the ASQ Certified Six Sigma Green Belt, and ASCM’s CPIM for planning and inventory work. None is required by law.
Time it takes

Moving from the floor to supervisor usually takes several years. Degree holders in trainee programs may supervise within one to two years. Plant manager typically comes after many years of larger roles, such as area manager or operations manager, often a decade or more.
First job

The common entry point is production associate or machine operator, then lead. With a degree, the usual first role is production supervisor or supervisor trainee, often on second or third shift, where new supervisors commonly start.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a production supervisor?

Not always. Many production supervisors are promoted from operator or lead roles based on experience and reliability, with only a high school diploma. A degree in industrial engineering, manufacturing or business helps you move up faster and is usually expected for plant manager jobs, especially at larger companies.
How long does it take to become a plant manager?

It usually takes many years. A typical path runs from production supervisor to area or department manager to operations manager, then plant manager. That often means a decade or more of manufacturing experience. A bachelor’s degree, a track record with safety and quality results, and Lean or Six Sigma skills can shorten the climb.

steps: Basic education

Most employers prefer a high school diploma or GED, though some entry-level line jobs hire without one. Basic math, reading measurements, shop classes and career and technical education programs in high school or community college give you a head start.
Hiring screens

Expect a drug test, a background check and sometimes a basic skills or mechanical aptitude test. Many plants also expect you to stand for long shifts, lift parts, and work nights, weekends or rotating shifts.
On-the-job training

No state license is required for production work. Training happens on the job and usually lasts from a few days to a few months. It covers safety rules, lockout/tagout, the machines on your line, quality checks and how to read work instructions.
Optional certifications

Some workers earn the MSSC Certified Production Technician (CPT) credential, or NIMS credentials for machining work. If you drive a forklift, OSHA rules require training and evaluation before you operate it, and the employer usually provides this.
First job

Most people start as an assembler, packer, line worker or machine operator trainee. Many are hired directly, and others come in through a staffing agency on a temp-to-hire basis. With experience, workers move into machine setup, quality inspection or team lead roles.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a production worker?

No. Production workers do not need a college degree or a license. Many employers prefer a high school diploma or GED, and some hire without one. Employers train new hires on the job, so reliability, safety awareness, basic math and a willingness to work shifts matter more than formal schooling.
How long does it take to become a machine operator?

You can often start an entry-level machine operator job right away and learn the basics in a few weeks of on-the-job training. Running complex equipment such as CNC machines on your own, or doing machine setup, usually takes one to two years or more, sometimes with a community college certificate or an apprenticeship.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in information systems, computer science, business, accounting or engineering. The best field depends on the product. Finance software favors accounting, HR software favors human resources and technical products favor computer science. Some companies hire people without a degree if they already know the product well.
Technical and product skills

Learn how business software is configured and connected. Useful skills include SQL, data migration, spreadsheets, REST APIs and basic scripting. You also need to run workshops, write requirements and explain technical choices to customers. Hands-on time inside the actual product matters more than general theory.
Vendor certification

There is no state license for this work. Many software makers run their own certification programs, such as Salesforce Certified Administrator or Microsoft Certified credentials for Dynamics 365. Employers and implementation partners often expect you to earn one soon after hiring. Some consultants later add the PMP from PMI.
First job

Common entry points are technical support, implementation specialist, business analyst, junior or associate consultant, and system administrator at a company that uses the product. Working as the in-house expert who runs a tool for your employer is a frequent route into consulting for the vendor or a partner firm.
Time it takes

After a degree, people usually spend one to three years in support, analyst or associate roles before leading customer implementations on their own. Senior consultants who design complex integrations across several systems typically have five or more years of hands-on project work.
qa: Do you need a license to be a professional services consultant?

No. No US state licenses this work. Instead, employers look at product knowledge, project experience and vendor certifications. Many software companies offer their own exams, such as Salesforce or Microsoft Dynamics 365 certifications, and partner firms often require consultants to hold them. A project management credential like the PMP can help but is rarely required at entry level.
How long does it take to become an implementation consultant?

Most people take four years to earn a bachelor’s degree, then one to three years in a related role such as technical support, business analyst or system administrator. Some move faster by joining a vendor or partner firm as an associate consultant and earning a product certification within their first year.

steps: Graduate degree

Most four-year colleges and universities require a doctorate, usually a PhD, for tenure-track jobs. Some fields use other terminal degrees, such as an MFA in creative arts or a JD in law. Community colleges often hire instructors with a master’s degree and graduate coursework in the subject.
Teaching and research

Doctoral students build experience as teaching assistants and by publishing research. A doctorate usually takes five to seven years after a bachelor’s degree. Strong publications, conference talks and teaching evaluations shape the academic job application.
Postdoc

In the sciences and some other fields, most new PhDs complete one or more postdoctoral positions, often lasting two to five years in total, before getting a faculty job. Postdocs build a publication record and often apply for their own research grants.
First job

The usual first job is assistant professor on the tenure track, or a non-tenure-track lecturer, instructor or adjunct position. Adjunct and lecturer roles mainly involve teaching and are a common way in at community colleges and for part-time teaching.
Tenure

Tenure-track faculty usually go up for tenure after about six years, based on research, teaching and service. Tenure usually brings promotion to associate professor, and full professor follows after more years. There is no state license, though some fields, such as nursing, require faculty to hold a professional license.
Time it takes

Expect about ten to fifteen years after high school to reach a tenure-track job: four for a bachelor’s degree, five to seven for a doctorate and often a postdoc. Earning tenure usually takes about six more years.
qa: How long does it take to become a professor?

Usually ten years or more after high school. A bachelor’s degree takes four years and a PhD usually five to seven more. Many fields then expect one or more postdocs before a tenure-track assistant professor job. Earning tenure usually takes about six more years. Community college teaching can start sooner with a master’s degree.
Do you need a license to be a professor?

No license is required to teach at a college or university. Hiring depends on your degree, research and teaching record. Some programs, such as nursing, require faculty to hold a professional license in their field, and clinical faculty in medicine must be licensed to treat patients.

steps: Education

Most program coordinators have a bachelor’s degree in a field tied to the program, such as public health, social work, education, public administration or nonprofit management. Some community programs hire people with an associate degree and relevant experience.
First job

Common ways in are program assistant, administrative assistant, case aide, outreach worker or intern at a nonprofit, school, hospital or government agency. National service programs such as AmeriCorps and volunteer work also give experience running schedules, events and records.
Grant rules

Coordinators on federally funded programs must follow grant rules, including the Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR 200, and track spending, participants and outcomes for reports. Many learn this on the job or through short grants management courses.
Background checks and training

Programs serving children, older adults or patients usually require a criminal background check, and some require fingerprinting, CPR and first aid training, or training on reporting child abuse. Health programs may also require HIPAA privacy training.
Certification

No license or certification is required. Some coordinators earn the CAPM (Certified Associate in Project Management) from the Project Management Institute, and later the PMP. Others take certificates in nonprofit management, volunteer management or grants management.
Time it takes

With a bachelor’s degree, many people land a coordinator role after one to two years as an assistant, intern or service member. Moving up to program manager or director usually takes another three to five years.
qa: Can you become a program coordinator without experience?

It is possible but uncommon. Most coordinators first gain one to two years as a program assistant, intern, case aide or volunteer. Some new graduates get hired directly, especially after internships or a year of national service such as AmeriCorps. Strong organization, writing and spreadsheet skills help you stand out.
What certification helps a program coordinator?

None is required. A common choice is the CAPM (Certified Associate in Project Management) from the Project Management Institute, which shows basic project skills, followed later by the PMP. Coordinators in nonprofits sometimes take certificates in grants management or volunteer management, and health programs may require HIPAA privacy training.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree. Common fields are business, engineering, computer science, or the field the projects serve, such as construction or health care. Some people study project management directly, but no single major is required.
First job

Most people start as a project coordinator, project analyst, or assistant project manager. Others move in from a technical or operations role where they already help plan work, track deadlines, and coordinate across teams.
Entry certification

The CAPM from the Project Management Institute (PMI) suits people with little experience. It requires 23 hours of project management education and passing an exam. It is optional, but it can help a first application stand out.
PMP certification

There is no state license for this work. Many employers prefer or expect the PMP from PMI. With a four-year degree, you need 36 months of experience leading projects and 35 hours of project management education before the exam. Without a degree, you need 60 months of experience.
Program and agile credentials

People who go on to oversee several related projects may later earn PMI’s PgMP. In software and tech, employers often want agile skills, shown through credentials such as the PMI-ACP or Certified ScrumMaster.
Time it takes

Most people spend three to seven years after college moving from coordinator to project manager. Leading a full program across many teams usually takes several more years of experience on top of that.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a project manager?

No license or certification is legally required. Still, many employers prefer the PMP from the Project Management Institute, and some job postings, especially in government contracting and large companies, list it as a requirement. Newer workers can earn the CAPM first, then the PMP once they have enough experience leading projects.
How long does it take to become a program manager?

It usually takes a bachelor’s degree plus many years of work. Most people spend several years as a project coordinator and then project manager before they lead a program that spans many teams. In total, that often means five to ten years of experience after college, depending on the industry and employer.

steps: Education

Many programmers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. An associate degree or self-study can also work, especially at smaller employers. CNC programmers for machine tools usually come through a machining or manufacturing technology program at a community college or trade school.
Core languages and tools

Learn the languages your target field uses. Game studios lean on C++ and C#. Older companies often run COBOL, Java or SQL on mainframe and business systems. Machine tool programmers work in G-code and CAM software, and they also need to read blueprints and understand the machining process.
Portfolio of work

Employers want proof you can write working code. Build small games, tools or programs and share the source code publicly. CNC candidates can show parts they programmed and machined. A good portfolio often matters as much as a degree, and sometimes more.
Optional certifications

No state license is required to work as a programmer. Some people add vendor or language certifications to stand out. In manufacturing, machining credentials from NIMS are recognized by many employers, but they are not required by law.
First job

Common entry points are junior programmer, programming intern or QA tester at a game studio. In manufacturing, many people start as CNC machinists or operators and move into programming. At older companies, IT support or trainee programs in legacy systems can lead to a programmer role.
Time it takes

Most people need two to four years of school or focused self-study before their first programming job. CNC programmers often spend a few years as machinists first. Reaching a fully independent programmer role usually takes another one to three years on the job.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a programmer?

No. A computer science degree is common and helps with many employers, but it is not legally required. Many programmers get hired with an associate degree, self-study or a strong portfolio of working projects. Larger companies and game studios may still prefer a bachelor’s degree, so a degree widens your options.
Do programmers need a license or certification?

No license is required to work as a programmer in any US state. Certifications are optional. Some people earn vendor or language certifications, and machine tool programmers may earn NIMS machining credentials. Employers usually care more about your skills, your portfolio and your experience than about any certificate.

steps: Education

There is no license and no single required path. Many coordinators hold an associate or bachelor’s degree in business, management or a field tied to the industry, such as construction or IT. Strong organization, writing and spreadsheet skills matter as much as the degree.
First job

Many people start as an administrative assistant, office coordinator, project assistant or operations assistant, then take on scheduling, meeting notes and task tracking for a project team. In construction and engineering firms, project assistant and document control roles are common ways in.
Tools and methods

Coordinators keep schedules, task lists, risk and issue logs, and meeting minutes. Learning project scheduling software, spreadsheets and the basics of both waterfall and agile methods, such as Gantt charts, milestones and sprints, prepares you for most postings.
Certification

Certification is optional. The Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) from the Project Management Institute (PMI) is aimed at beginners. It requires a high school diploma and 23 hours of project management education, then an exam, and needs no prior project experience.
Time it takes
Entry-level coordinator jobs are open right after school or after a year or two in an administrative role. Preparing for the CAPM usually takes a few weeks to a few months of study.
Next step

After three to five years leading projects, depending on education, coordinators can qualify for the Project Management Professional (PMP) from PMI, which also requires 35 hours of training and an exam. Many coordinators move up to project manager.
qa: Can you become a project coordinator without experience?

Yes. It is one of the more common entry-level roles in project work. Employers often hire recent graduates or people with administrative, customer service or office experience who show strong organization and communication. A CAPM certification or a record of projects you tracked, even volunteer ones, can help a beginner stand out.
What certification is best for a project coordinator?

The most common is the Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) from the Project Management Institute. It needs no project experience, only 23 hours of project management education and a passing exam. After three to five years of experience leading projects, depending on education, many coordinators go on to the Project Management Professional (PMP).

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in business, engineering, information technology, construction management or the field the projects belong to. No single degree is required. Some colleges offer project management degrees or certificates, but experience usually counts for more.
First job

Most people start as a project coordinator, project assistant or associate project manager, handling schedules, meeting notes and status reports. Others move up from a role in their field, such as engineer, analyst or site supervisor, by taking on small projects first.
Entry certification

The CAPM from the Project Management Institute (PMI) is an optional starting credential. It needs no work experience, only 23 hours of project management education and a passing exam score. It can help a newcomer stand out for coordinator roles.
PMP certification

The PMP from PMI is the credential employers ask for most. It requires 35 hours of project management education plus 36 months leading projects with a four-year degree, or 60 months without one. You then pass the exam and earn 60 PDUs every three years to keep it.
Time it takes

Moving from a first coordinator job to a project manager title usually takes three to five years. Software and agile teams may also look for agile credentials, such as PMI-ACP, while construction employers often value field experience over certification.
qa: Do you need a license to be a project manager?

No. Project management has no state license in the US. Many employers prefer or require certification, most often the PMP from the Project Management Institute. Some fields add their own rules, so a construction project manager may work under a company’s contractor license, but the project manager role itself is not licensed.
How long does it take to become a project manager?

It usually takes three to five years after a bachelor’s degree. Most people spend that time as a project coordinator or in a related role, gaining the experience leading projects that employers and the PMP require. With a four-year degree, the PMP needs 36 months of that experience before you can sit the exam.

steps: Education

A high school diploma is the minimum, but many property managers have a bachelor’s degree in business, real estate, finance or hospitality. Courses in accounting, real estate law and customer service help. Commercial property roles more often expect a degree.
First job

The most common way in is a leasing consultant or leasing agent job, showing units, processing applications and signing leases. Others start as an assistant property manager, an administrative assistant at a management firm or a maintenance coordinator.
State license

Many states require a real estate broker or salesperson license to lease or manage property for others for a fee, while on-site employees of the owner are often exempt. Some states, such as Florida, separately license managers of condominium and homeowners associations. Requirements vary widely by state.
Fair housing and landlord law

Property managers must follow the federal Fair Housing Act, state landlord-tenant law and local rent and eviction rules. Most learn these through on-the-job training and fair housing courses, because mistakes in screening, advertising or evictions carry legal risk.
Certification
