Common credentials include the NALP and CAM (Certified Apartment Manager) from the National Apartment Association, the ARM and CPM (Certified Property Manager) from the Institute of Real Estate Management, and the RPA from BOMI International for commercial buildings. The higher ones require years of experience.
Time it takes

Most people move from leasing agent to assistant manager in one to two years, then to property manager after two to four years in total. Earning the CPM or managing a large portfolio usually takes several more years.
qa: Do you need a license to be a property manager?

It depends on the state. Many states require a real estate broker or salesperson license to lease or manage property for others for a fee, though on-site employees working for the owner are often exempt. A few states have a separate property management or community association manager license. Check with the state real estate commission where you work.
Can you become a property manager without experience?

Usually not directly. Most property managers start as leasing consultants or assistant property managers, where they learn leasing, rent collection, maintenance requests and fair housing rules. Small owners sometimes hire beginners with strong customer service or office experience. Credentials such as the CAM from the National Apartment Association help once you have some experience.

steps: Education

There is no required degree, but most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree. Common fields are English, communications, journalism, business and marketing. Strong writing and editing skills matter more than the exact major.
First job

Most people start as a proposal coordinator, proposal writer or proposal specialist. Others move over from technical writing, contracts administration, business development or program support, where they already help with bids.
Learn government contracting

For federal work, you learn how requests for proposals are built and evaluated. That includes the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), compliance matrices, color team reviews, past performance writing and agency procurement portals like SAM.gov.
Certification

No license is required. Many employers value certification from APMP, the Association of Proposal Management Professionals. Its levels include APMP Foundation, Practitioner and Professional. Defense contractors may also require a security clearance, which the employer sponsors.
Time it takes

Moving from coordinator to proposal manager usually takes three to five years of running pieces of bids. Capture manager roles often come later, after years of proposal work and some business development experience.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a proposal manager?

No license or certification is legally required. Many employers do prefer or ask for APMP certification, from the Association of Proposal Management Professionals, at the Foundation, Practitioner or Professional level. Proven experience winning bids, especially government contracts, usually counts most when hiring managers compare candidates.
How long does it take to become a proposal manager?

Most people need three to five years of proposal experience after a bachelor’s degree. They often start as a proposal coordinator or writer, then take on larger sections and whole bids. Moving into capture management, which shapes deals before the request for proposal is released, often takes several more years.

steps: Engineering degree

Most propulsion engineers earn a bachelor’s degree in aerospace or mechanical engineering, usually from an ABET-accredited program. Key courses include thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, heat transfer, combustion and gas dynamics. Some enter from chemical engineering, especially for rocket propellant work.
Hands-on projects

Employers look closely at practical experience. Students build it through internships, co-ops and university rocketry or engine teams, where they design, machine and test real hardware. Skills in CAD, MATLAB or Python, and analyzing test data make applicants stand out.
Citizenship and clearance

Much propulsion work falls under ITAR export rules, so many employers hire only US citizens or permanent residents. Defense and some space jobs also require a security clearance, which the employer sponsors after you are hired.
Optional license

Most propulsion jobs need no license, since engineers working for manufacturers are usually exempt from state licensing. Some take the FE exam near graduation and later earn a PE license, with requirements that vary by state, but few aerospace employers ask for it.
Graduate study

A master’s degree, which usually takes one to two years, is common for combustion, analysis and advanced design roles. Many employers help pay for it while you work. A PhD mainly suits research and new engine concepts.
First job

Most start as a junior propulsion engineer, test engineer or design engineer, often supporting engine test stands, building components or running simulations. Expect to work under senior engineers for the first few years before owning a full subsystem.
qa: Do you need a license to be a propulsion engineer?

Usually not. Most propulsion engineers work for aerospace or defense manufacturers, which are generally exempt from state engineering licensing. Some take the FE exam and later earn a PE license for career flexibility, and rules vary by state. Many jobs instead require US citizenship or permanent residency under ITAR, and some need a security clearance.
How long does it take to become a propulsion engineer?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in aerospace or mechanical engineering, then land an entry-level role. Those who add a master’s degree spend one to two more years. Becoming a senior engineer who leads engine design or testing usually takes several more years of work experience.

steps: Education

Many public administrators hold a bachelor’s degree in public administration, political science, public policy, economics or a field tied to the agency’s work. For management roles, a Master of Public Administration (MPA) is common, and many programs are accredited by NASPAA.
Applying

Federal jobs are posted on USAJOBS and graded on the General Schedule, with education and experience setting your starting grade. State and local governments post jobs on their own sites, and many fill positions through civil service exams or ranked lists. Veterans’ preference applies in federal and many state hiring.
Requirements

Most federal jobs require US citizenship, and many public jobs require a background check. Some positions add a security clearance, a driver’s license or a professional license. Hiring can take several months, so many people apply widely.
First job

Common first jobs are program assistant, management analyst, budget analyst, administrative officer or policy aide in a city, county, state or federal agency. Internships with local governments or legislative offices are a common way in for students.
Certification

No license is required for general public administration. Some managers earn the Certified Public Manager (CPM) through state programs accredited by the National Certified Public Manager Consortium. City and county managers may pursue the ICMA Credentialed Manager designation.
Time it takes

Entry-level government jobs are open to new graduates. An MPA usually takes about two years full time. Moving up to program manager or department head often takes many years, and civil service systems usually require competing for each promotion.
qa: How do you get a government job with no experience?

Start with entry-level and internship postings. The federal government lists jobs on USAJOBS and can set grades by education, so a bachelor’s degree alone can qualify you for some entry-level grades. State and local governments often use civil service exams. Read each posting’s qualifications closely and match your resume to them, since screening is strict.
What is a civil service exam?

A civil service exam is a test many state and local governments use to rank applicants for public jobs, such as clerical, police, fire and administrative roles. Scores often place you on an eligible list from which agencies hire. Exams and rules vary by government, and most federal jobs use online assessments and questionnaires instead.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Many start with a bachelor’s degree in public health, biology, economics, statistics or a social science. Courses in statistics, epidemiology and programming in R, SAS or Python are useful. Entry jobs exist at this level, but most analytical roles expect a graduate degree.
Graduate degree

The standard degree is a Master of Public Health (MPH), usually two years, ideally from a program accredited by the Council on Education for Public Health (CEPH). Health economists usually hold a master’s or PhD in economics, health economics or health services research. Epidemiologists often need an MPH or MS.
Certification

There is no license for most public health work. The Certified in Public Health (CPH) credential from the National Board of Public Health Examiners is optional. Health educators often earn the Certified Health Education Specialist (CHES) from the National Commission for Health Education Credentialing.
Fellowships

Government fellowships are a common way in. The CDC’s Public Health Associate Program takes recent graduates, and its Epidemic Intelligence Service trains field epidemiologists, mainly people with doctoral degrees. The Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) runs an applied epidemiology fellowship at health departments.
First job

Typical first jobs are research assistant, data analyst, program coordinator or epidemiologist at a health department, hospital, university or nonprofit. Health economics graduates often start as health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) analysts at consulting firms, insurers or drug companies, building cost-effectiveness models.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree and two for an MPH or another master’s. A PhD in epidemiology or health economics usually takes four to six more years. Research leadership roles in academia and industry often require the doctorate.
qa: How long does it take to become an epidemiologist?

Usually about six years after high school: four for a bachelor’s degree and two for an MPH or master’s in epidemiology. Some entry roles at health departments take bachelor’s graduates, but most epidemiologist jobs expect a master’s. Those who want to lead research or teach typically add a PhD, which takes several more years.
Do you need a certification to work in public health?

Usually not. There is no license for most public health jobs. The Certified in Public Health (CPH) credential shows broad knowledge, and some employers value it. Health educators often hold the CHES. Health economists rely on their degree, publications and modeling skills rather than a credential.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in public relations, communications, journalism, marketing or English. Courses in news writing, media relations and crisis communication help most. Strong writing matters more than the exact major, since the job is built on press releases, pitches and statements.
Internships

Internships at PR agencies, newsrooms, nonprofits or corporate communications teams are the usual way in. Many students complete one or more before graduating. They teach you how to pitch reporters, track coverage and handle press questions under deadline.
Writing portfolio

Build a portfolio of press releases, media pitches, social posts, op-eds and any coverage you helped secure. Hiring managers often ask for writing samples or give a writing test, so clean, fast, newsworthy writing is the main thing to show.
First job

The usual first job is PR assistant, account coordinator at an agency, or communications coordinator in-house. You build media lists, draft releases, monitor news and support senior staff during announcements and crises before pitching and speaking for clients yourself.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually one to three years in an entry-level role before holding a full specialist or account executive title. People moving over from journalism can often start at a higher level.
Optional accreditation

No license is required. After several years of experience, some specialists earn the Accreditation in Public Relations (APR), granted through the Universal Accreditation Board and supported by PRSA. It is voluntary and signals experience, but most employers do not require it.
qa: Do you need a license to work in public relations?

No. Public relations has no state license or required exam in the US. Employers look for a relevant degree, internship experience and strong writing samples. Some experienced practitioners choose to earn the voluntary Accreditation in Public Relations (APR), but it is not needed to get hired or to practice.
How long does it take to become a public relations specialist?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree in communications, journalism or a related field, often with internships along the way. They then usually work one to three years as a PR assistant or account coordinator before moving into a full specialist role. Former reporters can sometimes move in faster.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in business, marketing, communications, political science or public administration. No specific degree is required, and some companies hire people without one if they have a strong sales record.
First sales job

Most people start as a sales development representative or business development representative, booking meetings with agencies, schools and universities. Others enter from government, education or procurement jobs, bringing inside knowledge of how public bodies plan and buy.
Learn public buying rules

Learn how agencies buy: RFPs, RFQs, sole-source justifications, cooperative purchasing contracts and fiscal-year budget cycles. Federal sales follows the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) and often GSA Schedules. State, local and school buying rules vary by state and district.
Optional credentials

No license or exam is required. Some people earn NCMA certifications such as the Certified Federal Contracts Manager (CFCM) to show contracting knowledge. Defense and intelligence sales roles may require a security clearance, which is sponsored through an employer.
Time it takes

It usually takes two to five years of sales experience to reach a public sector account executive role. Many first close deals as an associate or commercial account executive, then move into a public sector territory with its own quota.
qa: Do you need a license to be a public sector account executive?

No. There is no license or required exam for this work. Your employer usually registers as a vendor, for example in SAM.gov for federal sales. In some states and cities, people who contact officials about pending contracts may have to register as lobbyists, so check the rules where you sell.
How long does it take to become a public sector account executive?

Usually two to five years after college. Most people spend one to two years as a sales or business development representative, then close deals in a junior account role. People coming from government or education jobs can sometimes move in faster because they already understand public budgets and procurement.

steps: Education

Many job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. It is not a strict rule. Employers also hire people who learned through community college courses, coding bootcamps or self-study, as long as they can show working code.
Core skills

Learn Python well, then Git, SQL, automated testing and the Linux command line. Next, pick a direction: Django, Flask or FastAPI for web backends, pandas and SQL for data pipelines, or machine learning libraries for AI tools.
Portfolio

Build a few real projects and publish the code online. Good examples are a small web API, a script that automates a task, or a data pipeline with clear documentation and tests. Contributing fixes to open source projects also counts.
Optional certifications

No license, state registration or exam is required to work as a Python developer. The Python Institute offers the PCEP and PCAP certifications, and cloud certifications can help for backend roles. Employers rarely require them and usually weigh projects and interviews more.
Time it takes

A degree usually takes four years. People who teach themselves or switch careers often need one to two years of steady study and project work before they are ready for an entry-level role. Hiring often includes coding tests and technical interviews.
First job

Common ways in are an internship, a junior or entry-level developer role, or test automation work. Others start as a data analyst, IT support specialist or systems administrator, write Python scripts on the job, and then move into a developer title.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a Python developer?

No. Many employers list a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field, but it is not legally required, and many developers are self-taught or come from bootcamps. Without a degree, a strong portfolio of working projects and good results in coding interviews matter even more.
How long does it take to become a Python developer?

With a computer science degree, it usually takes about four years, often with an internship along the way. Career changers who study on their own commonly need one to two years of consistent practice and project building before landing a junior role. No license or exam adds time to the process.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. Many QA engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information technology or a related field. Others come from unrelated degrees or no degree and learn testing through courses, self-study and practice projects.
Core skills

Learn how software is built and how to test it: writing test cases, reporting bugs clearly, and basic SQL. Then learn one programming language, such as Python, Java or JavaScript, plus Git and an automation tool like Selenium, Cypress or Playwright.
Optional certification

No license or exam is required to work in QA in the US. Some people earn the ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level (CTFL), offered in the US through ASTQB. A few employers list it, but practical skills and a portfolio usually matter more.
Portfolio

Build proof of your work. Write test plans and bug reports for real apps, and publish small automated test suites on GitHub. Hiring managers often ask you to walk through a project or complete a short testing exercise.
First job

The usual way in is an entry-level role such as QA tester, QA analyst or manual tester. Some people move over from customer support, help desk or other roles at a software company where they already know the product.
Time it takes

Learning enough to land a first testing job usually takes several months to two years, depending on your background. Moving from manual testing to a QA engineer or automation role often takes another one to three years on the job.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a QA engineer?

No. Many QA engineers have a degree in computer science or a related field, but it is not required. People without a degree often get in through an entry-level manual testing job, then learn programming and test automation to move up. A portfolio of test plans and automated tests helps show your skills.
Do you need a certification to be a QA engineer?

No license or certification is required in the US. The ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level (CTFL) is the most widely known testing certification, and some employers mention it in job postings. It can help beginners, but most employers care more about hands-on testing, programming and automation skills.

steps: Education

Most quality engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, industrial, manufacturing or a related engineering field. Courses in statistics, materials and manufacturing processes help most. Some people start as technicians with an associate degree and move up later, though many employers ask for a four-year degree for engineer titles.
Core tools to learn

Learn statistical process control, measurement system analysis, FMEA, root cause methods such as 8D, and reading GD&T on drawings. Know the quality system standards your industry uses, such as ISO 9001, AS9100 for aerospace, IATF 16949 for automotive or ISO 13485 for medical devices.
First job

Common first roles are quality technician, quality inspector, associate quality engineer or manufacturing engineer. Internships and co-op terms in a plant count heavily. Early work usually means writing inspection plans, handling nonconforming parts, running measurements and supporting audits under a senior engineer.
Certification

No license is required. Many employers value ASQ certifications, such as the Certified Quality Engineer (CQE) or Six Sigma Green Belt and Black Belt. The CQE requires several years of work experience, and a degree counts toward part of that requirement. Lead auditor training for an ISO standard is also common.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually one to three years in an entry or technician role before holding a full quality engineer title. Earning the CQE typically comes a few years into the career, once the experience requirement is met.
qa: Do you need a license to be a quality engineer?

No. Quality engineers in the US do not need a state license, and a Professional Engineer license is rarely required for this work. Employers instead look for an engineering degree, plant experience and often voluntary certifications from ASQ, such as the Certified Quality Engineer (CQE) or a Six Sigma belt.
How long does it take to become a quality engineer?

Usually about five to seven years in total. Most people spend four years earning an engineering bachelor’s degree, then one to three years as a quality technician, inspector or associate engineer. Those who start without a degree can get there by working up from technician roles, but it generally takes longer.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Classes in math, shop and blueprint reading help. Some people take a certificate or associate degree in quality technology, machining or manufacturing technology, which can lead to inspector jobs that use more advanced equipment.
First job

Many inspectors start as machine operators, assemblers or production workers and move into inspection after learning the parts. Others are hired straight into entry-level roles such as receiving inspector or final inspector, checking parts against drawings and sampling plans.
On-the-job training

New inspectors learn under a lead inspector or quality engineer. They practice with calipers, micrometers, height gauges and go/no-go gauges, read blueprints and GD&T, record results and tag rejected parts. Running or programming a coordinate measuring machine (CMM) usually comes later.
Certifications

There is no state license for general quality inspection. ASQ offers the Certified Quality Inspector (CQI) and Certified Quality Technician (CQT), which require work experience or education to sit for. Welding inspectors often earn the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) credential.
NDT and X-ray roles

Inspectors who use X-ray, ultrasonic or other nondestructive testing are usually certified by their employer to Level I or Level II under ASNT SNT-TC-1A or NAS 410, with classroom hours and supervised experience. Radiographers using radioactive sources must also meet NRC or state certification rules.
Time it takes

A basic inspector can be trained in a few weeks to a few months. Becoming a skilled CMM operator, certified quality inspector or NDT Level II inspector usually takes one to three years of hands-on experience.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a quality inspector?

No license or certification is required for most quality inspector jobs. Employers usually train new hires on the job. Credentials such as the ASQ Certified Quality Inspector (CQI) can help you get hired or promoted. Nondestructive testing and welding inspection jobs are different and often require ASNT-based employer certification or the AWS Certified Welding Inspector credential.
How long does it take to become a quality inspector?

You can start as an entry-level inspector with a high school diploma and a few weeks to a few months of on-the-job training. Gaining the skills for CMM work, a professional certification or nondestructive testing Level II usually takes one to three years of supervised experience in manufacturing.

steps: Education

Most quantitative researchers hold a master’s degree or PhD in mathematics, statistics, physics, computer science, financial engineering or a related field. Probability, statistics, linear algebra, stochastic calculus and machine learning matter most, along with programming in Python and often C++.
Research and coding skills

Employers want proof you can do research: a thesis, published papers, competition results or personal projects testing ideas on real data. Clean, fast code matters as much as math, since researchers build and test their own models and trading signals.
Internship

Many quants are hired through summer internships at trading firms, hedge funds and banks, taken during a master’s or PhD program. Recruiting usually opens many months ahead and includes timed tests and interviews on probability, statistics, coding and brain teasers.
Licenses

Quantitative researchers usually need no license. Some roles at broker-dealers that involve trading require FINRA registration, which starts with the Securities Industry Essentials (SIE) exam plus a role-specific exam the employer sponsors. The CFA and FRM are optional and rarely required for research roles.
First job

The usual first job is a junior quantitative researcher, quantitative analyst or quant developer role, often offered after a successful internship. New hires typically start by cleaning data, testing ideas from senior researchers and improving existing models before running their own strategies.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, then one to two years for a master’s or about five years for a PhD. Some strong candidates are hired straight from a bachelor’s program, especially into quant developer or trading roles.
qa: How long does it take to become a quantitative researcher?

Usually five to ten years after high school. Most quant researchers hold a master’s degree or PhD in a field like mathematics, statistics, physics or computer science, which adds one to six years after a bachelor’s degree. Many are hired through an internship during graduate school, and some exceptional candidates join straight from a bachelor’s program.
Do you need a license to be a quant?

Usually not. Quantitative researchers who build models and test strategies typically need no license. Some roles at broker-dealers that involve trading require FINRA registration, starting with the Securities Industry Essentials (SIE) exam and a role-specific exam, which the employer sponsors. Certifications like the CFA or FRM are optional.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most people start with a four-year degree in physics, electrical engineering, computer science or applied math. Key courses are linear algebra, quantum mechanics, probability and programming, usually in Python. Hardware builders add electronics, electromagnetics and optics.
Research experience

Join a university lab as an undergraduate or take a summer research program. Hands-on work with cryogenics, microwave electronics, lasers or quantum software kits counts for more than coursework alone. Contributing to open-source quantum software also helps.
Graduate degree

Many hardware and algorithm research roles expect a PhD in physics, electrical engineering, computer science or a related field. A master’s degree can be enough for engineering roles in control electronics, test, fabrication or quantum software.
License and clearance

There is no state license, required exam or standard certification for quantum engineers. Employers judge your degree, research and publications. Some government-funded or defense-related roles may require US citizenship or a security clearance.
Time it takes
A bachelor’s degree takes about four years. A PhD usually takes five to six more, so about nine to ten years in total. A postdoc, which many research-track people take, adds one to three years.
First job

PhD holders often start as postdoctoral researchers or research scientists. Others enter as engineers in RF and microwave electronics, cryogenics, optics or quantum software. Those with a bachelor’s degree often begin as lab technicians, test engineers or software developers on quantum teams.
qa: Do you need a PhD to become a quantum engineer?

Not always. Many research roles in quantum hardware and algorithms expect a PhD in physics, engineering or computer science. But engineers with a bachelor’s or master’s degree are also hired for control electronics, cryogenics, fabrication, testing and quantum software work, especially with strong lab or programming experience.
How long does it take to become a quantum engineer?

With a bachelor’s degree alone, about four years, though entry roles are mostly in supporting engineering or software work. The common research path adds a five-to-six-year PhD, for about nine to ten years in total. A postdoc adds another one to three years for those who take one.

steps: Education

No license or specific degree is required. Some React developers studied computer science, while many came through bootcamps or self-study. Learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript well first, since React builds on them, then add TypeScript.
React skills

Learn components, props, state and hooks, then routing, data fetching and form handling. Many teams also use TypeScript, a framework such as Next.js, testing tools and a state management approach. Accessibility and responsive design come up in interviews.
Portfolio

Build and deploy three or four polished projects, such as a dashboard pulling live data, an online store front end or a clone of a familiar app. Publish the code publicly and make each project work well on phones as well as desktops.
Certifications

There is no official React certification, and employers do not require one. Hiring depends on take-home projects, live coding of small interface components and questions about JavaScript, browser behavior and React itself. A strong portfolio matters far more than any certificate.
First job

The usual first job is junior front-end developer, junior React developer or junior full-stack developer. Agencies, startups and product companies all hire React developers. Some move in from web design, QA testing or support roles where they already worked with web interfaces.
Time it takes

Career changers often reach a first React job after one to two years of focused study and projects. A computer science degree takes about four years. Developers who already know JavaScript can usually learn React itself in a few months.
qa: How long does it take to become a React developer?

If you start from zero, plan on one to two years of focused learning to cover HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript and React, and to build a portfolio employers take seriously. If you already know JavaScript, learning React well enough for a junior role usually takes a few months. A computer science degree takes about four years.
Is there a certification for React developers?

React has no official certification, and US employers do not require one. Some online courses issue certificates, but hiring managers mostly look at deployed projects, public code, take-home assignments and live coding interviews. Time spent building polished, working apps usually helps more than collecting certificates.

steps: Education

Most corporate real estate managers hold a bachelor’s degree in real estate, finance, business, economics, urban planning or a related field. Coursework in finance, accounting, contracts and property valuation helps most. Some people later add a master’s degree in real estate or an MBA, but it is rarely required to get started.
First job

People usually start as a real estate analyst, lease administrator, transaction coordinator or junior analyst at a commercial brokerage, developer or corporate real estate team. These roles teach lease abstraction, financial modeling, site research and how deals are negotiated and closed.
License, if any

Managing property for your own employer usually does not require a real estate license, but rules vary by state. Some people get licensed while working in brokerage first. License names differ by state: many states license new agents as salespersons, while others, such as Colorado and Illinois, license them as brokers.
Optional credentials

No certification is required, but some employers value them. Options include the Master of Corporate Real Estate (MCR) from CoreNet Global and the CCIM designation, which requires courses, qualifying experience and a final exam. Each credential sets its own eligibility rules, so check the issuing body’s current requirements.
Time it takes

There is no set timeline. After a four-year degree, people commonly spend several years in analyst, leasing or brokerage roles before managing a company’s portfolio, site selection or large leases on their own. Experience with real deals matters more than any single credential.
qa: Do you need a real estate license to be a corporate real estate manager?

Usually not. Employees who handle leases and purchases for their own company are often not required to hold a license, but rules vary by state. Many managers came from commercial brokerage and got licensed there. In states that license new agents, the license may be called salesperson or broker depending on the state.
How do you get into corporate real estate?

Most people earn a bachelor’s degree in real estate, finance, business or a related field, then take an entry role such as real estate analyst, lease administrator or commercial brokerage analyst. After several years handling leases, site searches and deal analysis, they move into managing real estate for a company.

steps: Basic requirements

Most states require you to be at least 18 or 19, hold a high school diploma or GED, and pass a background check, often with fingerprints. No college degree is needed for an entry-level license, though some agents study real estate, business or finance.
Pre-licensing course

Every state requires approved pre-licensing education before the exam. The number of hours varies widely by state, from a few dozen to well over a hundred, and covers property law, contracts, agency, financing and fair housing. Many people finish it online.
State exam and license

After the course, you pass the state real estate exam, which usually has a national section and a state law section, then apply to the state real estate commission. Most states call the first license a salesperson license, while some use titles such as sales associate or broker.
Sponsoring broker

A new license is usually active only while you work under a licensed broker, who supervises your deals and holds client funds. New agents often choose a brokerage for its training and leads. Many also join the National Association of Realtors, which is required to use the Realtor title.
Leasing agents

Rules for leasing agents differ. Many states require a real estate license to lease property for others, some offer a limited leasing license, and some exempt on-site apartment leasing staff employed by the owner or management company. Check with your state real estate commission.
Time it takes

Getting licensed usually takes a few weeks to a few months, depending on course hours and exam dates. Most states require continuing education to renew. Becoming a broker usually takes two or more years of experience, more coursework and another exam.
qa: Do you need a license to be a real estate agent?

Yes. Every state requires a real estate license to help others buy, sell or rent property for pay. You usually complete state-approved pre-licensing courses, pass a state exam and a background check, and work under a licensed broker. Some states exempt on-site apartment leasing staff who work directly for an owner or management company.
How long does it take to become a real estate agent?

Usually a few weeks to a few months. Required pre-licensing course hours vary by state, and many people finish them part time or online. After that you pass the state exam, apply for the license and join a sponsoring broker. Building a steady flow of clients often takes a year or more.

steps: Education

Most receptionist jobs ask for a high school diploma or GED. No college degree is needed. Classes in office skills, keyboarding and business communication help, and speaking a second language, often Spanish, is a plus in many areas.
Customer service experience

Employers value experience dealing with the public. Many receptionists come from retail, food service, call centers or hotel work, where they learned to stay calm, handle complaints and multitask. Volunteering at a front desk also counts.
Training on the job

Most training happens on the job and usually takes a few days to a few weeks. You learn the phone system, scheduling or check-in software, visitor and security procedures, and how the office wants calls and messages handled.
Medical or legal settings

Receptionists in clinics must follow HIPAA privacy rules and often learn insurance verification and medical terms. Some earn the CMAA (Certified Medical Administrative Assistant) from the National Healthcareer Association. Law firm receptionists must keep client matters confidential.
Time it takes

You can usually start as a receptionist within a few weeks of applying. There is no license, apprenticeship or required exam. Becoming fully comfortable with a busy front desk typically takes a few months.
Next steps

Many receptionists move on after one to three years to administrative assistant, office manager, medical office coordinator, hotel front desk supervisor or customer service roles. Learning office software, bookkeeping basics or medical billing makes the move easier.
qa: Can you become a receptionist without experience?

Yes. Receptionist is one of the most common entry-level office jobs, and many employers train new hires. A high school diploma, a friendly phone manner, basic computer skills and reliability are often enough. Experience in retail, food service or customer service helps, because it shows you can handle the public.
Do you need a certification to be a receptionist?

No certification or license is required, and most receptionists learn on the job. In medical offices, some employers prefer a credential such as the CMAA (Certified Medical Administrative Assistant) from the National Healthcareer Association, and all clinic staff must follow HIPAA privacy rules. Elsewhere, typing and office software skills matter more than certificates.

steps: Education

Most employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business, psychology or communications, but many hire without one. Staffing agencies often value sales skill, phone confidence and drive over a specific degree. Experience in the field you’ll recruit for, such as nursing or IT, can also help.
No license needed

Individual recruiters do not need a state license. Some states regulate employment agencies, especially those that charge fees to job seekers, so agency owners should check local rules. Learning basic employment law, such as equal employment opportunity rules, matters more day to day.
First job

Common entry points are recruiting coordinator, sourcer, HR assistant or junior recruiter at a staffing agency. Coordinators schedule interviews and handle candidate communication. Sourcers search job boards and professional networks to find candidates. Agency roles often hire people from sales or customer service backgrounds.
Building core skills

On the job you learn to write job postings, screen resumes, run phone screens, use an applicant tracking system and search for passive candidates. You also learn to work with hiring managers, present offers and keep candidates engaged through every stage of hiring.
Optional certifications

Certifications are not required, but some recruiters earn the SHRM-CP from SHRM or the PHR from HRCI, especially in corporate HR teams. Both expect some HR knowledge or experience. Short sourcing and recruiting courses can also show commitment to employers.
Time it takes

Many people land a first recruiting coordinator or sourcer role within a few months of starting their search. Moving up to a full-cycle recruiter who manages roles from posting to offer usually takes one to three years of hands-on experience.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a recruiter?

Not always. Many corporate employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business, psychology or a related field. Staffing agencies often hire people without a degree if they have strong communication and sales skills. Experience in customer service, sales or a specific industry can substitute for formal education in many recruiting jobs.
Do recruiters need a license or certification?

Individual recruiters do not need a state license, though some states regulate employment agencies that place workers. Certification is optional. Some recruiters, especially in corporate HR departments, earn the SHRM-CP or PHR to show HR knowledge. Most employers care more about proven results, like filling roles and building strong candidate pipelines.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in human resources, business, psychology or communications. Many also hire people with an associate degree or a high school diploma plus solid office or customer service experience. No license, registration or required exam exists for this work in any state.
Office and people experience

Build a record of organized, people-facing work. Jobs or internships that involve juggling calendars, answering phones and emails, handling confidential records and keeping several tasks on track show employers you can manage the steady flow of candidates and interviews.
Tools and basics

Get comfortable with shared calendars, video meeting tools, spreadsheets and applicant tracking systems. Learn the basics of hiring paperwork, such as offer letters, background check steps and Form I-9, along with candidate privacy and equal employment opportunity rules.
Optional certification

Certification is not required, but some coordinators earn the aPHR from HRCI, which is designed for people new to HR. Others later pursue the SHRM-CP from SHRM. Check each body’s current eligibility rules before applying.
First job

Common ways in are HR assistant, administrative assistant, receptionist, recruiting intern or coordinator at a staffing agency. Moving internally from an assistant role to recruiting coordinator is a frequent path, since you already know the company’s hiring process.
Time it takes

Some graduates land the role right after a recruiting or HR internship. Others usually spend one to two years in an administrative or HR support job first. There is no set training period or apprenticeship.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a recruiting coordinator?

Not always. Many postings prefer a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business or a related field, but plenty of employers hire people with an associate degree or high school diploma who show strong scheduling, communication and organization skills from office, HR assistant or customer service jobs. There is no license or required exam for this role.
How long does it take to become a recruiting coordinator?

It can take very little time if you finish a degree and a recruiting internship, since some people are hired straight out of school. Others usually spend one to two years in an administrative, receptionist or HR assistant role before moving into recruiting coordination. Optional certifications such as the aPHR can be added along the way.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business, psychology, communications or a related field. No specific degree is required, and some teams hire on experience alone. Classes in data analysis, spreadsheets and marketing help with the systems and employer brand sides of the work.
First job

Most people start as a recruiting coordinator. They schedule interviews, post jobs and keep candidate records clean in the applicant tracking system. Others move in from HR assistant, sourcer or recruiter roles. This is where you learn how hiring really runs day to day.
Systems and data skills

Become the person on the team who knows the applicant tracking system best. Learn to build reports, track measures like time to fill and source of hire, and work in spreadsheets and dashboards. Volunteer for tool rollouts, process fixes and career page updates.
Optional certification

No license or exam is required for this work. Some people earn the SHRM-CP from the Society for Human Resource Management, or the aPHR or PHR from HRCI, to show HR knowledge. Employers usually value hands-on systems and process experience more than any credential.
Time it takes

Moving into a recruiting operations role usually takes two to four years after starting as a coordinator or in a related HR job. Small companies often blend coordinator and operations duties, which can speed the move. Later steps include recruiting operations manager or talent acquisition systems lead.
qa: Do you need a certification to work in recruiting operations?

No. There is no license or required exam for recruiting operations in the US. Some people choose the SHRM-CP, aPHR or PHR to show HR knowledge, but most employers care more about proven skill with an applicant tracking system, reporting and hiring processes than about a certificate.
What is the best entry-level job for getting into recruiting operations?

Recruiting coordinator is the most common starting point. Coordinators schedule interviews, manage candidate data and use the applicant tracking system every day. Those who take on reporting, clean up workflows or help launch new tools are often the ones promoted into recruiting operations after a few years.

steps: Education

Most regional sales directors hold a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing or a field tied to what they sell, such as engineering or life sciences. An MBA is common at some companies but rarely required. There is no general license for sales leadership.
First job

Most start in an entry-level sales role, such as sales development representative, inside sales representative or territory sales representative, then move up to account executive. Years of meeting or beating quota are the main proof employers look for.
Sales management

The usual next step is first-line sales manager, leading a team of reps: hiring, coaching, forecasting and managing a pipeline. Directors are expected to have led managers or several teams, and to plan territories and quotas.
Industry licenses

Some industries add licenses. Selling securities requires FINRA registration and exams such as the SIE and Series 7, and supervisors often need the Series 24. Insurance and real estate sales require state licenses. Medical device sales needs no license, but hospitals often require vendor credentialing.
Time it takes

Reaching regional director usually takes ten years or more, including several years as an account executive and several as a sales manager. Strong results and deep experience in one industry can speed this up.
qa: How long does it take to become a regional sales director?

Usually ten years or more. Most people spend several years as sales representatives and account executives meeting quota, then several more as sales managers leading a team, before running a region. Strong results, experience in one industry and leading other managers can shorten the path.
Do you need a license to be a sales director?

Not usually. General sales leadership needs no license. Some industries are different: securities salespeople and their supervisors must register with FINRA and pass exams such as the Series 7 and Series 24, and insurance and real estate sales require state licenses. Check the rules for the products your region sells.

steps: Education

Most employers want a bachelor’s degree in a science or engineering field, such as biology, chemistry, pharmacy, biomedical engineering or nursing. Some people add a master’s degree or graduate certificate in regulatory affairs or regulatory science. This can help career changers show focused knowledge.
Related experience

Many people come in from nearby work: quality assurance, clinical research, lab work, manufacturing or technical writing. These roles teach how products are tested, made and documented. Regulators such as the FDA review exactly those records closely.
First job

A common first job is regulatory affairs associate or regulatory coordinator. You compile submission documents, track deadlines, keep records current and help prepare filings to the FDA or other agencies. A senior specialist usually reviews your work.
No license required

No government license is required to work in regulatory affairs. What employers want is solid knowledge of the rules for their product type, such as FDA regulations for drugs, medical devices, biologics or food, and how submissions are put together.
Optional certification

The Regulatory Affairs Certification (RAC) from RAPS is the best-known credential in the field. It is voluntary, but some employers list it as preferred. RAPS recommends hands-on regulatory experience before taking an exam, so many people earn it after a few years of work.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree. After that, people usually spend two to five years as an associate or in a related role before holding a specialist title. Career changers from science roles often move faster.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a regulatory affairs specialist?

No. There is no required license or certification. The Regulatory Affairs Certification (RAC) from RAPS is voluntary, though some employers prefer it. Many people get hired with a science degree and related experience, then decide whether to pursue the RAC after working in the field for a while.
How long does it take to become a regulatory affairs specialist?

Usually about six to nine years from the start of college. That includes a four-year science or engineering degree, then two to five years as a regulatory associate or in related work like quality assurance or clinical research. People already working in life sciences can often move into the role sooner.

steps: Bachelor’s and prerequisites

Physical and occupational therapy programs are graduate level, so most people first earn a bachelor’s degree in exercise science, kinesiology, biology or psychology. Prerequisites often include anatomy, physiology, statistics and psychology. Many programs also ask for observation hours with a licensed therapist.
Graduate degree

Physical therapists need a Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) from a CAPTE-accredited program, which usually takes about three years. Occupational therapists need a master’s or doctoral degree from an ACOTE-accredited program, which usually takes two to three years.
Clinical training

Both degrees include supervised clinical work. Physical therapy students complete full-time clinical rotations in settings such as hospitals and outpatient clinics. Occupational therapy students complete Level I and Level II fieldwork, with Level II lasting at least 24 weeks full-time.
National exams

Physical therapists take the National Physical Therapy Examination (NPTE), run by the Federation of State Boards of Physical Therapy. Occupational therapists take the NBCOT certification exam, which grants the OTR credential. Both exams are taken after graduation.
State license

Every state requires physical and occupational therapists to be licensed. After passing the national exam, you apply to the state board, and some states add a law or jurisprudence exam. Licenses must be renewed, usually with continuing education.
First job and timeline

Most new therapists start as staff therapists in hospitals, outpatient clinics, skilled nursing facilities, schools or home health. Expect about six to seven years after high school. Some physical therapists later add a residency and earn board certification as a clinical specialist.
qa: How long does it take to become a physical or occupational therapist?

Usually six to seven years after high school. A physical therapist needs a bachelor’s degree and then a three-year DPT program. An occupational therapist needs a bachelor’s degree and then a two- to three-year master’s or doctoral program. Both then pass a national exam and get a state license. Assistant roles take about two years through an associate degree.
Do you need a license to be a physical or occupational therapist?

Yes. Every state licenses both. Physical therapists must pass the NPTE, and occupational therapists must pass the NBCOT exam, after graduating from an accredited program. Some states add a jurisprudence exam. Physical therapist assistants and occupational therapy assistants are also licensed or regulated in most states.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in computer science, mathematics, statistics or a related field. Key courses include linear algebra, probability, optimization and Python programming. Many also take graduate-level machine learning and reinforcement learning courses before they finish.
Graduate study

Research roles usually expect a PhD in machine learning or a related field, which typically takes four to six years. Some people enter with a master’s degree and strong engineering skills. They often start as research engineers rather than research scientists.
No license or exam

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in any state. No certification is a standard way in. Employers judge candidates on published papers, code they have written and their skill at running large training experiments.
Research record

Candidates build a record by publishing papers at major machine learning conferences, releasing open-source code and doing research internships at AI labs during graduate school. Hands-on work with reward models, policy optimization and large-scale model training counts heavily.
Time it takes

With a PhD, the path usually takes eight to ten years after high school: four years for a bachelor’s degree and four to six years of doctoral study. A master’s route is shorter, though the first role is often more engineering focused.
First job

The usual first step is a research internship during graduate school. That often leads to a research scientist or research engineer role on a team that trains models. Some move over from machine learning engineering after strong results on training work.
qa: Do you need a PhD to be a reinforcement learning researcher?

Not always, but most research scientist roles expect one. A PhD shows you can run original research and publish it. People with a master’s or bachelor’s degree do get in, usually as research engineers, by showing strong coding skills, open-source work and experience training large models. Some later move into research scientist roles.
How long does it take to become a reinforcement learning researcher?

On the PhD route, it usually takes eight to ten years after high school: four years for a bachelor’s degree and four to six years of doctoral research. On a master’s route, it is often five to six years, though the first job is usually more engineering focused. No license or exam adds time.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing, communications or a related field, but some hire on experience alone. Coursework in negotiation, finance or contract basics helps, since the job turns on pricing, terms and deadlines.
No license needed

Renewals management has no state license, registration or required exam in the US. Optional sales or customer success certificates exist, but employers rarely ask for one. They care more about a track record of keeping customers and hitting renewal targets.
First job

Most people start as a renewals specialist or representative, customer success associate, inside sales representative or junior account manager. These roles teach you to manage a list of accounts, track contract end dates, handle pricing pushback and work inside a CRM system.
Build a renewal record

Move toward owning a book of accounts with clear renewal and upsell goals. Learn to forecast which contracts are at risk, negotiate multiyear terms, and work with legal, finance and support teams. Numbers like retention and expansion become the proof you show hiring managers.
Time it takes

Moving from an entry role to renewals manager usually takes two to five years. Some managers carry their own accounts, while others lead a team of renewals representatives. The team lead version usually expects more years and some coaching or supervisory experience.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a renewals manager?

Not always. Many job postings list a bachelor’s degree in business or a related field as preferred, but experience often matters more. People who have worked in customer success, account management or inside sales and can show strong retention and upsell results are regularly hired without a specific degree.
How long does it take to become a renewals manager?

It usually takes two to five years. Most people begin in an entry role such as renewals representative, customer success associate or inside sales representative. After building a record of on-time renewals and added sales, they move up to managing larger accounts or leading a renewals team.

steps: Education

No license is required. Most reporting analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in business, finance, accounting, economics, information systems or a related field. Courses in statistics, accounting and databases help, since the work combines numbers, data systems and business rules.
Data skills

Learn advanced Excel, including pivot tables, lookups and formulas, then SQL to pull data from databases. Most jobs also use a business intelligence tool such as Power BI or Tableau to build dashboards and scheduled reports.
Regulatory reporting

Reporting for regulators is a specialty. Banks file Call Reports, public companies file reports with the SEC, and insurers file statutory statements with state regulators. Learning the rules and controls behind these filings, and reconciling figures with care, opens specialized roles.
Certifications

Certifications are optional. Tool certifications such as Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate or Tableau certifications show skill. In finance, some analysts later pursue accounting credentials such as the CPA, which is a state license with its own education and exam rules.
First job

Common first jobs are reporting analyst, junior data analyst, financial analyst, operations analyst or business intelligence analyst. Many people also move in from accounting, customer operations or administrative roles where they built the team’s spreadsheets and reports.
Time it takes

You can start as a reporting analyst right after a bachelor’s degree, or within a year or two of building Excel, SQL and dashboard skills in another role. Senior reporting or reporting manager roles usually take several years.
qa: How long does it take to become a reporting analyst?

Many people start as reporting analysts straight after a four-year bachelor’s degree in business, finance or a related field. Others move in after a year or two in operations, accounting or administrative roles, once they can build reports in Excel, query data with SQL and create dashboards in a tool such as Power BI or Tableau.
Can you become a reporting analyst without experience?

Yes, many entry-level reporting analyst jobs accept new graduates or career changers. Show skill with a portfolio: a few dashboards built from public data, SQL queries and a written summary of what the numbers show. Internal moves are common too, where someone who builds their team’s reports is promoted into a formal analyst role.

steps: Education

Most research analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, accounting, statistics, mathematics or a related field. Employers look for strong skills in financial statements, spreadsheets and clear writing. Some learn Python, SQL or on-chain data tools, especially for quantitative or crypto research.
Build a writing sample

Because the job is writing up what the numbers say, a sample matters. Many people publish their own company, market or protocol reports, or build models from public filings, to show they can find data, reach a view and explain it in plain terms.
First job

The usual way in is a research associate or junior analyst role. You support a senior analyst by updating models, gathering data, checking numbers and drafting parts of reports. Internships during college often lead to these roles.
FINRA exams if required

Analysts who write equity research at a FINRA member broker-dealer must pass the SIE plus the Series 86 and Series 87, with sponsorship from the firm. Those who passed CFA Level I and II may be exempt from the Series 86. Most other research roles need no license.
Optional credentials

Many analysts pursue the CFA charter from CFA Institute, which involves three exam levels and relevant work experience. It is not legally required but is widely respected in investment research. Some quantitative analysts add statistics or data science training instead.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then usually two to four years as an associate before covering companies, markets or protocols on your own. Completing the CFA program often takes several more years alongside work.
qa: Do you need a license to be a research analyst?

It depends on where you work. Analysts who produce equity research at a FINRA member broker-dealer must pass the SIE, Series 86 and Series 87 through a sponsoring firm. Analysts at asset managers, consulting firms, data providers or crypto companies usually need no license, though employers may value the CFA charter.
How long does it take to become a research analyst?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree, then start as a research associate or junior analyst. Moving up to a lead analyst who covers companies, sectors or protocols on their own usually takes another two to four years, depending on the employer and the quality of your work.

steps: Science background

Most research program managers have a degree in a science or engineering field, and many hold a master’s or PhD. Some come from research administration instead, with a degree in business or public administration. Understanding how research works matters more than any single field.
First job

Common starting roles are research coordinator, lab manager, grants or contracts administrator, project coordinator or postdoc taking on project duties. These jobs build skills in budgets, timelines, reporting and working with researchers, sponsors and outside partners.
Grants and rules

Managers of funded research need to know sponsor rules, including the federal grant rules known as the Uniform Guidance, and policies of funders such as NIH and NSF. Work with human or animal subjects also involves IRB and animal care committee rules.
Certification

There is no license. Optional certifications include the Project Management Professional (PMP) from the Project Management Institute and the Certified Research Administrator (CRA) from the Research Administrators Certification Council. Both require work experience before you can sit for the exam.
Time it takes

Most people work three to five years as a coordinator, administrator or scientist before managing a research program. PhD holders who move over from the bench may get there sooner if they already ran projects, budgets or teams.
qa: How do you become a research program manager?

Most people come from one of two directions. Scientists with a master’s or PhD take on project duties in a lab, then move into program management. Others start as research coordinators or grants administrators and learn budgets, compliance and reporting. A few years of experience and optional certifications such as the PMP or CRA help.
What certification helps a research program manager?

None is required. The Project Management Professional (PMP) from the Project Management Institute is the most widely recognized for program and project roles. In universities and research institutes, the Certified Research Administrator (CRA) shows knowledge of grants and sponsor rules. Both require documented work experience before the exam.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Start with a bachelor’s degree in the field you want to research. That might be biology, chemistry, physics, computer science or another science. Join a faculty lab as an undergraduate to learn how experiments are designed, run and written up.
Graduate degree

Most research scientist roles expect a PhD in the relevant field. Some industry teams, especially in AI and software, also hire people with a master’s degree and strong research experience. The PhD is where you learn to lead your own projects.
Publication record

Hiring managers look at what you have published. That usually means peer-reviewed papers in your own field’s respected journals, or its main conferences in fields such as AI where conferences carry more weight. Released code, datasets or methods others use also count.
No license needed

There is no general license or exam for research scientists in the US. Work with human subjects, animals, hazardous chemicals or radioactive materials requires training and approval through your institution, and some of these areas also follow federal rules.
Postdoc or first job

Many new PhDs take a postdoctoral position first, especially in academia and the life sciences. Others enter industry directly as research scientists. People without a PhD often start as research assistants, lab technicians or research engineers and move up.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree and usually four to six more for a PhD. A postdoc can add one to several years. Industry roles in AI may be reached sooner by people who already have strong published work.
qa: Do you need a PhD to be a research scientist?

Usually, yes. Most universities, government labs and many companies expect a PhD for research scientist titles. Some industry teams, especially in AI, hire people with a master’s degree or strong publications instead. Without a PhD, people often start as research assistants, technicians or research engineers and grow into scientist roles over time.
How long does it take to become a research scientist?

It commonly takes eight to ten years after high school. That includes four years for a bachelor’s degree and usually four to six years for a PhD. Many people then spend one to several years as a postdoctoral researcher before landing a permanent research scientist job, especially in academia and the life sciences.

steps: Basic requirements

Retail work needs no license or degree. Many stores hire from age 16, and some from 14 or 15. Workers under 18 may need a state work permit, and child labor laws limit their hours. A high school diploma helps but is often not required.
Skills to bring

Employers look for friendly customer service, basic math, cash handling and reliability. Being free to work evenings, weekends and holidays matters a lot. School jobs, volunteering or helping in a family business all count as useful experience.
First job
Most people start as a sales associate, cashier or stock associate. Seasonal holiday hiring each fall is a common way in, and good seasonal workers are often kept on afterward.
On-the-job training

Training is paid and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks. You learn the register, returns, store policies, theft prevention and safety. Stores that sell alcohol or tobacco follow state age rules, and some states require seller training.
Time it takes
You can often start within a few weeks of applying. Moving up to key holder or shift lead, the people who open and close the store, usually takes six months to two years of steady work.
Moving up

From shift lead, the usual path is assistant store manager, then store manager. Some people take business or retail management courses along the way, but most promotions come from experience, sales results and dependability.
qa: Do you need experience to work in retail?

No. Retail is one of the most common first jobs, and many stores hire people with no work history. Employers train new hires on the register, products and store rules. Showing a friendly attitude, good attendance and open availability, especially on weekends and holidays, often matters more than past experience.
How old do you have to be to work in retail?

Federal law allows 14 and 15 year olds to work in many retail jobs with limits on hours. Many stores still set their own minimum at 16 or 18. State rules vary, and minors may need a work permit. Selling alcohol or tobacco usually has a higher minimum age set by each state.

steps: Education

No degree is required. Many employers prefer a high school diploma or GED, but plenty of stores hire students who are still in high school. Classes in basic math, communication or business help with handling cash and talking to customers.
Minimum age and work permits

Most large retailers hire at 16 or older, and some require 18. Workers under 18 may need a work permit, depending on state law. Stores that sell alcohol or tobacco often set a higher minimum age for running the register.
On-the-job training

Training happens in the store. New hires usually spend a few days to a few weeks learning the register, payment and return rules, stocking, product knowledge and safety, often by shadowing an experienced associate.
Optional credentials

No license or exam is required. Some people earn optional retail credentials, such as those offered through the NRF Foundation, to show customer service and sales basics. Most hiring managers care more about reliability, availability and a friendly manner.
Time it takes
Most people can start working within one to two weeks of applying. Feeling fully comfortable with the register, the stock and the products usually takes one to three months on the job.
First job

Retail is often a person’s first job. Common ways in are seasonal holiday hiring and part-time cashier or stock associate roles. With experience, associates can move up to keyholder, shift lead or department supervisor.
qa: Do you need experience to be a retail sales associate?

No. Retail sales associate is one of the most common entry-level jobs in the US, and stores train new hires on the register, stocking and store policies. Any customer-facing experience helps, including volunteering, school activities or food service, but many people are hired with no work history at all.
Do you need a high school diploma to work in retail?

Not always. Many retailers prefer a high school diploma or GED, especially for full-time or supervisor roles, but plenty hire high school students for part-time and seasonal work. Minimum age rules vary by employer and state law, and most large stores hire at 16 or older.

steps: Education

Most revenue accountants hold a bachelor’s degree in accounting. Some have a finance or business degree plus enough accounting courses. Useful classes include intermediate accounting, auditing and accounting information systems, since the job applies ASC 606 rules to real contracts.
First job

Few people start in revenue roles. The usual way in is a staff accountant job in a company’s accounting team or an audit associate job at a public accounting firm. There you learn the close process, journal entries, reconciliations and how auditors test revenue.
Learn ASC 606

Revenue work centers on ASC 606, the US standard for revenue from contracts with customers. You learn its five steps, from identifying the contract to recognizing revenue as obligations are met. Companies that also report under international rules use IFRS 15.
CPA license

No license is required to work as a revenue accountant, but many employers prefer a CPA, especially for senior roles. Earning it means passing the Uniform CPA Exam and meeting your state’s education and experience rules. Requirements vary by state.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a degree, then usually two to four years in general accounting or audit before moving into a dedicated revenue accountant role. Senior revenue and technical accounting jobs often come after five or more years.
qa: Do you need a CPA to be a revenue accountant?

No. There is no license required to work as a revenue accountant. Many employers still prefer or ask for a CPA, especially for senior and manager roles, because the work involves judgment on complex accounting rules. Getting a CPA means passing the Uniform CPA Exam and meeting your state’s education and experience requirements, which vary by state.
How long does it take to become a revenue accountant?

Most people need about six to eight years. That usually means four years for a bachelor’s degree in accounting, then two to four years as a staff accountant or audit associate. Those first jobs teach the close process and how revenue is tested, which prepares you to apply ASC 606 contract by contract.

steps: Education

Most RF engineers earn a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, ideally from an ABET-accredited program. Key courses include electromagnetics, circuit design, signals and systems, microwave engineering and communications. Lab time with network analyzers, spectrum analyzers and oscilloscopes matters as much as grades.
Hands-on practice

Internships with wireless, aerospace or defense teams give real test bench experience. Student projects also help, such as building antennas, joining a satellite team or working on radio hardware. An FCC amateur radio license is easy to earn and shows real interest in radio.
Graduate study

Many antenna, radar and microwave circuit design roles prefer a master’s degree, which usually takes one to two years. Network roles at wireless carriers and tower companies often hire with a bachelor’s degree alone.
License and clearance

Most RF jobs require no license. The PE license in electrical engineering, which starts with the FE exam, is optional and matters mainly for consulting or public infrastructure work. Defense and radar employers often require US citizenship and a security clearance, which the employer sponsors after hiring.
Time it takes
Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, plus one to two more for a master’s. Leading designs on your own usually takes another three to five years of work under senior engineers.
First job

Common first jobs are junior RF engineer, RF test engineer, or RF optimization and drive test engineer for cellular networks. Test and validation roles build the measurement skills that lead into design work.
qa: Do you need a license to be an RF engineer?

No license is required for most RF engineering jobs in the US. A PE license is optional and mainly useful for consulting or public projects. Some technician roles that service aviation or maritime radio equipment call for the FCC General Radiotelephone Operator License (GROL). Defense work often needs a security clearance instead.
How long does it take to become an RF engineer?

It usually takes four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and start in an entry-level RF role. Many design jobs prefer a master’s degree, adding one to two years. Becoming a fully independent RF designer typically takes another three to five years of hands-on experience.

steps: Education

Most risk managers hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, accounting, mathematics, statistics or business. Banks and trading firms often favor quantitative majors. A master’s degree in finance, financial engineering or business helps for senior or market risk roles but is not required everywhere.
First job

People usually start as a risk analyst, credit analyst, internal auditor or compliance analyst. In insurance and corporate settings, a first job in claims, underwriting or insurance buying is also common. These roles teach how losses happen and how controls are tested.
Certifications

No license is required to work as a risk manager. Many employers value the FRM from GARP or the PRM from PRMIA for financial risk. The CFA helps in investment firms, and the ARM from The Institutes is common in corporate and insurance risk.
Exams and experience

The FRM has two exams, and GARP requires two years of relevant full-time work experience before you are certified. Many people study while working as analysts. Other credentials also combine exams with work experience requirements.
Time it takes

Moving from a first analyst job to a risk manager title usually takes five to ten years. The pace depends on the employer, the type of risk and whether you add a graduate degree or certification along the way.
qa: Do you need a license to be a risk manager?

No. There is no state or federal license for risk managers in the US. Employers instead look for a relevant degree, several years of experience and often a certification such as the FRM from GARP, the PRM from PRMIA or the ARM from The Institutes. Some finance roles may ask for other credentials depending on the firm.
How long does it take to become a risk manager?

Most people spend four years on a bachelor’s degree, then about five to ten years in roles like risk analyst, credit analyst or internal auditor before becoming a manager. Earning the FRM or a master’s degree during that time can speed up promotion, especially at banks and investment firms.

steps: Education

Most roles ask for a high school diploma or GED. An associate degree or coursework in robotics, mechatronics, electronics or computer science helps, but many operators are hired without one. Comfort with computers, game controllers, VR headsets and careful note taking matters more than a specific degree.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam to operate robots for testing or data collection in the US. Employers set their own standards. Some value general safety training, such as an OSHA 10-hour course, and any prior work around machines, warehouses or labs.
Build relevant skills

Practice skills employers test for: steady hand control with joysticks or motion-capture gear, following detailed task scripts, spotting and logging errors, and basic troubleshooting. Hobby robotics, drone flying, 3D printing or lab and manufacturing work can show you handle equipment carefully and consistently.
On-the-job training

New hires usually learn the specific robot, teleoperation rig and data tools at work. Training covers safety zones, emergency stops, recording sessions to quality standards and reporting hardware faults. Expect a few days to several weeks of supervised practice before working on your own.
Time it takes
