Yes. Many solutions engineers studied business, science or other fields and gained technical skills through work in support, IT, implementation or development. Employers care most about whether you can understand the product, solve customer problems and explain technical ideas clearly. A track record of hands-on technical work matters more than the specific degree.

steps: Education

No specific degree is required. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree, often in business, human resources, psychology or communications. People also come in from sales, customer service or research jobs. Strong writing and comfort with online research matter more than the major.
First job in recruiting

Most sourcers start as a recruiting coordinator, recruiting assistant or researcher at a staffing agency, or in a sales role that involves cold outreach. These jobs teach how hiring works, how to read résumés and how to talk with people who aren’t job hunting.
Search and outreach skills

Learn Boolean search strings, advanced search engine operators and the search features in professional networking sites and applicant tracking systems. Practice finding contact details, mapping teams at target employers and writing short messages that get replies from passive candidates.
License and certification

No state requires a license or exam to work as a sourcer. Some people take short sourcing courses or certifications from training providers, and some later earn HR credentials such as SHRM-CP. Employers mostly judge you on results like response rates and hires.
Time it takes

With a related first job, many people move into a dedicated sourcing role within one to two years. Specializing in hard-to-fill areas like engineering or healthcare, then moving up to senior sourcer or full-cycle recruiter, usually takes a few more years.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a sourcer?

Not always. Many job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in business, human resources or psychology, but plenty of sourcers get in without one. Experience as a recruiting coordinator, agency researcher or sales rep, plus strong search and writing skills, often counts as much as a degree.
Do you need a certification to be a sourcer?

No. There is no license or required certification for sourcers in the US. Some people take sourcing courses to learn Boolean search and outreach, and some HR professionals earn SHRM-CP, but hiring managers mainly look at whether you can find qualified people and get them to reply.

steps: Education

There is no license. Most spend analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in supply chain management, business, finance, economics or data analytics. Courses in statistics, databases and purchasing matter most, since the work means cleaning and grouping large sets of invoice and purchase order data.
First job

Common first jobs are procurement analyst, purchasing assistant, junior buyer, accounts payable analyst or junior data analyst. Accounts payable and buying roles teach how purchase orders, invoices and contracts flow, which is the raw material of spend analysis.
Data skills

Employers expect advanced spreadsheet skills and often SQL and a business intelligence tool. Learn to classify spend by category and supplier, often with a taxonomy such as UNSPSC, find duplicate suppliers and off-contract buying, and model savings from price or volume changes.
Certification

Certification is optional. The Certified Professional in Supply Management (CPSM) from the Institute for Supply Management (ISM) is the best known in procurement and requires exams plus several years of experience. Some analysts add the Certified Supply Chain Professional (CSCP) from ASCM.
Time it takes

Entry-level analyst roles are open to new graduates with strong data skills. Senior analyst roles usually ask for a few years of procurement or finance experience, and category manager or sourcing manager is a common next step.
qa: What certification is best for a procurement analyst?

No certification is required. The best known in procurement is the Certified Professional in Supply Management (CPSM) from the Institute for Supply Management, which requires passing exams and several years of supply management experience. Some analysts choose the Certified Supply Chain Professional (CSCP) from ASCM. Data skills such as SQL often matter more at entry level.
Can you become a spend analyst without experience?

Yes. Many companies hire new graduates with degrees in supply chain, business, finance or analytics as procurement or spend analysts. Strong spreadsheet skills, some SQL and a project that cleans and analyzes purchasing data help most. Others move in from accounts payable, purchasing or general data analyst roles.

steps: Education

There is no license. Most sponsorship managers hold a bachelor’s degree in sports management, marketing, communications or business. Sports management programs often include internships with teams, leagues or events, which matter more to employers than the degree itself.
Internships

Internships with teams, leagues, venues, festivals, nonprofits or sponsorship agencies are the usual way to get noticed. Many sports and event employers hire entry-level staff from their own interns, so working game days or events while in school helps.
First job

Common first jobs are sponsorship or partnership coordinator, activation coordinator, account coordinator at an agency, or inside sales for a sports team. Activation roles deliver what sponsors bought, such as signage, hospitality and promotions, and teach contracts in practice.
Skills to build

Sponsorship work combines sales and service. Learn to build proposals, value assets such as naming rights and media, negotiate contracts, track deliverables and report results to sponsors. On the buying side, brands expect you to measure the return on each sponsorship.
Time it takes

Moving from coordinator to sponsorship manager usually takes several years. Director roles typically ask for a record of selling, renewing and growing sponsor revenue, plus strong contacts in sports, entertainment or events.
qa: How long does it take to become a sponsorship manager?

Usually several years after a bachelor’s degree. Most people start as interns, then work as sponsorship, partnership or activation coordinators, or in team ticket sales, before managing their own sponsor accounts. Progress depends mainly on a record of selling, renewing and delivering sponsorships rather than on any credential.
Do you need a license to work in sponsorships?

No. There is no license or required certification for sponsorship managers in the US. Employers hire on sales results, contract and activation experience, and contacts in sports, entertainment or events. Sports agents who represent athletes are a different job, regulated by many states and certified by players’ unions.

steps: Education

No license is required. Many SQL developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information systems, mathematics or business analytics, while others learn SQL through community college courses or self-study. Learn relational database concepts, normalization and data modeling.
SQL skills

Go beyond basic queries to joins, window functions, common table expressions, indexes and query tuning. Learn to write stored procedures, functions and views in at least one database, such as SQL Server with T-SQL, Oracle with PL/SQL, or PostgreSQL.
Reporting and ETL tools

Many SQL developer jobs also involve reporting and moving data between systems. Learn a reporting tool such as SSRS or Power BI and the basics of ETL, using tools such as SSIS, to load and clean data.
Certifications

Certifications are optional but can help. Database vendors offer them, such as the Oracle Database SQL Certified Associate, and Microsoft offers certifications for its data platform. Employers usually test SQL skills directly with written queries or a technical interview.
First job

Common first jobs are junior SQL developer, database developer, report writer, data analyst or database support technician. Many SQL developers start in a business role, such as operations or finance, writing queries for their team, then move into a dedicated database role.
Time it takes

You can learn useful SQL in a few months. Reaching a junior SQL developer role usually takes one to two years of practice and work with real data, or a four-year degree. Becoming a senior database developer usually takes five or more years.
qa: How long does it take to become a SQL developer?

You can learn basic SQL queries in a few weeks and solid skills in a few months. Landing a SQL developer job usually takes one to two years of practice with real data, often in an analyst or report writer role first. Senior SQL developers who tune performance and design databases typically have five or more years of experience.
What certification helps a SQL developer?

No certification is required. Database vendors offer optional ones, such as the Oracle Database SQL Certified Associate, and Microsoft offers certifications for its data platform, including SQL Server and Azure. They can help when an employer uses that vendor’s database, but most employers still test SQL skills directly with written queries or technical interviews.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, computer science or a related field. Engineers focus on programming and security. Finance and legal people study capital markets, securities and payments. Some later earn a law degree or a master’s in finance.
Core blockchain skills

Learn how blockchains such as Ethereum work, how ERC-20 tokens are built and how stablecoin reserves are held and reported. Developers usually learn Solidity and smart contract auditing basics. Non-engineers learn custody, wallets and on-chain settlement through online courses, documentation and hands-on testing.
Licenses and registrations

There is no license for this job title. Firms that issue stablecoins usually need state money transmitter licenses or a charter. If you sell or structure tokenized securities at a broker-dealer, FINRA registration such as the Series 7 may be required. Rules vary by firm and role.
First job

Common entry points are blockchain developer, fintech or bank analyst, fund operations, treasury or payments analyst, or compliance analyst at a crypto exchange or digital asset firm. Experience in traditional bonds, funds or payments is valued because tokenization copies those products onto a blockchain.
Time it takes

Expect a four-year degree plus usually two to five years of related work before moving into a dedicated stablecoin or tokenization role. People already working in securities, payments or software engineering can often move over faster by building blockchain skills on the side.
qa: Do you need a license to work on stablecoins or tokenization?

No personal license exists for this work. Companies may need state money transmitter licenses, trust charters or federal approval to issue stablecoins. If your job involves selling or structuring tokenized securities at a broker-dealer, you may need FINRA registrations such as the Series 7. Requirements depend on the employer and your exact duties.
What degree do you need to work in asset tokenization?

There is no required degree. Most people hold a bachelor’s in finance, economics, computer science or law-related studies. Engineers need strong programming skills and smart contract knowledge. Business, product and compliance roles favor finance or legal training plus a clear understanding of securities rules, custody and how blockchains settle transactions.

steps: Education

There is no required degree or license. Most staff engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field, though some are self-taught or came through a coding bootcamp. What matters is a deep grasp of systems design, data structures and the main languages a company uses.
First job

Nobody starts as a staff engineer. The usual way in is an entry-level software engineer role, often after an internship, followed by promotion to mid-level and then senior engineer. Each level adds scope, from single features to whole services and the teams that depend on them.
Senior engineer years

Most people spend several years as a senior engineer before the staff step. Staff candidates show impact beyond their own team: leading designs that several teams use, fixing problems no one else could, writing clear technical documents and mentoring other engineers.
Staff promotion

Most staff engineers are promoted internally, where a committee reviews their work against a written career ladder. Others are hired from outside after a long interview loop with system design, coding and behavioral rounds, where past projects and their results carry great weight.
Time it takes

It usually takes eight or more years of professional experience to reach staff level, though this varies widely by company. Principal engineer, the next level at many companies, often takes several more years and is reached by far fewer people.
qa: How long does it take to become a staff engineer?

Most staff engineers have eight or more years of experience, though it varies widely by company. The usual path runs from entry-level software engineer to mid-level and senior engineer, then staff. Promotion depends on proven impact across several teams, not on years alone, so some reach it sooner and many never do.
Is there a certification for staff engineers?

No. There is no license or certification for staff or principal engineers. Companies judge candidates on their track record: systems they designed, hard problems they solved, design documents they wrote and engineers they helped grow. Cloud or vendor certifications can help in some jobs but do not lead to a staff title.

steps: Education

Most statisticians hold a master’s degree in statistics, biostatistics or mathematics, and research or academic roles often require a PhD. A bachelor’s degree in statistics or mathematics can lead to analyst roles. Key subjects are probability, mathematical statistics, regression, experimental design and sampling.
Software skills

Learn R and SAS, which are widely used in research and clinical trials, plus Python and SQL. Practice with real data sets, simulation and reproducible reports. Clear writing about what the results do and do not show matters as much as the math.
Internships and research

Internships at government statistical agencies, health research groups, drug makers and survey firms give experience with real studies. Graduate students often gain experience as research or teaching assistants, analyzing data for professors or campus consulting services.
Accreditation

No state license is required. The American Statistical Association offers voluntary accreditation: GStat for early-career statisticians and PStat for experienced ones. Federal statistician jobs set their own coursework requirements, and clinical trial roles expect knowledge of FDA rules.
First job

Common first jobs are statistical analyst, biostatistician, research associate, survey statistician or data analyst. Government agencies, universities, hospitals, drug makers and research firms hire many new graduates, often directly from master’s programs.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree and one to two more for a master’s, so most statisticians start working about five to six years after high school. A PhD usually takes another four to six years.
qa: How long does it take to become a statistician?

Usually about five to six years after high school: a four-year bachelor’s degree in statistics or mathematics, then a one to two year master’s degree, which most statistician jobs expect. Research and academic positions often require a PhD, which usually takes four to six more years. Some start as data analysts with a bachelor’s degree.
Is there a certification for statisticians?

No license is required, but the American Statistical Association offers voluntary accreditation. GStat is for statisticians early in their careers with a graduate degree, and PStat is for experienced statisticians who show professional competence and ethics. Most employers do not require either, but they can strengthen a resume, especially for consulting or expert work.

steps: Education

Most storage engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information technology, computer engineering or a related field. Some enter with an associate degree or military IT training plus strong hands-on experience. Coursework in operating systems, networking and Linux is most useful.
First job

Few people start as storage engineers. The usual way in is a role such as help desk technician, data center technician, backup administrator or systems administrator. In these jobs you handle servers, disks, backups and restores, and you learn how data moves across a network.
Build storage skills

While working, learn RAID, SAN and NAS systems, iSCSI and Fibre Channel, file systems, snapshots, replication and backup software. Get comfortable with cloud object storage and scripting in Bash, PowerShell or Python. A home lab with virtual machines helps you practice safely.
Certifications

No state license or required exam exists for this work. Many employers value vendor or industry certifications, such as the SNIA Certified Storage Professional, NetApp Certified Data Administrator, CompTIA Server+ or AWS certifications. Pick the ones that match the systems used where you want to work.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then usually two to five years in systems or backup roles before moving into a storage engineer title. People who already work in IT can often make the move faster by taking on storage projects.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a storage engineer?

No. There is no license or required exam for storage engineers in the US. Certifications are optional, but they can help you get hired. Common choices include the SNIA Certified Storage Professional, NetApp Certified Data Administrator, CompTIA Server+ and AWS certifications. Hands-on experience with real storage systems usually matters more to employers than any single credential.
How long does it take to become a storage engineer?

It usually takes six to nine years in total. Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree in IT or computer science, then two to five years working as a systems administrator, backup administrator or data center technician. Those roles build the server, network and backup skills needed before stepping into a storage engineer job.

steps: Education

No license or set degree is required. Most employers ask for a high school diploma or equivalent. A degree in business, retail management or a related field can speed things up, and some large retailers hire graduates straight into management trainee programs.
Start on the floor

Most store managers begin as sales associates, cashiers or stock workers. This is where you learn the register, merchandising, inventory counts, loss prevention and how to handle difficult customers. Reliability and strong sales or service results get you noticed for promotion.
Supervisor or keyholder

The next step is usually shift supervisor, keyholder or department lead. You open and close the store, run shifts, handle cash deposits and direct other staff. This is your first real experience scheduling people and solving problems without a manager present.
Assistant store manager

Most people serve as assistant manager before running a store. You help with hiring, training, payroll hours, sales targets, ordering and reading store reports. Many companies expect you to cover for the store manager and show you can hit numbers on your own.
Role-specific certificates

Some stores need extra training. Grocery and food stores often require a certified food protection manager, and rules vary by state and county. Stores selling alcohol, tobacco or pharmacy items may need state or local responsible-sales training. Optional retail and customer service credentials also exist.
Time it takes

Moving from entry-level associate to store manager commonly takes several years, often three to six, depending on the company, store size and your results. Management trainee programs for degree holders can shorten this to one or two years.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a store manager?

No. Many store managers have only a high school diploma and worked their way up from sales associate through supervisor and assistant manager. A degree in business or retail management helps, especially at large chains, and can qualify you for management trainee programs that move faster. Proven experience leading staff and hitting sales goals usually matters most.
How long does it take to become a store manager?

It usually takes several years of retail experience, often three to six, moving from associate to shift supervisor to assistant manager. The pace depends on the company, store size and your performance. Graduates who join a retailer’s management trainee program can sometimes run a store within one to two years.

steps: Education

Most employers expect a bachelor’s degree in supply chain management, business, finance, economics or engineering. Courses in negotiation, contract basics, cost analysis and spreadsheets help most. Some managers later earn an MBA, but it is rarely required to get in.
First job

Most people start as a buyer, purchasing agent, procurement analyst or sourcing specialist. You compare supplier quotes, place orders, track spend and learn how purchase terms and contracts work. Some come from engineering, finance or operations roles instead.
Certification

No state license is required. Many employers value the CPSM from the Institute for Supply Management (ISM) or the CSCP from ASCM. Public-sector buyers often pursue the CPPB or CPPO. These usually require some work experience plus passing exams.
Category experience

Next comes a senior sourcing or category role where you own spend for an area such as IT, raw materials, logistics or services. You run RFPs, negotiate multiyear contracts and track supplier cost, quality and risk.
Time it takes

Becoming a strategic sourcing manager commonly takes five to eight years of procurement experience after a bachelor’s degree. People who lead large negotiations and show measurable savings early can move up faster.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a strategic sourcing manager?

No certification or license is legally required. Many employers still prefer or list credentials such as the CPSM from the Institute for Supply Management or the CSCP from ASCM. Government buyers often earn the CPPB or CPPO. Proven experience negotiating contracts and managing suppliers usually matters more than any single credential.
How long does it take to become a strategic sourcing manager?

Most people need a four-year bachelor’s degree and then about five to eight years in procurement. A common path runs from buyer or procurement analyst to sourcing specialist or category manager, then to strategic sourcing manager. Timelines vary with company size, the value of spend you handle and the results you can show.

steps: Education

Most structural engineers earn a bachelor’s degree in civil engineering from an ABET-accredited program, with courses in statics, mechanics of materials, structural analysis, and steel and concrete design. Many employers prefer a master’s in structural engineering. For aircraft and rocket structures, a degree in aerospace or mechanical engineering is more common.
FE exam

Many students take the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam near graduation. Passing it lets you register with your state board as an engineer in training (EIT) or engineer intern (EI), the usual first step toward a license.
Supervised experience

Most states require about four years of progressive engineering experience, usually under a licensed Professional Engineer, before granting a PE license. Some states count a master’s degree toward part of this time. Requirements vary by state.
PE or SE license

Licensure requires passing the NCEES PE Civil: Structural exam or the NCEES Structural Engineering (SE) exam, depending on your state. Many state boards let you take an exam before you finish your experience, with the license issued once it is complete. A few states require a separate SE license to design certain structures.
Time it takes
Expect about eight years from starting college to a PE license: four years of school and about four years of experience. An SE license, where a state requires it, usually takes longer.
First job

Most people start as a junior structural engineer or engineer in training at a structural or civil engineering consulting firm. Others start as design engineers or stress analysts in aerospace or manufacturing. You run calculations, build models, and draft details while a licensed engineer reviews your work.
qa: Do you need a license to be a structural engineer?

You need a state PE license to sign and seal building or bridge designs or to offer engineering services to the public. Rules vary by state, and a few require an SE license for some structures. Many engineers who design aircraft, rockets, or products for a manufacturer work without a license under industrial exemptions, though employers may still value one.
How long does it take to become a structural engineer?

You can start working after a four-year bachelor’s degree, or after five to six years if you add a master’s. Earning a PE license usually takes about four more years of supervised experience plus passing the required exams, so licensure often comes around eight years after starting college.

steps: Be enrolled in school

Most summer internships require you to be a current college student, usually a sophomore or junior, and often returning to school in the fall. Some programs take high school students or recent graduates. No license or exam is needed. A declared major related to the work helps, but many employers accept a range of fields.
Build a resume

Put together a one-page resume listing coursework, campus jobs, clubs, volunteer work and class projects. Your school’s career center can review it and run mock interviews. For design, writing or software roles, a small portfolio or code samples often matters more than grades.
Apply early

Large employers, especially in finance, consulting and tech, often open summer applications the fall before, sometimes nearly a year ahead. Smaller firms and nonprofits hire later, into spring. Use campus career fairs, school job boards and direct applications. Applying to many openings is normal.
Interviews and work authorization

Expect a phone screen, then one or more interviews, which may include technical questions or a case exercise. International students on an F-1 visa usually need Curricular Practical Training (CPT) approved through their school before starting. Some schools also offer academic credit for internships.
Time it takes

The search usually runs two to six months from first application to offer. The internship itself typically lasts ten to twelve weeks, from late May or June through August. Many students complete one or two summer internships before graduating.
Return offer

Strong interns are often offered a full-time job starting after graduation, or a second summer internship. A return offer usually depends on your final project, manager feedback and the company’s hiring needs that year. If none comes, the experience still strengthens later applications.
qa: When should you apply for a summer internship?

Start looking the fall before the summer you want to intern. Banks, consulting firms and large tech companies often fill many spots by late fall or winter. Smaller companies, government offices and nonprofits may keep hiring into March or April. Check your school’s career center calendar and apply as soon as postings open.
Are summer internships paid?

Many are, especially at large companies. Under federal law, unpaid internships at for-profit employers are allowed only when the intern, not the employer, is the primary beneficiary, based on a Department of Labor test. Some states have stricter rules. Unpaid roles are more common at nonprofits and government agencies, and some students receive academic credit instead.

steps: Education or trade start

There are two common starts. Some superintendents earn a bachelor’s degree in construction management, construction science or civil engineering. Many others go to work in a trade right after high school, such as carpentry, concrete or electrical work, and learn construction on the job. Employers accept both paths.
Field experience

Years on job sites matter most. Trade workers usually move up to lead hand and then foreman, running their own crew. Degree holders often start as a field engineer or project engineer, handling layout, submittals and RFIs while learning from an experienced superintendent.
Safety training

Employers usually expect the OSHA 30-Hour Construction course, and many also want first aid and CPR. Depending on the work, you may need training in fall protection, scaffolds, excavation or confined spaces. You will be the person responsible for safety on site.
First job

The usual first job with the title is assistant superintendent. You run part of a project, such as one building, floor or phase. You write daily reports, coordinate subcontractors, check work against the drawings and walk inspections under a lead superintendent.
Optional certifications

No certification is required to work as a superintendent. Some people take the AGC Supervisory Training Program. Others later earn the Certified Construction Manager (CCM) credential from CMAA, which requires years of experience. These credentials can help you get onto larger commercial projects.
Time it takes

With a degree, it usually takes about five to ten years to run a site on your own. Coming up from the trades, it often takes ten years or more. Large or complex projects such as hospitals or high-rises usually call for more experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a construction superintendent?

Usually not. In most cases the construction company holds the contractor’s license, not the superintendent. Some states and cities have their own site supervisor or qualifier rules for certain types of work, so requirements vary by location. Employers almost always expect OSHA 30-Hour Construction training, and some ask for added safety training.
Do you need a degree to become a construction superintendent?

No. Many superintendents never went to college. They worked their way up from a trade to foreman and then to assistant superintendent. A degree in construction management or civil engineering can speed up the path and is preferred by some large general contractors. Proven field experience still counts the most.

steps: Education

Most supervisor jobs ask for a high school diploma or GED. A college degree is not usually required for shift or floor roles, though an associate’s or bachelor’s degree in business or a related field can help in larger companies or for later moves into management.
Frontline experience

Nearly everyone starts by doing the work they will later oversee, such as stocking, production, food service, customer service or warehouse jobs. Employers want people who know the tasks, the equipment and the common problems firsthand, usually after one to three years on the floor.
Lead or trainer role

The usual step up is a team lead, shift lead or trainer position. You start assigning tasks, training new hires, covering breaks and handling small problems. This shows a manager you can direct people and stay calm when something goes wrong.
Safety and industry training

There is no general supervisor license. Many employers expect OSHA 10-hour or 30-hour training in construction, manufacturing or warehousing. In food service, many states and local health codes require a certified food protection manager on site. Requirements vary by industry and state.
Time it takes

Moving from a frontline job to supervisor usually takes two to five years, depending on the company and industry. Some employers run internal leadership programs that shorten this, and fast-growing workplaces often promote reliable workers sooner.
First job

The first supervisor job is most often an internal promotion at the same company, overseeing a shift or small crew you already know. Hiring an outside supervisor usually requires prior lead or supervisory experience in the same type of work.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a supervisor?

Usually not. Most shift and floor supervisor jobs ask for a high school diploma or GED plus experience in the work. A degree in business or a related field can help in larger companies or when moving up to manager, but proven experience and leadership on the job matter most to employers.
How long does it take to become a supervisor?

Most people take two to five years. They spend one to three years in a frontline job, then often serve as a team lead or shift lead before being promoted. Timing depends on the industry, company size and how quickly openings come up. Internal leadership programs can shorten the path.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, industrial, manufacturing or materials engineering. Some accept a related technical degree with strong shop floor experience. Courses in statistics, metrology, materials and manufacturing processes help most, since the job is judging how parts are made and measured.
First job

Few people start in supplier quality. The usual first job is quality engineer, manufacturing engineer or process engineer inside a plant. Some move up from quality technician or inspector roles. There you learn blueprints, GD&T, gauges, root cause analysis and corrective action before working with outside suppliers.
Industry tools and standards

Learn the standards your industry uses. Automotive work relies on IATF 16949 and the AIAG core tools such as APQP, PPAP, FMEA and MSA. Aerospace uses AS9100 and AS9102 first article inspection. Medical device work follows ISO 13485 and FDA rules. Most roles also expect ISO 9001 knowledge.
Auditor training

Because the job means auditing suppliers, many people take internal or lead auditor training for ISO 9001 or an industry standard. Employers often provide this. It teaches how to plan an audit, collect evidence, write findings and follow up on supplier corrective actions.
Certifications

No license is required. Employers often value ASQ certifications such as Certified Quality Engineer (CQE), Certified Supplier Quality Professional (CSQP) or Six Sigma Green Belt or Black Belt. ASQ requires several years of work experience for most of these, with credit for a degree.
Time it takes

Expect four years for the degree, then usually two to five years in quality or manufacturing roles before moving into a supplier quality and development engineer position. Travel to supplier sites is common, so a clean driving record and a passport can help.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a supplier quality engineer?

No license or certification is legally required. Many employers prefer or ask for ASQ credentials such as the Certified Quality Engineer (CQE) or Certified Supplier Quality Professional (CSQP), plus lead auditor training. In automotive and aerospace jobs, hands-on knowledge of PPAP, APQP or AS9102 often matters as much as any certificate.
How long does it take to become a supplier quality engineer?

Most people need a four-year engineering degree and then two to five years of experience as a quality, manufacturing or process engineer. That time builds skills in root cause analysis, measurement and audits. People with a strong plant background sometimes move in faster, especially when they already know the industry standards their employer uses.

steps: Education

Most employers want a bachelor’s degree in supply chain management, business, operations management, industrial engineering or a related field. Courses in statistics, forecasting, inventory control and accounting help. Some people enter with an associate degree or warehouse experience and finish a degree while working.
Spreadsheet and system skills

Planners spend their days in data. Build strong Excel skills, including pivot tables and lookups, and learn how ERP systems handle orders, inventory and production schedules. Internships or class projects using real planning software make a resume stand out.
First job

Most people start as a junior planner, inventory analyst, buyer, material planner, production scheduler or logistics coordinator. These roles teach how orders, suppliers, lead times and stock levels connect before you own a full demand or supply plan.
Optional certification

No license is required. Many planners earn the CPIM (Certified in Planning and Inventory Management) or CSCP (Certified Supply Chain Professional) from ASCM, formerly APICS. Some in purchasing earn the CPSM from ISM. Employers often value these but rarely require them for entry roles.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually one to three years in an entry role before holding a full supply chain planner title. Moving into senior planning or management often takes several more years of experience.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a supply chain planner?

No. There is no license or required certification for supply chain planners in the US. Many employers list the CPIM or CSCP from ASCM as preferred, especially for senior roles. Most people earn one after gaining some work experience, since the exams cover planning, inventory and operations concepts used on the job.
How long does it take to become a supply chain planner?

Most people take about five to seven years in total. That usually means a four-year bachelor’s degree in supply chain, business or a related field, followed by one to three years as an analyst, buyer, scheduler or coordinator. Strong spreadsheet and ERP skills can shorten the time to a planner title.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in supply chain management, business, operations management, industrial engineering or a related field. Courses in statistics, forecasting and operations are especially useful. Some people get in with an associate degree plus experience in a warehouse, production or purchasing setting.
Tools and skills

Learn spreadsheets well, including pivot tables and lookups. Get comfortable with ERP and MRP systems, which planners use daily to read demand, inventory and lead times. Internships or co-op roles in purchasing, logistics or production give the hands-on practice employers look for.
First job

Typical entry roles are supply chain analyst, inventory analyst, material planner, junior buyer or production scheduler. Some people move in from warehouse, customer service or purchasing jobs after learning how orders and stock move through the business.
Certification

No license is required. Many planners earn ASCM’s CPIM (Certified in Planning and Inventory Management) after a year or two of work, and later the CSCP (Certified Supply Chain Professional). Employers usually list these as preferred rather than required.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a degree, then one to three years in an analyst or junior planner role before owning a planning area. Moving into a supply chain manager job typically takes five or more years of experience, often including leading projects or people.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a supply chain planner?

No. There is no license or required certification for this work in the US. Many employers prefer candidates with ASCM’s CPIM or CSCP, and purchasing-focused roles may value ISM’s CPSM. These show you know planning, inventory and forecasting methods, but a related degree and hands-on experience with ERP systems usually matter more for getting hired.
How long does it take to become a supply chain manager?

Most people spend four years earning a bachelor’s degree, then several years working as an analyst, buyer or planner. Moving into a manager job usually takes five or more years of experience, including leading projects or people. A master’s degree or a certification such as CSCP can help, but it does not replace work experience.

steps: Education

Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information technology or a related field. An associate degree or self-study can also work, especially for entry roles. What matters most is a working grasp of networking, operating systems and how software fails.
Hands-on skills

Build the skills interviews test: Linux and Windows command lines, reading log files, basic SQL queries, HTTP and APIs, and a scripting language such as Python or Bash. A home lab where you break and fix things on purpose is good practice.
Certifications

No license or certification is required by law. Many people add CompTIA A+ or CompTIA Network+ to get past screening for entry roles. Later, vendor credentials such as Cisco’s CCNA or Microsoft and AWS certifications help when an employer supports those platforms.
First job

Most people start in help desk, IT support or Tier 1 customer support, answering tickets and following set procedures. Escalating cases well, writing clear ticket notes and learning the product deeply is how you move up to Tier 2 or support engineer work.
Time it takes

Some graduates with a related degree go straight into a junior support engineer role. Coming from help desk, it usually takes one to three years of ticket experience to land the title, depending on how complex the product is.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a technical support engineer?

No. A degree in computer science or IT helps, and some software companies list one, but many support engineers got in through help desk work, certifications such as CompTIA A+ and self-taught skills. Showing you can read logs, reproduce faults and explain fixes clearly often counts more than the degree itself.
How long does it take to become a technical support engineer?

It usually takes one to three years. Most people first work in help desk or Tier 1 support, learning troubleshooting and the product, then move into a support engineer role. Someone with a related degree and strong technical skills can sometimes start as a junior support engineer right away.

steps: Education

There is no license and no required degree for this work. Many employers prefer a bachelor’s degree in business, communications or a related field, but plenty accept a high school diploma when it is backed by solid support experience.
First job

Most people start as a customer support agent or customer service representative, answering tickets, calls or chats. This is where you learn the ticketing software, the product, and the metrics managers are judged on, such as response time, resolution time and customer satisfaction scores.
Senior agent or team lead

The usual next step is senior agent, team lead or support supervisor. You handle escalations, coach newer agents, review ticket quality and help build schedules. Showing you can raise a team’s numbers matters more here than any credential.
Optional certifications

No exam is required. Some leads take voluntary certifications from industry groups such as HDI, or training in workforce management, coaching or project management. These can help a resume stand out but are rarely a hiring requirement.
Time it takes

Moving from a first agent job to support manager usually takes three to six years. People who take on hiring, scheduling and reporting tasks early, or who join a fast growing team, often move up sooner.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a customer support manager?

Not always. Many job postings list a bachelor’s degree in business, communications or a related field as preferred, but employers often accept several years of support experience instead. Proven results as a team lead, such as better response times and quality scores, usually count more than the degree itself.
How long does it take to become a customer support manager?

It usually takes three to six years. Most people spend one to three years as a support agent, then one to three years as a senior agent or team lead before moving into a manager role. The pace depends on company size, team growth and how much leadership work you take on.

steps: Education

Many employers ask for an associate or bachelor’s degree in information technology, computer science or a related field. No degree is legally required. Some people enter through a certificate program or self-study, practicing on a home lab with virtual servers, then prove their skills on the job.
Entry certifications

CompTIA A+ and CompTIA Network+ are common starting points. They cover hardware, operating systems and networking basics. Many help desk postings list them, and they help people without a degree get a first interview.
First job

Most system administrators start at a help desk or as an IT support technician. You reset passwords, set up laptops and fix user problems. This work teaches accounts, permissions and how a company’s systems connect, which is the core of the admin role.
Platform certifications

As you move up, employers look for proof of skill on the systems they run. Common choices include Microsoft certifications for Windows Server and Microsoft 365, Red Hat Certified System Administrator (RHCSA) or CompTIA Linux+ for Linux, and CompTIA Security+. Security+ is often required for Department of Defense and defense contractor jobs.
Time it takes

Moving from help desk to a system administrator title usually takes two to four years. People with a degree and an IT internship sometimes start as junior administrators right after school. Without a degree, expect more time in support roles first.
qa: Do you need a license to be a system administrator?

No. There is no state or federal license for system administrators in the US. Certifications such as CompTIA Security+, RHCSA or Microsoft certifications are voluntary, but many employers expect them. Government and defense contractor jobs often require a specific certification like Security+ and may also require a security clearance.
How long does it take to become a system administrator?

It usually takes two to four years of IT work after training. Most people first spend time at a help desk or in desktop support, learning accounts, permissions and networking. A two- or four-year degree adds time up front but can shorten the climb. Some people with strong certifications and home lab experience move up faster.

steps: Education

Most systems engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in engineering, often electrical, mechanical, aerospace, computer or systems engineering. Employers often prefer programs accredited by ABET. Courses in requirements, controls, software and probability are useful, since the job ties many disciplines together.
First job

Few people start with the title systems engineer. Most begin as a design, test, integration or software engineer on one part of a product. That work teaches how subsystems behave and fail, which is the base for coordinating the whole system later.
Systems engineering experience

Over several years, engineers take on requirements writing, interface definition, verification planning and trade studies. Many move into a systems role on the same program. In defense and aerospace, much of this work also requires a US security clearance, which the employer sponsors.
Graduate study

A master’s degree in systems engineering or a related field is common but not required. Many engineers earn it part time while working. It can help with promotion to lead or chief systems engineer roles.
Certification

No license is required for most systems engineering jobs. Some employers value INCOSE certification: ASEP for early career, then CSEP and ESEP, which require documented systems engineering experience. A Professional Engineer license is optional and matters mainly when signing off on public works.
Time it takes

Expect four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually three to five years of engineering work before holding a true systems engineer role. Senior and lead positions typically come after ten or more years of experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a systems engineer?

Usually not. Most systems engineers work in industry, where no state license is required. Some earn INCOSE certifications such as ASEP or CSEP to show their skills. A Professional Engineer license is optional and mostly matters for work that affects public safety and needs a licensed engineer’s approval. Defense jobs often require a security clearance instead.
How long does it take to become a systems engineer?

Most people need about seven to nine years. That includes a four year engineering degree and usually three to five years working in design, test, integration or software before moving into a systems role. A part time master’s degree in systems engineering can be earned during those working years and may speed up promotion.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most people enter with a four-year bachelor’s degree in computer science or computer engineering. Focus on the core systems courses: operating systems, compilers, computer architecture, networking and databases. Some compiler, database internals and research-heavy roles favor a master’s or PhD.
Low-level programming skills

Learn C and C++ deeply, and increasingly Rust. Get comfortable with Linux, debuggers, profilers, memory management, concurrency and reading assembly. Build small projects such as a shell, a memory allocator, a toy compiler or a simple key-value store.
Open-source work

Contributing to open-source operating systems, compilers, databases or networking tools is a common way to prove ability. Accepted patches show you can read large codebases, follow review and write careful code.
Internships

Internships during college on infrastructure, storage, networking, embedded or compiler teams give real systems experience. They often turn into full-time offers and matter more than grades to many hiring teams.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required certification for this work in the US. Employers judge you through coding interviews, systems and design questions, and your track record of shipped or published code.
First job

The usual entry point is a junior software engineer role on an infrastructure, kernel, storage, embedded or compiler team. Some people move in after a few years of general software work. Expect two to five years before owning core systems code alone.
qa: Do you need a license to be a systems software engineer?

No. The US has no state license, registration or required certification for software engineers, including those who write operating systems, compilers, databases or networking code. Employers rely on technical interviews, your degree, internships and visible work such as open-source contributions to decide whether you are ready.
How long does it take to become a systems software engineer?

Most people spend four years on a bachelor’s degree in computer science or computer engineering, then start in a junior role. It usually takes another two to five years of hands-on work before you are trusted with core kernel, compiler or database code. A master’s or PhD adds time but can open specialized roles.

steps: Education

Most tax analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in accounting. Finance or economics can work if you add courses in financial accounting and federal income tax. Some people later earn a Master of Taxation or Master of Accountancy, which also helps meet CPA credit-hour rules.
First job

The usual way in is a tax associate or staff tax accountant role at a public accounting firm. There you prepare corporate returns, work out tax provisions and learn filing rules. Some people start directly on a corporate in-house tax team instead.
Licensing

No license is required to work as a tax analyst inside a company. Many employers prefer a CPA, though. Each state sets its own CPA rules. Most require 150 semester hours, but several now accept a bachelor’s degree plus extra supervised work experience.
Exams

CPA candidates pass the Uniform CPA Examination. It has three core sections, plus one discipline section, and Tax Compliance and Planning fits this work. Another option is the IRS Enrolled Agent credential, earned by passing the Special Enrollment Examination. It covers federal tax only.
International tax skills

For work across several countries, you learn transfer pricing, foreign tax credits, withholding taxes and how each country’s filing deadlines work. Most of this comes on the job, often by moving onto an international tax team after a year or two.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree. Most people then spend one to three years as an associate before they hold a tax analyst title. If you also earn a CPA, it often takes five to seven years in total.
qa: Do you need a CPA to be a tax analyst?

No. A CPA is not legally required to work as a tax analyst inside a company, and many analysts are hired with only an accounting degree. Many employers prefer it, though, especially for senior roles. The CPA exam includes a Tax Compliance and Planning section, and licensing rules vary by state.
How long does it take to become a tax analyst?

Most people need about five to seven years. That covers a four-year accounting degree plus one to three years as a tax associate at an accounting firm or on a corporate tax team. Some graduates are hired straight into entry-level tax analyst roles, which shortens the path.

steps: Education

Most tech leads hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. Some get in through self-study or a coding bootcamp plus a strong portfolio. No degree is legally required, but many employers list one in postings.
First job
The usual way in is a junior or entry-level software engineer role. There you learn to ship code as part of a team, use version control, write tests, and both give and receive code reviews.
Senior engineer experience

Most people work as a senior software engineer before leading. That means owning features end to end, designing systems, handling production issues, and becoming the person others ask for help. Employers want proof you make sound technical decisions on your own.
Leadership practice

Before getting the title, take on lead work. Mentor newer engineers, write design documents, break projects into tasks, run planning meetings and coordinate with product managers. Many tech leads are promoted from within after doing this informally for a while.
Licenses and certifications

There is no license, registration or required exam for tech leads in the US. Optional credentials, such as cloud platform certifications or Certified ScrumMaster, can help on a resume but rarely replace hands-on experience leading engineers.
Time it takes
Most people reach a tech lead role after roughly five to eight years as a software engineer, on top of any degree. Smaller or fast-growing teams sometimes promote strong engineers sooner.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a tech lead?

No. There is no license or required certification for tech leads in the US. Employers look for years of software engineering experience, strong code and design skills, and a record of mentoring or coordinating others. Optional credentials like cloud certifications or Certified ScrumMaster can help, but they rarely substitute for real leadership experience.
How long does it take to become a tech lead?

It usually takes about five to eight years of working as a software engineer, after any degree or training. Most people move from junior engineer to senior engineer first, then take on informal lead duties such as mentoring and planning before being given the tech lead title. Some smaller companies promote faster.

steps: Education

Many employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information technology, engineering or a related field. Others accept equivalent hands-on experience instead. A business or communications degree can also work when it comes with strong, proven technical skills in the product area.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam for technical account managers. Some people earn optional certifications, such as a vendor certification in the product they support, a cloud platform certification, or ITIL Foundation for IT service management. Employers usually value these as a plus, not a requirement.
First job

Most people start in a related technical role. Common entry points are technical support engineer, support specialist, implementation consultant, systems administrator or solutions engineer. These jobs teach the product, how customers set it up, and how problems get escalated and fixed.
Customer-facing experience

Before moving up, build a record of working directly with customers. Handle escalations, lead troubleshooting calls, write clear incident summaries and help plan upgrades or migrations. Hiring managers look for people who can explain technical issues to both engineers and business contacts.
Time it takes

There is no fixed timeline. Beyond any degree or training, most people spend two to five years in support, implementation or engineering roles before landing a first technical account manager job. Deep knowledge of one product or industry can shorten that.
Moving into the role

Many technical account managers move in through an internal transfer, since they already know the product and its customers. Some companies hire associate or junior technical account managers who start with a small set of accounts under a senior colleague.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a technical account manager?

Not always. Many job postings ask for a bachelor’s degree in computer science, IT, engineering or a related field, but plenty of employers accept equivalent experience instead. What matters most is proven technical skill with the product or platform, plus a record of working well with customers in support or implementation roles.
How long does it take to become a technical account manager?

There is no set timeline or required exam. Beyond any degree or training, most people spend two to five years in technical support, implementation, systems administration or engineering roles first. Those with deep knowledge of one product, or who transfer internally at a company they already know, can sometimes move in faster.

steps: Education

Most technical product managers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering, or another engineering field. Some come from math, physics, or information systems. An MBA is sometimes seen, but it is not required. For this role, technical depth usually matters more than a business degree.
Hands-on technical work

Most people first spend a few years as software engineers, site reliability or DevOps engineers, data engineers, or solutions engineers. This builds the credibility to talk with engineering users about APIs, system design, scaling, reliability, and tradeoffs.
No license required

There is no license, registration, or required exam for this work in any state. Optional credentials, such as the Certified Scrum Product Owner (CSPO) from Scrum Alliance or a cloud platform certification, can show knowledge. Employers rarely require them.
Take on product tasks

While still in a technical role, take on product work. Write specs, gather feedback from developers who use your tools, help own a roadmap for an internal service or API, and lead a small launch. Internal transfers are a very common way in.
First job

Common first titles are associate product manager or product manager on a platform, infrastructure, or developer tools team. Some people step in from technical program manager, solutions engineer, or developer relations roles.
Time it takes
There is no set timeline. Counting a four-year degree and a few years of engineering or related work, many people reach a technical product manager title six to nine years after starting college.
qa: Do you need to know how to code to be a technical product manager?

You usually do not write production code in this job. However, most employers expect you to understand code, APIs, and system architecture well enough to discuss design choices with engineers. Many technical product managers worked as software engineers first, and a computer science or engineering background is common.
How long does it take to become a technical product manager?

There is no fixed path. Most people earn a bachelor’s degree in computer science or engineering, then work a few years in a technical role such as software engineer before moving into product. In total, it often takes six to nine years after starting college. No license or exam is required.

steps: Education

Most technical program managers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, engineering, information systems or a related technical field. Some come from other majors but build strong technical knowledge through work. A master’s degree or MBA can help but is rarely required.
Hands-on technical work

Employers expect you to understand how software or hardware is actually built. Many people spend several years as a software engineer, QA engineer, systems engineer or IT specialist first. That background lets you discuss architecture, tradeoffs and risks with engineers.
Cross-team project experience

Before taking the title, most people volunteer to coordinate releases, track dependencies across teams, run sprint ceremonies or lead a launch. This shows you can plan schedules, manage risks and keep many groups aligned without direct authority over them.
Optional certifications

There is no license for this work. Some employers value the PMP from PMI, the PMI-ACP or the Certified ScrumMaster credential from Scrum Alliance. These are optional, and many technical program managers have none. Proven delivery of complex projects counts more.
Time it takes

There is no set timeline. Most people move into the role after roughly three to five or more years in engineering, IT or project management work following their degree. Some reach it sooner through an associate or entry-level program role.
First job

Common entry points are associate technical program manager, project manager or project coordinator on an engineering team, or scrum master. Many technical program managers also move over internally from an engineering role at the same company.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a technical program manager?

No. There is no required license or certification. Some employers like to see the PMP from PMI or a Certified ScrumMaster credential, but many technical program managers have neither. Hiring managers focus more on technical understanding and a record of delivering complex projects across several teams.
How long does it take to become a technical program manager?

It usually takes a bachelor’s degree plus several years of experience, often three to five or more, in software engineering, IT or project management. People who already lead cross-team work as engineers can sometimes move into the role sooner, especially through an internal transfer or an associate-level position.

steps: Education

Most technical recruiters hold a bachelor’s degree, often in business, human resources, psychology or communications. Some come from computer science or a bootcamp-free self-taught tech background. No specific degree is required, and some employers hire people without one who show strong sales or communication skills.
Learn the technology

You need enough technical knowledge to screen engineers. Learn how software roles differ, such as frontend, backend, DevOps and data engineering. Understand common languages, frameworks and cloud tools well enough to read a resume, ask follow-up questions and spot mismatched experience.
First job

The usual way in is as a recruiting coordinator, sourcer or junior agency recruiter. Coordinators schedule interviews and manage candidate flow. Sourcers search profiles, code repositories and job boards to find engineers and send first outreach messages. Agency roles often hire people with sales experience.
Full-cycle recruiting

Next you move into full-cycle work: meeting hiring managers, writing role requirements, screening candidates, managing technical interviews and closing offers. You build a track record of filled engineering roles, which matters more to employers than any credential.
Optional certification

There is no license to recruit in the US. Some recruiters later earn HR credentials such as the SHRM-CP from SHRM or the PHR from HRCI. These are optional and more useful if you plan to move into broader HR or talent leadership.
Time it takes

Moving from coordinator or sourcer to a full technical recruiter usually takes one to three years. People who already work in tech, such as former engineers or IT support staff, can sometimes move in faster because they already know the roles.
qa: Do you need a license or certification to be a technical recruiter?

No. There is no state or federal license for technical recruiters in the US. Employers care most about your record of hiring engineers and your grasp of technical roles. Optional credentials like the SHRM-CP or PHR exist, but they are general HR certifications and are rarely required for recruiting jobs.
Can you become a technical recruiter without a tech background?

Yes. Many technical recruiters start with no coding experience and learn on the job, often as sourcers or coordinators. You do need to learn how engineering roles, languages and tools fit together so you can screen candidates well. Reading job descriptions, talking with engineers and taking basic programming courses all help.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree. Common majors are English, communications, journalism and technical communication. A degree in computer science, engineering or a science is also valued, especially for software and API documentation, where you must understand what developers do.
Tools and technical skills

Learn to write in Markdown and basic HTML, use Git, and follow a style guide. Many teams use docs-as-code workflows or structured authoring such as DITA. API writers should be able to read code samples and test REST API calls.
Writing portfolio

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work. Employers judge you mainly on writing samples. Build a portfolio with a user guide, a how-to article and an API reference. Contributing to open-source project documentation gives you public, reviewed work to show.
Optional certificate

Some people take a college certificate program in technical communication, especially when changing careers. These programs teach audience analysis, editing and documentation tools. They are not required, and most hiring managers weigh your samples and subject knowledge more heavily than any credential.
First job

Common entry points are junior technical writer, documentation specialist or content writer roles. Many writers move in from related jobs instead, such as customer support, quality assurance, software engineering or lab work, where they already know the product and start writing its documentation.
Time it takes

The usual path is a four-year degree plus a few months building a portfolio. Career changers who already hold a degree and have technical experience often make the switch in six months to a year of focused practice and job searching.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a technical writer?

No. Technical writing has no license, registration or required exam in the US. Some people complete a college certificate program in technical communication, but employers care far more about writing samples, knowledge of the subject area and comfort with tools such as Markdown and Git. A strong portfolio usually matters more than any credential.
How long does it take to become a technical writer?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree, then a few months building a portfolio before landing a first role. If you already have a degree and work experience in software, engineering or support, you can often move into technical writing in six months to a year by building samples and applying.

steps: High school basics
Most employers ask for a high school diploma or GED. Classes in math, shop, electronics or auto repair help, as does any hands-on work fixing cars, appliances, computers or machines at home.
Technical training

Many technicians complete a certificate or associate degree in a field such as automotive, HVAC, electronics or industrial maintenance at a community college or trade school. Programs usually run from several months to two years. Some employers train new hires on the job instead.
Certifications

Which credential you need depends on the equipment. Automotive technicians often earn ASE certification after gaining work experience. Servicing stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment requires EPA Section 608 certification, while servicing motor vehicle air conditioning requires EPA Section 609 certification.
State license

Many technician jobs need no state license. Some trades do, such as HVAC or electrical work in many states, often after supervised hours or an apprenticeship. Requirements vary by state and sometimes by city, so check local rules for your specialty.
First job

People usually start as a helper, trainee, apprentice or entry-level technician, such as a lube technician or maintenance helper. You work under an experienced technician, learn diagnostic tools and build the experience that certifications and promotions require.
Time it takes

Working on your own usually takes six months to two years of training and experience. Specialties with state licenses or formal apprenticeships, like electrical work, often take longer, commonly several years.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a technician?

It depends on the specialty. Many technician jobs require no certification to start. Automotive employers often prefer ASE certification. Federal rules require EPA Section 608 certification for stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning work and EPA Section 609 certification for motor vehicle air conditioning. Some trades also need a state license, which varies by state.
How long does it take to become a technician?

Most people become technicians in about six months to two years, through a certificate or associate degree program, on-the-job training or both. Reaching a senior level or earning certifications that require work experience takes longer. Licensed trades with formal apprenticeships, such as electrical work, often take several years.

steps: Education

Most technology consultants hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information systems, engineering or business with a technology focus. Some later add an MBA or a master’s in information systems to move into senior or strategy roles. Coursework in databases, networking, project management and business process helps.
No license required

There is no state license or required exam to work as a technology consultant in the US. Employers judge you on your degree, your hands-on experience with specific systems, and your ability to explain technical choices to business clients in plain language.
First job

Many people start as a business analyst, systems analyst, IT support specialist, developer or junior analyst at a consulting firm. These roles teach you how systems are set up and used, how projects run, and how to gather requirements from the people who will use the technology.
Certifications

Certifications are optional but often expected for the systems you advise on. Common ones include cloud credentials such as AWS Certified Solutions Architect or Microsoft Azure certifications, Salesforce certifications, CompTIA certifications, ITIL for IT service management, and the PMP from PMI for project leadership.
Build a specialty

Consultants usually focus on an area such as cloud migration, cybersecurity, ERP or CRM systems, data and analytics, or a specific industry like healthcare or finance. Leading parts of real implementations and documenting results gives you the track record clients and hiring managers look for.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, then usually two to five years of work in analyst, IT or development roles before holding a full consultant title. Graduates hired directly into consulting firms start as analysts and typically advance after two to three years.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a technology consultant?

No certification is legally required. Many employers still prefer or ask for credentials tied to the systems you work on, such as AWS or Microsoft Azure cloud certifications, Salesforce certifications, ITIL, or the PMP from PMI. They show you know a platform or method, but real project experience usually matters more.
How long does it take to become a technology consultant?

Most people need about four years for a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information systems or business, plus two to five years of experience in roles like business analyst, systems analyst or developer. Some graduates join consulting firms right away as analysts and earn the consultant title within two to three years.

steps: Education

Most telecommunications engineers hold a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering or telecommunications engineering. Key subjects are signals and systems, electromagnetics, digital communications, networking and RF design. Some technicians move up through associate degrees and experience.
Technical skills

Learn radio frequency planning, propagation, antennas and spectrum, plus IP networking, routing and the mobile network core. Knowledge of LTE and 5G standards from 3GPP, fiber optics and test equipment is expected. Scripting in Python helps automate network work.
Licenses

Most telecom engineers need no license. Technicians who repair some aviation and maritime radio transmitters need an FCC General Radiotelephone Operator License (GROL). Engineers who sign and seal designs for public projects may need a state Professional Engineer (PE) license, earned through the FE exam, experience and the PE exam.
First job

Common first jobs are RF engineer, drive test engineer, field engineer, network operations center engineer or junior network engineer at a mobile carrier, equipment vendor or engineering contractor. Some start as tower or field technicians and move into engineering with a degree.
Time it takes

Expect four years for an engineering degree. Moving from junior to senior telecom engineer usually takes about five or more years. A PE license, where needed, usually requires about four years of qualifying experience after the degree plus two exams.
qa: Do you need a license to be a telecommunications engineer?

Usually not. Most telecom engineers work without a license. Engineers who sign and seal designs for public projects may need a state Professional Engineer (PE) license, and technicians who repair some aviation or maritime radio transmitters need an FCC General Radiotelephone Operator License (GROL). Requirements vary by state and job.
How long does it take to become a telecommunications engineer?

Usually about four years, the time it takes to earn a bachelor’s degree in electrical, computer or telecommunications engineering. Many graduates then start as RF, field or network engineers at carriers or equipment vendors. Reaching a senior role typically takes five or more years, and earning a PE license, where needed, takes about four years of experience.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in business, marketing, communications or a related field. Some hire people with only a high school diploma and a strong sales record. Technical products such as medical devices, industrial equipment or farm supplies often favor a degree or background in a matching field.
First sales job

Most people start as an inside sales representative, a sales development representative or an outside sales representative. These roles teach prospecting, cold calling, working in a CRM and closing deals. Others move in from customer service, retail management or a technical role in the same industry.
Licenses and driving record

Territory sales itself has no license. Some products do. Selling insurance requires a state insurance producer license, and selling securities requires FINRA exams such as the SIE and Series 7. Because the job means daily travel, employers almost always require a valid driver’s license and a clean driving record.
Track record

Employers hire territory managers on proof of results. Keep a record of quotas you met, new accounts you won and revenue you grew. Voluntary sales certifications exist, but most hiring managers weigh your numbers and industry contacts more heavily than any certificate.
Time it takes

It usually takes two to five years of sales experience after school. Some companies promote strong outside reps to territory manager within a year or two. Others hire experienced sellers from competitors who already know the area’s customers.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a territory sales manager?

Not always. Many employers list a bachelor’s degree in business or marketing, but a proven record of meeting sales quotas often counts for more. People without a degree usually get in through inside sales or retail sales, then move to outside sales and a territory once they show steady results.
How long does it take to become a territory sales manager?

Usually two to five years after school. Most people first spend time in inside sales or as an outside sales representative, learning to find customers and close deals. Strong performers can be given their own territory sooner, especially in industries where they already know the products and the local buyers.

steps: Education

Most employers want a bachelor’s degree in electrical, mechanical, aerospace or computer engineering. A degree in engineering technology also works for many test roles. Useful courses include circuits, materials, vibration, heat transfer, statistics and data acquisition.
Hands-on experience

Internships, co-ops and student projects matter a lot. Employers look for time spent wiring sensors, running test rigs, using oscilloscopes and thermal chambers, writing test scripts and turning raw data into clear reports.
Licenses and certifications

No state license is required for this work. Some engineers take the FE exam early on. Later, the ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer (CRE) or Certified Quality Engineer (CQE) can help. Defense and aerospace jobs often expect familiarity with MIL-STD-810 environmental test methods.
First job

Many people start as a test technician, lab technician or junior test engineer. They run test procedures written by others, set up fixtures, log results and flag failures before they write their own test plans.
Time it takes
Expect about four years for the degree. After that, it usually takes two to five years of lab work to plan full validation programs on your own, covering thermal, vibration, shock and life testing.
qa: Do you need a license to be a test engineer?

No. Hardware test and validation engineers do not need a state license. A PE license is rarely asked for in this field. Employers care more about an engineering degree, lab experience and knowledge of test standards.
