Optional certifications such as the ASQ Certified Reliability Engineer can strengthen a resume later in a career.
Can you become a test engineer without an engineering degree?

Sometimes. Some people start as test or electronics technicians with an associate degree or military training. They learn test equipment on the job and move up to engineer over several years. Many employers still prefer a bachelor’s degree for engineer titles, especially in aerospace, defense and medical devices.

steps: Bachelor’s degree

Most thermal and fluids engineers earn a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering, usually from an ABET-accredited program. Aerospace or chemical engineering also works. Core courses include thermodynamics, heat transfer and fluid mechanics. The degree usually takes four years.
Internships and co-ops

Students often complete internships or co-op terms in product design, testing, HVAC or energy systems. This is where many first learn thermal and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation tools, run lab tests and build the hands-on record employers look for.
FE exam

Many graduates take the Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) exam from NCEES near the end of school or soon after. Passing earns Engineer in Training or Engineer Intern status in most states. It is the first step toward a PE license.
First job

The usual way in is an entry-level mechanical engineer, test engineer or junior thermal analyst role. Typical work includes cooling electronics, sizing pumps and heat exchangers, running simulations and checking designs against test data under a senior engineer.
PE license if needed

A Professional Engineer (PE) license is optional for most industry roles. It is needed to sign off on public work such as building systems. Most states require about four years of supervised experience and passing the NCEES PE Mechanical exam, often the Thermal and Fluid Systems version. Rules vary by state.
Advanced study

Some engineers earn a master’s degree in mechanical engineering, focused on heat transfer or fluid dynamics. It is common for advanced simulation, research and aerospace roles. Many people complete it part time while working, usually in one to three years.
qa: Do you need a license to be a thermal engineer?

Usually not. Most thermal engineers work for manufacturers under an industrial exemption, so no PE license is required. A Professional Engineer license is needed if you approve designs for the public, such as building heating and cooling systems. Requirements vary by state. They usually include passing the FE exam, about four years of experience and the PE exam.
How long does it take to become a thermal engineer?

Most people need about four years to earn a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering and can start in an entry-level role right after. Becoming a fully independent thermal engineer usually takes another two to four years on the job. Earning a PE license or a master’s degree adds more time.

steps: Education

Most analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in cybersecurity, computer science, information technology or intelligence studies. Some come from political science or international relations, which helps with tracking nation-state groups. Employers care more about skills than the exact major, but a degree is commonly listed.
Core technical skills

Learn networking, operating systems, log analysis and how malware and phishing campaigns work. Study frameworks analysts use every day, such as MITRE ATT&CK, the Diamond Model and the Cyber Kill Chain. Practice writing short, clear reports, because warning others is the heart of the job.
Certifications

No license is required. Many people start with CompTIA Security+ or CompTIA CySA+. Threat-focused options include GIAC Cyber Threat Intelligence (GCTI) and EC-Council’s Certified Threat Intelligence Analyst (CTIA). These are optional, but they help when you lack direct experience.
First job

The usual way in is a security operations center (SOC) analyst or incident response role, where you triage alerts and learn real attacker behavior. Others enter through military or government intelligence work. Government and contractor roles often require a security clearance, which the employer sponsors.
Time it takes

Few people are hired straight into threat intelligence. Expect a degree or equivalent study, then usually two to five years in security operations, incident response or intelligence before moving into a dedicated threat intelligence analyst role.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a threat intelligence analyst?

No license or certification is legally required. Many employers still like to see CompTIA Security+ or CySA+, and threat-specific credentials such as GIAC Cyber Threat Intelligence (GCTI) can set you apart. Hands-on experience in a SOC or incident response role, plus clear written reports, usually matters more than any single certificate.
Can you become a threat intelligence analyst without a degree?

Yes, it is possible, though many postings list a bachelor’s degree. People without one usually get in through IT support or SOC analyst jobs, military intelligence service, or strong certifications and a portfolio of public research, such as write-ups on malware or phishing campaigns. Experience tracking real threats is what employers weigh most.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, manufacturing or plastics engineering. Courses in materials, machining, heat transfer and CAD matter most. Some people instead earn a two-year degree in tool and die or mold technology and move up from the shop floor.
Shop floor or apprenticeship

Many strong tooling engineers first worked as toolmakers or moldmakers. A registered tool and die or moldmaker apprenticeship usually takes about four years of paid on-the-job training plus classroom hours. Engineering graduates gain similar knowledge through co-ops and time spent beside machinists and press operators.
Design skills

You need to model molds, dies and fixtures in 3D CAD, read and apply GD&T, and understand how parts shrink, cool and eject. Learning mold flow simulation and progressive die layout makes you far more useful in your first role.
Licenses and certifications

No license is required for this work. Optional credentials can help, such as the SME Certified Manufacturing Engineer (CMfgE), the ASME GD&T Professional certification, or NIMS credentials for those coming from the trades. A PE license is rarely needed.
First job

Graduates often start as junior tooling engineers, manufacturing or process engineers, or mold designers. Former toolmakers often move into tool design or tooling engineer roles at the shop where they trained.
Time it takes
Expect four years for a degree or apprenticeship, then usually two to five more years before you design complex molds or dies on your own and lead tool builds with outside shops.
qa: Do you need a license to be a tooling engineer?

No. Tooling and molding engineers in the US do not need a state license. Most employers want an engineering degree or years of toolmaking experience. Optional certifications, such as the SME Certified Manufacturing Engineer (CMfgE) or the ASME GD&T Professional, can strengthen a resume but are not required.
Can a toolmaker become a tooling engineer without a degree?

Yes, many do. Experienced tool and die makers or moldmakers who learn CAD and design principles often move into tool design and tooling engineer roles. Some employers still prefer a degree for engineering titles, so some toolmakers take part-time engineering or technology courses while working.

steps: Education

Most firms hire traders with a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, mathematics, statistics, computer science or engineering. Quantitative trading roles often prefer a master’s or PhD in a math-heavy field. Programming skills, especially Python, are increasingly expected, along with strong probability and statistics.
Internships

Summer internships, usually after the junior year of college, are the main route into trading at banks and trading firms. Many full-time offers come from these programs. Interviews often test mental math, probability puzzles, market knowledge and how you make decisions under pressure.
FINRA exams

Traders at broker-dealers usually pass the SIE exam plus the Series 57, and some roles also need the Series 7 or Series 63. The firm must sponsor you for the representative-level exams, so most people take them in their first months on the job.
Futures and commodities

People who handle customer business in futures or commodities usually need the Series 3, which is required for NFA registration. Some trading roles, such as certain buy-side or proprietary positions, need no license at all. Requirements depend on the firm and what is traded.
First job

The usual first job is trading assistant, junior trader or trading analyst on a desk, working under senior traders. You start by booking trades, managing positions and building models. Some people move onto a desk from risk, operations or research roles.
Time it takes

Expect a four-year degree, then often one to three years as a junior before you manage your own book or trading limits. Quantitative traders with graduate degrees may take longer to start but can move faster once hired.
qa: Do you need a license to be a trader?

It depends on the role. Traders at broker-dealers usually must pass the SIE and the Series 57, with firm sponsorship, and some also need the Series 7 or Series 63. Futures traders handling customer business usually need the Series 3. Some buy-side and proprietary trading roles require no license.
How long does it take to become a trader?

Most traders finish a four-year degree in finance, economics, math or a related field, then join a desk as a trading assistant or junior trader. Licensing exams are usually done in the first months. It often takes one to three more years before a trader runs their own positions.

steps: Education

Most people earn a bachelor’s degree in computer science, computer engineering, electrical engineering, or math. Coursework in operating systems, computer networks, data structures, and computer architecture matters most. A master’s degree helps some candidates but is not required by most employers.
Low-latency skills

Employers look for strong C++ (sometimes Java or Rust), Linux, multithreading, and networking down to TCP, UDP, and multicast. Learning how exchanges work, including order books, matching rules, and protocols like FIX, sets candidates apart. Personal projects such as a simple matching engine show this skill well.
Internship

Many trading firms, exchanges, and banks hire through summer software engineering internships, often aimed at juniors. Interviews are hard and focus on algorithms, systems design, and sometimes math or probability puzzles. A strong internship often leads to a full-time offer.
FINRA registration if required

There is no license for this work in general. At broker-dealers that are FINRA members, engineers primarily responsible for designing or significantly changing algorithmic trading strategies must register as Securities Traders, which means passing the SIE and Series 57 exams. The firm sponsors this after hiring.
First job

The usual first job is a new-graduate software engineer on a trading, market data, or exchange connectivity team. Others start in general backend or systems roles elsewhere and move into trading after building low-latency or high-performance experience.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree, often with one or two internships along the way. Working on the most latency-critical parts of a trading stack, like order gateways or matching engines, usually takes another two to five years of hands-on experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be a trading systems engineer?

Usually not. Most trading systems engineers need no license or certification. The main exception is at FINRA member broker-dealers, where engineers primarily responsible for designing or significantly modifying algorithmic trading strategies must register as Securities Traders by passing the SIE and Series 57 exams. Employers typically sponsor this after hiring, so you don’t need it to apply.
How long does it take to become a trading systems engineer?

Most people need a four-year degree in computer science or a related field, then join a trading firm, exchange, or bank as a new-graduate software engineer. Some get there directly through internships. Others spend two to five years in systems or backend roles first. Owning core low-latency components usually takes several years of experience.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree. Common fields are education, human resources, business, communications and organizational psychology. Technical and product trainers are sometimes hired on strong job experience alone, without a related degree.
Know the work firsthand

Many trainers first do the work they later teach, such as sales, customer support, software, health care or manufacturing. Volunteering to onboard new hires, write how-to guides or lead team sessions builds a teaching track record before you change roles.
Learn course design

Study how adults learn and how courses are built, including models like ADDIE and common e-learning authoring tools. Short courses or a certificate in instructional design help. Keep a portfolio of sample lesson plans, slide decks, job aids and short e-learning modules.
Optional certification

No license is required to train employees or customers. Some trainers earn the APTD or, with more experience, the CPTD from the Association for Talent Development. Product trainers may need the vendor’s own certification in the product they teach.
First job

Common ways in are training coordinator, training assistant, onboarding specialist or a part-time peer trainer on your current team. Moving into a training role inside the company where you already work is one of the most common paths.
Time it takes

There is no set timeline. Many people spend a four-year degree plus a few years working in their field before becoming a full-time trainer. Moving up to senior trainer or training manager usually takes several more years.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a corporate trainer?

No. There is no state license or required certification for corporate or product trainers. Some choose the APTD or CPTD from the Association for Talent Development to show their skills. Software and equipment trainers may need the vendor’s own certification. Most employers care more about job experience, presentation skills and sample courses you have built.
How long does it take to become a trainer?

It usually takes a bachelor’s degree plus a few years of experience in the field you will teach. Some people move into training sooner by taking on onboarding or coaching duties in their current job. Others start as a training coordinator and grow into a full trainer role over one to three years.

steps: Education

Most travel coordinator jobs ask for a high school diploma, and many prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree in hospitality, tourism, business or a related field. Classes in geography, a foreign language and customer service are useful.
First job

Many people start as an administrative assistant who books travel for a team, a travel agent, or a reservations agent at an airline, hotel or travel management firm. These jobs teach booking systems, fare rules and handling last-minute changes.
Booking skills

Coordinators learn global distribution systems and online booking tools, airline fare rules, hotel contracts, passport and visa requirements, and company travel policy. Most of this is learned on the job within several months, along with duty of care for travelers abroad.
Certification

No license is needed to coordinate travel for your own employer. Optional credentials include the GTP (Global Travel Professional) from the Global Business Travel Association and the CTA (Certified Travel Associate) from The Travel Institute. They show knowledge of travel programs and booking.
Seller of travel rules

If you sell travel to the public rather than book for an employer, a few states, including California, Florida, Hawaii and Washington, require sellers of travel to register with the state. In-house corporate travel staff usually fall outside these rules.
Time it takes

You can often start as a junior travel coordinator within a few months, especially with booking or office experience. Moving up to travel manager, who runs the travel program and negotiates with airlines and hotels, usually takes five or more years.
qa: Do you need a license to be a travel coordinator?

No license is needed to book travel for your own employer. A few states, including California, Florida, Hawaii and Washington, require businesses that sell travel to the public to register as sellers of travel. Optional credentials such as the GTP from the Global Business Travel Association can help you stand out, but they are not required.
Can you become a travel coordinator without experience?

Yes, many people do. Administrative assistants who book trips for their team often move into travel coordinator roles. Others start as reservations agents or travel agents. Strong organization, attention to detail and calm problem solving matter most, and employers usually train new coordinators on their booking tools and travel policy.

steps: Education

Most treasury analysts hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting or economics. Courses in corporate finance, financial markets, accounting and statistics help most. Strong Excel skills matter, and some employers also look for experience with SQL or a treasury management system.
Internship or related experience

An internship in corporate finance, accounting or a bank’s cash management area gives you practice with bank reconciliations, cash forecasting and payments. Employers often prefer candidates who have already handled real cash or banking data.
First job

Many people start as a cash analyst, staff accountant, financial analyst or treasury associate. Others come from commercial banking roles in treasury services. From there they move into a treasury analyst job covering cash positioning, forecasting, bank relationships and foreign exchange or interest rate exposure.
No license required

No state license or required exam applies to corporate treasury work. Hiring is based on your degree, skills and experience. Some roles that involve trading or giving investment advice at a financial firm can bring separate registration rules, but a typical company treasury job does not.
Certification

The Certified Treasury Professional (CTP) credential from the Association for Financial Professionals (AFP) is the best-known certification in the field. It requires relevant work experience and a passing score on an exam. Some analysts also pursue the CFA later. Neither is required to get hired, but both help with advancement.
Time it takes

Expect about four years for a bachelor’s degree. Many people then spend one to three years in an accounting, finance or banking role before landing a treasury analyst position. Earning the CTP usually comes a few years into the career.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a treasury analyst?

No. Corporate treasury work has no license or required exam, and many analysts are hired with just a finance or accounting degree. The Certified Treasury Professional (CTP) credential from the Association for Financial Professionals is valued by employers and can help you move up. It requires work experience first, so most people earn it after a few years on the job.
How long does it take to become a treasury analyst?

It usually takes about four to six years. That includes a four-year bachelor’s degree in finance, accounting or economics. Some graduates are hired straight into treasury, but many first work one to three years as a staff accountant, financial analyst or bank cash management associate before moving into a treasury analyst role.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree, though no specific major is required. Common fields include communications, psychology, criminal justice, political science, public policy and law. Fluency in a second language or deep knowledge of a region or online community is a real advantage for review work.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for trust and safety work in the US. No single certification is standard either. Some people take short courses or join professional groups such as the Trust & Safety Professional Association to learn the field’s vocabulary and meet people already working in it.
First job

The usual way in is a content moderator or content reviewer role, often a contract job with an outsourcing vendor that reviews content for a platform. Others come in from customer support, fraud or risk analysis, investigations, or policy research roles where they already handle abuse reports.
On-the-job training

New hires learn the platform’s community guidelines, how to escalate threats, and legal duties such as reporting child sexual abuse material to NCMEC. Training also covers appeals, consistent decision making, and wellness practices, since the work means regular exposure to disturbing content.
Time it takes

Most people spend about one to three years in moderation, support or investigations before moving into a trust and safety specialist role. Specialists who later write policy or lead enforcement programs usually have several more years of experience behind them.
Building toward specialist

To move up, build a record of accurate decisions and handling complex escalations. Basic data skills such as spreadsheets or SQL help with spotting abuse patterns. Clear writing matters, because specialists draft policy language, explain enforcement decisions and respond to user appeals.
qa: Do you need a degree to work in trust and safety?

Many entry-level content moderator jobs ask only for a high school diploma, good judgment and strong reading skills. Specialist, policy and analyst roles usually ask for a bachelor’s degree, often in communications, psychology, criminal justice, policy or law. Relevant moderation or investigations experience can sometimes count in place of a specific degree.
How long does it take to become a trust and safety specialist?

It usually takes one to three years after starting in a related role. Most specialists begin as content moderators, support agents or fraud analysts, learn platform policies and escalation work, then move into specialist roles. There is no license or exam to pass, so the timeline depends mainly on experience and performance.

steps: Education

Most UI designers hold a bachelor’s degree in graphic design, visual communication, interaction design or a related field. A degree is common but not required. Some people enter through short courses or self-study, learning typography, color, layout, grids and visual hierarchy on their own.
Design tools and skills

Employers expect fluency in interface design tools such as Figma, plus working knowledge of design systems, components, icon design, accessibility basics and responsive layouts for web and mobile. Knowing how HTML and CSS work helps you hand off designs that developers can build.
Portfolio

The portfolio is what gets you hired. Build three to five case studies that show real screens, the problem, your choices on type, color and spacing, and how the design changed. Redesigns, freelance work, volunteer projects and class work all count if they look polished.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for UI designers in the US. Certificates from courses can show effort, but employers judge you mainly on your portfolio, your eye for detail and how you explain your design decisions.
Time it takes

Through a degree, it usually takes about four years to be ready for an entry role. Career changers with a related background often build enough skill and portfolio work in one to two years of focused practice.
First job

Common first roles are junior UI designer, junior visual designer, production designer or design intern. Many people also start as graphic or web designers and move toward interface work by taking on app and website screens.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a UI designer?

No. Many UI designers have a degree in graphic design or a related field, and some employers list one, but it is not legally required. Plenty of people get hired through self-study or short courses. What matters most is a strong portfolio showing polished interface work and clear reasoning behind your design choices.
How long does it take to become a UI designer?

It usually takes one to four years. A bachelor’s degree in design takes about four years. People who already have visual or graphic design skills can often build a job-ready portfolio in one to two years of steady practice. Your first junior role then adds the real product experience employers look for.

steps: Education

Most employers want a bachelor’s degree in business, finance, economics, accounting, math or a related field. Some mortgage and small commercial underwriting roles accept an associate degree or a high school diploma plus experience in lending or insurance operations.
First job

Many people start as an underwriting assistant, an underwriter trainee or, in lending, a loan processor. These roles teach how a file is built, which documents matter and how guidelines are applied before you make decisions on your own.
On-the-job training

Insurers and lenders usually train new underwriters in-house. You work under a senior underwriter who reviews your decisions. Your authority to approve larger or riskier cases grows as you show sound judgment.
No license usually required

Insurance underwriters generally do not need a state license, unlike agents and adjusters. Mortgage underwriters usually do not need an NMLS license, which applies to loan originators. Rules and employer policies vary by state, so check before you apply.
Professional designations

Many employers expect or pay for designations. Common ones are the CPCU and AU from The Institutes for property and casualty work, and the FLMI from LOMA for life insurance. You earn them by passing a series of exams while working.
Time it takes

Usually four years for a degree, then one to three years as a trainee or assistant before you handle your own accounts with real authority. Senior underwriter roles often take five or more years of experience.
qa: Do you need a license to be an underwriter?

In most cases, no. Insurance underwriters in the US generally do not need a state license, and mortgage underwriters usually fall outside NMLS loan originator licensing. Employers often value designations such as the CPCU or AU instead. Rules can vary by state and employer, so check the requirements for the job you want.
How long does it take to become an underwriter?

Most people spend about four years earning a bachelor’s degree, then one to three years as a trainee or assistant before underwriting on their own. Earning a designation like the CPCU while working often takes a few more years. Moving over from a related job, such as loan processor, can shorten the path.

steps: Education

Most employers ask for a bachelor’s degree. Common fields are human resources, business, communications and psychology, but the major matters less than showing you can plan events, write clearly and talk easily with students. Campus jobs in career services, admissions or student groups give useful early experience.
First job

Most people start as a recruiting coordinator, HR assistant or agency recruiter. These roles teach interview scheduling, resume screening, applicant tracking systems and working with hiring managers. Some move over from university career services or admissions offices, where they already know how campuses and student schedules work.
No license required

No license, registration or exam is required to work as a university recruiter in any state. Employers hire based on recruiting experience, organization, event planning and comfort working with students, faculty and campus career staff.
Optional certifications

Some recruiters earn the SHRM-CP from SHRM or the PHR from HRCI to show broad HR knowledge. Both are voluntary, and the PHR requires prior HR experience. Many campus recruiters also join NACE, the National Association of Colleges and Employers, for training and recruiting standards.
Time it takes

After a four-year degree, people often spend one to three years in coordinator or general recruiting work before moving into a dedicated campus role. Large employers run the biggest internship and graduate programs, so most university recruiter jobs are found there.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a university recruiter?

No. There is no required license or certification for university recruiting in the US. Some recruiters choose the SHRM-CP or PHR to show general HR knowledge, and many join NACE for training. Employers care most about recruiting experience, organization skills and the ability to connect with students and campus career offices.
How long does it take to become a university recruiter?

Most people need a bachelor’s degree, which usually takes four years, plus one to three years of experience as a recruiting coordinator, HR assistant or general recruiter. Some people who worked in university career services or admissions move into campus recruiting faster because they already understand how colleges and student hiring cycles work.

steps: Education

No single degree is required. Many UX designers study human-computer interaction, interaction design, graphic design, psychology or computer science. Others come from unrelated fields and learn through short courses, online classes or self-study. Employers care more about what you can show than which degree you hold.
Core skills and tools

Learn user research, wireframing, prototyping, information architecture and usability testing. Get comfortable in a common design and prototyping tool, and learn the basics of accessibility standards and how developers build interfaces. Practice by interviewing real people and testing your designs with them.
Portfolio of case studies

A portfolio is the main thing hiring managers review. Build three to five case studies that show the problem, your research, sketches, iterations, testing with users and the result. Redesigns of real apps, volunteer projects for nonprofits and freelance work for small businesses all count.
License or certification

There is no license, state registration or required exam for UX design in the US. Private certificates exist, but they are optional and rarely a hiring requirement. A strong portfolio and the ability to explain your design decisions matter far more.
Time it takes

A four-year degree is one route. Career changers who already have related skills often build a job-ready portfolio in about six months to two years of steady practice. Getting the first role can take extra time, since entry-level openings are competitive.
First job

Common first roles are UX design intern, junior UX designer, junior product designer or UX research assistant. Many people also move in sideways from graphic design, front-end development, customer support or marketing by taking on UX work inside their current company.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a UX designer?

No. Many UX designers have degrees in design, psychology or computer science, but no degree is legally required. Some employers list a bachelor’s degree in postings, yet most hiring decisions rest on your portfolio. Clear case studies that show research, testing with users and thoughtful design choices can open doors without a related degree.
How long does it take to become a UX designer?

It usually takes six months to two years for someone changing careers to learn the skills and build a portfolio, depending on time spent and prior experience. A related four-year degree is another path. Landing the first job may take longer, so many people start with internships, freelance projects or UX tasks in their current role.

steps: Education

Most people start with a bachelor’s degree in psychology, anthropology, sociology, human-computer interaction, marketing or a related field. Courses in research methods, statistics and interviewing matter most. Many in-house and senior roles prefer a master’s or PhD in HCI, human factors or a social science, though it is not always required.
Learn the methods

Practice user interviews, usability testing, surveys, field observation and card sorting. Learn to recruit participants, write a screener and discussion guide, get informed consent, and turn notes into clear findings. Class projects, volunteer work for nonprofits and studies of real apps or websites all give useful practice.
Build a portfolio

Employers judge you mostly on case studies. Each one should show the question you asked, the method you chose and why, who took part, what you found, and what changed in the product. Remove names and any confidential details so participants and clients stay protected.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for UX or market research in any US state. Optional certificates in UX or market research exist, and some employers mention them, but hiring usually rests on your methods, your portfolio and how clearly you present findings.
First job

Common entry roles are research assistant, research coordinator, usability test moderator, market research analyst and junior UX researcher. Many people also move over from UX design, product support, customer service, data analysis or academic research labs, bringing domain knowledge that teams value.
Time it takes

A bachelor’s degree usually takes four years, and a master’s adds one to two more. Career changers with a related background often need six months to two years of study and portfolio projects before landing a first research role.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a UX researcher?

Most UX researchers have at least a bachelor’s degree, often in psychology, anthropology, sociology, HCI or marketing. Many employers prefer a master’s for in-house research roles. Still, people without a related degree do get in by learning research methods, building a strong portfolio of case studies, and starting in a nearby role such as research coordinator or analyst.
Do you need a license or certification to be a UX researcher?

No. No US state requires a license, registration or exam to work as a UX or market researcher. Some optional certificates exist, and a few employers list them as a plus. Hiring managers mostly look for solid research methods, sound ethics with participants, clear writing and a portfolio showing how your findings shaped real products.

steps: Education

Most people hold a bachelor’s degree in business, finance, economics, accounting, engineering or computer science. Coursework in corporate finance, accounting and statistics helps most. An MBA is common among value consultants, especially at larger software companies, but it is rarely required.
Related first job

Few people start in value engineering. Common earlier roles are management consultant, financial analyst, FP&A analyst, sales engineer, solutions consultant, customer success manager or industry specialist. Any job where you built business cases or spoke with customers about results counts.
Core skills

Learn to build clear spreadsheet models of ROI, total cost of ownership, payback period and net present value. Practice customer discovery, turning operational data into dollar figures and presenting a business case to finance leaders. Deep knowledge of one industry, such as manufacturing, healthcare or IT, makes your numbers more credible.
No license required

There is no license, registration or required exam for this work in the US. Employers judge you on sample business cases and modeling skill. Note that the Certified Value Specialist (CVS) from SAVE International belongs to a different field, construction and design value engineering, not sales.
Time it takes

Expect a four-year degree plus usually two to five years in a related role before landing a dedicated value position. People already inside a software company, such as sales engineers or analysts, can often move over sooner.
First value job

The usual entry point is a value consultant, value analyst or business value associate role on a software vendor’s value engineering team. You build ROI models and business cases that support account executives on new deals and renewals.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a value engineer in software sales?

No. There is no license or required certification for value engineers who support sales. Employers look for strong financial modeling, business acumen and customer-facing experience. Some people take financial modeling or value selling courses, but a portfolio of real business cases and ROI models matters far more than any certificate.
How do you get into value engineering without experience?

Most people enter from a related job rather than straight from school. Roles in consulting, financial analysis, sales engineering, solutions consulting or customer success build the right skills. Inside a software company, volunteering to build ROI models for sales deals is a common way to move into a value consultant role.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. Many editors study film, video production, communications or journalism at a college or community college. Others learn on their own through online courses and practice. What employers check most is whether you can shoot, cut and finish clean, well-paced video.
Software skills

Learn at least one major editing program, such as Adobe Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, Final Cut Pro or Avid Media Composer. Add basic color correction, audio mixing and motion graphics. Optional credentials like Adobe Certified Professional or Avid Certified User can help, but no certification is required.
Build a portfolio

Make a short demo reel and an online portfolio of your best work. Include different formats, such as social clips, interviews, promos and a longer story piece. Personal projects, volunteer work for nonprofits and class assignments all count if they look professional.
Drone license if needed

No license is needed to shoot or edit video. If you fly a drone for paid work, the FAA requires a Remote Pilot Certificate under Part 107, which means passing a knowledge test. Shooting on public or private property may also need location permits or releases.
First job

Most people start as a production assistant, assistant editor, logger or junior video producer at a marketing agency, news station or production company. Freelancing on small social media and event projects is another common entry. Assistant editors learn workflows, media management and how to take notes from directors.
Time it takes

Expect about two to four years of study or self-directed practice before steady paid work. Moving from assistant to lead editor or producer usually takes a few more years. Film and TV editors may later join the Motion Picture Editors Guild once they work on union productions.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a video editor?

No. A degree in film, communications or media production helps you learn the craft and make contacts, but it is not required. Many working editors are self-taught. Employers mostly hire based on a demo reel, a portfolio of finished projects and skill with editing software like Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve or Avid Media Composer.
How long does it take to become a video editor?

Most people need about two to four years of training and practice to get steady paid work, whether through a degree or self-study. Many start as production assistants, assistant editors or freelancers on small projects. Reaching lead editor or producer roles on larger projects usually takes several more years of experience.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. Many motion designers study graphic design, animation, film or digital media at a college or community college. Others learn on their own through online courses and practice, which employers often accept if the work is strong.
Software skills

Learn the tools employers name most: Adobe After Effects for animation, Premiere Pro or a similar editor for cutting video, and often Cinema 4D or Blender for 3D. Basic camera, lighting and audio skills help when the job includes filming.
Certification

No license or exam is required to work as a motion designer in the US. Some people take the Adobe Certified Professional exams to show software skill, but employers rarely require them and judge mostly on your reel.
Demo reel and portfolio

Build a short demo reel of your best motion work, usually one to two minutes, plus a portfolio site with full projects. Include marketing spots, explainer or training videos and social clips that show both animation and editing.
First job

Common entry points are junior motion designer, video editor, production assistant or in-house content creator at a marketing team or agency. Freelance gigs and internships also help you build client work and references.
Time it takes

Most people need about two to four years of study and practice to land a first paid role. Reaching a mid-level motion designer position usually takes a few more years of steady client or in-house work.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a motion designer?

No. Many motion designers hold degrees in graphic design, animation or film, but employers mostly hire based on your demo reel and portfolio. Self-taught designers who show strong animation, editing and design work can get hired, especially at agencies, startups and in-house marketing teams.
How long does it take to become a motion designer?

It usually takes two to four years to build the skills and reel needed for a first job, whether through a degree or self-study. Learning After Effects and a video editor well, then producing several finished projects, is what most people need before applying for junior roles.

steps: Education

Most employers expect a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, business or a related field. Courses in markets, trading and accounting help. No single degree is required, and some people at crypto exchanges come in from trading or tech backgrounds instead.
First job

Most people start in client services, account management, sales support or a junior analyst role at a bank, broker-dealer, exchange or trading firm. There you learn the products, client onboarding, KYC and compliance checks, and how large clients trade.
Exams if required

If the role involves securities business at a FINRA member broker-dealer, you usually pass the SIE exam and the Series 7, which needs sponsorship by a member firm. Many states also require the NASAA Series 63 or Series 66. Many crypto exchange roles need no exam. It depends on the firm and the products.
Build a client record

Next you take on larger accounts and show you can keep and grow them. Employers look for knowledge of market structure, liquidity, fees, trading platforms and APIs, plus the ability to handle urgent issues for funds, firms and very active traders.
Time it takes

There is no fixed timeline. Many people reach a VIP or institutional coverage role after several years in client-facing finance or trading jobs. Promotion depends on your track record, your network and the needs of the firm.
qa: Do you need a license to be an institutional relationship manager?

It depends on the firm. If you handle securities business at a FINRA member broker-dealer, you usually need to pass the SIE exam and the Series 7, and many states also require the Series 63 or 66. Many crypto exchange and some bank roles need no license. Check each job posting for what the employer expects.
How long does it take to become a VIP relationship manager?

Most people first earn a bachelor’s degree, then spend several years in client services, account management or sales support before covering the biggest clients. The timeline is not fixed. It depends on how quickly you build a record of keeping and growing accounts and on openings at your firm.

steps: Education

There is no license for visual merchandising or merchandise planning. Visual merchandisers often study visual merchandising, fashion merchandising, interior design or art, though many learn on the job. Buyers and planners usually have a bachelor’s degree in fashion merchandising, business, marketing or retail management.
Retail experience

Most people start on the sales floor as a retail sales associate, stock associate or store visual lead. Store work teaches how customers shop, how stock moves and how displays affect sales, which employers in both visual and buying roles look for.
Portfolio

Visual merchandisers need a portfolio of displays, windows, store layouts or mockups, with photos and sketches. Skills in planograms, basic design software and lighting help. Buyers and planners instead show skill with Excel, sales data and inventory planning.
First job

Common first jobs are visual merchandising associate, display assistant, merchandising assistant, assistant buyer or allocation analyst. Many retailers run training programs for new graduates that rotate through buying, planning and allocation.
Time it takes

Visual merchandising roles can open after one to two years of retail experience. Becoming a visual manager or buyer usually takes three to five years or more. Senior merchant and merchandising director roles follow many years of results.
qa: Can you become a visual merchandiser without experience?

Usually not directly, but the first step is easy to take. Most visual merchandisers start as retail sales or stock associates and help with displays, then move to a visual lead or associate role. A portfolio of photos of windows, displays or styling work, even from school projects, helps you get noticed.
How long does it take to become a buyer?

Usually three to five years or more. Most buyers start as merchandising assistants, allocation analysts or assistant buyers after a bachelor’s degree, often through a retail training program. They then move to associate buyer and buyer as they show results with sales data, vendors and inventory. There is no license or required certification.

steps: Education

Most directors and VPs of engineering hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, software engineering or a related field. Some enter through self-study or a bootcamp. A master’s degree or MBA is optional and rarely required, though some leaders add one later.
Years as an engineer

Nearly everyone starts as a software engineer. They spend several years designing, building and running production systems, often reaching senior or staff level. Credibility on technical decisions comes from this hands-on work.
First management role

The usual first step into leadership is engineering manager or team lead. You run one team, hire engineers, give feedback, handle performance reviews and plan delivery with product partners. Many people move into this role from inside their own team.
Managing managers

Next comes senior engineering manager or director. You lead several teams through their managers, set technical direction, own budgets and headcount, and shape how the organization builds and ships. A strong record here is what qualifies people for VP roles.
No license required

There is no license, state registration or required exam for this work. Some leaders take management training or earn cloud or security certifications, but employers mainly judge a track record of growing teams, delivering products and hiring well.
Time it takes

Reaching director usually takes about 8 to 12 years from the first engineering job. VP of engineering often takes 12 to 15 years or more. At startups, people may reach these titles faster, with smaller teams.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a VP of engineering?

A degree is not legally required, and there is no license for the role. Most VPs of engineering do hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science or a related field. What matters most is years of engineering experience followed by a record of managing teams and managers successfully.
How long does it take to become a director of engineering?

It usually takes about 8 to 12 years. Most people spend several years as software engineers, then two to four years as engineering managers before leading multiple teams. At small or fast-growing companies the path can be shorter, while large companies often expect more experience at each level.

steps: Education

Most VPs of sales hold a bachelor’s degree, often in business, marketing, communications or economics, though many employers accept any field. An MBA is common at larger companies but rarely required. No degree replaces a proven record of hitting quota.
First sales job

Most start as a sales development representative (SDR) or business development representative (BDR), prospecting and booking meetings for account executives. Others start in inside sales, retail sales or customer success. Strong performers usually move up to account executive within one to two years.
Quota-carrying track record

Promotion depends on results. Future leaders usually spend several years as account executives, beating quota, closing larger deals and learning forecasting, pipeline management and CRM tools. Coaching newer reps or serving as a team lead shows you can lead, not just sell.
Sales management

The next step is first-line sales manager, leading a team of reps and owning the team’s number. From there, people move to director or regional director, managing managers, hiring, setting territories and quotas, and reporting forecasts to executives.
Licenses in some fields

There is no general license for sales leaders. Regulated industries differ. Securities sales requires FINRA registration, and supervisors often need a principal exam such as the Series 24. Insurance and real estate sales require state licenses, and requirements vary by state.
Time it takes

Reaching VP of sales often takes about 8 to 15 years from a first sales job. It can be faster at small or fast-growing startups. Many people hold their first VP title at a smaller company before leading sales at a larger one.
qa: Do you need a degree to become a VP of sales?

Not always. Most VPs of sales have a bachelor’s degree, and many job postings list one, but employers care most about a record of hitting revenue targets and building teams. An MBA can help at larger companies. People without degrees do reach VP, usually by rising through the ranks at one company.
How long does it take to become a VP of sales?

It often takes about 8 to 15 years. A typical path runs from SDR or BDR to account executive, then sales manager, director and VP. Startups and fast-growing companies can move strong performers up faster, while large companies usually expect more years leading managers before promoting someone to VP.

steps: Education

Many vulnerability management specialists hold a degree in cybersecurity, computer science or information technology, but experience and certifications often count as much. No license is required. Learn networking, Windows and Linux administration, and how software patches and configuration changes are rolled out.
First job

Most people start in IT support, system administration or a security operations center analyst role. Patching servers or triaging alerts teaches how systems really run, which helps you judge which vulnerabilities matter and how to get them fixed without breaking things.
Core skills

Learn to run vulnerability scanners, read CVE entries and CVSS scores, and use sources such as CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog to set priorities. Scripting in Python or PowerShell, cloud security basics and clear reporting to system owners are expected.
Certifications

Common certifications include CompTIA Security+ for entry level and CompTIA CySA+ for analysts. Defense and federal contractor roles often require specific certifications under DoD 8140 and may need a security clearance. Requirements vary by employer.
Time it takes

With a degree or IT background, expect one to three years in IT or security operations before moving into a dedicated vulnerability management role. Senior roles that run the program for a whole company usually take five or more years.
qa: What certification do you need for vulnerability management?

No certification is legally required, but CompTIA Security+ is a common entry-level requirement, and CompTIA CySA+ fits analyst roles that include vulnerability management. Defense contractor and federal jobs often require certifications under the DoD 8140 framework. Hands-on experience with vulnerability scanners and patching usually matters as much as any certificate.
Can you get into vulnerability management without experience?

Rarely as a first job. Most specialists start in IT support, system administration or a security operations center, where they learn patching, networks and how vulnerabilities are exploited. Building a home lab, scanning your own systems and earning CompTIA Security+ can help you move into a vulnerability analyst role within one to three years.

steps: Basic requirements

No license or degree is needed. Most employers hire people 18 or older, and many prefer a high school diploma or GED but do not always require one. Expect a background check and drug screen at many employers, and be ready to stand, walk and lift for a full shift.
Getting hired

Many people get in through seasonal hiring before the holidays or through a staffing agency that places temporary warehouse workers. Temp and seasonal roles often turn into permanent jobs for reliable workers. Prior work in retail stockrooms, delivery or food service helps but is rarely required.
On-the-job training

Training happens on site and usually lasts a few days to a couple of weeks. New associates learn safety rules, handheld scanners, the warehouse management system, and the site’s standards for receiving, picking, packing and shipping. Most sites then track speed and accuracy against set rates.
Forklift training

OSHA requires employers to train and evaluate anyone who drives a forklift or other powered industrial truck, with re-evaluation at least every three years. This certification is usually given by the employer and may not carry over to a new job. Federal child labor rules bar workers under 18 from operating forklifts.
Time it takes

You can usually start working within days or a few weeks of applying. Getting comfortable with the pace and the systems typically takes a few months. Forklift training can often be completed in a few days once an employer offers it.
First job and next steps

The usual first job is an entry-level picker, packer, loader or receiving associate. With experience, people move into equipment operator, inventory control, shipping clerk, team lead or shift supervisor roles. Some later study logistics or supply chain management to move into planning or management.
qa: Do you need a certification to be a warehouse associate?

No. There is no license or required certification for general warehouse work, and most employers train new hires on the job. The main exception is driving a forklift or similar equipment. OSHA requires employers to train and evaluate operators before they drive, so forklift certification usually comes from the employer rather than an outside class.
Do you need experience to work in a warehouse?

Usually not. Most warehouse associate jobs are entry level, and many employers hire people with no prior experience, especially during seasonal peaks or through staffing agencies. They mainly look for reliability, the ability to handle physical work for a full shift, and a willingness to follow safety rules. Experience mostly matters for equipment operator and lead roles.

steps: Education

Most wealth managers hold a bachelor’s degree in finance, economics, accounting or business, and a bachelor’s degree is also required for CFP certification. Courses in investments, tax, estate planning and insurance give the base that wealthy clients expect.
First job

Common ways in are client service associate, paraplanner, associate advisor or financial advisor trainee at a wealth firm, bank or broker-dealer. These roles prepare plans, handle account paperwork and learn client service under a senior advisor.
Licenses

Advisors who give investment advice usually register as investment adviser representatives, which in most states requires the Series 65, or the Series 66 with the Series 7. Selling securities through a broker-dealer requires the SIE and Series 7. Selling insurance or annuities requires a state insurance license.
CFP certification

The Certified Financial Planner (CFP) certification from CFP Board is the most recognized planning credential. It requires a bachelor’s degree, approved coursework, passing the CFP exam, 6,000 hours of professional experience or 4,000 hours through an apprenticeship, and meeting ethics standards.
Advanced credentials

Wealth managers serving very wealthy families often add the Certified Private Wealth Advisor (CPWA) from the Investments & Wealth Institute or the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) charter. Trust and estate specialists may earn the Certified Trust and Fiduciary Advisor (CTFA).
Time it takes

Securities licenses can be earned within a few months of being hired. The CFP usually takes two to three years to complete because of the experience requirement. Most people work several years as associates before managing their own wealthy clients.
qa: What licenses do you need to be a wealth manager?

Most wealth managers who give investment advice register as investment adviser representatives, which in most states requires the Series 65, or the Series 66 together with the Series 7. Those selling securities through a broker-dealer also need the SIE and Series 7, and selling insurance or annuities requires a state insurance license.
How long does it take to become a Certified Financial Planner?

Often two to three years. You need a bachelor’s degree, CFP Board approved education, a passing score on the CFP exam and 6,000 hours of professional experience, or 4,000 hours through an apprenticeship. Many people finish the coursework in about a year while working, then complete the experience requirement.

steps: Learn the core skills

Start with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the languages every website is built on. Then add a front-end framework, a back-end language such as Python, PHP or JavaScript on Node.js, basic databases, Git for version control, responsive design and web accessibility.
Education or training

Many web developers hold a bachelor’s degree in computer science, information technology or a related field. Others take a two-year associate degree, a coding bootcamp or teach themselves with online courses. Employers usually care more about what you can build than how you learned it.
No license required

There is no state license, registration or required exam for web developers in the US. Optional vendor certifications exist, but most employers do not expect them. Your skills and your work samples do the job a license does in other fields.
Build a portfolio

Put together several working sites or apps you built yourself, with the code on a public repository such as GitHub. Small paid or volunteer projects for local businesses, nonprofits or open-source projects show you can work to real requirements and deadlines.
Time it takes

Self-study or a bootcamp plus portfolio building usually takes about six months to two years before someone is hired. An associate degree takes about two years and a bachelor’s degree about four years, often with an internship along the way.
First job

Most people start as a junior or entry-level web developer, front-end developer or development intern. Others come in through related roles such as website support, content management, QA testing or freelance site building, then move into full development work.
qa: Do you need a degree to be a web developer?

No. A degree in computer science or a related field helps, and some employers ask for one, but many web developers are self-taught or trained through a bootcamp or associate degree. What gets you hired is a portfolio of working sites and solid skills in HTML, CSS, JavaScript and at least one back-end technology.
How long does it take to become a web developer?

It usually takes about six months to two years of focused study and project work to land a first job through self-study or a bootcamp. A bachelor’s degree route takes about four years. Either way, building real projects and a portfolio is what makes you ready for an entry-level role.

steps: High school basics

Most employers want a high school diploma or GED. Classes in shop, math, blueprint reading and drafting help. Many high schools and career centers offer welding courses where students first learn safety and basic processes like stick, MIG and TIG welding.
Welding training program

Most welders complete a certificate program at a technical school or community college, which usually takes several months to a year. Some earn a two-year associate degree. Programs cover welding processes, metal cutting, blueprint and weld symbol reading, metallurgy basics and shop safety.
Apprenticeship option

Some people enter through a paid apprenticeship run by unions, contractors or employers, usually lasting three to five years. Apprentices combine on-the-job hours under experienced welders with classroom instruction. This path is common for pipe welding, structural steel and pipefitting work.
Welding certification tests

There is no general state license for welders, but employers expect certification. Welders take hands-on weld tests to codes such as AWS D1.1 for structural steel, ASME Section IX for pressure piping or AWS D17.1 for aerospace. Certifications are tied to a process and position and must be kept current.
First job

Common first jobs are welder helper, production welder or fabrication shop welder. New welders often start on simpler, repetitive welds and move to pipe, pressure vessel or aerospace work as they pass harder tests and build a record of sound welds.
Advancing and inspecting

With several years of experience, welders can move into lead or supervisor roles or become inspectors. The AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) credential requires documented work experience and passing an exam. Some local governments also require their own welder certification for certain structural work.
qa: Do you need a license to be a welder?

Most states do not issue a general welder license. Instead, employers require welder certifications earned by passing weld tests to a specific code, such as AWS D1.1 or ASME Section IX. Some cities and states have their own requirements for structural or public works welding, so requirements vary by location and job.
How long does it take to become a welder?

A basic certificate program usually takes several months to a year, and some people start entry-level jobs right after. An associate degree takes about two years. Apprenticeships usually run three to five years. Reaching skilled pipe or aerospace welding often takes several years of experience and passing more demanding certification tests.

steps: Education

Most Workday specialists hold a bachelor’s degree in human resources, business, accounting, finance or information systems. No specific degree is required. Employers care more that you understand the HR, payroll or finance work the system supports.
Related work experience

Many people start in HR, payroll, benefits, accounting or a general HRIS role. This teaches the business processes you will later configure, such as hiring, compensation, time tracking or the general ledger.
Getting Workday access

Workday does not sell its training or certification to the general public. You usually gain hands-on access by working for a company that uses Workday or for a consulting firm that is an official Workday partner. Volunteering as a super user during an implementation is a common way in.
Certification

There is no license for this work. Employees of Workday customers can pursue Workday Pro certification in areas such as HCM, Payroll or Integrations. Partner consultants earn certification through Workday’s partner training. Both require keeping skills current with Workday’s regular updates.
First job

Common first roles are HRIS analyst, Workday analyst, payroll systems analyst or associate consultant at a Workday partner. You typically start with reports, business process changes and user support before handling full configuration.
Time it takes

After a degree, it usually takes one to three years of related work to move into a dedicated Workday role. Reaching senior consultant or lead analyst level often takes several more years of project experience.
qa: Do you need a certification to become a Workday specialist?

No license is required, and many analysts at Workday customer companies work without formal certification. However, consulting firms that are Workday partners generally expect their consultants to be certified. Customer employees can earn Workday Pro certification, which helps show skill in a specific area such as HCM or Payroll.
Can you get Workday certified on your own?

Generally, no. Workday limits its official training and certification to employees of companies that use Workday and to employees of its partner firms. Most people get certified after being hired into a role with Workday access, often an HRIS, payroll or finance systems job, and then completing training through their employer.

steps: Education

There is no set degree for this work. Many analysts studied business, mathematics, statistics, economics or operations management. Others have no degree and learn on the job. Strong spreadsheet skills, basic statistics and comfort with numbers matter more than a specific major.
First job

Many workforce management analysts start on the phones as contact center agents or team leads. From there they move into real-time analyst or scheduler roles, watching queues during the day, adjusting breaks and updating staffing as contacts come in.
Forecasting skills

The core skills are forecasting call or ticket volume, sizing staff with the Erlang C formula or simulation, and building schedules that meet service level goals. Most analysts learn this through on-the-job training and the workforce management software their employer uses.
Training and certification

No license is required. Professional groups such as the Society of Workforce Planning Professionals offer training, conferences and certification, and software vendors often train and certify users of their tools. Some analysts also learn SQL, Python or data visualization to build better forecasts.
Time it takes

Moving from contact center agent to real-time analyst often takes one to two years. Becoming a full workforce management analyst who owns forecasts and long-range capacity plans usually takes another one to three years of hands-on work.
Senior roles

Experienced analysts can become workforce management managers, capacity planners or operations analysts. Senior roles often cover several sites or channels, such as phone, chat and email, and plan hiring and budgets months ahead.
qa: Can you become a workforce management analyst without experience?

It is hard to start in this role with no experience at all. Most analysts first work as contact center agents, then move into real-time analyst or scheduler jobs. People with a degree in statistics, math or business and strong spreadsheet skills sometimes get hired directly as junior analysts, especially at large contact centers.
How long does it take to become a workforce management analyst?

Usually two to four years for people who start in a contact center. A typical path is one to two years as an agent or team lead, then time as a real-time analyst or scheduler, before owning forecasts and schedules. Graduates with strong math or data skills may move faster.

steps: Education

There is no required degree. A high school diploma is the minimum, but many employers prefer an associate or bachelor’s degree in business administration, hospitality, facilities management or a related field. Coursework in budgeting, office software and communication helps.
First job

Most people start as a receptionist, front desk associate, office assistant or administrative assistant. These roles teach visitor check-in, mail and deliveries, supply ordering, vendor contact and the daily rhythm of running a shared space.
Build facilities skills

Take on tasks like booking rooms, tracking maintenance requests, planning desk moves and helping with emergency drills. Learn the workplace and facilities software your employer uses. This hands-on experience is what hiring managers look for most.
Safety training

No license is required, but employers often value safety training. Common options include an OSHA 10-hour general industry course, first aid and CPR certification, and serving as a fire warden or floor safety lead in your building.
Optional certifications

Certifications are not required to start. Some coordinators later earn the Facility Management Professional (FMP) credential from IFMA or the Certified Administrative Professional (CAP) from IAAP to show skills and move toward facilities or office manager roles.
Time it takes

Most people reach a workplace coordinator role after one to three years in front desk or administrative work. Those with a related degree or strong event and operations experience can sometimes move in sooner.
qa: Do you need a license or certification to be a workplace coordinator?

No. There is no state license for workplace coordinators. Employers hire based on office, front desk and operations experience. Optional credentials like IFMA’s Facility Management Professional (FMP) or basic safety training such as OSHA 10-hour, first aid and CPR can strengthen an application, but they are rarely required for entry-level roles.
How long does it take to become a workplace coordinator?

It usually takes one to three years. Most people start as a receptionist or administrative assistant, then take on duties like supplies, visitor management, room bookings and office moves. Once they can handle the space, vendors and safety tasks on their own, they are ready to apply for coordinator roles.
